COMPANY LAW : Where pursuant to order of Court, a One-Man Committee was constituted to oversee identification, recovery and distribution of proceeds from sale of assets of various chit fund companies to verified claimants, Enforcement Directorate was directed to extend all necessary assistance to Committee, as and when sought, for purpose of implementation of various orders of Court, particularly with respect to identification, recovery and allied matters concerning assets of respective
HC directs symbolic possession of property as co. convicted of siphoning of funds to avoid overdue payment
HC upholds attachment of properties as company served as conduit to channelize funds from shell/paper companies

COMPANY LAW : Where in a complaint filed by appellant, an FIR was registered against respondent for offence under section 420 and 120B of IPC, since investigation was still underway and respondent was main beneficiary of alleged fraudulent transaction, High Court exceeded its inherent jurisdiction under section 482 CrPC by allowing petition filed by respondent for release of funds withheld by BSE thus, order passed by High Court was to be set aside
CL: Where a shareholder failed to give proof or evidence regarding non-compliance of statutory requirements by company, order for investigation could not be entertained
HC directs appointment of expert to find out a feasible payout method for disbursement of investor’s money

SEBI : Where a committee was appointed to manage affairs of company and to make sure that sale of assets of company were to ensure that depositors be refunded their amounts, expert was to be appointed to assist committee in its task to evolve a feasible practicable method for disbursement of various amounts to depositors and investors
CL: Unless circumstance suggested that company was doing any fraudulent business or attempted to defraud its creditors or members, investigation into affairs of company could not be directed

COMPANY LAW : Where NCLT directed company to open a separate bank account, in which rent income and other amount collected would be deposited thenceforth which could be utilized for payment of statutory dues subject to satisfaction of NCLT, however, said direction of NCLT was not complied by defendant-directors and Civil Court did not take into account prima facie blameworthy conduct of defendants and permitted them to liquidate fixed deposits held by company to pay statutory dues, impugned order of Civil Court was to be set aside
ED directed to assist One-Man Committee in identifying, recovering, and distributing assets of chit fund firms: HC

COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'

CL : Where allegations were that respondents in collusion with other entities had siphoned off funds, CLB was entitled to pierce corporate veil to find out truth of allegations and if allegations were found proved, CLB in exercise of its rights and powers under section 402 entitled to pass an order to recover amounts so siphoned off from such third parties/entities

COMPANY LAW: Where respondent, claiming to be a shareholder, alleged fraudulent transfer of shares and sought investigation, Tribunal validly exercised its inherent power under rule 43 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to appoint an independent auditor for forensic examination without requiring a specific application, such power being independently vested to ensure effective justice without causing unfair prejudice to appellants

CL: Where respondent-company had not furnished information in respect of its affairs, to Chartered Accountants appointed by Court which it was reasonably expected to furnish, Central Government was to be directed to order investigation into affairs of respondent-company
HC directs Govt. to order investigation into Co's affairs as it didn't furnish info to CA appointed by Court

CL : Where a company tried to alienate its properties without following procedure laid down in its Memorandum and Articles of Association, and despite various complaints, ROC did not took action to stop illegal act of company, as power to appoint Special Officer was vested with ROC, writ Court would not be a proper forum to agitate said issue
CL: Where circumstances suggested that business of company was being conducted with intend to defraud petitioner and its members, investigation into affairs of respondent No. 1 was to be ordered
COMPANY LAW : Powers under sections 241, 337 and 339 could not be possibly utilized in order that a person who may be head of some other organization be roped in and his or her assets be attached
Recovery from director couldn’t be made without indicating what steps were taken to trace assets of Co.: HC
No order for investigating into affairs of co. as alleged issue was already sub-judice
CL : Where company failed to refund investors as per SEBI's directions in earlier order, company was to be directed to deposit entire amount to SEBI immediately

CL: Where there were allegations of manipulation of accounts by company which raised inference of misappropriation and diversion of funds with intent to defraud creditors, petition to direct Central Government to take steps to investigate into affairs of company was to be allowed

COMPANIES LAW/SEBI : Where suit was filed before High Court praying for declaration that names of defendants as shareholders in register of company were recorded fraudulently, NCLT was not competent to enquire into allegation of fraud and such suit was maintainable before High Court

COMPANY LAW : Where NCLT directed company to open a separate bank account, in which rent income and other amount collected would be deposited thenceforth which could be utilized for payment of statutory dues subject to satisfaction of NCLT, however, said direction of NCLT was not complied by defendant-directors and Civil Court did not take into account prima facie blameworthy conduct of defendants and permitted them to liquidate fixed deposits held by company to pay statutory dues,
NCLT has inherent powers to cause an audit of a/c during a fraud investigation into affairs of Co.: NCLAT
CL : No order for investigating into affairs of co. as alleged issue was already sub-judice

COMPANY LAW/ARBITRATION : Where while exercising power under section 36 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Single Judge passed an order appointing court receiver in respect of properties, since said order was neither an order under Order XLIII of Code of Civil Procedure nor appealable under section 37, appeal against same was held to be not maintainable
Shares transferred to Investor fund for safekeeping couldn't be property of Central Govt.: HC
PMLA attachment order against appellant invalid as no investigation was conducted on proceeds of crime from investors
SC admits writ plea; directs SEBI to auction assets of Companies running illegal ‘CIS’ and to refund monies to investors

COMPANY LAW: Without circumstances suggesting that business of company was being conducted in a fraudulent manner with intent to defraud creditors, investigation into affairs of said company only on basis of irregularities in financial statements, could not have been ordered

COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where CBI issued freeze orders against appellant company during an investigation into an alleged crime committed by 'D' however, appellant company was in no way connected to concerned investigation, freeze orders made against appellant company's properties were redundant qua investigation and condition imposed to furnish bank guarantee in furtherance of said orders was to be set aside
CL : In terms of provisions of Act, Tribunal does not have power to give direction to a company to issue duplicate shares to its shareholders

COMPANY LAW : Where a company and its directors were alleged by its homebuyer of acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds of said company to its sister concern, RoC having been failed to exercise their statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of homebuyers and investors of said company,
'Fraud Investigating Officer' can investigate into affairs of a Co. on basis of opinion of Govt.

COMPANY LAW : Where petitioner/homebuyer alleged that promoters and directors of respondent company 'TCSPL' had misappropriated and siphoned off funds collected from innocent homebuyers into various shell/sister concerns and sought directions to respondents/Central Government to take cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against management of 'TCSPL' as well as its shell/sister group of companies, in view of complexity of factual narrative and interwoven set of legal proceedings, Central Government was directed to entrust investigation to Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO)
Authority appointed under Maharashtra protection of depositors Act couldn't supersede powers of Company Court: HC

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where provisional attachment order was passed against appellant company under PMLA on ground that appellant had misrepresented before Ministry of Coal to get allocation of Coal Block,in absence of any predicate offence having been registered and investigated with respect to flow of investment from outsider investors into appellant company, attempt by respondent Directorate to make such flow of funds as proceeds of crime failed
HC directed fresh examination to ensure that sum indicated in seized docs was undisclosed investment

FEMA, BANKING & INSURANCE : Where Additional Director of Enforcement had reasons to believe that properties seized from premises of respondent company was proceeds of crime involved in money laundering, impugned order by Single Judge directing Additional Director to release properties seized to respondent was to be set aside
CLB permitted petitioner to inspect bank account of respondent Co. to ensure that funds were utilized judicially

Company Law : Where petitioner/homebuyer alleged that promoters and directors of respondent company 'TCSPL' had misappropriated and siphoned off funds collected from innocent homebuyers into various shell/sister concerns and sought directions to respondents/Central Government to take cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against management of 'TCSPL', as well as its shell/sister group of companies,

SEBI's order restraining appellant, chairman of company ‘P’, unsustainable as no specific statutory violation was imputed: SAT

COMPANY LAW/SEBI ACT: Where appellant company was carrying business of collective investment schemes without obtaining certificate of registration from SEBI and it had failed to prove that it had returned entire amount to contributors, impugned order passed by SEBI to refund monies to investors could not be interfered with

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

HELD: There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

with the order of the Single Judge allowing injunction application restraining CGH and KCP from proceeding with the arbitration and dismissing application filed by the appellants under section 45 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. [Para 120]

Power of Company Law Board to review: On behalf of ORE and Athappan, it was mainly contended that the CLB has no power to review its own order, especially, in the guise of a clarification. [Para 137] It is fairly well-settled that the CLB does not have the power of review. It is, however, open to the CLB to exercise its inherent powers and to make such orders as may seem necessary to meet the ends of justice. The CLB has power to review and recall its orders which have been wangled through fraud or misrepresentation. [Para 141]

In its earlier order dated 13-8-2008, the CLB has recorded categorical findings:- (i) conduct of KCP having regarded CEPL's funds as though his own funds is burdensome, harsh and wrongful; (ii) movement of funds from CEPL as traced by the auditors is not supported by any approvals from the Board of CEPL. (iii) KCP had taken enormous steps in safeguarding and enhancing the value of CPL properties as well as bringing VML out of sickness thereby saving its vast extent of properties and settling all dues of workmen which is in contravention of the JVA/Articles of CEPL. (iv) KCP is accountable for not having diligently discharged its statutory duties cast on him. On those factual findings, in its order dated 13-8-2008, CLB observed that the very purpose of CEPL could not have been achieved in terms of JVA and in the light of those factual findings directed CEPL to return a sum of Rs. 75 crores and Rs.4 crores invested by ORE and Athappans respectively along with interest at 8 per cent. In the said order, the CLB also permitted KCP to utilise the money to return the said amount to ORE and Athappans and in the meanwhile directing that VML shall not alienate or sell any of its immovable properties till payment is made to ORE. The CLB also made provision that in the event of failure to make the repayment within the specified time, CEPL, CGH, KCP and VML were to duly convey the immovable properties of VML, i.e., 17.15 acres of land in favour of ORE and 7.80 acres of land in favour of Athappans. When the CLB has recorded categorical findings that CEPL neither carried out nor could accomplish its business plan in accordance with terms of JVA and directed return of sum of Rs.75 crores and Rs.4 crores, it was not justified in modifying its earlier order permitting KCP to deal with 50 per cent of the money lying with State Bank of India. [Para 142]

Given the sequence of events, if KCP is placed in position to manage CEPL, he would again try to divert the amount to innumerable subsidiary companies floated by him, the CLB was not justified in directing ORE and NA to deposit the share certificates with the Bench Officer. Having found that KCP had not discharged his statutory duties and that he was not prudent in managing CEPL, the CLB was not justified in directing payment of 50 per cent of the deposit lying with the State Bank of India. [Para 143]

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

HELD: Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

Also, there cannot be any difference of opinion by any of the parties that the Central Government can very well invoke section 212(1)(c), i.e. in the public interest and order investigation into the affairs of the petitioner company. HEADNOTE: Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with Order XXXIX, rule 4 and Order XLIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Court - Jurisdiction of - Case of revision petitioners was that first respondent-company had filed Form II and Form FCGPR with Reserve Bank of India along with certificates issued by statutory auditor of company and Company Secretary stating that it had allotted certain shares to first revision petitioner - Subsequently, it was found that to deprive revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to first revision petitioner - First respondent also filed a suit before civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to first revision petitioner - Revision petitioners filed revision petition under article 227 of Constitution for setting aside said interim order on grounds that trial court had no jurisdiction to decide issue as same issue was pending before CLB and that order of trial court granting interim injunction was non-speaking one - Whether revision petitioners could not invoke jurisdiction of High Court under article 227, since they had two concurrent remedies, namely, to get order of trial court varied, vacated or discharged as per order XXXIX, rule 4 of Code and to file an appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(r) of Code - Held, yes

FACT: The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

HELD: The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

In the aforesaid case, the Court passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company.

Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but ‘for any other purpose’, and ‘any other purpose’ would include such public interest purpose.

HELD: Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

order of attachment was not having information that an OL had been appointed - Further, it was not that OL had made an application to provide an opportunity of hearing and had been denied - Rather, 'Birla Solar' remain unrepresented and it was they who were relevant party to inform about appointment of liquidator - Whether thus, order of Adjudicating Authority did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 18, 21, 22, 28 and 29] FACT: A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

HELD: The provision for hearing is given under section 8(1). Section 5(1) provides for attachment against 'any person' in possession of proceeds. At the relevant time defendant was in possession of the proceeds. The Competent Authority passed the order of attachment was not having information that an Official Liquidator has been appointed. The information was given only to the Adjudicating Authority.[Para 17]

Exchange deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company in compliance with the order passed by the Custodian. Section 3(5) lays down that the Custodian can take assistance of any other person while exercising his powers or for discharging his duties under this section and under section 4. When a fax message was sent to the Calcutta Stock Exchange for information and necessary action, the Calcutta Stock Exchange had no option but to deactivate the terminal of the petitioner-company. [Para 11] The plea taken by the petitioner-company was that K was one of the shareholders of the petitioner-company (though he resigned later on) and his holding which was raised to 97.94 per cent was subsequently brought down to 68 per cent. But the fact remained that K was practically the owner of that company; though in order to escape the clutches of law, he had resigned as one of the directors. But the fact remained that the petitioner-company was started by K in 1994 and it was a debatable question as to whether the company was established by K from the tainted money earned by him during 1-4-1991 to 6-6-1992. That matter was yet to be decided by the competent forum. But the petitioner-company rushed to file the instant writ petition and challenged the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange as well as the National and Mumbai Stock Exchanges. It was not the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was sought to be challenged but in fact what was sought to be challenged was the order passed by the Custodian. Therefore, the view taken by the Single Judge to the extent that that could not be interfered with in extraordinary writ jurisdiction was well-founded. It was a question which was yet to be decided by the Special Court as to whether all the money for establishing the petitioner-company was tainted money or the petitioner-company which had been established by K was from any other source which did not have the tinge of that tainted money. That question could not have been decided in the instant pro- ceeding. More so, by virtue of the notification dated 20-11-2001 and the public notice issued on 24-11-2001 all the properties of all the persons who were notified and that of K stood attached. The 20-11-2001 not- ification clearly said that all the properties movable or immovable or both belonging to persons/entities would stand attached by virtue of section 3(3) of the Act of 1992 and similarly in the public notification dated 24-11-2001, the same was reiterated for notice of all concerned that from the date of the aforesaid notification any property movable or imm- ovable or both belonging to the notified persons/entities would stand attached and it would only be dealt with by the Custodian in such manner as the Special Court may direct. It was also made clear in the public notice dated 24-11-2001 that the provisions of the Act of 1992 have overriding effect on all other laws and all the companies and firms were directed to take notice that the property belonging to the notified persons/entities stood attached and it was not permissible to have any transaction of any kind relating to the attached properties of the notified persons/entities except with the direction of the Special Court. It was also mentioned in the public notice that all those who had dealings with such attached properties of the notified persons/entities should intimate to the Custodian the details of such properties. Therefore, in view of those facts, the assets and properties of K were attached and if the petitioner-company sought any remedy, the remedy lay in the Special Court which alone has jurisdiction to provide remedy and that Court is held by no less than a sitting Judge of the High Court. Therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter which was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Special Court. There was no occasion for the Single Judge to have unnecessarily entered into the question whether the Calcutta Stock Exchange was a ‘State’ within the meaning of article 12 or not. In fact, that question did not directly fall for determination. In substance what the petitioner-company wanted to challenge was the basic order of the Custodian, as the Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted in terms of the direction issued by the Custodian. Therefore, it was only an incidental action, and the basic challenge was to the notification notifying K as a notified person under section 3(2) of the Act of 1992. No executing agency who has implemented the order can be held responsible. The Calcutta Stock Exchange was only an executing agency and since the said K was notified person and he floated the company in 1994, all his assets stood attached, and, therefore, it deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company preventing it from doing any trading activity in Calcutta Stock Exchange. Therefore, it was not an action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was under challenge. The Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted as per the direction given by the Custodian as executing agency and if the petitioner-company had any grievance against the order passed by the Custodian, then it had remedy under the Act of 1992

The blocking of substantial funds in another company when the main object was not investment, diversion of project money to various bodies incorporated or unincorporated, the laxity in the collection of loans, the unusual facility of allowing repayment of principal with interest still outstanding, payment of substantial commission to a private company, substantial increase in the cost of materials and wasteful expenses all went to show that the funds of the company had gone out to third parties and were not easily recoverable. Only such a kind of investigation would establish the link, if any, between the ultimate beneficiary and those incharge of the management of the funds of the company. Ultimately, the investigation might not be able to establish any link. However, prima facie opinion could be formed on the basis of facts available to warrant the investigation. It might be only through a detailed probe that the intention, if any, behind the above acts resulting in substantial loss to various interests in society through the company could be established. If the above acts were done intentionally (mens rea), adverse consequences may follow including penalising the guilty. Establishing mens rea is the purpose behind any legal framework of this kind. It is essential to invoke such provisions where the funds of public and creditors are vested in the hands of a few individuals for the benefit of the former. . The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator. The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

338 relates to 'Liability where proper accounts not kept'. On the other hand, section 339 relates to the 'Liability for fraudulent conduct of business'. As per sub-section (2) of section 339, if any business of the company has been carried on with intent as mentioned in sub-section (1), any person who is or were parties carrying on of the business are also liable for action under section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 47] Section 340 empowers the Tribunal to assess damages against delinquent directors or any other person who has taken part in the promotion or formation of the company, or any person, who is or has been a Director, Manager, Company Liquidator or officer of the company and has misapplied, or retained, or become liable or accountable for, any money or property of the company if found to be guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. The Tribunal, after inquiry into the conduct of such person(s), Director(s), Manager(s) etc. can order him to repay or restore the money or property or any part thereof. [Para 48]

The liability under sections 339 and 340 also extend to partners or directors of firms or other companies in terms of section 341. [Para 49]

Therefore, on an application under sub-section (2) of section 241, the Tribunal can pass not only any order under Chapter XVI and if it is read with section 246, it will be evident that sections 339, 340 and 341 being applicable mutatis mutandis, in relation to an application made to the Tribunal under section 241, the Tribunal can pass order in terms of those extended provisions. [Para 50]

This apart under section 420, the Tribunal is empowered to pass such orders as it thinks fit after giving the parties to any proceeding before it, a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Tribunal has also inherent powers to make such orders as may be necessary for meeting the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Tribunal under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. [Para 51]

Therefore, if sub-section (4) of section 242 is read with sections 339 and 340 and section 221, it is clear that apart from 'freezing of assets of company on inquiry and investigation', it is also open to the Tribunal to freeze the assets of any person, including other companies and individuals, even during inquiry and investigation of fraud under section 212. [Para 52]

Insofar as the order dated 2-4-2018 is concerned, it is found that by the said order the Tribunal, while modified its earlier order dated 23-2-2018, practically exonerated 'S' (respondent No. 43); 'G' (respondent No. 44); 'SS' (respondent No. 51); M (respondent No. 52) and R (respondent No. 53) by holding that those respondents had no complicity in the matter and they had no role to play in the financial fraud in question. The Tribunal failed to appreciate that it was dealing with the question of vacating the interim order passed under sub-section (4) of section 242, read with sections 221, 241(2), 339 and 340. While considering the question of modification or vacating the interim order passed under section 242 and 221, it was not open to the Tribunal to pass an order which is final in nature, amounting to exonerating one or other respondent particularly, when the allegation of fraud is pending investigation by the SFIO. [Para 54]

Though it was brought to the notice of the Tribunal that the respondent companies, individuals including existing and erstwhile Directors, partners, trustees, beneficiaries and their associates or subsidiaries and firms had exposure with the PNB and are prima facie found to be beneficiaries of the fraud, without waiting for the report of the SFIO it was not open to the Tribunal to exonerate some of the respondents from the charges. Sections 397 and 398 fall under Chapter VI of the Companies Act, 1956 which provide the power of the tribunal for prevention of oppression and mismanagement. These provisions enable any member of a company, who complains that affairs of a company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the public interest or in a manner oppressive to any member or members, to apply to the Tribunal for an order under the sections. [Para 43]

Section 456 of the Act, 1956 gives wide powers to the Liquidator of the company-in-liquidation to take into his custody or under his control, any property, effects or actionable claims to which the company is or appears to be entitled enabling him to approach the Magistrate concerned within whose jurisdiction such property, effects or actionable claims or any book of account or other documents of the company may be found to take possession thereof and deliver possession thereof to the Liquidator. Further, the powers of the Liquidator under section 457 of the Act, 1956 are also wide ranging. It is not the case of the Official Liquidator that the powers conferred on it by virtue of the aforesaid provisions are inadequate for purpose of detection of the irregularities like the allegation of diversion of funds, etc. that caused it to move this Court for referring the matter to the SFIO. It should not appear to the Court that the Official Liquidator seeks referral of the matter to the SFIO for the reason that it finds itself inadequate to exercise the powers conferred on the Official Liquidator by the aforesaid sections of the Act. [Para 45]

As reflected in the 'Allegations Table', the list of the properties of the company-in-liquidation is with the Official Liquidator. Nothing has been demonstrated on behalf of the Official Liquidator to show what steps have been taken for sale of the properties already in its possession. Further, the Official Liquidator is required to exercise its powers conferred under sections 283, 290 of the Act, 2013 and related provisions which, to some extent correspond to the provisions of sections 456 and 457 of the Act, 1956 to ensure possession of the properties of the company-in-liquidation and seek orders of the Courts for disbursal of the dues of the depositors. FACT: The instant application had been filed by an Ex-Director of the Company-in-liquidation to recall the order dated 13-12-2019 passed by writ Court, whereby, writ Court had directed the Special Frauds Investigating Office, to recommence the investigation into the affairs of the company-in-liquidation that was started pursuant to an order dated 18-7-2008 passed by writ Court in the said company petition. As reflected in the order dated 13-12-2019, the Official Liquidator in its Report urged that the original sale deeds of the properties of the company-in-liquidation should be directed to be produced. Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. In regard to the function of a balance-sheet, it may be stated to be an endeavour to show the share capital, reserves (distinguishing those which are available for distribution as dividends from those reserves not regarded as so available) and the liabilities of the company at the date on which it is prepared and the manner in which the total sums represented then are distributed over several types of assets. In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Also, a balance-sheet is known as a statement of net worth assets and liabilities and it is called as 'Statement of financial position'. In the Companies Act, it is the duty of the directors of a company to see that the regular and correct account books are kept. [Para 31]

Normally, it is the duty of the directors and the management to ensure that the provisions of the Companies Act have been complied with. However, where there is contravention of a legal requirement by a company, which has a bearing on the accounts and transactions of the company, an auditor would in the normal course of his inquiry become aware of such a contravention which needs to be brought to the notice of the shareholders. In short, an auditor should, however, not merely state the facts, leaving it to be inferred that a contravention of legal requirements has taken place, but he should spell out that in his opinion a contravention of the law has taken place. Further, an auditor is the eyes and ears of the disparate shareholders' community. Moreover, the only individual who has an access to the books of account of a company, apart from the concerned company itself, is the auditor. [Para 32]

As far as our country is concerned, a share is not merely a chose-in-action, it is also as per the definition of a share or a debenture under section 82 a 'movable property'. However, shares or debentures become equivalent to 'goods' as per the decision in Kunhunni Elaya Nayar v. P.N. Krishna Pattar [1942] 12 Comp. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. Moreover, it represents the interest of the holder measured for the purposes of liability and dividend by a sum of money. [Para 34]

HELD: Under sub-article (2) of article 226, the power conferred on the High Court to issue directions, orders or writs can be exercised by the Court in relation to territories within which the cause of action wholly or in part arises for the exercise of such powers. If cause of action or part of cause of action has not arisen or the person fails to demonstrate such cause of action, as having arisen within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court, issue of any writ or direction would be without jurisdiction. [Para 14]

As per clause (f) of section 45-I of the RBI Act, the first petitioner was a NBFC because it received deposits under a scheme or arrangement and admittedly obtained licence under the provisions of that Act. Further, under section 45QA thereof, the first petitioner was under obligation to repay every deposit accepted by it. If the deposit was not repaid, the aggrieved party could file application before the CLB which might direct the NBFC to make payment of such deposit. Any order passed by the CLB was appealable order before the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the company had its registered office. Thus, the High Court of Andhra Pradesh was not a Court to which an appeal would lie under section 10F of the Companies Act. [Para 19]

The counter-affidavit filed by the third respondent and the letters addressed by depositors as well as Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, would show that no cause of action whatsoever arose in the State of Andhra Pradesh, much less in Hyderabad. [Para 20]

It was reasonable to infer that the petitioners had intentionally withheld the information from the Court and obtained order. It was also reasonable to infer that petitioners having failed to obtain necessary orders of bail or otherwise, had approached the Court and chose to file the writ petition seeking the relief the granting of which would pre-empt any authority in the country to investigate further into the acts of malfeasance and misfeasance and deny justice to the depositors. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 depositors and none of them was resident or hailed from Hyderabad or Andhra Pradesh. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Compromise and arrangement - A scheme of compromise and/or arrangement between applicant company ‘E’ and its creditors was sanctioned by Company Judge - After that, a creditor of applicant resorted to arbitration proceedings against applicant and executing Court attached property of applicant and also directed sale of property - Applicant and its two unsecured creditors filed company applications claiming relief with regard to setting aside of aforesaid auction sale - By an order dated 12-2-2004, a committee of unsecured creditors was appointed by Court under Chairmanship of then Company Registrar of Court and other five members, which was to take steps to dispose of specified property of applicant so as to repay dues of unsecured creditors - However, then board of directors of applicant resolved to assign job of intended sale of suit property to ‘N’ and ‘D’, directors of applicant, and ‘P’, who was ex-director of ‘G’ company - Thereafter, suit property was conveyed in favour of ‘G’ company - Subsequently, conveyance deed in respect of suit property was executed by ‘G’ company in favour of ‘K’ company - Aforesaid development took place without knowledge of committee appointed by Court for sale of suit property - Committee submitted its report on basis of which Court issued notices to respective companies and directed parties, in particular ‘K’ company to maintain status quo of suit property as on that date till disposal of proceedings - Whether since applicant-company was party to proceedings before High Court as well as before executing Court which issued order of attachment and order of sale of suit property, transfer of suit property by applicant in favour of ‘G’ company without seeking permission of Court was illegal and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, ‘G’ company had no valid title in suit property and it could not have validly transferred suit property to ‘K’ company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, sale of suit property was illegal and non-existent and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether once Court found that suit property was transferred by applicant in violation of order of Court to which it was a party and same was in force, it would necessarily follow that transfer so effected by applicant was illegal and non-existent in law - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, instant case was an act of commission and omission in connivance and as a part of conspiracy to act in breach of order of Court to encash property of applicant and also to defeat claims and rights of creditors of applicant - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, criminal action was to be initiated against all erring persons who were directly or indirectly concerned with transaction-in-question, which was intended to overreach orders of Court of law and to defeat claim of creditors - Held, yes - Whether both applicant company and ‘G’ company were to be directed to bring back amount of sale proceeds with interest for payment of same to ‘K’ company and property-in-question was to be reauctioned for payment of dues of creditors - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 237, read with section 10, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Whether ‘Court’ referred to in section 237 is court having jurisdiction under section 10 and no other court - Held, yes - Whether under section 237(a)(ii), court can appoint directly inspector(s) to investigate into affairs of company - Held, no - Whether court can only make a declaration that affairs of company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by Central Government - Held, yes - Whether power of Company Law Board under section 237(b) is a bar to exercise of discretionary jurisdiction of court under section 237(a)(ii) - Held, no - Whether mere allegations are insufficient to support an application to court to act under section 237(1)(ii) and material placed before court should be such as to satisfy court that a deeper probe into affairs of company is desirable in interests of company itself - Held, yes - Whether court can pass a declaration under section 237(a) for a fishing expedition - Held, no - Whether an isolated instance of mismanagement is enough for court to declare that an investigation is required - Held, no - Whether existence of circumstances described under section 237(b) may sway court to pass an order under section 237(a)(ii) also but it is not always mandatory that court can pass a declaration only if conditions under section 237(b) exist - Held, yes - Whether power of court under section 237(a)(ii) is equal to power of CLB under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether unlike CLB, there are no restrictions placed on Court even though Court will exercise its judicial discretion only on sufficient materials and only after it is convinced that situation warrants an investigation in interest of company as a whole - Held, yes - Whether when a discretionary order under section 237(a)(ii) is passed by proper court with jurisdiction, unless there are compelling grounds appellate court will not interfere - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent was an equity shareholder and the promoter of the appellant-company. He was also appointed as the Chairman of the company. Subsequently, the company came out with public issue which was subscribed in excess of 14 times the offer. Thereafter, the respondent filed petition under section 237(a)( ii ) before the Company Judge seeking to direct the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company. It was alleged that no first annual general meeting of the company was held as convened in time.

The managing director, ‘M’ had been fraudulently mismanaging the company in utter disregard of the interest of the shareholders and was acting in an autocratic and oppressive manner. He created false and fabricated documents with nefarious motive to oust the respondent and other members of the board of directors who opposed the misutilisation and misappropriation of public funds. He created documents and minutes purporting to remove the petitioner and others who opposed the mismanagement and oppression. Though on the public issue, shares were over subscribed to the tune of 14 times and huge amounts were collected from the public, shares were neither allotted properly nor amounts refunded to the applicants whose application for shares were not accepted.

It was further alleged that 1200 complaints had been filed against ‘M’ by the subscribers to whom the amounts were not refunded and that ‘M’ had misappropriated, misutilised and mismanaged the funds collected through public issue and diverted the funds for his private purposes. The company opposed the petition. The Company Judge found that the submission of the Central Government supported the respondent’s allegations and concluded that a deeper probe was necessary and passed an order declaring that affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Court itself.

On appeal :

HELD: By virtue of the power under section 237(a )(ii), the Court cannot appoint directly inspector or inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company but only make a declaration that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Once such an order is passed it is mandatory for the Central Government to conduct such investigation by appointing competent persons as inspectors.
