Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - Pursuant to an advertisement made by an investment company inviting general public to subscribe in various fixed deposits and saving schemes, appellants subscribed to scheme - As on date of maturity certificates issued were not honoured appellants lodged an fir with police station - On application of appellants, Magistrate directed attachment of said company’s properties - Thereafter, appellants filed criminal revision petition, alleging that notwithstanding order of attachment, properties were either disposed of or dealt with in a manner contrary to order of attachment - Additional District and Sessions Judge rejected said petition on ground that appellants had no locus standi to file a revision petition - Against said order, appellants filed petitions, but same were also dismissed by High Court - Whether, on facts, without entering into matter relating to contempt of court, concerned court was to be directed to work out details and modalities as to how properties of said company could be sold to get highest price so that dues of creditors and liabilities could be paid - Held, yes

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc. - Company Judge is a Court within meaning of section 476 of Code of Criminal Procedure

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  Company Court itself is not invested with any power of investigation under section 237 and all that it can do is to consider plea of petitioners as to whether it is a fit case to direct Central Government to do so

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - A Company Judge has no jurisdiction to enforce an order against persons other than those mentioned in section 185 of 1913 Act

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - A Company Judge has no jurisdiction to enforce an order against persons other than those mentioned in section 185 of 1913 Act

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Powers of Court under section 237(a )(ii) are not circumscribed in any way

Section 452 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 - Punishment - For wrongful withholding of property - Whether inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash interlocutory orders can be invoked only in case of exceptional case of illegality or lack of jurisdiction in interlocutory order - Held, yes - Whether where Magistrate had found that prima facie company had a right to possession of disputed property, he could have granted interlocutory relief under section 630(2), prior to conclusion of trial under section 630(1) - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where order of Magistrate under section 630(2) directing possession of disputed property to appellant company was an interlocutory relief based on prima facie assessment of facts and did not conclusively decide ongoing trial under section 630(1), there was no exceptional case of illegality or lack of jurisdiction in interlocutory order of lower court calling for exercise of inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 11]COMPANY LAW: Where order of Magistrate under section 630(2) was an interlocutory relief based on prima facie assessment of facts and did not conclusively decide ongoing trial under section 630(1), inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. could not have been invoked to quash interlocutory orders

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc. - Court need not first determine that person to be examined actually possesses information

Section 263 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Appointment of Directors -  Court cannot interfere in management of company and cannot direct a company to induct non-shareholders as Directors merely on basis of allegations that those non-shareholders had invested money from undisclosed sources by undisclosed modes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - There is nothing in section 237(a )(ii) to say that a person should first approach Central Government before coming to Court

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

Section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Compromise and arrangement - A scheme of compromise and/or arrangement between applicant company ‘E’ and its creditors was sanctioned by Company Judge - After that, a creditor of applicant resorted to arbitration proceedings against applicant and executing Court attached property of applicant and also directed sale of property - Applicant and its two unsecured creditors filed company applications claiming relief with regard to setting aside of aforesaid auction sale - By an order dated 12-2-2004, a committee of unsecured creditors was appointed by Court under Chairmanship of then Company Registrar of Court and other five members, which was to take steps to dispose of specified property of applicant so as to repay dues of unsecured creditors - However, then board of directors of applicant resolved to assign job of intended sale of suit property to ‘N’ and ‘D’, directors of applicant, and ‘P’, who was ex-director of ‘G’ company - Thereafter, suit property was conveyed in favour of ‘G’ company - Subsequently, conveyance deed in respect of suit property was executed by ‘G’ company in favour of ‘K’ company - Aforesaid development took place without knowledge of committee appointed by Court for sale of suit property - Committee submitted its report on basis of which Court issued notices to respective companies and directed parties, in particular ‘K’ company to maintain status quo of suit property as on that date till disposal of proceedings - Whether since applicant-company was party to proceedings before High Court as well as before executing Court which issued order of attachment and order of sale of suit property, transfer of suit property by applicant in favour of ‘G’ company without seeking permission of Court was illegal and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, ‘G’ company had no valid title in suit property and it could not have validly transferred suit property to ‘K’ company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, sale of suit property was illegal and non-existent and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether once Court found that suit property was transferred by applicant in violation of order of Court to which it was a party and same was in force, it would necessarily follow that transfer so effected by applicant was illegal and non-existent in law - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, instant case was an act of commission and omission in connivance and as a part of conspiracy to act in breach of order of Court to encash property of applicant and also to defeat claims and rights of creditors of applicant - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, criminal action was to be initiated against all erring persons who were directly or indirectly concerned with transaction-in-question, which was intended to overreach orders of Court of law and to defeat claim of creditors - Held, yes - Whether both applicant company and ‘G’ company were to be directed to bring back amount of sale proceeds with interest for payment of same to ‘K’ company and property-in-question was to be reauctioned for payment of dues of creditors - Held, yes

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

Section 543 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power of court to assess damages against delinquent directors, etc. - Court is competent to proceed against non-resident foreigner directors and pass a decree   In an application under section 235 of the 1913 Act the Court can be asked to examine into the conduct of non-resident foreigner directors and compel them to pay the amount in respect of which they have committed breach of trust. The proceeding is in the nature of a suit for recovery of monies wrongfully converted by a person who happens to be a non-resident foreigner. If this proceeding is instituted by way of a suit, the provisions of sections 19 and 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable and since the cause of action arises within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, though the defendants - the persons who are liable to account - reside in a foreign territory, a suit can very well be laid and summons served in the manner provided by the rules and a decree can be passed. This does not necessarily involve any process to compel his attendance in order to submit himself for examination. If on the receipt of notice served in the manner provided under the rules, the concerned director does not choose to appear, the Court can come to a conclusion on the material placed before it on behalf of the applicant as to the conduct of the director in the matter and decide about his liability to the applicant or to the company and an order can be made directing the particular director to bring in any amount which he has misapplied, retained or in respect of which he has committed breach of trust or misfeasance which order will be in the nature of a decree. How and in what manner the decree will be treated by the foreign Court is immaterial, for, the decree is nevertheless valid though it may be treated as a nullity by the foreign Court. It is also equally unnecessary to consider whether such a decree can be enforced against such director. The Court is competent to pass such a decree by virtue of the local or municipal law governing the exercise of such jurisdiction. If the concerned director has any properties within the jurisdiction of the State, such an order can very well be executed against those properties and if there are no such properties, the order will have the same force and effect as a decree passed in a suit against a non-resident foreigner.
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Failure of Government to disclose to Court materials to justify order would lead to quashing of order

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Held, yes [Para 38]  Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'
Section 155 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Power of court to rectify register of members -  A fraudulent transfer does not defeat title of true owner, and Court can strike off name of transferee
Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Court - Jurisdiction of - Inherent powers of Court cannot be invoked when express provisions are there

II Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases Before an investigation can be ordered by Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244 Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) The nature of an investigation to be ordered depends very much on the power of the Central Government which would be exercised if the Court so orders. For instance, the consequences of an order directing investigation have to be seen from the various provisions which govern such questions. Section 241 deals with the report of the Inspector and sections 242, 243 and 244 deal with what is to be done once a report has been made. Under section 242, a prosecution can be ordered. Under section 243, an application for winding up of the company on a petition under sections 397 and 398 can be instituted. Under section 244, proceedings for recovery of damages or property can be instituted. The result of an investigation can thus result either in prosecution or an application under sections 397 and 398 or a suit for recovery of damages or any property, which has been misapplied on account of misfeasance or mismanagement. Therefore, before an investigation can be ordered by the Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in the manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244. It is unnecessary to order an investigation merely because a shareholder feels aggrieved at the manner in which the company’s business is going on.

Section 543 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power of court to assess damages against delinquent, directors, etc - Court has power even to order delivery of books of company which are in possession of somebody else
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.

VII Section 11 Special Courts (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Discharge of liabilities Third person coming into possession of properties of notified parties under illegal agreements, cannot be allowed to retain them A.K. Menon v. Fairgrowth Financial Services Ltd. [1994] 81 Comp. Cas. 508 (Bom.) (Special Court) In case of statutory attachments which requires distribution of property it is the Special Court which has to recover the properties for the purposes of effective distribution under section 11(2) of the Act. One of the main objects of the Act being to recover large amounts of public money which have gone into private pockets and there being statutory attachment of properties of notified parties, such statutory attachments would operate even if the properties are in the hands of a third party pursuant to an illegal contract. After attachment, such properties can only be dealt with under the directions of the instant court. All such property must, therefore, be available for distribution under section 11(2). It, thus, cannot be argued that even after a statutory attachment, the third party must be allowed to deal with the properties as the notified party will not be assisted by the Court. The Court will not be assisting notified parties.The Court is safeguarding properties purchased from public monies from further alienation and ensuring that they are available for distribution under section 11. The question of applying the principle of pari delicto to such cases does not arise at all. To accept such an argument would amount to meaning that if an agreement is legal, then the Special Court can recover attached properties, but if an agreement is illegal, the Special Court must allow a transfer to take place. It can hardly be said that the third person who has come into possession of properties of notified parties, under illegal agreements, must be allowed to retain them. Such an argument cannot be accepted.
Rule 9  of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 - Inherent Powers of Court - Court has inherent powers to make such order necessary to do justice on facts of case
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  An order of Company Court directing investigation in exercise of powers under section 237(a)(ii ) is not a judgment determining rights of parties

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where in commercial property project admeasuring 115 acres respondent had a claim of only Rs. 4 crores, High Court could not stall entire project with injunction order, however, no third party rights were to be created in respect of subject properties till orders were passed in winding up petition filed by respondent against developer

Section 4  of the Special Court (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Contracts Entered Fraudulently May Be Cancelled -  Under Special Court Act Custodian has no power to pass any order in nature of a decree directing payment by any party to notified party

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - Order, which Court can pass directing delivery of money, property, etc., to liquidator, can only be against persons enumerated in section 468

Section 433 read with  section 443 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which company may be wound up - Petitioner challenged winding up order on ground that company was not given opportunity of hearing and as such order was in breach of principles of natural justice - Whether where company judge had painstaking and studiously gone into whole financial aspects through a questionnaire and information regarding relevant transactions was also sought and affidavits were filed showing company's financial position, order of company judge for winding up could not be challenged on ground of non-hearing of company - Held, yes - Whether Court has ample powers to recommend investigation and give directions for filing first information report with regard to any apparent fraud by company and those in-charge of company - Held, yes
Section 634A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Enforcement of court orders

Section 633 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Powers of Court to Grant Relief in Certain Cases - Before exercising discretion under section 633 Court has to make an enquiry in accordance with section 4(2) of Code of Criminal Procedure

Section 635 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Enforcement of orders of one court by other courts - In view of provision of section 635, any order made by company court under section 446(2)(b) must be treated as a decree for purpose of recovering money ordered to be recovered in favour of company

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a )(ii) there should be a proceeding already before Court; even a petition simpliciter can be entertained
Section 633 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Powers of court to grant relief in certain cases - Court referred to in section 633 need not be only Criminal Court

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, which had given huge loans to respondent- companies, sought for investigation under section 237(b) by Central Government into affairs of respondent-companies and their promoter-directors for fraudulently and unlawfully making wrongful gain and having committed misfeasance, thereby causing pecuniary losses to petitioner - Siphoning-off of huge amount by respondents through 250 front companies in fraudulent manner was indicated by income-tax authorities also - Whether since without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by respondents in cheating petitioner and siphoning-off of public money, enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered and Central Government was to be directed to appoint inspectors for enquiry - Held, yes

I. Section 478 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to order public examination of promoters directors, etc. - Court can order examination only of that person who is suggested as being guilty of fraud in official liquidator's report
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Court has no jurisdiction to appoint an Inspector to investigate company's affairs
Section 634 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Enforcement of orders of courts -  Orders passed under the Act, are not orders having force of a decree for purpose of Court Fees Act

facts.text:
The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

The first petitioner, a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) registered under the Companies Act, 1956 having its registered office in Madhya Pradesh, was promoted by the second respondent with the objectives of carrying on the business of financing, money-lending, bills discounting, hire-purchasing, leasing, etc. The company evolved a scheme known as SFDR whereunder deposits collected from the investors were to be utilized for allotment of shares to them and also to be invested in other companies. The petitioners alleged that they collected non-interest yielding/profit-sharing investments in the form of equity and invested in equity shares. According to them, there were baseless rumours of cheating against first petitioner and, therefore, some of the members of public filed complaints against them in various police stations. It was alleged that there were serious threats to their lives and in spite of repeated requests to the SHOs to extend proper protection, the police officer was instead of protecting the petitioners, were compelling them to repay deposits collected by the company, and that some investors had attacked the office of the second petitioner and threatened him with physical abuses. Therefore the petitioners sought protection from third respondent - police officer. The third respondent, on the other hand, denied all the allegations.

On writ, the petitioners sought for relief (i) to declare the action of the respondents in not taking necessary prohibitive steps for the safety of the petitioners as illegal and unconstitutional, (ii) to declare the action of respondents in calling upon the petitioners to make payments on the basis of civil transactions between petitioners and their investors/shareholders as arbitrary, illegal and unjust and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14, 19, 20 and 21 of the Constitution of India and constitutional guarantees under articles 50 and 300A of the Constitution of India; (iii) to issue a direction to first respondent, namely, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), New Delhi, to centralize all the alleged complaints against petitioners, if any, and carry out investigation in accordance with law, (iv) to issue a consequential direction to police to take such steps as were necessary for protection of petitioners and not to harass petitioners on the back of civil complaints; and (v) to direct respondents to carry out their investigations, if any, on the complaints against petitioners strictly in accordance with the procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

The Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner to take charge of the movable and immovable properties, who after visiting various places, reported that there were no substantial money deposits in the name of the company but there were deposits in the name of the second petitioner’s wife and personal accounts. According to the report, properties were sold under Revenue Recovery Act by the bank, cold storage units were still under construction and the Indore office was seized by the police in some criminal case. A letter from a depositor informed that all the depositors belonged to New Delhi and Indore, and that they were cheated by the petitioners against whom FIR was lodged at New Delhi. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 investors who were cheated and all of them did not belong to Andhra Pradesh.

When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. held.text:
Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

The Reserve Bank of India was directed to appoint at least three auditors with other necessary staff to carry out the inquiry and assist the Deputy Commissioner of Police in carrying out such inquiry:

Respondent No. 2 was directed, inter alia, to state on oath in an affidavit the following:—

(i) The list of their movable and immovable properties and all assets and the location thereof;

(ii) The list of their bank accounts and the particulars thereof, including the names and addresses of the banks and the amounts therein.

There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. Section 3(5) lays down that the Custodian can take assistance of any other person while exercising his powers or for discharging his duties under this section and under section 4. When a fax message was sent to the Calcutta Stock Exchange for information and necessary action, the Calcutta Stock Exchange had no option but to deactivate the terminal of the petitioner-company. [Para 11] The plea taken by the petitioner-company was that K was one of the shareholders of the petitioner-company (though he resigned later on) and his holding which was raised to 97.94 per cent was subsequently brought down to 68 per cent. But the fact remained that K was practically the owner of that company; though in order to escape the clutches of law, he had resigned as one of the directors. But the fact remained that the petitioner-company was started by K in 1994 and it was a debatable question as to whether the company was established by K from the tainted money earned by him during 1-4-1991 to 6-6-1992. That matter was yet to be decided by the competent forum. But the petitioner-company rushed to file the instant writ petition and challenged the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange as well as the National and Mumbai Stock Exchanges. It was not the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was sought to be challenged but in fact what was sought to be challenged was the order passed by the Custodian. Therefore, the view taken by the Single Judge to the extent that that could not be interfered with in extraordinary writ jurisdiction was well-founded. It was a question which was yet to be decided by the Special Court as to whether all the money for establishing the petitioner-company was tainted money or the petitioner-company which had been established by K was from any other source which did not have the tinge of that tainted money. That question could not have been decided in the instant pro- ceeding. More so, by virtue of the notification dated 20-11-2001 and the public notice issued on 24-11-2001 all the properties of all the persons who were notified and that of K stood attached. The 20-11-2001 not- ification clearly said that all the properties movable or immovable or both belonging to persons/entities would stand attached by virtue of section 3(3) of the Act of 1992 and similarly in the public notification dated 24-11-2001, the same was reiterated for notice of all concerned that from the date of the aforesaid notification any property movable or imm- ovable or both belonging to the notified persons/entities would stand attached and it would only be dealt with by the Custodian in such manner as the Special Court may direct. It was also made clear in the public notice dated 24-11-2001 that the provisions of the Act of 1992 have overriding effect on all other laws and all the companies and firms were directed to take notice that the property belonging to the notified persons/entities stood attached and it was not permissible to have any transaction of any kind relating to the attached properties of the notified persons/entities except with the direction of the Special Court. It was also mentioned in the public notice that all those who had dealings with such attached properties of the notified persons/entities should intimate to the Custodian the details of such properties. Therefore, in view of those facts, the assets and properties of K were attached and if the petitioner-company sought any remedy, the remedy lay in the Special Court which alone has jurisdiction to provide remedy and that Court is held by no less than a sitting Judge of the High Court. Therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter which was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Special Court. There was no occasion for the Single Judge to have unnecessarily entered into the question whether the Calcutta Stock Exchange was a ‘State’ within the meaning of article 12 or not. In fact, that question did not directly fall for determination. In substance what the petitioner-company wanted to challenge was the basic order of the Custodian, as the Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted in terms of the direction issued by the Custodian. Therefore, it was only an incidental action, and the basic challenge was to the notification notifying K as a notified person under section 3(2) of the Act of 1992. No executing agency who has implemented the order can be held responsible. The Calcutta Stock Exchange was only an executing agency and since the said K was notified person and he floated the company in 1994, all his assets stood attached, and, therefore, it deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company preventing it from doing any trading activity in Calcutta Stock Exchange. Therefore, it was not an action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was under challenge. The Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted as per the direction given by the Custodian as executing agency and if the petitioner-company had any grievance against the order passed by the Custodian, then it had remedy under the Act of 1992

Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13]

From a plain reading of sections 542 and 543 as a whole, as it is evident that the statute itself is very clear and there is no ambiguity with regard to entitlement to filing an application under sections 542 and 543, the principle of law of casus omissus cannot be supplied by the Court in the absence of any necessity. [Para 17]

From the said finding, it would be evident that the application under sections 542 and 543 preferred by the administrator of the company-in-liquidation was not maintainable, nor the Company Judge was empowered to impose a fine in lieu of imprisonment under section 542(3). In such a background, there was no other option, but to set aside the impugned order passed by the Company Judge. [Para 18]

The impugned order of the Company Judge was to be set aside, accordingly, and the appeals were to be allowed. [Para 19]

The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Generally speaking, presumption is in favour of existence of the jurisdiction of the civil courts rather than exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil courts. Normally, the civil courts' jurisdiction has following three dimensions : (a) it must have jurisdiction regarding the subject-matter; (b) it should have pecuniary jurisdiction; and (c) it must have territorial jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [Para 30]

In regard to the function of a balance-sheet, it may be stated to be an endeavour to show the share capital, reserves (distinguishing those which are available for distribution as dividends from those reserves not regarded as so available) and the liabilities of the company at the date on which it is prepared and the manner in which the total sums represented then are distributed over several types of assets. In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Also, a balance-sheet is known as a statement of net worth assets and liabilities and it is called as 'Statement of financial position'. In the Companies Act, it is the duty of the directors of a company to see that the regular and correct account books are kept. [Para 31]

Normally, it is the duty of the directors and the management to ensure that the provisions of the Companies Act have been complied with. However, where there is contravention of a legal requirement by a company, which has a bearing on the accounts and transactions of the company, an auditor would in the normal course of his inquiry become aware of such a contravention which needs to be brought to the notice of the shareholders. In short, an auditor should, however, not merely state the facts, leaving it to be inferred that a contravention of legal requirements has taken place, but he should spell out that in his opinion a contravention of the law has taken place. Further, an auditor is the eyes and ears of the disparate shareholders' community. Moreover, the only individual who has an access to the books of account of a company, apart from the concerned company itself, is the auditor. [Para 32]

The CLB may pass such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process of the Bench as per regulation 44 and that power is similar to the power of a civil court under section 151 of the Code. [Para 33]

As far as our country is concerned, a share is not merely a chose-in-action, it is also as per the definition of a share or a debenture under section 82 a 'movable property'. However, shares or debentures become equivalent to 'goods' as per the decision in Kunhunni Elaya Nayar v. P.N. Krishna Pattar [1942] 12 Comp. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. Moreover, it represents the interest of the holder measured for the purposes of liability and dividend by a sum of money. [Para 34]

Under the TNPID Act, there are two procedures. There are provisions which deal with the property of financial establishments like the company after an FIR is registered. There are also provisions for trial and punishment of financial establishments and persons responsible for running them under section 5 of TNPID Act. Once the charge sheet is filed under the TNPID Act, the Special Court alone will have jurisdiction to deal with the financial establishment and its properties. The charge sheet or the final report has not yet been filed in this case. [Para 18]

Under section 3 of the TNPID Act, the Government on being satisfied that the financial establishment is not likely to return the deposits or make payment of interests, may pass an order attaching the money or other properties procured in the name of the establishment or in the name of any other person from the deposits collected by the financial establishment. The Government can also transfer the property so attached to the control of the Competent Authority constituted under section 4 of TNPID Act. [Para 19]

Section 7(8) of TNPID Act also empowers the Special Court to issue directions for equitable distribution of monies attached or realized out of the sale of the properties among the investors/depositors. Such order is to be passed on an application made by the Competent Authority. [Para 21]

Having regard to the number of depositors and the huge stakes involved, it would be a mammoth task to identify the investors, identify the lands that have been purchased, value the land and realize the actual value by way of sale of properties. It would be appropriate if a committee is constituted consisting inter alia of Competent Authority under TNPID Act, representatives from the Revenue Department, representatives from the legal fraternity, representatives from the Economic Offences Wing, representatives of SEBI and a team of Chartered Accountants to carry out the task of identifying the investors, identifying the lands that have been purchased, getting the land valued and raising funds for settlement of dues of investors/depositors by actual sale of landed properties. It will be open to the Committee to engage Chartered Accountants of repute, valuers, lawyers and to employ such other professional services, as the Committee might deem it necessary. The advertisement shall be published in at least two English newspapers and two Tamil newspapers having wide circulation in the State of Tamil Nadu. [Para 24]

All depositors/investors of the company should apply to the Committee with details of their investments and documents in support of their claims within the time stipulated in the advertisement. The Committee shall take necessary steps to identify the properties of the company, its sister concerns, Directors and transferees, to ascertain the location, marketability and title thereto and thereafter proceed to sell the properties. The Committee may obtain the assistance of a team of experts of the revenue department and a competent legal team to perform the acts mentioned above. [Para 26]

The amounts realized from out of the sale of the properties shall be deposited in a special account opened for this purpose, which may jointly be operated by any two members of the committee nominated by the Chairperson. [Para 27]

In case the amounts realized are not sufficient to settle the claims of all depositors/investors in full, the depositors/investors shall be paid on pro rata basis in proportion with the amounts deposited by them in the company as substantiated by cogent documents. It is fairly well-settled that the CLB does not have the power of review. It is, however, open to the CLB to exercise its inherent powers and to make such orders as may seem necessary to meet the ends of justice. The CLB has power to review and recall its orders which have been wangled through fraud or misrepresentation. [Para 141]

In its earlier order dated 13-8-2008, the CLB has recorded categorical findings:- (i) conduct of KCP having regarded CEPL's funds as though his own funds is burdensome, harsh and wrongful; (ii) movement of funds from CEPL as traced by the auditors is not supported by any approvals from the Board of CEPL. Moreover, as held in New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Dy. Secretary, Ministry of Finance [1966] 36 Comp.
