Whether it is in the nature of removal of the blot of a court conviction, increase in the number of directors on the Board beyond twelve, remuneration of directors or its increase, holding offices or places of profit by the directors and their qualification or disqualification or loans to them or loans and investments in their related companies (for return investment in the parent company’s shares as cross-holdings) or contracts or arrangements in which they are interested or sole-selling-buying agencies in which they are suspected to be interested or suspension of powers or supersession of the directors by those nominated in case of mismanagement/change in the constitution of the Board or investigation into the affairs of a company or the ownership of the shares as well as the appointment and remuneration of the managerial persons or changes in the company’s name or its situation from one State to another or unclaimed dividends, it is entirely at the highest level in the Ministry at New Delhi with the obligation of an Annual Report on its working being placed on the table of the Parliament on which there is hardly any debate. Public issues, listing and insider-trading, among others, is controlled by SEBI. Matters left to shareholders and investors include the fiduciary obligations of company promoters/directors/managerial persons, fund-raising and maintenance, dividends and bonus, political contributions, financial sickness and as contributories in winding up. The power of the general meeting is reserved for formal compliances connected with the yearly maintenance of companies and fund-raising and maintenance, with no way made visible to get back their investments robbed by the wrongdoers in control of companies. As to judicial review, as a result of the latest amendments to the Act, excepting the Supreme Court all High Court jurisdiction has been divested and transferred to the Tribunals and continued with the Criminal Courts for the levy of enhanced fines, many of them open for compounding out of court under section 621A, and imprisonment for infractions remaining only as a mere threat with the few of Government prosecutions bringing not much significant deterrence. The singular offence that is punishable with imprisonment alone extending up to five years under the Act is the application made for subscription of shares in a fictitious name by the investors, under section 68A(1).

If in any return, report, certificate, balance sheet, prospectus, statement or other document required by or for the purposes of any of the provisions of the Act, any person making a statement that is false in any material particular knowingly, (not wilfully, as under section 438 of the English Act, thus widening the scope of the section) or which omits any material fact knowing it to be material, the person making the same incurs the liability to be punished under section 628. But to sustain a prosecution under the section, proof of guilty mind of knowledge of falsity is essential - P.P. Looke v. N.J. Mathew [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 790 (Ker.).

26.26-6-4a DIRECTORS OWE THEIR DUTIES TO THE COMPANY - The directors owe their duties to the company, and it is the company or in the name of the company at the instance of shareholders where allowed or the creditors if the company’s solvency is not sufficient to pay its debts in full (for which reason the shareholders lose their power to ratify the acts of directors), that those duties can be enforced, but not at the instance of the employees as employees while the company is a going concern. A single shareholder will not succeed to bring an action for any recovery of profit made by the director, unless the action is brought as a derivative action, Prudential Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1982) 1 All ER 354 (CA). CHAPTER 284

PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER *PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER*

284.1 Background note284.1 Background note

The Court/Tribunal has been vested with the power to restrain fraudulent persons from managing companies under section 203 of the Act, in a case before it by way of a disqualification order passed, where —

(a) a person is convicted of any offence in connection with the promotion, formation or management of a company, or

(b) in the course of its winding up, a person is found guilty of an offence punishable under section 542 of the Act, irrespective of his conviction, or

(c) a person is otherwise guilty while being an officer of the company of any fraud, or misfeasance in relation to the company or of any breach of duty to the company.

284.2 Disqualification order284.2 Disqualification order

The Court/Tribunal may make an order that a person convicted as above shall not, without the leave of the Court/Tribunal, be a Director or, in any other way - whether directly or indirectly be concerned or take part in the promotion, formation or management of a company, for such period not exceeding five years as may be specified in the order.

284.3 Who can apply ?284.3 Who can apply ?

Any person who is or has been a member or creditor of the company or the liquidator or Official Liquidator may apply to the Court/Tribunal for making the disqualification order by following the procedure under section 203.

284.4 Violation of disqualification order284.4 Violation of disqualification order

Acting in contravention of disqualification order entails punishment by a prison term upto two years or fine extending to fifty thousand rupees or both, for each such offence.

Illustration

In a case, winding up petitions were filed, but the winding order was not passed. At that stage a petition under section 203 seeking a disqualification order was filed. The alleged breach of duty against the company consisted of further issue of capital in violation of the provision in the Articles made by the Directors allotting the shares in the names of the Directors themselves and their relatives without first offering them proportionately to the members of the company. Held that the case called for a disqualification order against all the Directors for two years (with an alternate arrangement put in place for management of the company, meanwhile) - K.K. Roller Flour Mills (P.) Ltd. v. Utkal Flour Mills (P.) Ltd. [2005] 63 SCL 35 (Ori.).

Need for performance and propriety audit of company contracts 1.27-5 It is a paradox that the law never dictates how companies are run although companies are the creatures of the law. Law is just a factor but not the key factor, and there is a serious limitation to law reform in company affairs, which in the main are nothing but company contracts and their working. Private individuals entering into commercial contracts as they like are, inter alia, subject to the rule of caveat emptor, or beware buyer, and it ought to stand to reason to ask why the same cannot and should not apply to company contracts brought about by the Managing Director or Chief Executive or his cronies personally, who at best is an agent for a term with nothing for him to lose under the contracts that he makes day-in-and-day-out for and on behalf of the company, and everything to gain personally for himself if he chooses with no questions to be asked by any. The legality of the arbitrary character of the shrouded company contracts under cover of the so called business secrets, and the large number of compromises and waivers of obligations under them commonly found in any company of considerable size, are prima facie questionable on grounds of propriety but in the face of the general apathy of the Boards of directors are going unchallenged, though these form the bulk of company management in its essence, and it is an impropriety of the highest degree to leave it totally free and invitingly open to misuse.

The Company Law is sheltering the companies and company managers by not providing any deterrence in that behalf except in the case of a prospectus for public offer of securities, and expressly not conceding the locus standi to the shareholders or depositors or debt instrument holders, who stand on a different footing from sundry trade creditors, in the name of avoidance of multiplicity of litigation against the companies, on the British model, where there are other modes of deterrence like the public run scare apart from legal redress familiar to many in matters of this kind since ages unlike in India.

1.27-6 The important question that arises here is whether this arrangement provides even a semblance of balance between private interest and public interest in the so called public company in India, where the scare of public run is operative against the banks, and it is absent in every other walk of life. In companies, the residuary control of the general body at a duly convened meeting is limited to the slated subjects and those present and voting, in line with the legislative procedure except the matters reserved to the postal ballot in which company contracts do not figure, and the shareholders’ interest is nil as to the company’s affairs as those are disallowable for want of prior notice to the company, reducing the general meetings of companies to a near farce; while the legal remedies available against erring companies as to their contracts are scanty and little known unless those accumulate and amount to ‘mismanagement’, and therefore ineffectual. External voucher audit coupled with internal audit of the so called ‘commensurate level’ and the Audit Committee of Directors introduced by section 292A of the Act, without specifying the items to be seen and leaving the whole to the august Board of Directors to decide, is no answer to it, because the businessmen would not brook it and the law-makers would not get to it, for obvious reasons. Perhaps, conditioned in our mind-set as we are by the UK model, though it is patently unsuited in the Indian milieu without re-formulation, our Company Law will never find an answer to this core question of exercise of unqualified power with non chalance; or, it should be accepted in law whether fair or unfair that there is nothing ‘public’ in a public company except it being synonymous with their right to tap the capital markets at large by public offers to fund private contracts.

The above conditions satisfy the definition of the Benami transaction u/s 2(9) of the PBPT Act, 1988. Thus I have reason to believe and I am satisfied that the property in the form of Flat having details discussed above, is a Benami property as per section 2(8) of the PBPT Act, 1988."

The notice under Section 24(1) was answered by the Writ Petitioner/Company. The Company denied that the provisions of the 1988 Act are at all applicable to the facts of the present case. The Company took the stand that, if at all, the IO has jurisdiction only to inquire under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act (for short the IT Act). The reply to the Section 24(1) notice (supra) was finally considered by the IO vide his order under Section 24(4) of the 1988 Act. The IO, inter alia, concluded that both the paper and the fund trails connecting to the purchase of the scheduled property in issue, inter alia, point to fictitious/non-transparent/non-visible entities. The IO found, on the basis of the available materials, that the funds utilised in the name of the Company to purchase the property in issue belonged to person/persons whose identities have not been disclosed. The usufructs of the purchase, although ostensibly in the name of the Company, may be ultimately beneficial to the non-transparent/Fictitious/non-visible entities behind the suspected benami purchase. Therefore, the IO ordered that the provisional attachment under section 24(3) shall continue till the Adjudicating Authority (for short AA) further adjudicates under section 24(3) of the 1988 Act.

The company filed a writ petition challenging the initiation of proceedings by IO under section 24(1) and attachment of property under section 24(4) and reference to Adjudicating Authority. The company contended that, in view of the decision reported in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 at Paragraph 7 thereof, the question of fictitious entities behind the fund alleged to have been utilised by the Company for the purchase of the property in issue would not be attracted in law since, such fictitious entities are not referable to the shareholders of the Company, who carry no fiduciary interest connected to the property of the Company. The law as elucidated in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 (supra), inter alia, permits the shareholders to only participate in the profits of the Company in the form of dividends without being required to exercise any participatory involvement in its immovable assets. Therefore, the fundamentals of the proceeding initiated by the IO under section 24(1) and 24(4) are misconceived. The Respondents/Revenue contended that the profile of the investments made by the Company as evident from the facts collected by the IO connected to the purchase of the scheduled property traces its source to funds from fictitious entities which are required to be identified. On the basis of the materials available to the IO, the Company is believed to be acting as the benamidar, or, apropo the current lingo in vogue of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), Government of India, a shell or "dabba" company of investors at large.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

HELD: There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

Power of Company Law Board to review: On behalf of ORE and Athappan, it was mainly contended that the CLB has no power to review its own order, especially, in the guise of a clarification. [Para 137] It is fairly well-settled that the CLB does not have the power of review. It is, however, open to the CLB to exercise its inherent powers and to make such orders as may seem necessary to meet the ends of justice. The CLB has power to review and recall its orders which have been wangled through fraud or misrepresentation. [Para 141]

In its earlier order dated 13-8-2008, the CLB has recorded categorical findings:- (i) conduct of KCP having regarded CEPL's funds as though his own funds is burdensome, harsh and wrongful; (ii) movement of funds from CEPL as traced by the auditors is not supported by any approvals from the Board of CEPL. (iii) KCP had taken enormous steps in safeguarding and enhancing the value of CPL properties as well as bringing VML out of sickness thereby saving its vast extent of properties and settling all dues of workmen which is in contravention of the JVA/Articles of CEPL. (iv) KCP is accountable for not having diligently discharged its statutory duties cast on him. On those factual findings, in its order dated 13-8-2008, CLB observed that the very purpose of CEPL could not have been achieved in terms of JVA and in the light of those factual findings directed CEPL to return a sum of Rs. 75 crores and Rs.4 crores invested by ORE and Athappans respectively along with interest at 8 per cent. In the said order, the CLB also permitted KCP to utilise the money to return the said amount to ORE and Athappans and in the meanwhile directing that VML shall not alienate or sell any of its immovable properties till payment is made to ORE. The CLB also made provision that in the event of failure to make the repayment within the specified time, CEPL, CGH, KCP and VML were to duly convey the immovable properties of VML, i.e., 17.15 acres of land in favour of ORE and 7.80 acres of land in favour of Athappans. When the CLB has recorded categorical findings that CEPL neither carried out nor could accomplish its business plan in accordance with terms of JVA and directed return of sum of Rs.75 crores and Rs.4 crores, it was not justified in modifying its earlier order permitting KCP to deal with 50 per cent of the money lying with State Bank of India. [Para 142]

Given the sequence of events, if KCP is placed in position to manage CEPL, he would again try to divert the amount to innumerable subsidiary companies floated by him, the CLB was not justified in directing ORE and NA to deposit the share certificates with the Bench Officer. Having found that KCP had not discharged his statutory duties and that he was not prudent in managing CEPL, the CLB was not justified in directing payment of 50 per cent of the deposit lying with the State Bank of India. [Para 143]

HEADNOTE: Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with Order XXXIX, rule 4 and Order XLIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Court - Jurisdiction of - Case of revision petitioners was that first respondent-company had filed Form II and Form FCGPR with Reserve Bank of India along with certificates issued by statutory auditor of company and Company Secretary stating that it had allotted certain shares to first revision petitioner - Subsequently, it was found that to deprive revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to first revision petitioner - First respondent also filed a suit before civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to first revision petitioner - Revision petitioners filed revision petition under article 227 of Constitution for setting aside said interim order on grounds that trial court had no jurisdiction to decide issue as same issue was pending before CLB and that order of trial court granting interim injunction was non-speaking one - Whether revision petitioners could not invoke jurisdiction of High Court under article 227, since they had two concurrent remedies, namely, to get order of trial court varied, vacated or discharged as per order XXXIX, rule 4 of Code and to file an appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(r) of Code - Held, yes

FACT: The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

HELD: The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. SEBI received several complaints from investors of the respondent-company to the effect that the cheques issued by the company had been dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the bank account of the respondent-company, that the office of the respondent- company had become non-functional, that directors of the respondent-company had gone defaulter and had more or less gone underground and that the funds received by the respondent had been diverted to the group companies. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. It sought the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investors’ moneys from being filtered away.

HELD: Prima facie it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agriculture productions, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of this empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company’s moneys are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

As held in DDA v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. The concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. Absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court while acting under article 142/226 from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. In India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity. In the aforesaid case, the Court passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but ‘for any other purpose’, and ‘any other purpose’ would include such public interest purpose.

HELD: Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34]

order of attachment was not having information that an OL had been appointed - Further, it was not that OL had made an application to provide an opportunity of hearing and had been denied - Rather, 'Birla Solar' remain unrepresented and it was they who were relevant party to inform about appointment of liquidator - Whether thus, order of Adjudicating Authority did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 18, 21, 22, 28 and 29] FACT: A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

HELD: The provision for hearing is given under section 8(1). Section 5(1) provides for attachment against 'any person' in possession of proceeds. At the relevant time defendant was in possession of the proceeds. The Competent Authority passed the order of attachment was not having information that an Official Liquidator has been appointed. The information was given only to the Adjudicating Authority.[Para 17]

Section 3(5) lays down that the Custodian can take assistance of any other person while exercising his powers or for discharging his duties under this section and under section 4. When a fax message was sent to the Calcutta Stock Exchange for information and necessary action, the Calcutta Stock Exchange had no option but to deactivate the terminal of the petitioner-company. [Para 11] The plea taken by the petitioner-company was that K was one of the shareholders of the petitioner-company (though he resigned later on) and his holding which was raised to 97.94 per cent was subsequently brought down to 68 per cent. But the fact remained that K was practically the owner of that company; though in order to escape the clutches of law, he had resigned as one of the directors. But the fact remained that the petitioner-company was started by K in 1994 and it was a debatable question as to whether the company was established by K from the tainted money earned by him during 1-4-1991 to 6-6-1992. That matter was yet to be decided by the competent forum. But the petitioner-company rushed to file the instant writ petition and challenged the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange as well as the National and Mumbai Stock Exchanges. It was not the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was sought to be challenged but in fact what was sought to be challenged was the order passed by the Custodian. Therefore, the view taken by the Single Judge to the extent that that could not be interfered with in extraordinary writ jurisdiction was well-founded. It was a question which was yet to be decided by the Special Court as to whether all the money for establishing the petitioner-company was tainted money or the petitioner-company which had been established by K was from any other source which did not have the tinge of that tainted money. That question could not have been decided in the instant pro- ceeding. More so, by virtue of the notification dated 20-11-2001 and the public notice issued on 24-11-2001 all the properties of all the persons who were notified and that of K stood attached. The 20-11-2001 not- ification clearly said that all the properties movable or immovable or both belonging to persons/entities would stand attached by virtue of section 3(3) of the Act of 1992 and similarly in the public notification dated 24-11-2001, the same was reiterated for notice of all concerned that from the date of the aforesaid notification any property movable or imm- ovable or both belonging to the notified persons/entities would stand attached and it would only be dealt with by the Custodian in such manner as the Special Court may direct. It was also made clear in the public notice dated 24-11-2001 that the provisions of the Act of 1992 have overriding effect on all other laws and all the companies and firms were directed to take notice that the property belonging to the notified persons/entities stood attached and it was not permissible to have any transaction of any kind relating to the attached properties of the notified persons/entities except with the direction of the Special Court. It was also mentioned in the public notice that all those who had dealings with such attached properties of the notified persons/entities should intimate to the Custodian the details of such properties. Therefore, in view of those facts, the assets and properties of K were attached and if the petitioner-company sought any remedy, the remedy lay in the Special Court which alone has jurisdiction to provide remedy and that Court is held by no less than a sitting Judge of the High Court. Therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter which was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Special Court. There was no occasion for the Single Judge to have unnecessarily entered into the question whether the Calcutta Stock Exchange was a ‘State’ within the meaning of article 12 or not. In fact, that question did not directly fall for determination. In substance what the petitioner-company wanted to challenge was the basic order of the Custodian, as the Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted in terms of the direction issued by the Custodian. Therefore, it was only an incidental action, and the basic challenge was to the notification notifying K as a notified person under section 3(2) of the Act of 1992. No executing agency who has implemented the order can be held responsible. The Calcutta Stock Exchange was only an executing agency and since the said K was notified person and he floated the company in 1994, all his assets stood attached, and, therefore, it deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company preventing it from doing any trading activity in Calcutta Stock Exchange. Therefore, it was not an action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was under challenge. The Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted as per the direction given by the Custodian as executing agency and if the petitioner-company had any grievance against the order passed by the Custodian, then it had remedy under the Act of 1992

It might be only through a detailed probe that the intention, if any, behind the above acts resulting in substantial loss to various interests in society through the company could be established. If the above acts were done intentionally (mens rea), adverse consequences may follow including penalising the guilty. Establishing mens rea is the purpose behind any legal framework of this kind. There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator. The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

HEADNOTE: Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - In regard to the function of a balance-sheet, it may be stated to be an endeavour to show the share capital, reserves (distinguishing those which are available for distribution as dividends from those reserves not regarded as so available) and the liabilities of the company at the date on which it is prepared and the manner in which the total sums represented then are distributed over several types of assets. In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Also, a balance-sheet is known as a statement of net worth assets and liabilities and it is called as 'Statement of financial position'. In the Companies Act, it is the duty of the directors of a company to see that the regular and correct account books are kept. [Para 31]

Normally, it is the duty of the directors and the management to ensure that the provisions of the Companies Act have been complied with. However, where there is contravention of a legal requirement by a company, which has a bearing on the accounts and transactions of the company, an auditor would in the normal course of his inquiry become aware of such a contravention which needs to be brought to the notice of the shareholders. In short, an auditor should, however, not merely state the facts, leaving it to be inferred that a contravention of legal requirements has taken place, but he should spell out that in his opinion a contravention of the law has taken place. Further, an auditor is the eyes and ears of the disparate shareholders' community. Moreover, the only individual who has an access to the books of account of a company, apart from the concerned company itself, is the auditor. [Para 32]

As far as our country is concerned, a share is not merely a chose-in-action, it is also as per the definition of a share or a debenture under section 82 a 'movable property'. However, shares or debentures become equivalent to 'goods' as per the decision in Kunhunni Elaya Nayar v. P.N. Krishna Pattar [1942] 12 Comp. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. Moreover, it represents the interest of the holder measured for the purposes of liability and dividend by a sum of money. [Para 34]

HELD: Under sub-article (2) of article 226, the power conferred on the High Court to issue directions, orders or writs can be exercised by the Court in relation to territories within which the cause of action wholly or in part arises for the exercise of such powers. If cause of action or part of cause of action has not arisen or the person fails to demonstrate such cause of action, as having arisen within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court, issue of any writ or direction would be without jurisdiction. [Para 14]

As per clause (f) of section 45-I of the RBI Act, the first petitioner was a NBFC because it received deposits under a scheme or arrangement and admittedly obtained licence under the provisions of that Act. Further, under section 45QA thereof, the first petitioner was under obligation to repay every deposit accepted by it. If the deposit was not repaid, the aggrieved party could file application before the CLB which might direct the NBFC to make payment of such deposit. Any order passed by the CLB was appealable order before the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the company had its registered office. Thus, the High Court of Andhra Pradesh was not a Court to which an appeal would lie under section 10F of the Companies Act. [Para 19]

The counter-affidavit filed by the third respondent and the letters addressed by depositors as well as Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, would show that no cause of action whatsoever arose in the State of Andhra Pradesh, much less in Hyderabad. [Para 20]

It was reasonable to infer that the petitioners had intentionally withheld the information from the Court and obtained order. It was also reasonable to infer that petitioners having failed to obtain necessary orders of bail or otherwise, had approached the Court and chose to file the writ petition seeking the relief the granting of which would pre-empt any authority in the country to investigate further into the acts of malfeasance and misfeasance and deny justice to the depositors. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 depositors and none of them was resident or hailed from Hyderabad or Andhra Pradesh. [Para 21]

After perusing the various documents on record, the affidavit in support of the writ petition as well as the report of the Advocate Commissioner, the irresistible conclusion was that the petitioners had no cause of action to file the writ petition and no part of cause of action arose within the territorial jurisdiction of the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The categorical averment made by the third respondent that the petitioners had not lodged any complaint with police station, Mir Chowk and that the petitioners had never approached them and that there was no complaint made against them, stood unrebutted thereby supporting the view that no part of cause of action arose in Andhra Pradesh. Therefore, the High Court had no territorial jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition. [Para 22]

The report of the Advocate Commissioner would show that the petitioners had not approached the Court with clean hands. The attempt to suppress the facts was glaring. Only to make out case within the jurisdiction of the High Court ,bald allegations were made against respondents 2 and 3 which were proved to be false, and baseless and that showed that the petitioners were not only guilty of suppressio veri, suggestio falsi, but these proceedings were not bona fide. These proceedings were only a sharp practice designed to abuse the process of law and take unfair advantage from depositors/investors and law enforcing agencies. At every movement and at every stage the petitioners made a mockery of rule of law. The extraordinary special jurisdiction under article 226 is never intended to redress the spurious grievance of persons like petitioners to force miscarriage of justice. [Para 25]

FACT: The respondent was an equity shareholder and the promoter of the appellant-company. He was also appointed as the Chairman of the company. Subsequently, the company came out with public issue which was subscribed in excess of 14 times the offer. Thereafter, the respondent filed petition under section 237(a)( ii ) before the Company Judge seeking to direct the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company. It was alleged that no first annual general meeting of the company was held as convened in time.

The managing director, ‘M’ had been fraudulently mismanaging the company in utter disregard of the interest of the shareholders and was acting in an autocratic and oppressive manner. He created false and fabricated documents with nefarious motive to oust the respondent and other members of the board of directors who opposed the misutilisation and misappropriation of public funds. He created documents and minutes purporting to remove the petitioner and others who opposed the mismanagement and oppression. Though on the public issue, shares were over subscribed to the tune of 14 times and huge amounts were collected from the public, shares were neither allotted properly nor amounts refunded to the applicants whose application for shares were not accepted.

It was further alleged that 1200 complaints had been filed against ‘M’ by the subscribers to whom the amounts were not refunded and that ‘M’ had misappropriated, misutilised and mismanaged the funds collected through public issue and diverted the funds for his private purposes. The company opposed the petition. The Company Judge found that the submission of the Central Government supported the respondent’s allegations and concluded that a deeper probe was necessary and passed an order declaring that affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Court itself.

On appeal :

HELD: By virtue of the power under section 237(a )(ii), the Court cannot appoint directly inspector or inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company but only make a declaration that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Once such an order is passed it is mandatory for the Central Government to conduct such investigation by appointing competent persons as inspectors.

In order to make quick and easy money, the directors of ‘GAL’ started accepting inter-corporate deposits/loans of huge amounts from various parties against the security of bookings of Maruti cars during the nineties when Maruti cars were selling like hot cakes. During those good old days, over hundred crores were stated to have been collected by GAL from various parties. It appeared that that money was collected without any intention of paying back to the investors/depositors. When the depositors/investors asked for refund of their money, they were not paid back by GAL and so they started approaching ‘M’ for getting back their money since their deposits were secured by the Maruti bookings. Pursuant to an understanding between GAL and ‘M’, GAL’s managing director executed indemnity bond on behalf of GAL and also personal guarantee bond indemnifying ‘M’ against any kind of demands against it by GAL’s investors from whom GAL had taken inter-corporate loans against non-existent bookings of Maruti cars. ‘G’ also executed a personal guarantee bond in favour of ‘M’. Both father and son had admitted that GAL had secured loans from the public against non-existent bookings of Maruti cars. The petitioner was one of the creditors of GAL who had approached the Court for winding up of GAL. When notice of the company petition was given to GAL, it had entered appearance and right from the beginning, not only GAL had started coming out with proposals for liquidating the liabilities of its creditors but DAL also came forward to re-pay the debts of GAL so that GAL was not wound up by the Court. It also appeared that proposals and assurances given by GAL as well as DAL during the pendency of winding up proceedings to avoid passing of order of its winding up and to save the reputation of ‘S’ Group of companies were never intended to be honoured by the directors of both those companies. ‘G’ gave an undertaking in order, dated 2-2-1998, that DAL had immovable property at Sikandara Road, which would be sold and its money would be utilized for meeting the amount due to the creditors and in case, it was not sold within a period of three and half months and the amounts which were due to the creditors who were before the Court were not paid off or any other favourable arrangement securing the monies of the creditors was not reached within the said period, the property No. 1, would be deemed to have been attached and would be sold under the supervision of the Court. GAL after the passing of the order, dated 2-2-1998, regarding deemed attachment of the property had been contending before the Court that ‘G’, the then Chairman of DAL had no authority to bind the said company by making a statement before the Court that property No. 1, would be sold in order to liquidate the liabilities of GAL since GAL had nothing to do with DAL. So recalling of the order dated, 2-2-1998, whereby it was ordered by the Court that, in case, the debts of the creditors of GAL were not paid off within the period of 3½ months, property No. 1 would be deemed to have been attached and become liable to be sold under the supervision of the Court, was sought. However, that was not done and so an appeal was filed before the Division Bench by, DAL. Pursuant to the liberty given by the Division Bench in that appeal, DAL had moved a review application before the company court seeking review of the order, dated 2-2-1998. In that application also it was contended that ‘G’ had no authority to bind the said company of which he was the chairman during those days since its board of directors had not authorized him to make the statement before the Court which he had made on 2-2-1998. Before that application could be disposed of, an amendment application came to be filed by DAL seeking amendment in its review application to the effect that even if ‘G’ was considered to be competent to make the statement which he made on 2-2-1998 that statement was ultra vires the company’s Memorandum and Articles of Association since it was not one of the objects of the company to offer security of its own assets for the repayment of debts of another company. Both the review petition as well as the amendment application, however, were not pursued and were finally dismissed for non-prosecution on 13-8-2009. Then an application was filed for revival of those applications but that application also was dismissed for non-prosecution on 18-3-2010
