A non-existent entity cannot ratify any action which it could not have initiated : there is no director, no secretary, no principal officer. The company having been dissolved there is no entity/person who can authorise anyone. A shareholder of erstwhile company cannot claim any right, title or interest in any particular asset/property of the company. Then there is no question of executing any power of attorney as authorised signatory. [Para 37] The legal position is well settled that on dissolution, properties of a company vest in the Government. By virtue of section 654 of the 1985 Act even if the property of the company is not sold (as per the plaintiff), the property has vested in the crown. Then there is no question of any person, including a shareholder, staking a claim to the property; and, thus, filing a plaint by self or through a power of attorney holder. [Para 39]

On a conjoint reading of provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 653 of the 1985 Act it is apparent that a company or any member or creditor can apply to a Court if the company or member or creditor feels aggrieved by the name of the company having been struck off from the register. The Court is required to be satisfied that at the point of time when the name of the company was struck off from the register, the company was carrying on business or was in operation, or otherwise, that it is just that the company be restored to the register. Therefore, the person applying for restoration has to be a person who is aggrieved. The concept of ’aggrieved’ here means that the order of striking off has resulted in a situation which is detrimental to the applicant, viz., company or any member or creditor. Therefore, unless the applicant is ’aggrieved’ there is no question of making an application seeking restoration. Upon an application being made the Court is required to ascertain whether the company was carrying on business or was in operation at the time of the striking off the name from the register. In effect, it means that the reasonable belief entertained by the Registrar of Companies under section 652(1) of the 1985 Act is found to be incorrect. For the Court to record such a finding there must be some material available on record. The other alternative contention which permits the Court to exercise discretion requires that ’it is just’ that the company be restored to the register. This requirement has to be backed by facts and circumstances prevailing in a given situation so as to enable the Court to exercise discretion in favour of the applicant, namely that the action of the Registrar striking off the name of the company of the register would result in creating a situation which is unfair and unjust to the applicant. [Para 46]

In the instant case, admittedly, the plaintiff could not seek restoration on the ground that it was carrying on business or was in operation at the time when its name was struck off, as the plaintiff had applied that its name be struck off from the register as the company was not carrying on business or was not in operation. In light of the fact that an application had been moved, it was not necessary to deal with the alternative situation whether it would be permissible for the Court to exercise discretion on the basis of the consequence of striking off being unjust to the applicant. Suffice it to state that there had to be cogent and sufficient material in that regard. [Para 47]

Section 654 of the 1985 Act stipulates that property and rights of a dissolved company are deemed to be bona vacantia and, accordingly, belong to the Crown. Once this was the position, the plaintiff could not seek any relief on the basis of being owner of the property without either impleading Crown or putting it to notice. [Para 48]

In the aforesaid factual matrix even if the plaintiff had moved an application seeking restoration of the company to the register it was not necessary to await outcome of such application. Considering the fact that an order of arrest was operating against the defendant it was not possible to do so, especially in light of the fact that the plaintiff was not inclined to permit vacation of the ex parte interim order of arrest. [Para 49]

In the aforesaid fact situation it was not possible to state that these were procedural defects which did not go to the root of the matter and should not be permitted to defeat a just cause. The plaintiff had failed to make out a case. [Para 53]

In the result, the OJMCA was allowed and as a consequence the suit was dismissed. The order of the arrest of the vessel was vacated/set aside. [Para 54]

HEADNOTE: Section 457 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Powers of liquidator - Whether Company Court while exercising jurisdiction in an application under sections 433, 434 and 439 has power to appoint a provisional liquidator giving him liberty to sell properties, not merely property standing in name of company but also properties standing in names of other companies on premise that such assets have been created with funds collected by company - Held, yes

FACT: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

HELD: STATUTORY POWERS OF OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR

The powers of provisional liquidator appointed by the Company Court under section 450(3) the same powers as that the liquidator himself has. The extensive powers of the liquidator are delineated under section 457. [Para 4]

EXTENT OF DIRECTIONS THAT THE COMPANY COURT COULD PASS

Even apart from the powers of the liquidator which are co-extensive with the powers of the provisional liquidator, the Court itself has the power under section 477 at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator to summon before it any officer of the company or person knowing or suspected to have in his possession any property or books or papers of the company or known or suspected to be indebted to the company. This power which the Company Court has under section 477 is wide enough to pass even an ex parte order to secure the interest of the persons moving the application for winding up. Having regard to such wide powers of the Company Court, it is untenable to contend that the Company Court could not have directed as regards the properties which, on a prima facie finding, were also the assets of the company. The order of the Company Court was unexceptional if it was noticed that the Company Court had also given liberty to show that the assets standing in the name of other companies did not belong to the company against which liquidation proceedings had been initiated. Indeed, no prejudice could be said to be caused by such an order. Further, section 533 enables the liquidator to apply for disclaimer of onerous property. Section 535(4), while fastening the liquidator to disclaim certain properties, makes it possible for any third party for approaching the liquidator himself staking his claim to the property which is taken possession of by the liquidator or in respect of which proceedings are taken for sale. Having regard to the scheme of the Act protecting the interest of third parties and controlling the discretion of the liquidator by overall supervision of the Company Court, it would be untenable to contend that the directions given by the Company Court at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator were not in conformity with law. [Para 5]

DISPOSITION

The sole contention raised by the appellant was, therefore, without any substance and the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

FACT: The company-in-liquidation, which was a ‘Nidhi’ started by the appellant, collapsed after collecting huge amounts of deposits from the public at large under certain schemes. On winding up petitions preferred by the affected persons, the Company Judge appointed an administrator, besides the Official Liquidator, to look into the affairs of the company. Since the Company Judge also made an observation to the effect that there was prima facie fraud of massive proportions having been committed by the appellants along with other board members of company-in-liquidation, the administrator appointed by the Court filed an application under sections 542 and 543 seeking for a declaration that those persons were liable to be prosecuted for the fraudulent diversion of the funds. The appellant contested the application denying all the allegations and also raised the question of maintainability of the same, but the Company Judge, while passing penal order against the appellant, also held that the application preferred by the administrator was maintainable.

On appeal to the Division Bench :

HELD: Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

If it could be shown that the affairs of the company were being conducted in a manner which was prejudicial to the public interest, then the order of the CLB was justified. The powers under section 408 are to be sparingly used and it is only if the CLB is satisfied that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner which is prejudicial to public interest, that the order can be passed. [Para 12] It is also a well-settled principle of law that it is not necessary that to invoke the powers under section 408, the damage should have already taken place. The powers of the Central Government under section 408 are preventive in nature and can be exercised in order to ensure that in future the affairs of the company are not conducted in a manner which is prejudicial to the public interest. An order under section 408 may not be able to cure the illegal or prejudicial act which may already have been performed, but can be used to prevent further damage. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the admitted facts were that the company had been unable to comply with the orders of the CLB and pay off the public depositors. The explanation of the company that it could not comply with the orders of the CLB due to the fact that its produce ‘Loratadine’ could not be sold in the US market; and that the global deposit receipts could not be utilized, could not be accepted. Both those circumstances were already in existence when the earlier order was passed by the CLB. At that time, the company itself had given various options to the CLB to pay off all the depositors. The CLB passed directions. That order of the CLB had attained finality and the company should have cleared the public debt in accordance with the orders of the CLB. The company, in fact, had not fulfilled its obligations and instead had diverted the funds to various other parties. One could not lose sight of the fact that thousands of pensioners, widows and other members of the public had invested their funds in the company. The company’s accounts should be above board. No doubt, in commercial transactions, there may be instances when a company may lose money, yet the totality of circumstances has to be seen while adjudicating whether the affairs of the company are being run in a manner which may be prejudicial to the public interest. [Para 14]

There were certain facts which had not been controverted. The first was that instead of servicing the public debt and repaying the depositors, the company had invested a sum of Rs. 67.75 crores in shares of associated companies. Admittedly, the company had invested huge amounts in its sister company ‘M’ Ltd. The annual report for the year 2002-03 showed that the company off loaded its investment and ‘M’ Ltd. ceased to be a subsidiary of the company. Thereafter, that company again became a subsidiary of the company a couple of years later. There was sufficient material on record to show that more than Rs. 67 crores had been diverted to other companies out of the funds of the company. That money could have been better utilized by paying off the public debt. [Para 15]

Another factor, which showed that the affairs of the company were not being run properly, was that the company had made a provision for writing-off outstanding debts of Rs. 126.25 crores as non-recoverable on 30-9-2003. In the previous year, the outstanding debts were less than Rs. one crore. The company had failed to explain as to how an increase of Rs. 124 crores in the bad debts had taken place in a period of less than one and a half years. Despite repeated queries in the matter, no proper answer could be given by the company. [Para 16]

It would also be pertinent to mention that even as per the report of the chartered accountants of the company itself, the accounts were not being properly maintained. It was being projected that the company was doing well and was making profit. However, if the note of the chartered accountants was taken into consideration, it appeared that said projection made by the company was also incorrect. [Para 17]

Section 207 enables the Registrar or the inspector to conduct inspection and inquiry and they are vested with all powers of the Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, while trying a suit in respect of; (a) the discovery and production of books of account; (b) summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath; (c) inspection of any books, registers and other documents of the company at any place. [Para 20]

The power to search and seizure is provided under section 209. Section 210 of the Act, 2013 empowers the Central Government, where it forms an opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company either, (a) on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208; (b) on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated; or (c) in public interest. Sub-section (2) thereof mandates the Central Government to order an investigation into the affairs of that company where an order is passed by a court or the Tribunal in any proceedings before it that affairs of a company ought to be investigated. [Para 21]

The establishment of SFIO is provided in section 211 of the Act, 2013, which also provides for its constitution by experts headed by a Director appointed by a notification by the Central Government. Once the provisions of Part VII of the Act, 1956 or Chapter XX of the Act, 2013 are brought into play, then the companies become subject to provisions of winding up and orders passed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

The Official Liquidator under the Act, 1956 and the Company Liquidator under the Act, 2013 are empowered to take into custody the company's properties and are vested with wide powers in that regard. [Para 29]

Wide ranging powers have been given to the liquidator for taking custody of the company's property under section 456 of the Act, 1956. All the properties and effects of the companies are deemed to be in custody of the Court/Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. [Para 30]

Similar powers are vested in the liquidator in section 283 of the Act, 2013, which provision also creates a legal fiction with regard to the custody of the properties and effects of the company being deemed to be with the Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. Wide ranging powers are provided by the Act, 2013 to the Tribunal which orders winding up of the company. Therefore, the purpose of the first proviso to section 226 of the Act, 2013 appears to be that since the Inspector would have taken into his custody the books and papers of the company or would have examined the various persons in exercise of his power under section 217 of the Act, 2013, or he would require papers and books for purpose of investigation initiated, he would bring to the knowledge of the Tribunal the steps taken by him or requiredto be taken, to enable the Tribunal to pass such orders as it may deem fit. This is in view of the fact that under section 283 of the Act, 2013 all the property of the company is deemed to be in the custody of the Tribunal. [Para 31]

It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that it has a panel of Chartered Accountants through whom the inspection and inquiries may be ordered. The sole purpose for which the Official Liquidator has sought for referring the matter to the SFIO was for detection of diversion of assets/funds of the company-in-liquidation. It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that the balance sheet, other books of account and documents are in possession of the Official Liquidator as well as the statement of affairs filed by the ex-director on behalf of the company-in-liquidation. [Para 32]

HEADNOTE: Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'

Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]

FACT: CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by the NCLT, wherein, the investors/homebuyers of 'C' including the petitioner, lodged their claims against 'C' before the resolution professional of 'C'.

However, the NCLAT on an appeal filed by the directors of 'C', passed an order setting aside the entire CIRP.

The order of NCLAT was challenged before the Supreme Court and an interim directions was passed to maintain status quo including the assets of 'C'.

The petitioner filed the instant writ petition praying for certain directions in the nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) to initiate and carry out appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for the acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds of the said company to its sister concern and freeze its assets.

Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. [Para 34] In the instant case, the Central Government by letter dated 17-2-2018 has directed the SFIO to investigate into the affairs of the respondent company, among other 114 entities. The investigation is currently undergoing and as such, as on date, being satisfied if so required, it is always open to the Central Government to file application under section 241(2), read with section 242 before the Tribunal. [Para 37]

In the interest of regulating the conduct of the company's affairs the interim order cannot be restrictive to any particular or individual person, including the company/companies, existing or erstwhile Officers and employees of the companies if investigation for alleged fraud is pending. [Para 38]

For the purpose of passing interim order, the Tribunal cannot fix the personal liability of delinquent Directors or Managers or Officers or other employees in absence of any specific evidence. Therefore, during the process of investigation and pendency of an application under section 241(2), read with section 242 and in view of powers conferred under section 221, the Tribunal is not only empowered to pass appropriate interim order against the company but also against any person or individual, including the order to desist. [Para 39]

Chapter XVI relates to 'Prevention of Oppression and Mismanagement'. An application to the Tribunal for relief in cases of oppression, etc. can be made by any eligible member(s) of the company under sub-section (1) of section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013, who complains about the oppression and mismanagement as stipulated in clauses (a) & (b) of sub-section (1). [Para 40]

On the other hand, the Central Government, if it is of the opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, it may itself apply to the Tribunal under sub-section (2) of section 241 for an order under Chapter XVI of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 41]

The power of Tribunal is wide enough as is evident from sub-section (1) of section 242 in terms of which 'it may make such order as it thinks fit', with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained of. [Para 42]

Sub-section (2) of section 242 is inclusive power without prejudice to the generality of the powers under sub-section (1), which includes regulation of conduct of affairs of the company in future; the purchase of shares or interests; restrictions on the transfer or allotment of the shares of the company; termination, setting aside or modification, of any agreement etc. [Para 43]

Sub-section (4) of section 242 empowers the Tribunal, on the application of any party to the proceeding to make any interim order which it thinks fit for regulating the conduct of the company's affairs upon such terms and conditions as appears to it to be just and equitable. [Para 44]

From the aforesaid provisions, it is clear that on an application made by the Central Government alleging affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, the Tribunal can pass any order in terms of Chapter XVI, which includes section 242 and other provisions under the said Chapter. [Para 45]

Section 246 is part of Chapter XVI, the provisions mentioned therein will be also covered by sub-section (2) of section 241. Therefore, in an application made by the Central Government alleging conduct of the company in a manner prejudicial to public interest, the provisions of sections 337 to 341 will be also applicable mutatis mutandis to an application made to the Tribunal under section 241 or section 245. [Para 46]

Section 337 deals with 'Penalty for frauds by officers' whereas section 338 relates to 'Liability where proper accounts not kept'. On the other hand, section 339 relates to the 'Liability for fraudulent conduct of business'. As per sub-section (2) of section 339, if any business of the company has been carried on with intent as mentioned in sub-section (1), any person who is or were parties carrying on of the business are also liable for action under section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 47]

HELD: The petitioner only wanted to take over the company subject to the approval by the BIFR and the BIFR had not approved the scheme and ordered for winding up. If that was so, he could not claim the amounts as an ex-managing director of the company-in-liquidation. The company court directed the third respondent (APSFC) to stay outside the winding up proceedings and proceed against the properties belonging to the company-in-liquidation only. If the property which did not belong to the company and belonged to the third parties like the petitioner, the company court would not exercise any power to grant permission to APSFC to proceed against the properties belonging to the third parties. If the third respondent seized the property which did not belong to the company, then the petitioner could take appropriate proceedings against APSFC for release of such property which did not form part of the assets of the company. But the Court would not direct the APSFC or the official liquidator to release the seized property which did not belong to the company. With regard to the amounts invested by the petitioner in the company in liquidation, his position would be like that of an unsecured creditor and as and when the properties of the company in liquidation were sold, he could submit his claim and establish his claim before the Official Liquidator like an unsecured creditor. But at this stage, the court could not order for refund of the amount alleged to have been invested by the petitioner. Similarly, an amount of Rs. 2 lakhs paid by the petitioner to the second and third respondents each as ’upfront’ amount could not also be directed to be released, as the same was also paid on behalf of the company in liquidation. Admittedly, the petitioner claimed that the property belonged to him and the same was not the property of the company and he brought in the said machinery pursuant to the interim orders passed by the BIFR and it was open for the petitioner to approach the BIFR for appropriate orders for the return of the machinery or any money invested by him pursuant to the interim orders granted by the BIFR, and the petitioner was also at liberty to approach the BIFR for seeking appropriate relief.

headnotes.text: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc - Though statement of official liquidator is confidential, there is nothing to prevent Court from referring to averments made in it, in order to determine whether order should be revoked

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc - An ex parte order is not final and in proper cases Court has power to discharge same

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  Under section 237(a)( ii), power of Court is invoked for directing Central Government to order investigation by concerned inspectors

Section 58A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Public deposits - Pursuant to an advertisement made by an investment company inviting general public to subscribe in various fixed deposits and saving schemes, appellants subscribed to scheme - As on date of maturity certificates issued were not honoured appellants lodged an fir with police station - On application of appellants, Magistrate directed attachment of said company’s properties - Thereafter, appellants filed criminal revision petition, alleging that notwithstanding order of attachment, properties were either disposed of or dealt with in a manner contrary to order of attachment - Additional District and Sessions Judge rejected said petition on ground that appellants had no locus standi to file a revision petition - Against said order, appellants filed petitions, but same were also dismissed by High Court - Whether, on facts, without entering into matter relating to contempt of court, concerned court was to be directed to work out details and modalities as to how properties of said company could be sold to get highest price so that dues of creditors and liabilities could be paid - Held, yes

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc. - Company Judge is a Court within meaning of section 476 of Code of Criminal Procedure

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 -Collective Investment Scheme-Respondent and certain other plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rate of returns which were not consistent with normal returns in such schemes - Cheques issued by respondent were dishonoured for want of fund and director/promoters of company were not traceable - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with high risk factors involved in such schemes, it is necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating these companies - It was prayed that pending drafting of regulations appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people - Whether in view of fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence and also fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize such property - Held, yes - Whether respondents should be restrained from operating their bank accounts and investigation by police with power to attach properties could be ordered - Held, yes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  Company Court itself is not invested with any power of investigation under section 237 and all that it can do is to consider plea of petitioners as to whether it is a fit case to direct Central Government to do so

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - A Company Judge has no jurisdiction to enforce an order against persons other than those mentioned in section 185 of 1913 Act

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - A Company Judge has no jurisdiction to enforce an order against persons other than those mentioned in section 185 of 1913 Act

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Powers of Court under section 237(a )(ii) are not circumscribed in any way

Section 452 of the Companies Act, 2013/ Section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 - Punishment - For wrongful withholding of property - Whether inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash interlocutory orders can be invoked only in case of exceptional case of illegality or lack of jurisdiction in interlocutory order - Held, yes - Whether where Magistrate had found that prima facie company had a right to possession of disputed property, he could have granted interlocutory relief under section 630(2), prior to conclusion of trial under section 630(1) - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where order of Magistrate under section 630(2) directing possession of disputed property to appellant company was an interlocutory relief based on prima facie assessment of facts and did not conclusively decide ongoing trial under section 630(1), there was no exceptional case of illegality or lack of jurisdiction in interlocutory order of lower court calling for exercise of inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 11]COMPANY LAW: Where order of Magistrate under section 630(2) was an interlocutory relief based on prima facie assessment of facts and did not conclusively decide ongoing trial under section 630(1), inherent powers of High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. could not have been invoked to quash interlocutory orders

Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc. - Court need not first determine that person to be examined actually possesses information

Section 263 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Appointment of Directors -  Court cannot interfere in management of company and cannot direct a company to induct non-shareholders as Directors merely on basis of allegations that those non-shareholders had invested money from undisclosed sources by undisclosed modes

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - There is nothing in section 237(a )(ii) to say that a person should first approach Central Government before coming to Court

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Official Liquidator - Custody of company's property - Official Liquidator of company under liquidation put under seal two godowns claimed as belonging to applicant trust on basis of documentry evidence and only given on rent for a period to company under liquidation - However, in a writ, Division Bench had directed Police Officials to investigate properties of certain persons including that of applicant to find out as to whether directors of company siphoned off company's property - Whether, it would be proper to order police to complete investigation within four weeks and if same would not be complied with, impugned properties should be handed over to applicant - Held, yes

Section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Compromise and arrangement - A scheme of compromise and/or arrangement between applicant company ‘E’ and its creditors was sanctioned by Company Judge - After that, a creditor of applicant resorted to arbitration proceedings against applicant and executing Court attached property of applicant and also directed sale of property - Applicant and its two unsecured creditors filed company applications claiming relief with regard to setting aside of aforesaid auction sale - By an order dated 12-2-2004, a committee of unsecured creditors was appointed by Court under Chairmanship of then Company Registrar of Court and other five members, which was to take steps to dispose of specified property of applicant so as to repay dues of unsecured creditors - However, then board of directors of applicant resolved to assign job of intended sale of suit property to ‘N’ and ‘D’, directors of applicant, and ‘P’, who was ex-director of ‘G’ company - Thereafter, suit property was conveyed in favour of ‘G’ company - Subsequently, conveyance deed in respect of suit property was executed by ‘G’ company in favour of ‘K’ company - Aforesaid development took place without knowledge of committee appointed by Court for sale of suit property - Committee submitted its report on basis of which Court issued notices to respective companies and directed parties, in particular ‘K’ company to maintain status quo of suit property as on that date till disposal of proceedings - Whether since applicant-company was party to proceedings before High Court as well as before executing Court which issued order of attachment and order of sale of suit property, transfer of suit property by applicant in favour of ‘G’ company without seeking permission of Court was illegal and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, ‘G’ company had no valid title in suit property and it could not have validly transferred suit property to ‘K’ company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, sale of suit property was illegal and non-existent and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether once Court found that suit property was transferred by applicant in violation of order of Court to which it was a party and same was in force, it would necessarily follow that transfer so effected by applicant was illegal and non-existent in law - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, instant case was an act of commission and omission in connivance and as a part of conspiracy to act in breach of order of Court to encash property of applicant and also to defeat claims and rights of creditors of applicant - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, criminal action was to be initiated against all erring persons who were directly or indirectly concerned with transaction-in-question, which was intended to overreach orders of Court of law and to defeat claim of creditors - Held, yes - Whether both applicant company and ‘G’ company were to be directed to bring back amount of sale proceeds with interest for payment of same to ‘K’ company and property-in-question was to be reauctioned for payment of dues of creditors - Held, yes

Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

Section 543 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power of court to assess damages against delinquent directors, etc. - Court is competent to proceed against non-resident foreigner directors and pass a decree   In an application under section 235 of the 1913 Act the Court can be asked to examine into the conduct of non-resident foreigner directors and compel them to pay the amount in respect of which they have committed breach of trust. The proceeding is in the nature of a suit for recovery of monies wrongfully converted by a person who happens to be a non-resident foreigner. If this proceeding is instituted by way of a suit, the provisions of sections 19 and 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable and since the cause of action arises within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, though the defendants - the persons who are liable to account - reside in a foreign territory, a suit can very well be laid and summons served in the manner provided by the rules and a decree can be passed. This does not necessarily involve any process to compel his attendance in order to submit himself for examination. If on the receipt of notice served in the manner provided under the rules, the concerned director does not choose to appear, the Court can come to a conclusion on the material placed before it on behalf of the applicant as to the conduct of the director in the matter and decide about his liability to the applicant or to the company and an order can be made directing the particular director to bring in any amount which he has misapplied, retained or in respect of which he has committed breach of trust or misfeasance which order will be in the nature of a decree. How and in what manner the decree will be treated by the foreign Court is immaterial, for, the decree is nevertheless valid though it may be treated as a nullity by the foreign Court. It is also equally unnecessary to consider whether such a decree can be enforced against such director. The Court is competent to pass such a decree by virtue of the local or municipal law governing the exercise of such jurisdiction. If the concerned director has any properties within the jurisdiction of the State, such an order can very well be executed against those properties and if there are no such properties, the order will have the same force and effect as a decree passed in a suit against a non-resident foreigner.
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Failure of Government to disclose to Court materials to justify order would lead to quashing of order

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

Section 206, read with section 210, of the Companies Act, 2013 - Investigations and inquiries - Power to - CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by NCLT, wherein, investor/homebuyers of 'C' including petitioner, lodged their claims before resolution professional - However, NCLAT passed an order setting aside entire CIRP - Said order was challenged before Supreme Court, which passed an interim direction to maintain status quo with regard to assets of 'C' - Petitioner filed instant writ petition praying for directions in nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) for initiating and carrying out appropriate inquires and investigation against management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds - It was noted that unscrupulous promoters/ex-directors running affairs of 'C' and its group of companies had committed repeated or multiple acts of siphoning off funds which had reached ears of RoC as several investors had already written to RoC to initiat action against 'C' and yet no action was taken - Whether RoC must exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets of 'C' and its group of companies and safeguard legitimate interests and rights of petitioner - Held, yes - Whether since there were compelling and justifiable grounds to pass directions so as to safeguard interests of petitioner and those who were similarly placed in larger public interest, interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against ex directors of 'C', to inspect affairs of 'C' and also to call for records of books of account of all related companies of 'C' - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 18, 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where RoC failed to exercise its statutory and public duties in arresting pilferage, siphoning off of assets and safeguard legitimate interests of investors of company 'C', interim directions were to be passed directing RoC to initiate appropriate legal action against alleged directors and to inspect affairs of 'C'
Section 155 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Power of court to rectify register of members -  A fraudulent transfer does not defeat title of true owner, and Court can strike off name of transferee
Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Court - Jurisdiction of - Inherent powers of Court cannot be invoked when express provisions are there

II Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases Before an investigation can be ordered by Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244 Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) The nature of an investigation to be ordered depends very much on the power of the Central Government which would be exercised if the Court so orders. For instance, the consequences of an order directing investigation have to be seen from the various provisions which govern such questions. Section 241 deals with the report of the Inspector and sections 242, 243 and 244 deal with what is to be done once a report has been made. Under section 242, a prosecution can be ordered. Under section 243, an application for winding up of the company on a petition under sections 397 and 398 can be instituted. Under section 244, proceedings for recovery of damages or property can be instituted. The result of an investigation can thus result either in prosecution or an application under sections 397 and 398 or a suit for recovery of damages or any property, which has been misapplied on account of misfeasance or mismanagement. Therefore, before an investigation can be ordered by the Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in the manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244. It is unnecessary to order an investigation merely because a shareholder feels aggrieved at the manner in which the company’s business is going on.

Section 543 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power of court to assess damages against delinquent, directors, etc - Court has power even to order delivery of books of company which are in possession of somebody else
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.

VII Section 11 Special Courts (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Discharge of liabilities Third person coming into possession of properties of notified parties under illegal agreements, cannot be allowed to retain them A.K. Menon v. Fairgrowth Financial Services Ltd. [1994] 81 Comp. Cas. 508 (Bom.) (Special Court) In case of statutory attachments which requires distribution of property it is the Special Court which has to recover the properties for the purposes of effective distribution under section 11(2) of the Act. One of the main objects of the Act being to recover large amounts of public money which have gone into private pockets and there being statutory attachment of properties of notified parties, such statutory attachments would operate even if the properties are in the hands of a third party pursuant to an illegal contract. After attachment, such properties can only be dealt with under the directions of the instant court. All such property must, therefore, be available for distribution under section 11(2). It, thus, cannot be argued that even after a statutory attachment, the third party must be allowed to deal with the properties as the notified party will not be assisted by the Court. The Court will not be assisting notified parties.The Court is safeguarding properties purchased from public monies from further alienation and ensuring that they are available for distribution under section 11. The question of applying the principle of pari delicto to such cases does not arise at all. To accept such an argument would amount to meaning that if an agreement is legal, then the Special Court can recover attached properties, but if an agreement is illegal, the Special Court must allow a transfer to take place. It can hardly be said that the third person who has come into possession of properties of notified parties, under illegal agreements, must be allowed to retain them. Such an argument cannot be accepted.
Rule 9  of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 - Inherent Powers of Court - Court has inherent powers to make such order necessary to do justice on facts of case
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.
Section 477 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to summon persons suspected of having property of company, etc.

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company affairs in other cases -  An order of Company Court directing investigation in exercise of powers under section 237(a)(ii ) is not a judgment determining rights of parties

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]COMPANY LAW : Where in commercial property project admeasuring 115 acres respondent had a claim of only Rs. 4 crores, High Court could not stall entire project with injunction order, however, no third party rights were to be created in respect of subject properties till orders were passed in winding up petition filed by respondent against developer

Section 4  of the Special Court (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Contracts Entered Fraudulently May Be Cancelled -  Under Special Court Act Custodian has no power to pass any order in nature of a decree directing payment by any party to notified party

Section 339 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Respondents invested Rs. 4 crores in a commercial project launched by real estate developer - Project, however, ran into trouble and construction was stalled - Neither possession was offered nor was assured return given to respondents - Respondents, thus, filed a petition for winding up of developer - There were several other investors who too had invested in project - Various complaints were filed against developer and its directors, which resulted in an FIR being registered - Subsequently, investigation thereon resulted in a charge sheet, wherein it was alleged that said developer siphoned off monies of investors including respondents to consortium of six land owning companies which were, related party companies of developer - Subsequently, said consortium of six companies purchased 11 properties extending to 115 acres of land for project mall - High Court, vide impugned judgment restrained these six companies from alienating aforesaid properties - Whether for a paltry amount claimed by respondents project admeasuring 115 acres could not be stalled however, developer was directed to give an undertaking that until further orders were passed in company petition for winding up, they would not create any third party rights in respect of subject properties - Held, yes - Whether therefore, order of High Court was not justified and was to be set aside - Held, yes. [Paras 19 and 20]

Section 468 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Delivery of property to liquidator - Order, which Court can pass directing delivery of money, property, etc., to liquidator, can only be against persons enumerated in section 468

Section 433 read with  section 443 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Circumstances in which company may be wound up - Petitioner challenged winding up order on ground that company was not given opportunity of hearing and as such order was in breach of principles of natural justice - Whether where company judge had painstaking and studiously gone into whole financial aspects through a questionnaire and information regarding relevant transactions was also sought and affidavits were filed showing company's financial position, order of company judge for winding up could not be challenged on ground of non-hearing of company - Held, yes - Whether Court has ample powers to recommend investigation and give directions for filing first information report with regard to any apparent fraud by company and those in-charge of company - Held, yes
Section 634A of the Companies Act, 1956 - Enforcement of court orders

Section 633 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Powers of Court to Grant Relief in Certain Cases - Before exercising discretion under section 633 Court has to make an enquiry in accordance with section 4(2) of Code of Criminal Procedure

Section 635 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Enforcement of orders of one court by other courts - In view of provision of section 635, any order made by company court under section 446(2)(b) must be treated as a decree for purpose of recovering money ordered to be recovered in favour of company

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - It is not necessary that for passing an order under section 237(a )(ii) there should be a proceeding already before Court; even a petition simpliciter can be entertained
Section 633 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Powers of court to grant relief in certain cases - Court referred to in section 633 need not be only Criminal Court

Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Petitioner, which had given huge loans to respondent- companies, sought for investigation under section 237(b) by Central Government into affairs of respondent-companies and their promoter-directors for fraudulently and unlawfully making wrongful gain and having committed misfeasance, thereby causing pecuniary losses to petitioner - Siphoning-off of huge amount by respondents through 250 front companies in fraudulent manner was indicated by income-tax authorities also - Whether since without investigation under section 237(b), it was not possible to discover true and correct facts and modus operandi adopted by respondents in cheating petitioner and siphoning-off of public money, enquiry under section 237(b) was to be ordered and Central Government was to be directed to appoint inspectors for enquiry - Held, yes

I. Section 478 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power to order public examination of promoters directors, etc. - Court can order examination only of that person who is suggested as being guilty of fraud in official liquidator's report
Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company's affairs in other cases - Court has no jurisdiction to appoint an Inspector to investigate company's affairs
