facts.text:
The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

The first petitioner, a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) registered under the Companies Act, 1956 having its registered office in Madhya Pradesh, was promoted by the second respondent with the objectives of carrying on the business of financing, money-lending, bills discounting, hire-purchasing, leasing, etc. The company evolved a scheme known as SFDR whereunder deposits collected from the investors were to be utilized for allotment of shares to them and also to be invested in other companies. The petitioners alleged that they collected non-interest yielding/profit-sharing investments in the form of equity and invested in equity shares. According to them, there were baseless rumours of cheating against first petitioner and, therefore, some of the members of public filed complaints against them in various police stations. It was alleged that there were serious threats to their lives and in spite of repeated requests to the SHOs to extend proper protection, the police officer was instead of protecting the petitioners, were compelling them to repay deposits collected by the company, and that some investors had attacked the office of the second petitioner and threatened him with physical abuses. Therefore the petitioners sought protection from third respondent - police officer. The third respondent, on the other hand, denied all the allegations.

On writ, the petitioners sought for relief (i) to declare the action of the respondents in not taking necessary prohibitive steps for the safety of the petitioners as illegal and unconstitutional, (ii) to declare the action of respondents in calling upon the petitioners to make payments on the basis of civil transactions between petitioners and their investors/shareholders as arbitrary, illegal and unjust and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14, 19, 20 and 21 of the Constitution of India and constitutional guarantees under articles 50 and 300A of the Constitution of India; (iii) to issue a direction to first respondent, namely, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), New Delhi, to centralize all the alleged complaints against petitioners, if any, and carry out investigation in accordance with law, (iv) to issue a consequential direction to police to take such steps as were necessary for protection of petitioners and not to harass petitioners on the back of civil complaints; and (v) to direct respondents to carry out their investigations, if any, on the complaints against petitioners strictly in accordance with the procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

The Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner to take charge of the movable and immovable properties, who after visiting various places, reported that there were no substantial money deposits in the name of the company but there were deposits in the name of the second petitioner’s wife and personal accounts. According to the report, properties were sold under Revenue Recovery Act by the bank, cold storage units were still under construction and the Indore office was seized by the police in some criminal case. A letter from a depositor informed that all the depositors belonged to New Delhi and Indore, and that they were cheated by the petitioners against whom FIR was lodged at New Delhi. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 investors who were cheated and all of them did not belong to Andhra Pradesh.

When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

The instant application had been filed by an Ex-Director of the Company-in-liquidation to recall the order dated 13-12-2019 passed by writ Court, whereby, writ Court had directed the Special Frauds Investigating Office, to recommence the investigation into the affairs of the company-in-liquidation that was started pursuant to an order dated 18-7-2008 passed by writ Court in the said company petition. As reflected in the order dated 13-12-2019, the Official Liquidator in its Report urged that the original sale deeds of the properties of the company-in-liquidation should be directed to be produced. He had further submitted that assets of the company-in-liquidation had been transferred to other companies in a clandestine manner and therefore, it was a fit case to be referred to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for investigation into the matter. The Official Liquidator had stated that the office of the Official Liquidator did not have the resources or the expertise to undertake an investigation into the diversion of funds, etc.

■

The petitioner, who was a homebuyer, claimed to have purchased a plot from ‘TCSPL’, in a real estate project named ‘Greenopolis’, which was envisioned to be developed in Gurugram, Haryana. Petitioner filed writ petition against TCSPL and its Ex-promoters / directors / management, accusing them of allegedly siphoning off approximately Rs. 1,664 crores collected from innocent homebuyers into its various shell/sister concerns. This misappropriation led to TCSPL being subjected to proceedings under the IBC before the NCLT with nearly 536 investors/claimants/homebuyers lodging their claims before the IRP.

■

While the matter was pending before the NCLT, three reports were submitted by the IRP and the Status Report, which, inter alia demonstrated as to how and in what manner the Ex promoters/directors/management of TCSPL had been siphoning off the funds.

■

The petitioner vide said petition was seeking invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of Writ Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, 1950, seeking certain directions against Registrar of Companies (RoC) and Union of India (UoI) through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for taking cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of TCSPL, as well as its shell/sister group of companies, for alleged action of manipulation of records and siphoning of funds to shell/sister companies based in Kolkata and elsewhere. Additionally, the petitioner sought reliefs in the nature of freezing the assets of such unscrupulous companies and their promoters/directors to safeguard the legal rights of the investors/claimants/homebuyers like the petitioner.

■

This, to safeguard the interest of the petitioner, as well as other similarly placed investors/claimants /homebuyers, RoC and UoI, were conjointly directed to initiate action and ensure step-wise compliance in terms of Section 206 to 210 of the Companies Act, 2013 and other analogous provisions in Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013, and thereby inspect the affairs of TCSPL and the related.

■

During the course of proceedings before Writ Court, an application was moved on behalf of the ACE Group, a renowned Real Estate Developer in Delhi and NCR for impleadment, which was allowed. Subsequently, ACE Group moved an application for the recall of the order. Prior to this, TCSPL had also moved an application to recall / modification of order.

■

The ACE Group submitted that although the order was directed at RoC and UoI to inspect the affairs of the TCSPL, they were directly affected, as the IRP had endeavoured to reclaim or repossess certain properties belonging to them, which have no nexus or connection with the TCSPL.

■

According to ACE Group, impugned order had wrongly portrayed it as a proxy of TCSPL. It was further stated that penal provisions under the Companies Act, 2013, appear to have been set in motion against the ACE Group of Companies without impleading them or issuing notice.

■

The One-Man Committee was constituted by the Court for the purpose of identification, recovery and distribution of proceeds from sale of assets of various chit fund companies to verified claimants.

■

The Enforcement Directorate was directed to extend all necessary assistance to the Committee, as and when sought, for the purpose of implementation of the various orders of this Court, particularly with respect to identification, recovery and allied matters concerning the assets of the respective companies or any issue incidental thereto.

During the CIRP, the CoC appointed Forensic Auditor to conduct a Forensic Audit and on receipt of the report, the RP filed application under section 66, read with sections 25(2), 69, 70 and other applicable sections inter alia seeking to attach the personal assets of three directors alleging that they were responsible for defrauding the creditors. Same was to be done in order to recover the total dues of Rs. 46.11 crores. By exercising power conferred on the Adjudicating Authority, the order was passed referring the matter to the Central Government for investigation through SFIO (Serious Fraud Investigation Office).

The appellant, a majority shareholder of the corporate debtor, contended that Adjudicating Authority was not conferred with power under section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 in absence of any amendment made in Schedule XI of the Code and, thus, had no jurisdiction to pass order under section 213 of the Companies Act.

The CLB had suspended the board of directors of the respondent-company by order dated 9-1-2009 and had authorized the Central Government to constitute a fresh board of the company. The Central Government had appointed six nominee directors on the board. In the meanwhile, the Central Government with a view to safeguard the interests of the company, its stakeholders and the public at large, filed instant application, ex parte seeking interim reliefs viz.; (i ) to implead ‘V’, being Chief Finance Officer as respondent No. 13; (ii) to direct the concerned respondents to disclose the bank accounts and both movable and immovable assets owned by them; and (iii) to restrain them from alienating, mortgaging, creating charge or lien or interest in those properties. In support, of the application, it was submitted that the Central Government had ordered investigation into the affairs of the company on consideration of the report of the RoC and that the Central Government might not be able to enforce the ultimate relief which might be granted under section 542, unless the concerned respondents were restrained from alienating any of their assets, thereby protecting the interests of the company and the stake-holders.

CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by the NCLT, wherein, the investors/homebuyers of 'C' including the petitioner, lodged their claims against 'C' before the resolution professional of 'C'.

However, the NCLAT on an appeal filed by the directors of 'C', passed an order setting aside the entire CIRP.

The order of NCLAT was challenged before the Supreme Court and an interim directions was passed to maintain status quo including the assets of 'C'.

The petitioner filed the instant writ petition praying for certain directions in the nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) to initiate and carry out appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for the acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds of the said company to its sister concern and freeze its assets.

Further the petitioner submitted that after raising funds from the investors/home buyers without any intention to complete the project, the ex-management of 'C' had altogether abandoned the project and despite the fact that entire information was brought to the knowledge of RoC, it was failing to perform its statutory duties to the detriment of large homebuyers and financial institutions.

The Official Liquidator had been appointed as a provisional liquidator of 'C' (in liquidation). 'C' and 'CR' had been ordered to be wound up and Court appointed Official Liquidator as the Liquidator.

The Official Liquidator, could not take possession of the registered office of the said Company (in liquidation), as the same was already sealed by the Economic Offences Wing. Crime Branch, Mumbai.

The Official Liquidator requested the Assistant Commissioner, Police, Economic Offences Wing, Crime Branch, Mumbai to handover the records/Books of Account of the Companies (in liquidation), if any, handover possession of the registered office of the company-in-liquidation i.e. 'C' (in liquidation).

The Single Judge also addressed the competence of the Special Committee to act during pendency of its extension application and the effect of the phrase “until further orders” in the order dated 12.09.2023.

On appeal:

■

The appellant and respondent no. 2 were both companies engaged in the trade of shares/securities and were registered with the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). On a complaint made by the appellant (through its Managing Director), under section 156(3) CrPC, an FIR was registered under section 420, 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). In this FIR, it was alleged that the appellant received a phone call by a person impersonating himself as their client 'B', to purchase 1 lakh shares of a company named 'APM Ltd.' After the purchase was executed, the said 'B' was called to confirm the purchase but he denied making any such call to the appellant for the above said purchase. A, an agent of the appellant company was said to have connived with the seller of the shares in question to defraud the appellant. The BSE was thus requested to stop payment to the seller of the shares.

■

Consequent to the FIR filed by appellant and the investigation it was revealed that around 72,000 shares (worth Rs. 15.90 lakhs) were sold by respondent no. 2. The charge sheet was filed against one A, who was said to have made the alleged phone call was the main accused as per the charge sheet, though respondent no.2 was revealed as the main beneficiary. Further, the charge sheet mentions that to ascertain the role of respondent no. 2, it would be necessary to arrest and interrogate main accused. Thus investigation was still underway. A meanwhile was absconding.

■

Subsequently, respondent no. 2 filed an application before Magistrate Court for the release of the money withheld by the BSE. This application was dismissed by an order dated 16-9-2016, holding that the role of respondent no. 2 was under investigation, and until investigation was finalized the release of the funds should not be allowed. Respondent no. 2 then filed a revision petition against the order dated 16-9-2016, which was also dismissed by an order dated 8-12-2016 passed by the Revisional Court.

■

While dismissing the revision petition, it was observed that the release of the funds will impact the rights of the appellant. The investigation was however, directed to be expedited. Being aggrieved by the order of the revisional court, respondent no. 2 filed a section 482 CrPC petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed this petition by impugned order and, directed the release of the sale value of the shares in favour of respondent no. 2.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

During the course of the winding-up proceedings of RPS Ltd., which was a financial company, the investigating committee found that the appellants had siphoned off the funds of RPS Ltd. and floated another company ‘A’ Ltd. The appellants were holding 81 per cent of shares in ‘A’ Ltd. and also had movable and immovable properties. On the basis of investigation report, the High Court directed the Official Liquidator to sell the shares of the appellants in ‘A’ Ltd. In the meanwhile, the High Court directed that money realised from the sale of ‘A’ Ltd.’s shares and some of the assets would be utilized exclusively for the payment to be made to the depositors of RPS Ltd. Simultaneously, the Economic Offences Wing also initiated action against RPS Ltd. under the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 1944 and attached the properties which were acquired out of the pecuniary sources that were believed to be procured from and out of the deposits collected from the depositors. The Tax Recovery Officer issued notice under section 222 to recover tax from the appellants towards capital gain out of the funds available with the Official Liquidator. On receipt of the said notice, the appellants filed applications. It was the common case of the appellants and the ITO that the capital gain tax was recoverable out of the funds available with the Official Liquidator from the sale of 81 per cent shares in ‘A’ Ltd. as per section 530(1)(a ) of the 1956 Act. But the Administrator objected to the same. The Single Judge dismissed application by holding that section 530 of the 1956 Act was not attracted for the disbursement of the sale consideration of 81 per cent of the shares of the appellants in ‘A’ Ltd.

The petitioner had purchased certain shares of third respondent-company. According to him, he had neither received any annual report nor notice of any extraordinary annual general meeting of the company since he purchased the shares of the company and further he could not get even a single rupee as return on his investment. Those facts were allegedly brought to the notice of the Registrar of Companies, but no action was taken on the matter. Therefore, the petitioner filed writ petition seeking a direction to the first respondent to appoint a competent person as investigator for investigating the affairs of the third respondent-company from 1995 onwards and to file a report in the High Court. The petitioner filed a suit for declaration, mandatory injunction and damages. During the investigations made by the CBI, in the matter of default in making payment to various investors by C Ltd., the agency registered criminal cases against directors of C Ltd. having cheated several thousands of investors, banks and financial institution through forgery, fraud and by corrupt/illegal business. Subsequently, the fourth respondent also filed an FIR against the appellant under Section 406, IPC alleging breach of trust with regard to the family jewellery belonging to the fourth respondent wherein she claimed that on 17.12.2010, the appellant changed her bank locker from a joint locker that she held with the second respondent to a locker singly held by her.

held.text:
Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

The Reserve Bank of India was directed to appoint at least three auditors with other necessary staff to carry out the inquiry and assist the Deputy Commissioner of Police in carrying out such inquiry:

Respondent No. 2 was directed, inter alia, to state on oath in an affidavit the following:—

(i) The list of their movable and immovable properties and all assets and the location thereof;

(ii) The list of their bank accounts and the particulars thereof, including the names and addresses of the banks and the amounts therein.

There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. [Para 53] On a combined reading of the law on the subject and applying it to the present context it is found, the depositors being citizens of the country were entitled to lodge complaint with regard to the non-refund of the deposits that they made with Saradha Group and police would be obliged to act upon such complaint and bring it to logical conclusion in accordance with the procedure laid down under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. In the instant case, SEBI would contend, time was still there. Hence, it would be premature for them to take further steps in this regard. The company did not have any registration either under the Chit Funds Act or under the SEBI Act and, thus, would attract appropriate penal measures under the relevant provisions of law and Reserve Bank of India would be obliged to advise the State in case their assistance would be needed. [Para 54]

Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. He prayed for appointment of investigation agency. He would be also approaching the Court for appointment of retired High Court Judge or a Supreme Court Judge to conduct the investigation.[Para 61]

The subsequent letter to CBI was rather a detailed exercise to narrate his version from setting up his empire up to the fall. He blamed several persons including some of them having political clout. In his letter, he referred to various persons from business and political circle, sports circle, some having access up to the President of India, to assure him no interference in his business by the State agencies. He requested CBI to carry out appropriate investigation. He described the said letter as "his last wish" before his death either by way of suicide or otherwise. He referred to a list of persons that we did not get from any of the parties or the State Administration. The CBI would say, they forwarded the letter to the State for action. [Para 62]

The petitioners tried to get support from the letter establishing nexus of persons attached to corridors of power involved in this scam who in exchange of illegal gratification assured him trouble free business that would warrant an independent agency to take up the cause.[Para 63]

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

What is Extraordinary/Exceptional Circumstance ?

The financial position of the respondent-company as admitted by the second respondent was that the balance sheet carried as on 10-9-2008, (a ) inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances, (b) accrued interest which was non-existent, (c) an understated liability on account of funds arranged by him, and (d) an overstated debtors position. The gap in the balance sheet had reportedly arisen on account of the inflated profits over a period of past several years. The desperate attempt of the second respondent to compensate the fictitious assets of the company by acquisition of ‘M’ miserably failed. In the words of respondent No. 11, the accounts of the company were unreliable. While considering the matters complained of on account of the massive financial fraud running into several thousands of crores of rupees, there would necessarily be need to examine the part played by the Chief Finance Officer of the company and, therefore, the proposed respondent, namely, the Chief Finance Officer, being interested in the subject-matter of the litigation, was a necessary party, without whom no order could effectively be made, in adjudicating the question of financial irregularities involved in the instant proceedings. Therefore, the Chief Finance Officer of the company was legally and directly interested in respect of the subject major controversies. The erstwhile directors and officers of the company were answerable for the whole of fraud unequivocally admitted by the second respondent. The Central Government, having satisfied with the prevailing state of affairs of the company, in exercise of powers under section 235, ordered investigation into the affairs of the company and further by virtue of section 240(1A) permitted the inspectors so appointed, to obtain information, books and papers related to MPL and MIL. Any order which might ultimately be passed against the delinquent officers, etc., under section 542 safeguarding the paramount interest of the company would be fruitful only if all their assets were maintained without any encumbrances whatsoever. The respondents, if on the other hand, were allowed to gain time to strip off their assets, there was no doubt that the company and its stakeholders would suffer irrepa-rable harm. The object was to preserve status quo, while the disputes were being adjudicated. There existed a strong prima facie case and the balance of convenience in favour of grant of the ex parte restraint order, as urged by the Central Government, to preserve the public interest at large. [Para 2] In view of the foregoing conclusions and in exercise of powers under section 403, it was deemed fit to order that (i) Chief Finance Officer ‘V’ of the company would be arrayed as respondent No. 13, to the instant proceedings; (ii) the respondents concerned should forward to the Bench Officer particulars of all their bank accounts, valuable movables and immovable properties owned in India or elsewhere outside India; (iii ) the concerned respondents should not alienate, charge, mortgage or sell any of their shares, securities and fixed assets, as the case may be, held and owned by them, without leave of the CLB, till disposal of the main petition. [Para 3]

It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that it has a panel of Chartered Accountants through whom the inspection and inquiries may be ordered. The provisions of the Act, 1956 and the Act, 2013 though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where the company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before the Tribunal, however, the same may not applicable in the case of the company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as the winding up order of the company-in-liquidation was passed by the Court much prior to the report of the Official Liquidator filed before this Court seeking investigation by the SFIO. Sections 397 and 398 fall under Chapter VI of the Companies Act, 1956 which provide the power of the tribunal for prevention of oppression and mismanagement. Where no information or explanation is so furnished, or the Registrar finds the information or explanation inadequate on his satisfaction that unsatisfactory state of affairs exists in the company and does not disclose a full and fair statement of the information required, he may, by another written notice, call on the company to produce for his inspection such further books of account, books, papers and explanations as he may require. [Para 17] Under sub-section (4) of section 206, where the Registrar is satisfied that the business of a company is being carried on for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or not in compliance with the provisions of the Act, 2013 or if the grievances of investors are not being addressed, he may call on the company to furnish any information or explanation on matters specified in the order. Sub-section (5) enables the Central Government also to direct inspection of books and papers of a company by an inspector appointed by it for the purpose. The penalty for non-compliance is also prescribed. [Para 18]

Section 207 enables the Registrar or the inspector to conduct inspection and inquiry and they are vested with all powers of the Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, while trying a suit in respect of; (a) the discovery and production of books of account; (b) summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath; (c) inspection of any books, registers and other documents of the company at any place. [Para 19]

The Registrar or inspector is mandated to submit a report in writing to the Central Government pursuant to an inquiry either under section 206 or 207, which may include a recommendation and further investigation into the affairs of the company is necessary along with reason. [Para 20]

The power to search and seizure is provided under section 209. Section 210 of the Act, 2013 empowers the Central Government, where it forms an opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company either, (a) on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208; (b) on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated; or (c) in public interest. Sub-section (2) thereof mandates the Central Government to order an investigation into the affairs of that company where an order is passed by a court or the Tribunal in any proceedings before it that affairs of a company ought to be investigated. [Para 21]

The establishment of SFIO is provided in section 211 of the Act, 2013, which also provides for its constitution by experts headed by a Director appointed by a notification by the Central Government. Section 212 provides for investigation into affairs of Company by SFIO. The procedure to be adopted by SFIO is also provided in this section. [Para 22]

Section 226 indicates that where winding up proceeding in respect of a company is pending before a Tribunal, that is to say, where winding up order has not been passed by a Tribunal, an investigation in the Chapter may be initiated, and no such investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason only of the fact that such winding up proceeding is pending. However, where a winding up order is passed by the Tribunal in a proceeding referred to in clause (c) of section 226 of the Act, 2013, the Inspector shall inform the Tribunal about the pendency of investigation proceedings before him and the Tribunal shall pass such order as it may deem fit. [Para 27]

Once the provisions of Part VII of the Act, 1956 or Chapter XX of the Act, 2013 are brought into play, then the companies become subject to provisions of winding up and orders passed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

The Official Liquidator under the Act, 1956 and the Company Liquidator under the Act, 2013 are empowered to take into custody the company's properties and are vested with wide powers in that regard. [Para 29]

Wide ranging powers have been given to the liquidator for taking custody of the company's property under section 456 of the Act, 1956. When an order is illegal, it cannot be severed by keeping the finding alone intact and setting aside that portion of the conclusion and remitting the matter to the company court to cure the defects. Likewise, it is also impossible for an appellate court to do the exercise of the company court when the Court has come to the conclusion that the order impugned is held to be an order passed against the statutory provisions. [Para 13] The company law is a special law and it provides certain inbuilt mandatory safeguards to be followed by the company court while passing orders and winding up as envisaged in the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959. The impugned order was an order against the statute and no judgment in the eye of law. [Para 16]

For the foregoing reasons, the order impugned in the instant appeal was to be set aside and the matter was to be remitted to the company court to pass orders on the petition in accordance with the statutory provisions. [Para 17]

Exchange deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company in compliance with the order passed by the Custodian. Section 3(5) lays down that the Custodian can take assistance of any other person while exercising his powers or for discharging his duties under this section and under section 4. When a fax message was sent to the Calcutta Stock Exchange for information and necessary action, the Calcutta Stock Exchange had no option but to deactivate the terminal of the petitioner-company. [Para 11] The plea taken by the petitioner-company was that K was one of the shareholders of the petitioner-company (though he resigned later on) and his holding which was raised to 97.94 per cent was subsequently brought down to 68 per cent. But the fact remained that K was practically the owner of that company; though in order to escape the clutches of law, he had resigned as one of the directors. But the fact remained that the petitioner-company was started by K in 1994 and it was a debatable question as to whether the company was established by K from the tainted money earned by him during 1-4-1991 to 6-6-1992. That matter was yet to be decided by the competent forum. But the petitioner-company rushed to file the instant writ petition and challenged the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange as well as the National and Mumbai Stock Exchanges. It was not the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was sought to be challenged but in fact what was sought to be challenged was the order passed by the Custodian. Therefore, the view taken by the Single Judge to the extent that that could not be interfered with in extraordinary writ jurisdiction was well-founded. It was a question which was yet to be decided by the Special Court as to whether all the money for establishing the petitioner-company was tainted money or the petitioner-company which had been established by K was from any other source which did not have the tinge of that tainted money. That question could not have been decided in the instant pro- ceeding. More so, by virtue of the notification dated 20-11-2001 and the public notice issued on 24-11-2001 all the properties of all the persons who were notified and that of K stood attached. The 20-11-2001 not- ification clearly said that all the properties movable or immovable or both belonging to persons/entities would stand attached by virtue of section 3(3) of the Act of 1992 and similarly in the public notification dated 24-11-2001, the same was reiterated for notice of all concerned that from the date of the aforesaid notification any property movable or imm- ovable or both belonging to the notified persons/entities would stand attached and it would only be dealt with by the Custodian in such manner as the Special Court may direct. It was also made clear in the public notice dated 24-11-2001 that the provisions of the Act of 1992 have overriding effect on all other laws and all the companies and firms were directed to take notice that the property belonging to the notified persons/entities stood attached and it was not permissible to have any transaction of any kind relating to the attached properties of the notified persons/entities except with the direction of the Special Court. It was also mentioned in the public notice that all those who had dealings with such attached properties of the notified persons/entities should intimate to the Custodian the details of such properties. Therefore, in view of those facts, the assets and properties of K were attached and if the petitioner-company sought any remedy, the remedy lay in the Special Court which alone has jurisdiction to provide remedy and that Court is held by no less than a sitting Judge of the High Court. Therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter which was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Special Court. There was no occasion for the Single Judge to have unnecessarily entered into the question whether the Calcutta Stock Exchange was a ‘State’ within the meaning of article 12 or not. In fact, that question did not directly fall for determination. In substance what the petitioner-company wanted to challenge was the basic order of the Custodian, as the Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted in terms of the direction issued by the Custodian. Therefore, it was only an incidental action, and the basic challenge was to the notification notifying K as a notified person under section 3(2) of the Act of 1992. No executing agency who has implemented the order can be held responsible. The Calcutta Stock Exchange was only an executing agency and since the said K was notified person and he floated the company in 1994, all his assets stood attached, and, therefore, it deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company preventing it from doing any trading activity in Calcutta Stock Exchange. Therefore, it was not an action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was under challenge. The Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted as per the direction given by the Custodian as executing agency and if the petitioner-company had any grievance against the order passed by the Custodian, then it had remedy under the Act of 1992

Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13]

From a plain reading of sections 542 and 543 as a whole, as it is evident that the statute itself is very clear and there is no ambiguity with regard to entitlement to filing an application under sections 542 and 543, the principle of law of casus omissus cannot be supplied by the Court in the absence of any necessity. [Para 17]

From the said finding, it would be evident that the application under sections 542 and 543 preferred by the administrator of the company-in-liquidation was not maintainable, nor the Company Judge was empowered to impose a fine in lieu of imprisonment under section 542(3). In such a background, there was no other option, but to set aside the impugned order passed by the Company Judge. [Para 18]

The impugned order of the Company Judge was to be set aside, accordingly, and the appeals were to be allowed. [Para 19]

The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Generally speaking, presumption is in favour of existence of the jurisdiction of the civil courts rather than exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil courts. Normally, the civil courts' jurisdiction has following three dimensions : (a) it must have jurisdiction regarding the subject-matter; (b) it should have pecuniary jurisdiction; and (c) it must have territorial jurisdiction to entertain the suit. [Para 30]

In regard to the function of a balance-sheet, it may be stated to be an endeavour to show the share capital, reserves (distinguishing those which are available for distribution as dividends from those reserves not regarded as so available) and the liabilities of the company at the date on which it is prepared and the manner in which the total sums represented then are distributed over several types of assets. In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Also, a balance-sheet is known as a statement of net worth assets and liabilities and it is called as 'Statement of financial position'. In the Companies Act, it is the duty of the directors of a company to see that the regular and correct account books are kept. [Para 31]

Normally, it is the duty of the directors and the management to ensure that the provisions of the Companies Act have been complied with. However, where there is contravention of a legal requirement by a company, which has a bearing on the accounts and transactions of the company, an auditor would in the normal course of his inquiry become aware of such a contravention which needs to be brought to the notice of the shareholders. In short, an auditor should, however, not merely state the facts, leaving it to be inferred that a contravention of legal requirements has taken place, but he should spell out that in his opinion a contravention of the law has taken place. Further, an auditor is the eyes and ears of the disparate shareholders' community. Moreover, the only individual who has an access to the books of account of a company, apart from the concerned company itself, is the auditor. [Para 32]

The CLB may pass such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of process of the Bench as per regulation 44 and that power is similar to the power of a civil court under section 151 of the Code. [Para 33]

As far as our country is concerned, a share is not merely a chose-in-action, it is also as per the definition of a share or a debenture under section 82 a 'movable property'. However, shares or debentures become equivalent to 'goods' as per the decision in Kunhunni Elaya Nayar v. P.N. Krishna Pattar [1942] 12 Comp. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. Moreover, it represents the interest of the holder measured for the purposes of liability and dividend by a sum of money. [Para 34]

Under the TNPID Act, there are two procedures. There are provisions which deal with the property of financial establishments like the company after an FIR is registered. There are also provisions for trial and punishment of financial establishments and persons responsible for running them under section 5 of TNPID Act. Once the charge sheet is filed under the TNPID Act, the Special Court alone will have jurisdiction to deal with the financial establishment and its properties. The charge sheet or the final report has not yet been filed in this case. [Para 18]

Under section 3 of the TNPID Act, the Government on being satisfied that the financial establishment is not likely to return the deposits or make payment of interests, may pass an order attaching the money or other properties procured in the name of the establishment or in the name of any other person from the deposits collected by the financial establishment. The Government can also transfer the property so attached to the control of the Competent Authority constituted under section 4 of TNPID Act. [Para 19]

Section 7(8) of TNPID Act also empowers the Special Court to issue directions for equitable distribution of monies attached or realized out of the sale of the properties among the investors/depositors. Such order is to be passed on an application made by the Competent Authority. [Para 21]

Having regard to the number of depositors and the huge stakes involved, it would be a mammoth task to identify the investors, identify the lands that have been purchased, value the land and realize the actual value by way of sale of properties. It would be appropriate if a committee is constituted consisting inter alia of Competent Authority under TNPID Act, representatives from the Revenue Department, representatives from the legal fraternity, representatives from the Economic Offences Wing, representatives of SEBI and a team of Chartered Accountants to carry out the task of identifying the investors, identifying the lands that have been purchased, getting the land valued and raising funds for settlement of dues of investors/depositors by actual sale of landed properties. [Para 22]

It will be open to the Committee to engage Chartered Accountants of repute, valuers, lawyers and to employ such other professional services, as the Committee might deem it necessary. The Committee shall insert an advertisement putting all concerned on notice of the constitution of the Committee under orders of the Court. The advertisement shall be published in at least two English newspapers and two Tamil newspapers having wide circulation in the State of Tamil Nadu. [Para 24]

All depositors/investors of the company should apply to the Committee with details of their investments and documents in support of their claims within the time stipulated in the advertisement. The claims shall be processed by the Committee and the list of depositors and their respective claims shall be finalised. Bogus claims can obviously be rejected. [Para 25]

The Committee shall take necessary steps to identify the properties of the company, its sister concerns, Directors and transferees, to ascertain the location, marketability and title thereto and thereafter proceed to sell the properties. The Committee may obtain the assistance of a team of experts of the revenue department and a competent legal team to perform the acts mentioned above. The committee may also constitute an accounting team to look into the bank accounts and other financial documents of the company, its Directors, its sister concerns, etc. and to ascertain whether there has been secretion of funds of the company. [Para 26]

The amounts realized from out of the sale of the properties shall be deposited in a special account opened for this purpose, which may jointly be operated by any two members of the committee nominated by the Chairperson. [Para 27]

In case the amounts realized are not sufficient to settle the claims of all depositors/investors in full, the depositors/investors shall be paid on pro rata basis in proportion with the amounts deposited by them in the company as substantiated by cogent documents. The FIR shall, however, be kept alive as the prosecution may have to continue if the amounts realized are not sufficient to pay the amounts due to all depositors/investors. [Para 28]

Since 'G' is a web of companies involved in committing fraud against public sector bank causing colossal loss to the public institution, there is every chance to believe that the persons involved in those companies can be at fault in respect to this fraud. All the companies referred in the oppression and mismanagement petition, prima facie are handwork of either Nirav Modi or Mehul Choksi. In this complexity, it is highly difficult to sniff out which company involved, which company not involved, who acted to which company. [Para 19]

Whenever any action or omission takes place in a company, though company is an independent entity equivalent to any other natural person, it will not get any momentum on its own for short of life in it, impetus will come into it only when it is driven by a natural person, so to the company, driver is a Board constituted with natural persons. Therefore, whenever company is involved in fraud, it will always point at the persons managing the affairs of the company. In this scenario, unless the persons (Directors and other key Managerial Personnel) involved are curtailed from dealing with not only the assets of the company but also the assets lying with the persons involved in committing fraud, it is next to impossible to claw back the proceeds of the fraud from the persons running the affairs of the companies. Here money being secreted out by colluding with some Bank officials, Competent Authority is conferred with powers to search and seize them; this section is nothing but to aid the same. [Para 20]

In view of this reason, when action against company/companies for getting back the money fraudulently taken out is permissible, if such money is routed to the persons managing through these companies, then it is obvious to construe that such companies have come into existence to be used as conduits to gulp down everything that comes to the company. That money is not in the books of at least companies in India. Linchpins in this fraud are not in India. Everybody knows it goes without saying that when granting consequential relief is imperative to attain the purpose of main relief, Courts can reach out to pass such reliefs as well. [Para 21]

It is the duty of Instant Court to see that innocent people are not burdened restraint order. There were no incriminating material placed as record showing that applicants were indulged or participated in anything that assisted or aided culprit indulged in fraud. Thus applicants deserves vacation of the restraint order in force. [Para 24]

Simple averment of saying that applicants working as Director in the companies which were made as Respondents in this case will not be good enough to say that applicants was also involved in the fraud played against Punjab National Bank. Power of Company Law Board to review: On behalf of ORE and Athappan, it was mainly contended that the CLB has no power to review its own order, especially, in the guise of a clarification. [Para 137]

It is fairly well-settled that the CLB does not have the power of review. It is, however, open to the CLB to exercise its inherent powers and to make such orders as may seem necessary to meet the ends of justice. The CLB has power to review and recall its orders which have been wangled through fraud or misrepresentation. [Para 141]

In its earlier order dated 13-8-2008, the CLB has recorded categorical findings:- (i) conduct of KCP having regarded CEPL's funds as though his own funds is burdensome, harsh and wrongful; (ii) movement of funds from CEPL as traced by the auditors is not supported by any approvals from the Board of CEPL. (iii) KCP had taken enormous steps in safeguarding and enhancing the value of CPL properties as well as bringing VML out of sickness thereby saving its vast extent of properties and settling all dues of workmen which is in contravention of the JVA/Articles of CEPL. (iv) KCP is accountable for not having diligently discharged its statutory duties cast on him. On those factual findings, in its order dated 13-8-2008, CLB observed that the very purpose of CEPL could not have been achieved in terms of JVA and in the light of those factual findings directed CEPL to return a sum of Rs. 75 crores and Rs.4 crores invested by ORE and Athappans respectively along with interest at 8 per cent. In the said order, the CLB also permitted KCP to utilise the money to return the said amount to ORE and Athappans and in the meanwhile directing that VML shall not alienate or sell any of its immovable properties till payment is made to ORE. The CLB also made provision that in the event of failure to make the repayment within the specified time, CEPL, CGH, KCP and VML were to duly convey the immovable properties of VML, i.e., 17.15 acres of land in favour of ORE and 7.80 acres of land in favour of Athappans. When the CLB has recorded categorical findings that CEPL neither carried out nor could accomplish its business plan in accordance with terms of JVA and directed return of sum of Rs.75 crores and Rs.4 crores, it was not justified in modifying its earlier order permitting KCP to deal with 50 per cent of the money lying with State Bank of India. [Para 142]

Given the sequence of events, if KCP is placed in position to manage CEPL, he would again try to divert the amount to innumerable subsidiary companies floated by him, the CLB was not justified in directing ORE and NA to deposit the share certificates with the Bench Officer.
