385.1 Background note385.1 Background note

The Central Government is empowered to appoint inspectors to investigate and report on the ownership of the company under certain circumstances.

385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company

An investigation into the ownership of the company may be ordered under the following circumstances :

385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own

The Central Government may, when it appears that there is good reason to do so, appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board

Where in the course of any proceedings before it, the Company Law Board declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall appoint one or more investigators and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.3 Scope of investigation385.3 Scope of investigation

While appointing inspectors, the Central Government may define the scope of investigation with regard to matters, period to which such inspection extends and limit the investigation to matters connected with particular shares or debentures.

385.4 Powers of Inspectors385.4 Powers of Inspectors

The inspectors shall have powers to examine persons on oath, inspect the books and papers. Refer para 384.9 for other provisions.

385.5 Inspector’s Report385.5 Inspector’s Report

The inspector shall forward his report to the Central Government. However, the Central Government shall not be bound to furnish the company or any other person with a copy of such report or any portion thereof, if there is a good reason for not divulging the contents thereof. In such a case, the Central Government shall require the Registrar to keep a copy of such report or parts of such report which could be divulged.

385.6 Expenses of Investigation385.6 Expenses of Investigation

The expenses of investigation shall be defrayed by the Central Government out of the moneys provided by the Parliament, unless it directs that the expenses or part thereof should be met by the applicants on whose application the investigation was ordered.

385.7 Imposition of restrictions385.7 Imposition of restrictions

Where it appears to the Company Law Board that for the purpose of investigation into ownership of the company, it is necessary to impose restrictions, it may by order direct that the shares shall be subject to the following restrictions for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the order viz.

u transfer of those shares shall be void;

u where shares are to be issued, they should not be issued and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void;

u no voting right shall be exercisable;

u no further shares shall be issued in right of those shares or in pursuance of any offer made to the holder thereof and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void ;

u except on liquidation no payment should be made for any sums due from the company on those shares, whether in respect of dividend or capital or otherwise.

385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures

Where a transfer of shares or debentures in a company has taken place and as a result thereof a change in the composition of the Board of Directors is likely to take place which would be prejudicial to the public interest, the Company Law Board may, by order, direct that—

u the voting rights in respect of those shares or debentures shall not be exercisable for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order.

u no resolution passed or action taken to effect a change in the composition of the Board of Directors before the date of the order unless it is confirmed by the Company Law Board.

u the transfer of shares in the company during such period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order, shall be void.

INVESTIGATION OF OWNERSHIP OF A COMPANY

Central Government can order investigation into ownership to decide who are really financially interested and who are in real control of the company.

Section 216(1) of Companies Act, 2013 provides that where it appears to the Central Government that there is a reason so to do, it may appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on matters relating to the company, and its membership for the purpose of determining the true persons—

(a)

who are or have been financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

(b)

who are or have been able to control or to materially influence the policy of the company.

(c)

who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company [clause (c) inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018].

Section 90 of Companies Act, 2013 substituted w.e.f. 13-6-2018 provides for declaration and register of beneficial interest. To support this provision, section 216 is amended w.e.f. 13-6-2018 to provide for investigation into beneficial ownership.

Central Government can appoint inspectors to investigate and report matters relating to company and its membership for purposes of determining the true persons who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company - section 216(1)(c) of Companies Act, 2013 inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018

Investigation if NCLT directs - Without prejudice to its powers section 216(1), the Central Government shall appoint one or more inspectors under that sub-section, if NCLT, in the course of any proceeding before it, directs by an order that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated as regards the membership of the company and other matters relating to the company, for the purposes specified in section 216(1) - Section 216(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Investigation under section 216 can be initiated or continued even if special resolution for voluntary winding up is passed or application in respect of oppression and mismanagement has been made or any winding up petition is filed or pending - section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250A of the 1956 Act].

Section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016. Of course, this section is not relevant now as provisions relating to voluntary winding up have been omitted vide Insolvency Code, 2016.

Imposition on restrictions during investigation on securities issued or to be issued by company - During investigation under section 216, NCLT can impose certain restrictions upon securities. Such restriction can be upto three years - section 222(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250(1) of the 1956 Act].

If despite such order, there is issue or transfer of securities, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 222(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Applicability of provisions to foreign company - The provisions of investigation of ownership apply to foreign company also [section 228 of Companies Act, 2013]

Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. These factors have contributed to encourage people at large to keep away from approaching the Courts on their disputes with others and swallow the losses unless compelled not for some little money alone as in the case of the common investors, or it forms the lesser evil faced by them, or it found advantageous to show as inescapable and vindicate their own position at any cost to the company or others. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

1.40 Administration of Law and Justice

Company Court

1.40-1 Primarily, Company Court is the High Court of the State in which the registered office of a given company is situated (it being reckoned by the longest time duration in the immediately preceding six months for winding up) section 10(1)(a) read with sub-section (3), or the jurisdictional District Court in the State to the extent the jurisdiction has been conferred by the Central Government in section 10(1)(b) read with sub-section (2) vide Notification GSR 663 of 29-5-1959 and GSR 1626 of 13.10.1966 conferring jurisdiction in respect of sections 89, 113, 118, 141, 144, 163, 196, 219, 234, 304, 307 and 614—generally—with some conditions. Consequent to the coming into force of Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which is yet to be notified, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) would be established (sections 10FB and 10FQ), in replacement of the Company Law Board which was in operation since 1-1-1964 introduced by the 1963 Amendment Act (section 10FA), and ousted the jurisdiction of High Court altogether so far as companies are concerned. With this, all Civil Court jurisdiction is barred with the exception of Constitutional powers of the High Court. Appeal against the orders of the Appellate Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court on questions of law. As against this, Taxation laws provide for reference of questions of law to the High Court [since shifted to the National Tax Tribunal formed recently, but halted by the ad interim order of the Bombay High Court in P.C. Joshi v. Union of India [2006] 282 ITR 39/152 Taxman 285] while jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is barred otherwise.

Puzzling mis-joinder of executive, civil and criminal adjudication

1.40-2 Under the Taxation and the economic laws enormous discretionary powers are vested in the Executive, subject to review of special Tribunals. In the same token, though companies are no Government, these are more or less equated to it in the philosophy of self-regulation subject to the purview of State-controlled Regulators of which SEBI partakes of the character both of a Corporate Regulator as well as a quasi-judicial Tribunal with powers of a Civil Court conferred on it in respect of calling for information from, undertaking inspection, conducting enquiries and audits of stock exchanges, mutual funds, other persons associated with the securities market, intermediaries and self-regulatory organizations in the securities market [section 10(i) and (3) of SEBI Act] and imposing penalties and/or fastening cease and desist orders.

Civil Court’s jurisdiction

1.40-3 Civil Court jurisdiction lies still in matters falling outside the purview of the NCLT in respect of protection of the property or prevention of invasion of related rights of the investors in shares or compensation for loss or damage like the remedies provided under section 62 (read with section 10), civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus under the Act and other civil matters connected to meetings, appointments of directors, debts and commercial disputes and torts subject to the jurisdiction being vested in the Court by Government Notification under section 10 and the Civil Procedure Code, and otherwise companies have been distanced from the Civil Court in the largest ever measure so far as shareholders are concerned.

Investor Help-lines

1.50 Ordinarily, in the absence of fraud or misfeasance in relation to the company or any breach of duty to the company alleged, there is no remedy in law against loss of investment in a company as a result of the company ceasing to be a going concern, it taken as an inherent risk in carrying on a business. In order to protect themselves from loss otherwise, the investors are expected generally to be aware of their rights with due recognition of their responsibilities to keep themselves informed about the developments in the affairs of the company where they have invested and to act, like participation in its meetings in person or by proxy individually or better still as a member in a kindred group of investors.

Investors’ rights

1.50-1 The investors’ rights in respect of shares include: (a) timely receipt of share certificates, whether on allotment or transfer/transmission, the abridged annual report each year and the notices for the general meetings and prompt refund of excess money paid with the share-application, dividend warrants, offers of rights shares on approval of the issue by the general body; (b) inspection of the statutory books and registers kept by the company as per the Act or to have copies in full or as extracts from the company; (c) to exercise the right of piloting members’ requisitioned resolutions/general meetings to force a change in the company’s course of affairs; (d) to commence civil and criminal proceedings against the company or the directors for defaults or infringements of their rights like oppression or mis-management; (e) to be the residual claimants or be liable as contributories on the company’s winding up; and (f) to prosecute the company and the directors for defaults under and offences against the Act or for the company to be wound-up by the Tribunal, if appropriate. Debenture or bond-holders’ rights are limited to receive the periodic returns and the return of the investment at maturity, to receive the debenture-trust-deed copy on request, and to seek the company’s winding up, if appropriate, before the Tribunal.

Trading and transfer of securities

1.50-2 As regards trading in and transfer of securities, the channels available to investors include :

(A) Trades - purchase and sale by private arrangement or via the trading floors established by the stock exchange where the securities are listed, the stock exchange route being free of the loss due to the risk of non-performance of delivery of securities and prompt payment of the consideration in the deals apart from getting the advantage of the market price at a little extra cost to the investors. While the securities are held, as owners they can raise finances against deposit of the securities.

(B) Grievances (to the low of which property rights of citizens in company or other securities have been summarily diluted as an administrative expedient to form part of Company Law)—the redressal channels available at present include the company and its Registrars first and foremost, besides the DCA and additionally in respect of listed companies, the SEBI/Stock Exchanges where the securities are listed, and the debenture-trustee in the case of debentures. Grievances in respect of Fixed Deposit Receipts in banks or financial institutions other than the Non-banking financial companies may be addressed to the RBI, but for company public deposits it is only the DCA to be approached.

Help-lines, minimal

1.50-3 Obviously, these help-lines are minimal at any rate for the vast domestic investors in a large country like India comprising of several States and divided controls to nurture investor confidence and encourage wider participation of common people in company securities, in the absence of well-known institutional remedies against wrongs available close at hand and at small cost, including provision of some measure of compensation against the perceived loss in investing in company shares compulsorily highlighted as a disclaimer in the offer documents, without it being an end in itself on its occurrence.

Whether it is in the nature of removal of the blot of a court conviction, increase in the number of directors on the Board beyond twelve, remuneration of directors or its increase, holding offices or places of profit by the directors and their qualification or disqualification or loans to them or loans and investments in their related companies (for return investment in the parent company’s shares as cross-holdings) or contracts or arrangements in which they are interested or sole-selling-buying agencies in which they are suspected to be interested or suspension of powers or supersession of the directors by those nominated in case of mismanagement/change in the constitution of the Board or investigation into the affairs of a company or the ownership of the shares as well as the appointment and remuneration of the managerial persons or changes in the company’s name or its situation from one State to another or unclaimed dividends, it is entirely at the highest level in the Ministry at New Delhi with the obligation of an Annual Report on its working being placed on the table of the Parliament on which there is hardly any debate. Public issues, listing and insider-trading, among others, is controlled by SEBI. Matters left to shareholders and investors include the fiduciary obligations of company promoters/directors/managerial persons, fund-raising and maintenance, dividends and bonus, political contributions, financial sickness and as contributories in winding up. The power of the general meeting is reserved for formal compliances connected with the yearly maintenance of companies and fund-raising and maintenance, with no way made visible to get back their investments robbed by the wrongdoers in control of companies. As to judicial review, as a result of the latest amendments to the Act, excepting the Supreme Court all High Court jurisdiction has been divested and transferred to the Tribunals and continued with the Criminal Courts for the levy of enhanced fines, many of them open for compounding out of court under section 621A, and imprisonment for infractions remaining only as a mere threat with the few of Government prosecutions bringing not much significant deterrence. The singular offence that is punishable with imprisonment alone extending up to five years under the Act is the application made for subscription of shares in a fictitious name by the investors, under section 68A(1).

26.26-6-4 COMPLAINTS BASED ON FIDUCIARY DUTIES - Complaints based on the fiduciary obligations per se of company promoters and directors or the managerial persons could be considered as covered by the general section 628/621 read with section 299(5) for false statements attracting imprisonment up to two years and also with fine with no limit specified. If in any return, report, certificate, balance sheet, prospectus, statement or other document required by or for the purposes of any of the provisions of the Act, any person making a statement that is false in any material particular knowingly, (not wilfully, as under section 438 of the English Act, thus widening the scope of the section) or which omits any material fact knowing it to be material, the person making the same incurs the liability to be punished under section 628. But to sustain a prosecution under the section, proof of guilty mind of knowledge of falsity is essential - P.P. Looke v. N.J. Mathew [1967] 37 Comp. Cas. 790 (Ker.).

26.26-6-4a DIRECTORS OWE THEIR DUTIES TO THE COMPANY - The directors owe their duties to the company, and it is the company or in the name of the company at the instance of shareholders where allowed or the creditors if the company’s solvency is not sufficient to pay its debts in full (for which reason the shareholders lose their power to ratify the acts of directors), that those duties can be enforced, but not at the instance of the employees as employees while the company is a going concern. A single shareholder will not succeed to bring an action for any recovery of profit made by the director, unless the action is brought as a derivative action, Prudential Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1982) 1 All ER 354 (CA). The Register of Directors’ Contracts required to be kept by the company under section 301is the open source for the shareholders as regards company contracts in which directors are interested. Filing a civil suit may be another option which is of considerable complexity, expense and time-consuming. But, such complaints are rare in our country.

CHAPTER 284

PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER *PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER*

284.1 Background note284.1 Background note

The Court/Tribunal has been vested with the power to restrain fraudulent persons from managing companies under section 203 of the Act, in a case before it by way of a disqualification order passed, where —

(a) a person is convicted of any offence in connection with the promotion, formation or management of a company, or

(b) in the course of its winding up, a person is found guilty of an offence punishable under section 542 of the Act, irrespective of his conviction, or

(c) a person is otherwise guilty while being an officer of the company of any fraud, or misfeasance in relation to the company or of any breach of duty to the company.

284.2 Disqualification order284.2 Disqualification order

The Court/Tribunal may make an order that a person convicted as above shall not, without the leave of the Court/Tribunal, be a Director or, in any other way - whether directly or indirectly be concerned or take part in the promotion, formation or management of a company, for such period not exceeding five years as may be specified in the order.

284.3 Who can apply ?284.3 Who can apply ?

Any person who is or has been a member or creditor of the company or the liquidator or Official Liquidator may apply to the Court/Tribunal for making the disqualification order by following the procedure under section 203.

284.4 Violation of disqualification order284.4 Violation of disqualification order

Acting in contravention of disqualification order entails punishment by a prison term upto two years or fine extending to fifty thousand rupees or both, for each such offence.

Illustration

In a case, winding up petitions were filed, but the winding order was not passed. At that stage a petition under section 203 seeking a disqualification order was filed. The alleged breach of duty against the company consisted of further issue of capital in violation of the provision in the Articles made by the Directors allotting the shares in the names of the Directors themselves and their relatives without first offering them proportionately to the members of the company. Held that the case called for a disqualification order against all the Directors for two years (with an alternate arrangement put in place for management of the company, meanwhile) - K.K. Roller Flour Mills (P.) Ltd. v. Utkal Flour Mills (P.) Ltd. [2005] 63 SCL 35 (Ori.).

A perusal of the notes to the statements of accounts at random bears testimony to this. Law is never of fundamental importance in company contracts, and if the law really or supposedly matters, contracting around is the answer, to give a semblance of compliance.

Need for performance and propriety audit of company contracts 1.27-5 It is a paradox that the law never dictates how companies are run although companies are the creatures of the law. Law is just a factor but not the key factor, and there is a serious limitation to law reform in company affairs, which in the main are nothing but company contracts and their working. Private individuals entering into commercial contracts as they like are, inter alia, subject to the rule of caveat emptor, or beware buyer, and it ought to stand to reason to ask why the same cannot and should not apply to company contracts brought about by the Managing Director or Chief Executive or his cronies personally, who at best is an agent for a term with nothing for him to lose under the contracts that he makes day-in-and-day-out for and on behalf of the company, and everything to gain personally for himself if he chooses with no questions to be asked by any. The legality of the arbitrary character of the shrouded company contracts under cover of the so called business secrets, and the large number of compromises and waivers of obligations under them commonly found in any company of considerable size, are prima facie questionable on grounds of propriety but in the face of the general apathy of the Boards of directors are going unchallenged, though these form the bulk of company management in its essence, and it is an impropriety of the highest degree to leave it totally free and invitingly open to misuse.

1.27-5a Question of good and proper dealing - Such questions of propriety do not fall to the lot of the statutory auditor, either. The C&AG of India has evolved a sound tradition, observed over the last five decades, of formal delegation of powers for contracting as well as the performance and propriety audit in Government companies in exercise of his power under section 619 of the Act; but, this has not caught on in general corporate audit in the country. The Company Law is sheltering the companies and company managers by not providing any deterrence in that behalf except in the case of a prospectus for public offer of securities, and expressly not conceding the locus standi to the shareholders or depositors or debt instrument holders, who stand on a different footing from sundry trade creditors, in the name of avoidance of multiplicity of litigation against the companies, on the British model, where there are other modes of deterrence like the public run scare apart from legal redress familiar to many in matters of this kind since ages unlike in India.

Shareholders’ control on company contracts negligible

1.27-6 The important question that arises here is whether this arrangement provides even a semblance of balance between private interest and public interest in the so called public company in India, where the scare of public run is operative against the banks, and it is absent in every other walk of life. In companies, the residuary control of the general body at a duly convened meeting is limited to the slated subjects and those present and voting, in line with the legislative procedure except the matters reserved to the postal ballot in which company contracts do not figure, and the shareholders’ interest is nil as to the company’s affairs as those are disallowable for want of prior notice to the company, reducing the general meetings of companies to a near farce; while the legal remedies available against erring companies as to their contracts are scanty and little known unless those accumulate and amount to ‘mismanagement’, and therefore ineffectual. External voucher audit coupled with internal audit of the so called ‘commensurate level’ and the Audit Committee of Directors introduced by section 292A of the Act, without specifying the items to be seen and leaving the whole to the august Board of Directors to decide, is no answer to it, because the businessmen would not brook it and the law-makers would not get to it, for obvious reasons. Perhaps, conditioned in our mind-set as we are by the UK model, though it is patently unsuited in the Indian milieu without re-formulation, our Company Law will never find an answer to this core question of exercise of unqualified power with non chalance; or, it should be accepted in law whether fair or unfair that there is nothing ‘public’ in a public company except it being synonymous with their right to tap the capital markets at large by public offers to fund private contracts.

Judicial review of contracting power of company management affecting public interest is another remedy

1.27-7 The trend now is towards judicial review of contractual power affecting public interest, generally : Jones v. Swansea City Council (1989) 3 All ER 162 (CA).

It was conceded that the subsidiary was a separate legal entity and not a mere emanation of the American parent and that it was selling its own goods as principal and not its parent’s goods as agent. Nevertheless, these sales were a means whereby the American company carried on its European business and it was held that the substance of the arrangement was that the American company traded in England through this agency of its subsidiary". 10.7-4a Exception is admissible either as public purpose or no real connection - A clutch of 13 foreign companies alleged to be belonging to one family trust formed into a ring to buy the shares of a company in India effectively for one man under NRI Schemes sponsored under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973, by the RBI to attract investments by NRIS, and it was urged before the Supreme Court that, in totality, the purchase of shares violated the FERA and that the corporate veils should be lifted to see the reality. It was refused on the ground that doing so would be defeating instead of promoting the aims of FERA which is a statutory enactment to attract investments into India, LIC v. Escorts Ltd. AIR 1986 SC 1370; Carrasco Investments Ltd. v. Special Director, Enforcement Directorate (1991) 2 Comp. LJ 339. A decree passed against a company cannot be satisfied by attachment and sale of properties belonging to other companies managed by the same group of directors, Punjab National Bank v. Breja Knipping Fasteners Ltd. [2001] 30 SCL 456 (Punj. & Har.).

10.7-4b Mere make-up found as a fact warrants lifting the veil - In Juggilal Kamalapat v. CIT, AIR 1969 SC 932, it was held that collusive foreclosing of managing agency agreement and assigning the managing agency by the partnership firm to a limited company in which the erstwhile partners of the firm became directors and continued as the managing agents, did not render the amount paid as compensation for loss of office as revenue expenditure in the hands of the paying managed company and a capital receipt in the hands of the dissolved partnership firm, avoiding tax at both ends, and the new company was no different from the dissolved firm, and that the Income Tax authorities were entitled to pierce the veil of the corporate entity and levy the tax.

10.7-4c Where the statute contemplates, veil can be lifted - The corporate veil may be lifted where the statute itself contemplates it or fraud or improper conduct is intended to be prevented, or a taxing statute or a beneficent statute is sought to be evaded or where associated companies are inextricably connected as to be, in reality, one concern, Life Insurance Corpn. of India v. Escorts Ltd. [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 548 (SC). The Court observed in Union of India v. Playworld Electronics (P.) Ltd. AIR 1990 SC 202, that: "The Court is entitled to lift the mask of corporate entity, if the concept is used for tax evasion, or to circumvent tax obligation, or to perpetuate fraud. However, tax-planning may be legitimate provided it is within the framework of the law. Colourable devices cannot be part of tax-planning". Various provisions of the Companies Act maintain a clear distinction between a company’s legal entity and its actions, assets, rights and liabilities and those of its shareholders’ from which it legally follows that lifting of the corporate veil is not permissible in law unless the statute clearly provides for it OR very compelling reasons exist such as prevention of fraud etc., Cotton Corpn. of India Ltd. v. G.C. Odusumathd [1999] 34 CLA 458/22 SCL 228 (Kar.).

10.7-4d Where experience claimed is experience on paper in the company’s name with the people of that experience not with it who left and made a new company, the claim is empty - With respect to experience to be reckoned for a tender and company mergers in the line, the Supreme Court observed that experience is not experience simply on paper in the name of a given company for the required duration when it has no experienced persons with it in order to ignore the new company having on its rolls the persons experienced in the field, in New Horizons Ltd. v. Union of India [1997] 89 Comp. Cas. 849/[1998] 15 SCL 148 (SC).

10.7-4e Illegal activities warrant lifting the veil - Where it is found that the corporate character has been used for committing illegalities and for defrauding people, corporate veil can be lifted with a view to rendering full justice to the affected parties, Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction (P.) Ltd. [1996] 4 Comp. LJ 233 (SC).

10.7-4f On a speculative plea, veil cannot be lifted - The doctrine of lifting of corporate veil cannot be applied to a plaintiff who is not a shareholder of a company but claims that the real holder will emerge on its lifting.

6.13

Where the investors in a private limited company are fictitious entities or untraceable, can the Department invoke confiscation proceedings under benami Act (PBPT Act, 1988) instead of the 1st proviso (2nd proviso w.e.f. AY 2023-24) to section 68?

In Macro Entertainment (P) Ltd. v. Union of India [2017] 87 taxmann.com 360 (Calcutta), the Initiating Officer (IO) issued a show cause notice u/s 24(1) of the PBPT Act which inter alia read as under:

"Material on record, marked as Annexure V, reveal that the entities which provided the consideration are either fictitious or non-traceable. It is evident from the above facts and circumstances that the consideration related to the transactions of the property in concern is provided by another person and it is held for the future benefit of another person whose identity is not known.

The above conditions satisfy the definition of the Benami transaction u/s 2(9) of the PBPT Act, 1988. Thus I have reason to believe and I am satisfied that the property in the form of Flat having details discussed above, is a Benami property as per section 2(8) of the PBPT Act, 1988."

The notice under Section 24(1) was answered by the Writ Petitioner/Company. The Company denied that the provisions of the 1988 Act are at all applicable to the facts of the present case. The Company took the stand that, if at all, the IO has jurisdiction only to inquire under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act (for short the IT Act). The reply to the Section 24(1) notice (supra) was finally considered by the IO vide his order under Section 24(4) of the 1988 Act. The IO, inter alia, concluded that both the paper and the fund trails connecting to the purchase of the scheduled property in issue, inter alia, point to fictitious/non-transparent/non-visible entities. The IO found, on the basis of the available materials, that the funds utilised in the name of the Company to purchase the property in issue belonged to person/persons whose identities have not been disclosed. The usufructs of the purchase, although ostensibly in the name of the Company, may be ultimately beneficial to the non-transparent/Fictitious/non-visible entities behind the suspected benami purchase. Therefore, the IO ordered that the provisional attachment under section 24(3) shall continue till the Adjudicating Authority (for short AA) further adjudicates under section 24(3) of the 1988 Act.

The company filed a writ petition challenging the initiation of proceedings by IO under section 24(1) and attachment of property under section 24(4) and reference to Adjudicating Authority. The company contended that, in view of the decision reported in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 at Paragraph 7 thereof, the question of fictitious entities behind the fund alleged to have been utilised by the Company for the purchase of the property in issue would not be attracted in law since, such fictitious entities are not referable to the shareholders of the Company, who carry no fiduciary interest connected to the property of the Company. The law as elucidated in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 (supra), inter alia, permits the shareholders to only participate in the profits of the Company in the form of dividends without being required to exercise any participatory involvement in its immovable assets. Therefore, the fundamentals of the proceeding initiated by the IO under section 24(1) and 24(4) are misconceived. The Respondents/Revenue contended that the profile of the investments made by the Company as evident from the facts collected by the IO connected to the purchase of the scheduled property traces its source to funds from fictitious entities which are required to be identified. On the basis of the materials available to the IO, the Company is believed to be acting as the benamidar, or, apropo the current lingo in vogue of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), Government of India, a shell or "dabba" company of investors at large.

Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective Investment Scheme -Investigation into - Petitioners, who were shareholders of respondent-company, filed petition stating that investment made by investors in pursuance of certain scheme floated by company promising 1025 per cent return was unsafe and amount collected by company had disappeared from company - They prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out - Whether even in absence of statutory provision, since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing aforesaid corporate veil which might amount to criminal offence appropriate directions could be issued by court to search and seize property of company - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent-company had floated an investment scheme promising high return on investment. It was called 'Project Grapes' and the return mentioned in the brochure was 1025 per cent. On the basis of said scheme the company collected huge amount from public and its shareholders. The petitioners, who were shareholder of the company, filed petition stating that the investment of shareholders was totally unsafe in such company and the amount collected by the company had disappeared and, therefore, prayed that an investigation was required to be carried out.

HELD: There is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that nationalised banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

Prima facie, it appeared that respondents No. 1 and 2 and such other companies which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, were committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under criminal law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 the Court could issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but "for any other purpose", and 'any othe r purpose' would include such public interest purpose.

Considering all the facts disclosed from the material on record and taking into consideration the submissions, for combating exploitation and to retrieve hard-earned money and/or life savings of innumerable investors the Court passed order directing an enquiry, freezing of accounts of respondent-companies and attachment of their properties and assets.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

The investors who had invested their money in the appellant-company, namely, ’IMFB’ Ltd. filed company petitions for its winding-up on account of its failure to repay the deposited amount in accordance with fixed schedule. The Company Judge, finding it to be a case of cheating and misappropriation of public funds with evil designs, allowed the petitions and ordered for winding-up of the appellant-company under section 433(e). The Official Liquidator was appointed and he was directed to exercise power under section 457, with authority to take into custody all movable and immovable properties of the appellant-company. He was further directed to auction properties of one of the sister concern of the appellant-company, i.e., ’IFCL’, also on ground that properties of said company were in reality properties belonging to the appellant-company.

Against aforesaid order, two sets of appeals were filed. First set of appeals was filed by the appellant-company wherein the order of its winding-up was challenged on various grounds. Second set of appeals was filed by the ’IFCL’ Ltd. on ground that there was no order of winding-up against it nor it was impleaded as a party in the company petitions and, therefore, even if the appellant-company was to be wound-up under the orders of the Court, no assets or properties of ’IFCL’ Ltd. could be taken possession of or could be put to auction.

On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

(xiii)

According to the Report of the Registrar of Companies, there was fraudulent/unlawful business carried on by the petitioner/CSITA and its management, which shall be unearthed only by proper enquiry and investigation by the SFIO.

Thus, according to the respondents 7 and 8, there is an urgent need to regulate the affairs of the company so as to ensure transparency and accountability. [Para 39]

The aforesaid allegations, in the opinion of this Court, cannot be slightly brushed aside as the same are heinous in nature. There cannot be any smoke without fire. While the culture of secrecy should be broken and a culture of accountability and transparency be practised, the culture of questioning is also a desirable element. Also, there cannot be any difference of opinion by any of the parties that the Central Government can very well invoke section 212(1)(c), i.e. in the public interest and order investigation into the affairs of the petitioner company. This Court has power to suo motu order investigation by SFIO. At this juncture, it is to be noted that there is no Civil Suit or Company Petition pending touching the issue involved herein. It is an admitted fact that the petitioner is now, available with all the impugned proceedings including the report of the Registrar of Companies. Their grievance is that the Central Government did not follow the relevant provisions as mandated under the Companies Act and they did not form an opinion, before ordering investigation by SFIO. It is also significant to point out that the petitioner stated in the affidavit filed in support of the writ petition in WP No. 25236 of 2018 that they are always ready and willing to face any enquiry conducted in accordance with law, besides the counsel for the petitioner during the course of argument, fairly submitted that the petitioner is inclined to co-operate with any kind of investigation to be done by the official respondents. [Para 40]

A repeated argument was made on the side of the respondents that there are sufficient materials available on record to order investigation into the affairs of the petitioner by SFIO. Even as per the statute as well as suo motu power, this Court can order such investigation. However, this Court is not inclined to do so, as it is not sitting in appeal over the decision of the Central Government in ordering investigation into the affairs of the company under section 212(1)(a) and (c) of the Act and scope of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, with regard to judicial review, is limited to the examination of decision making process and not the decision. [Para 41]

HEADNOTE: Section 10 of the Companies Act, 1956, read with Order XXXIX, rule 4 and Order XLIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Court - Jurisdiction of - Case of revision petitioners was that first respondent-company had filed Form II and Form FCGPR with Reserve Bank of India along with certificates issued by statutory auditor of company and Company Secretary stating that it had allotted certain shares to first revision petitioner - Subsequently, it was found that to deprive revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to first revision petitioner - First respondent also filed a suit before civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to first revision petitioner - Revision petitioners filed revision petition under article 227 of Constitution for setting aside said interim order on grounds that trial court had no jurisdiction to decide issue as same issue was pending before CLB and that order of trial court granting interim injunction was non-speaking one - Whether revision petitioners could not invoke jurisdiction of High Court under article 227, since they had two concurrent remedies, namely, to get order of trial court varied, vacated or discharged as per order XXXIX, rule 4 of Code and to file an appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(r) of Code - Held, yes

FACT: The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

HELD: The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Mr. Dada, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that, apart from the aforesaid facts, in the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has specifically held that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegali- ties or to defraud people. He prayed that immediate action be taken against the Directors who have siphoned off large amounts of investors under the guise of corporate veil.

7. Prima facie, it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life- long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister-companies or firms of the Directors or their relatives

8. In the case of Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd (supra ), the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose. The Court has also considered the concept of corporate entity and held that where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. After discussing other authorities, the Court has observed that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegal- ities or to defraud people and held as follows:

"Where, therefore, the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the corporate character and will look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to enable it to pass appropriate orders to do justice between the parties concerned. The fact that Tejwant Singh and members of his family have created several corporate bodies does not prevent this Court from treating all of them as one entity belonging to and controlled by Tejwant Singh and family if it is found that these corporate bodies are merely cloaks behind which lurks Tejwant Singh and/or members of his family and that the device of incorporation was really a ploy adopted for committing illegalities and/or to defraud people."

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appro-priate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Court has also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity and thereafter passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company in the aforesaid case.

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. [Para 53] On a combined reading of the law on the subject and applying it to the present context it is found, the depositors being citizens of the country were entitled to lodge complaint with regard to the non-refund of the deposits that they made with Saradha Group and police would be obliged to act upon such complaint and bring it to logical conclusion in accordance with the procedure laid down under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. In the instant case, SEBI would contend, time was still there. Hence, it would be premature for them to take further steps in this regard. The company did not have any registration either under the Chit Funds Act or under the SEBI Act and, thus, would attract appropriate penal measures under the relevant provisions of law and Reserve Bank of India would be obliged to advise the State in case their assistance would be needed. [Para 54]

Sudipta's Letter to SEBI on 1-4-2013 and CBI on 6-4-2013

Sudipta offered explanation to SEBI pleading innocence. According to him, the fall of the group was a result of wrong business decision and recession in the market. He prayed for appointment of investigation agency. He would be also approaching the Court for appointment of retired High Court Judge or a Supreme Court Judge to conduct the investigation.[Para 61]

The subsequent letter to CBI was rather a detailed exercise to narrate his version from setting up his empire up to the fall. He blamed several persons including some of them having political clout. In his letter, he referred to various persons from business and political circle, sports circle, some having access up to the President of India, to assure him no interference in his business by the State agencies. He requested CBI to carry out appropriate investigation. He described the said letter as "his last wish" before his death either by way of suicide or otherwise. He referred to a list of persons that we did not get from any of the parties or the State Administration. The CBI would say, they forwarded the letter to the State for action. [Para 62]

The petitioners tried to get support from the letter establishing nexus of persons attached to corridors of power involved in this scam who in exchange of illegal gratification assured him trouble free business that would warrant an independent agency to take up the cause.[Para 63]

Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

View in the Present Context

The Courts would definitely have power to direct CBI to conduct the investigation coupled with a direction upon the State authorities to co-operate with the CBI. However, the Court should be slow in exercising such power that could only be used in an extraordinary/exceptional circumstance. [Para 67]

FACT: The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. SEBI received several complaints from investors of the respondent-company to the effect that the cheques issued by the company had been dishonoured due to insufficient funds in the bank account of the respondent-company, that the office of the respondent- company had become non-functional, that directors of the respondent-company had gone defaulter and had more or less gone underground and that the funds received by the respondent had been diverted to the group companies. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. It sought the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investors’ moneys from being filtered away.

HELD: Prima facie it appears that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. Further, in agriculture productions, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country, where, otherwise, the farmers of this country would have become multi-millionaires by this time. It appears that, because of this empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company’s moneys are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

As held in DDA v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401 where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. The concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people. Absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court while acting under article 142/226 from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. In India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity. In the aforesaid case, the Court passed an appropriate order attaching certain properties of the Directors of the company.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors are being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but ‘for any other purpose’, and ‘any other purpose’ would include such public interest purpose.

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13] From a plain reading of sections 542 and 543 as a whole, as it is evident that the statute itself is very clear and there is no ambiguity with regard to entitlement to filing an application under sections 542 and 543, the principle of law of casus omissus cannot be supplied by the Court in the absence of any necessity. [Para 17]

From the said finding, it would be evident that the application under sections 542 and 543 preferred by the administrator of the company-in-liquidation was not maintainable, nor the Company Judge was empowered to impose a fine in lieu of imprisonment under section 542(3). In such a background, there was no other option, but to set aside the impugned order passed by the Company Judge. [Para 18]

The impugned order of the Company Judge was to be set aside, accordingly, and the appeals were to be allowed. [Para 19]

A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.
