Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Whether provisions of 1956 Act and 2013 Act though, do not prohibit investigation to be initiated where company has passed a special resolution for voluntary winding up or where other proceeding for winding of a company are pending before Tribunal, however, same may not applicable in case of company-in-liquidation, inasmuch as winding up order of company-in-liquidation is passed much prior to report of Official Liquidator filed before Court seeking investigation by SFIO - Held, yes [Para 38]  Section 210 of the Companies Act, 2013/Section 235 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation - Into affairs of company - Respondent company was ordered to be wound up and Official Liquidator (OL) took charge of assets and affairs of company - OL filed an application seeking an order for conducting an investigation into affairs of company-in-liquidation by SFIO alleging web of intrigue employed by company in-Liquidation and other group companies in defrauding investors and diversion of funds of company - It was also alleged that balance sheets and details of group companies were not furnished by ex-directors despite being asked to do so - Further, investigation was required into diversion of funds of company-in-liquidation for which expertise was not available with Official Liquidator - Said application was allowed by Writ Court - It was noted that balance sheet, other books of account and documents of Company-in-Liquidation were in possession of OL - All properties and effects of companies were deemed to be in custody of Court/Tribunal from date of order for winding up of company - Further, there was no evidence of any fraud conducted by Company or its ex-director that would merit referring matter to SFIO - As a matter of fact, allegation against company-in-liquidation regarding a web of intrigue employed by company could have been substantiated by specific references to entries made in balance sheet and other books of account of company-in-liquidation, which had not been done - To insinuate that office of OL did not have capacity or ability to detect diversion of funds, was not acceptable given fact that a panel of chartered accountant was admittedly available to assist OL in discharge of its duties - Whether under facts and circumstances of case, instant application to recall order by writ Court directing SFIO to commence investigation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 47]

On perusal of the records, particularly the copy of sale deeds filed by petitioner, it is found that though land was purchased in the name of ASBPL, the respondent no. 7 – company but there is no record evidencing that the amount for purchasing these land parcels were paid from the account of the company. Petitioner merely levelled an allegation that the money for land purchased by respondents in their names was paid from the company’s account but did not produce any proof of the same. The records could not get any evidence which suggest that the payment for purchase of these parcels of land was made by 1st respondent company. Hence, the allegation levels by the petitioner is not tenable because of lack of any evidence corroborating the allegation levelled by petitioner. It is further held that respondent''s contention that petition is barred by limitation is not tenable as the petitioner came to know about these activities in 2016 and petition was filed in the year 2018. It is a settled law that in the case of fraud the limitation starts from the date of knowledge of the fraud. Hence, the petition is well within the limitation. [Para 25]

This forensic audit report was taken on record as an evidentiary document as it is well settled law that a Forensic Audit Report serves as an evidentiary document and cannot, by itself, be treated as conclusive proof of any alleged misconduct or irregularity. In the light of this, the findings of the forensic audit are being examined in conjunction with the submissions made by the parties and the documentary evidence placed on record to determine their relevance in the present matter. Inspector’s Report 25.7-15 The Inspector may, and if so directed by the Central Government shall, make interim reports to it, and a final report on conclusion of the investigation; and such reports shall be admissible as evidence of the opinion of the Inspectors in any legal proceeding on any matter contained in them. It is not obligatory on the Central Government to prescribe the manner of making the inspector’s report or fix the time-limit of its submission, New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Finance (1966) 36 Comp. Cas. 512 (Cal.).

25.7-15a Duty of Central Government to send copy of report to company - It is the duty of the Central Government to forward a copy of the final report to the company investigated as well as the applicants under section 235 (2) if the Inspectors were appointed at their instance, or, to the Court/Tribunal, and may also cause it to be published, or copies supplied to any member or creditor of the company or the entities dealt in the report. DCA publishes such reports only selectively in public interest as the report is a privileged document within the meaning of sections 123 and 124 of the Indian Evidence Act, Swadeshi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Swadeshi Polytex (1982) 52 Comp. Cas. 483 (All).

25.7-16 Prosecution or winding up and proceedings for recovery of damages or property [Sections 242 & 243/244]

25.7-16a Prosecution - If it appears from the report, whether interim or final, to the Central Government that any person has been guilty of any offence attaching criminal liability, it may launch prosecution under section 242 against such person, and in that event, it becomes the duty of all officers, employees and agents of the company/other body corporate [other than the accused and as defined in section 240(6)] to give all assistance to the Central Government. Section 242 does not offend against Article 20(3) or Article 14 of the Constitution, Raja Narayan Bansilal v. Maneck Phiroz Mistry (1960) 30 Comp. Cas. 644 (SC), and section 242 does not divest the jurisdiction of a police officer under section 154, 156 or 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, M. Vaidyanathan v. Sub-Divisional Magistrate (1957) 27 Comp. Cas. 97 (Mad.); section 242 does not require a hearing to be given to the company before launch of prosecution, Titagarh Paper Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1986) 59 Comp. Cas. 94 (Cal.).

25.7-16b Act does not exclude CrPC - There is nothing in the Companies Act to exclude the Code of Criminal Procedure and the police in respect of cognizable offences under the Indian Penal Code committed in relation to the company’s affairs, Indian Express (Madurai) (P.) Ltd. v. Chief Presidency Magistrate (1974) 44 Comp. Cas. 106 (Mad.)

25.7-16c Winding up of the company - If from the Inspector’s report it appears to the Central Government that it is expedient to wind up the company or body corporate—if it is liable to be wound up under the Act—by reason of (a) the existence of circumstances that the company’s business was being conducted with intent to defraud the members/creditors or others or for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose or in a manner oppressive of any of its members, or if the company was formed for any fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or (b ) the persons connected with its formation or management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or its members, the Central Government may cause a petition/application to be filed before the Tribunal for winding up on the ground that it is just and equitable or for an order under section 397/398 regarding oppression and mismanagement or for both. Under section 203, the persons found to be fraudulent may be restrained from being a director, promoter or manager of a company up to five years, by the Tribunal. However, the privileged communications or information in the possession of legal advisors and bankers, though they may be related to the matters covered by the investigation, are immune from disclosure, section 251.

25.7-16-1 RECOVERY OF DAMAGES OR PROPERTY [SECTION 244] - If warranted in public interest in the opinion of the Central Government on perusal of the Inspector’s report, that any proceedings should be initiated for the recovery of damages or property due to any fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct in connection with the promotion or management of the affairs of the company or body corporate investigated, the Central Government may itself bring the proceedings for the purpose.

Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether since no right or interest or title can ever pass in favour of beneficiary of fraud and further, no action can be maintained which is founded in fraud, decree passed by Lok Adalat pursuant to a compromise entered into by and between parties therein in civil suit on file of Additional District Judge was to be declared as a nullity - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

The details of the outstandings from the group companies as also the details of the investments were available. It was seen that the company Judge had directed almost a detailed questionnaire and sought the information which was extremely relevant and which would give the complete picture regarding the financial status, etc., of the company. The information sought also appeared to be extremely relevant in coming to the conclusion as to whether the transactions were of bona fide nature or not. There was also a second affidavit filed on record before the order of the Court dated 17-8-2000 seeking further information and even in this affidavit, the financial scenario of the company and its dealings generally were highlighted. In fact, from a reading of those affidavits, it was clear that the company had access to all that was filed before the Court including the petitions. The Single Judge had painstakingly and studiously gone into the whole financial aspects giving a thorough picture of the financial status of the appellant-company itself as also vis-a-vis the other companies floated by it. The Judge had also taken stock of the various transactions with reference to the figures involved in those transactions. It was true that the Judge had made a reference to that report. However, he was completely convinced that there was no necessity of supplying the copy of every document on which the RBI had relied in support of its petitions. The company had a complete idea as to what was the stand of the RBI and what were the precise grounds on which the RBI was moving against it. The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator.

The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

On the basis of the earlier order of the Court the properties of the directors of Respondent No. 1 were attached. II Section 237 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases Before an investigation can be ordered by Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244 Delhi Flour Mills Co. Ltd., In re [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 33 (Delhi) The nature of an investigation to be ordered depends very much on the power of the Central Government which would be exercised if the Court so orders. For instance, the consequences of an order directing investigation have to be seen from the various provisions which govern such questions. Section 241 deals with the report of the Inspector and sections 242, 243 and 244 deal with what is to be done once a report has been made. Under section 242, a prosecution can be ordered. Under section 243, an application for winding up of the company on a petition under sections 397 and 398 can be instituted. Under section 244, proceedings for recovery of damages or property can be instituted. The result of an investigation can thus result either in prosecution or an application under sections 397 and 398 or a suit for recovery of damages or any property, which has been misapplied on account of misfeasance or mismanagement. Therefore, before an investigation can be ordered by the Court, there seems to be some sort of material required, which would result in proceedings being taken in the manner prescribed by section 242, 243 or 244. It is unnecessary to order an investigation merely because a shareholder feels aggrieved at the manner in which the company’s business is going on.

VII Section 11 Special Courts (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Discharge of liabilities Third person coming into possession of properties of notified parties under illegal agreements, cannot be allowed to retain them A.K. Menon v. Fairgrowth Financial Services Ltd. [1994] 81 Comp. Cas. 508 (Bom.) (Special Court) In case of statutory attachments which requires distribution of property it is the Special Court which has to recover the properties for the purposes of effective distribution under section 11(2) of the Act. One of the main objects of the Act being to recover large amounts of public money which have gone into private pockets and there being statutory attachment of properties of notified parties, such statutory attachments would operate even if the properties are in the hands of a third party pursuant to an illegal contract. After attachment, such properties can only be dealt with under the directions of the instant court. All such property must, therefore, be available for distribution under section 11(2). It, thus, cannot be argued that even after a statutory attachment, the third party must be allowed to deal with the properties as the notified party will not be assisted by the Court. The Court will not be assisting notified parties.The Court is safeguarding properties purchased from public monies from further alienation and ensuring that they are available for distribution under section 11. The question of applying the principle of pari delicto to such cases does not arise at all. To accept such an argument would amount to meaning that if an agreement is legal, then the Special Court can recover attached properties, but if an agreement is illegal, the Special Court must allow a transfer to take place. It can hardly be said that the third person who has come into possession of properties of notified parties, under illegal agreements, must be allowed to retain them. Such an argument cannot be accepted.

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29] Generally speaking, presumption is in favour of existence of the jurisdiction of the civil courts rather than exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil courts. Normally, the civil courts' jurisdiction has following three dimensions : (a) it must have jurisdiction regarding the subject-matter; (b) it should have pecuniary jurisdiction; and (c) it must have territorial jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In regard to the function of a balance-sheet, it may be stated to be an endeavour to show the share capital, reserves (distinguishing those which are available for distribution as dividends from those reserves not regarded as so available) and the liabilities of the company at the date on which it is prepared and the manner in which the total sums represented then are distributed over several types of assets. In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Also, a balance-sheet is known as a statement of net worth assets and liabilities and it is called as 'Statement of financial position'. In the Companies Act, it is the duty of the directors of a company to see that the regular and correct account books are kept. [Para 31]

Normally, it is the duty of the directors and the management to ensure that the provisions of the Companies Act have been complied with. However, where there is contravention of a legal requirement by a company, which has a bearing on the accounts and transactions of the company, an auditor would in the normal course of his inquiry become aware of such a contravention which needs to be brought to the notice of the shareholders. In short, an auditor should, however, not merely state the facts, leaving it to be inferred that a contravention of legal requirements has taken place, but he should spell out that in his opinion a contravention of the law has taken place. Further, an auditor is the eyes and ears of the disparate shareholders' community. As far as our country is concerned, a share is not merely a chose-in-action, it is also as per the definition of a share or a debenture under section 82 a 'movable property'. However, shares or debentures become equivalent to 'goods' as per the decision in Kunhunni Elaya Nayar v. P.N. Krishna Pattar [1942] 12 Comp. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. Moreover, it represents the interest of the holder measured for the purposes of liability and dividend by a sum of money. [Para 34]

1.40-9 Court’s Jurisdiction 1.40-9a Court & powers - Section 2(11) only defines ‘the court’ but not its powers, and where no notification has been issued by the Central Government under section 10(2) conferring the power on the District Court, ‘the court’ is the High Court, and in all cases there should be a provision in the Act for adjudication by ‘the court’, as may be seen in section 237(a), 630 or 633 and where it is not so specified it is not ‘the court’ as defined in section 2(11) that has the jurisdiction but it is the court having the jurisdiction under the general law, Inter Sales v. Reliance Industries Ltd. [2000] 26 SCL 355 (Cal.). The civil court’s jurisdiction with regard to a dispute of a civil nature is extensive in terms of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure unless barred by the statute either expressly or by implication. Even when the jurisdiction is specifically barred, if the provision so barring is not notified to have come into effect or after that the Tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure, the Civil Court’s jurisdiction to entertain the dispute of such nature is not barred. In other words, where there is no adequate and efficacious remedy available under the Act with regard to the dispute raised in the plaint, the Civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the dispute: Vijay Kumar Gupta v. Ram Naresh Singh [2004] 52 SCL 60 (Pat.). In any case, the Jurisdiction of the Civil Court is not barred by sections 9 and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure: Dwaraka Prasad Agarwal v. Ramesh Chandra Agarwala [2003] 117 Comp. Cas. 1/49 SCL 25 (SC).

1.40-9b Powers of Court - The powers of ‘the court’ as defined in section 2(11) of the Act, whether it is the High Court or the District Court, extend to adjudicate on the rights and obligations arising under the Act but not designed to function as common law courts in respect of every grievance arising in relation to a company. When the Law has no provision specifying the court’s jurisdiction regarding forfeiture of shares provided as a covenant in the company’s articles, the jurisdiction of the common law court is not ousted: Tej Prakash S. Dangi v. Coramandal Pharmaceuticals Ltd. [2002] 37 SCL 287 (AP). A challenge against the notice pursuant to section 283(1)(f) of the Act issued to a director for the non-payment of calls for over six months having the potential of not only to forfeit his shares but also cause the vacation of his office can be entertained by the Company Court K. Venkat Rao v. Rockwool (India) Ltd. [2002] 35 SCL 347 (AP) (FB).

1.40-9c Duplicate shares and provisions of Act - In regard to a dispute relating to the issue of duplicate shares, the Act provided no machinery for adjudication, and therefore it was held that the jurisdiction vested by section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code on the civil court was not ousted: Inter Sales v. Reliance Industries Ltd. [2000] 26 SCL 355 (Cal.). The allotment of shares was challenged by some members in the civil court on which the court directed the company to maintain status quo, but the company registered transfer of the shares. On the question of jurisdiction to adjudicate whether such transfer to the appellant was in contravention of the court’s interim order of injunction, it was held that it was a matter to be decided by the same civil court in the proceedings pending before it, and it could not be decided in an alien proceedings before the Company Court : National Organic Chemical Industries Ltd. v. Miheer H. Mafatlal [2004] 121 Comp. Cas. 519/54 SCL 96 (SC).

HELD: Under sub-article (2) of article 226, the power conferred on the High Court to issue directions, orders or writs can be exercised by the Court in relation to territories within which the cause of action wholly or in part arises for the exercise of such powers. If cause of action or part of cause of action has not arisen or the person fails to demonstrate such cause of action, as having arisen within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court, issue of any writ or direction would be without jurisdiction. [Para 14]

As per clause (f) of section 45-I of the RBI Act, the first petitioner was a NBFC because it received deposits under a scheme or arrangement and admittedly obtained licence under the provisions of that Act. Further, under section 45QA thereof, the first petitioner was under obligation to repay every deposit accepted by it. If the deposit was not repaid, the aggrieved party could file application before the CLB which might direct the NBFC to make payment of such deposit. Any order passed by the CLB was appealable order before the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the company had its registered office. Thus, the High Court of Andhra Pradesh was not a Court to which an appeal would lie under section 10F of the Companies Act. [Para 19]

The counter-affidavit filed by the third respondent and the letters addressed by depositors as well as Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, would show that no cause of action whatsoever arose in the State of Andhra Pradesh, much less in Hyderabad. [Para 20]

It was also reasonable to infer that petitioners having failed to obtain necessary orders of bail or otherwise, had approached the Court and chose to file the writ petition seeking the relief the granting of which would pre-empt any authority in the country to investigate further into the acts of malfeasance and misfeasance and deny justice to the depositors. The company court directed the third respondent (APSFC) to stay outside the winding up proceedings and proceed against the properties belonging to the company-in-liquidation only. If the property which did not belong to the company and belonged to the third parties like the petitioner, the company court would not exercise any power to grant permission to APSFC to proceed against the properties belonging to the third parties. If the third respondent seized the property which did not belong to the company, then the petitioner could take appropriate proceedings against APSFC for release of such property which did not form part of the assets of the company. But the Court would not direct the APSFC or the official liquidator to release the seized property which did not belong to the company. With regard to the amounts invested by the petitioner in the company in liquidation, his position would be like that of an unsecured creditor and as and when the properties of the company in liquidation were sold, he could submit his claim and establish his claim before the Official Liquidator like an unsecured creditor. But at this stage, the court could not order for refund of the amount alleged to have been invested by the petitioner. Similarly, an amount of Rs. 2 lakhs paid by the petitioner to the second and third respondents each as ’upfront’ amount could not also be directed to be released, as the same was also paid on behalf of the company in liquidation. Admittedly, the petitioner claimed that the property belonged to him and the same was not the property of the company and he brought in the said machinery pursuant to the interim orders passed by the BIFR and it was open for the petitioner to approach the BIFR for appropriate orders for the return of the machinery or any money invested by him pursuant to the interim orders granted by the BIFR, and the petitioner was also at liberty to approach the BIFR for seeking appropriate relief.

The powers of competent authority appointed under the MPID Act and the MPID Court does not supersede or prevail upon the powers of the Official Liquidator or of the Company Court under the provisions of the Companies Act. MPID Act is totally silent on the aspect relating to the winding up and thus if the financial establishment as defined under the provisions of the MPID Act is in winding up, then the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 would apply to such financial establishment; the MPID Act cannot take away the powers under the Companies Act. The provisions of the MPID Act and the Companies Act will have to be construed harmoniously by holding that on winding up of such companies which are financial establishment as defined under the provisions of the MPID Act, assets of such wound up companies would vest in the Official Liquidator and all the creditors including the depositors/investors can lodge their claims before the Official Liquidator. The MPID Act does not contemplate a situation of winding up of the financial establishment and for adjudication of the claims of other creditors and distribution of dividend to those creditors. Section 5(1)(d) of the WBPIDFE Act provides that where the State Government is satisfied that any financial establishment committing a default in repayment of deposit fraudulently, has transferred any of the property otherwise then in good faith and for consideration, it may in order to protect the interest of the depositors of such financial establishment by an order to be published in official gazette and recording reasons in writing attach the money or other property acquired either in the name of such financial establishment or in the name of any other person on behalf of such financial establishment. Sub-section (5) of section 5 of the WBPIDFE Act provides that the Competent Authority may make an application to Special Court or Designated Court for adjudicating any issue or subject matter pertaining to money or property or assets belonging to or ostensibly belonging to a financial establishment or any person mentioned in the order under sub-section (1) situated within the territorial jurisdiction of the Designated Court may be, for passing appropriate orders to give effect to the provisions. [Para 28]

Section 14 of the WBPIDFE Act provides the powers of Designated Court regarding attachment. Section 14(1) provides that upon receipt of an application under sub-section (4) of section 5, the Designated Court shall issue to the Financial establishment or to the person, whose property has been attached and vested in the competent authority under section 5, a notice accompanied by a copy of the application and affidavit together with an extract of evidence calling upon such financial establishment and person to show cause as to why the order of attachment should not be made absolute and property so attached sold in public auction. Section 14(3) provides that any person claiming an interest in the property attached or any portion thereof, may notwithstanding that no notice has been served upon him under this sub-section, raise an objection as aforesaid before the designated court at any time before an order is passed under sub-section (5) or sub-section (6). [Para 29]

HEADNOTE: Section 237, read with section 10, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Investigation of company’s affairs in other cases - Whether ‘Court’ referred to in section 237 is court having jurisdiction under section 10 and no other court - Held, yes - Whether under section 237(a)(ii), court can appoint directly inspector(s) to investigate into affairs of company - Held, no - Whether court can only make a declaration that affairs of company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by Central Government - Held, yes - Whether power of Company Law Board under section 237(b) is a bar to exercise of discretionary jurisdiction of court under section 237(a)(ii) - Held, no - Whether mere allegations are insufficient to support an application to court to act under section 237(1)(ii) and material placed before court should be such as to satisfy court that a deeper probe into affairs of company is desirable in interests of company itself - Held, yes - Whether court can pass a declaration under section 237(a) for a fishing expedition - Held, no - Whether an isolated instance of mismanagement is enough for court to declare that an investigation is required - Held, no - Whether existence of circumstances described under section 237(b) may sway court to pass an order under section 237(a)(ii) also but it is not always mandatory that court can pass a declaration only if conditions under section 237(b) exist - Held, yes - Whether power of court under section 237(a)(ii) is equal to power of CLB under section 237(b) - Held, no - Whether unlike CLB, there are no restrictions placed on Court even though Court will exercise its judicial discretion only on sufficient materials and only after it is convinced that situation warrants an investigation in interest of company as a whole - Held, yes - Whether when a discretionary order under section 237(a)(ii) is passed by proper court with jurisdiction, unless there are compelling grounds appellate court will not interfere - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent was an equity shareholder and the promoter of the appellant-company. He was also appointed as the Chairman of the company. Subsequently, the company came out with public issue which was subscribed in excess of 14 times the offer. Thereafter, the respondent filed petition under section 237(a)( ii ) before the Company Judge seeking to direct the Central Government to appoint inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company. It was alleged that no first annual general meeting of the company was held as convened in time.

The managing director, ‘M’ had been fraudulently mismanaging the company in utter disregard of the interest of the shareholders and was acting in an autocratic and oppressive manner. He created false and fabricated documents with nefarious motive to oust the respondent and other members of the board of directors who opposed the misutilisation and misappropriation of public funds. He created documents and minutes purporting to remove the petitioner and others who opposed the mismanagement and oppression. Though on the public issue, shares were over subscribed to the tune of 14 times and huge amounts were collected from the public, shares were neither allotted properly nor amounts refunded to the applicants whose application for shares were not accepted.

It was further alleged that 1200 complaints had been filed against ‘M’ by the subscribers to whom the amounts were not refunded and that ‘M’ had misappropriated, misutilised and mismanaged the funds collected through public issue and diverted the funds for his private purposes. The company opposed the petition. The Company Judge found that the submission of the Central Government supported the respondent’s allegations and concluded that a deeper probe was necessary and passed an order declaring that affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Court itself.

On appeal :

HELD: By virtue of the power under section 237(a )(ii), the Court cannot appoint directly inspector or inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company but only make a declaration that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated by an inspector appointed by the Central Government. Once such an order is passed it is mandatory for the Central Government to conduct such investigation by appointing competent persons as inspectors.

application which had been filed for recalling of order, dated 2-2-1998, whereby Court had ordered that in case of non-payment of dues of petitioning creditors within a period of 3½ months, said property would be deemed to have been attached and become liable to be sold under supervision of Court - Held, yes - Whether property No. 1 having stood attached by Court, had become liable to be sold after taking over its physical possession by Official Liquidator - Held, yes FACT: Respondent-GAL was appointed as a dealer of Maruti cars by Maruti Udyog Ltd. (‘M’). GAL was managed and controlled by one ‘G’ through his son. ‘G’ himself was the chairman of another automobile company in the group of companies by the name of DAL which was also selling Maruti cars. In order to make quick and easy money, the directors of ‘GAL’ started accepting inter-corporate deposits/loans of huge amounts from various parties against the security of bookings of Maruti cars during the nineties when Maruti cars were selling like hot cakes. During those good old days, over hundred crores were stated to have been collected by GAL from various parties. It appeared that that money was collected without any intention of paying back to the investors/depositors. When the depositors/investors asked for refund of their money, they were not paid back by GAL and so they started approaching ‘M’ for getting back their money since their deposits were secured by the Maruti bookings. Pursuant to an understanding between GAL and ‘M’, GAL’s managing director executed indemnity bond on behalf of GAL and also personal guarantee bond indemnifying ‘M’ against any kind of demands against it by GAL’s investors from whom GAL had taken inter-corporate loans against non-existent bookings of Maruti cars. ‘G’ also executed a personal guarantee bond in favour of ‘M’. Both father and son had admitted that GAL had secured loans from the public against non-existent bookings of Maruti cars. The petitioner was one of the creditors of GAL who had approached the Court for winding up of GAL. When notice of the company petition was given to GAL, it had entered appearance and right from the beginning, not only GAL had started coming out with proposals for liquidating the liabilities of its creditors but DAL also came forward to re-pay the debts of GAL so that GAL was not wound up by the Court. It also appeared that proposals and assurances given by GAL as well as DAL during the pendency of winding up proceedings to avoid passing of order of its winding up and to save the reputation of ‘S’ Group of companies were never intended to be honoured by the directors of both those companies. ‘G’ gave an undertaking in order, dated 2-2-1998, that DAL had immovable property at Sikandara Road, which would be sold and its money would be utilized for meeting the amount due to the creditors and in case, it was not sold within a period of three and half months and the amounts which were due to the creditors who were before the Court were not paid off or any other favourable arrangement securing the monies of the creditors was not reached within the said period, the property No. 1, would be deemed to have been attached and would be sold under the supervision of the Court. GAL after the passing of the order, dated 2-2-1998, regarding deemed attachment of the property had been contending before the Court that ‘G’, the then Chairman of DAL had no authority to bind the said company by making a statement before the Court that property No. 1, would be sold in order to liquidate the liabilities of GAL since GAL had nothing to do with DAL. So recalling of the order dated, 2-2-1998, whereby it was ordered by the Court that, in case, the debts of the creditors of GAL were not paid off within the period of 3½ months, property No. 1 would be deemed to have been attached and become liable to be sold under the supervision of the Court, was sought. However, that was not done and so an appeal was filed before the Division Bench by, DAL. Pursuant to the liberty given by the Division Bench in that appeal, DAL had moved a review application before the company court seeking review of the order, dated 2-2-1998. In that application also it was contended that ‘G’ had no authority to bind the said company of which he was the chairman during those days since its board of directors had not authorized him to make the statement before the Court which he had made on 2-2-1998. Before that application could be disposed of, an amendment application came to be filed by DAL seeking amendment in its review application to the effect that even if ‘G’ was considered to be competent to make the statement which he made on 2-2-1998 that statement was ultra vires the company’s Memorandum and Articles of Association since it was not one of the objects of the company to offer security of its own assets for the repayment of debts of another company. Fraud and deception are synonymous. [Para 36]

A non-existent entity cannot ratify any action which it could not have initiated : there is no director, no secretary, no principal officer. The company having been dissolved there is no entity/person who can authorise anyone. A shareholder of erstwhile company cannot claim any right, title or interest in any particular asset/property of the company. Then there is no question of executing any power of attorney as authorised signatory. [Para 37] The legal position is well settled that on dissolution, properties of a company vest in the Government. By virtue of section 654 of the 1985 Act even if the property of the company is not sold (as per the plaintiff), the property has vested in the crown. Then there is no question of any person, including a shareholder, staking a claim to the property; and, thus, filing a plaint by self or through a power of attorney holder. [Para 39]

On a conjoint reading of provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 653 of the 1985 Act it is apparent that a company or any member or creditor can apply to a Court if the company or member or creditor feels aggrieved by the name of the company having been struck off from the register. The Court is required to be satisfied that at the point of time when the name of the company was struck off from the register, the company was carrying on business or was in operation, or otherwise, that it is just that the company be restored to the register. Therefore, the person applying for restoration has to be a person who is aggrieved. The concept of ’aggrieved’ here means that the order of striking off has resulted in a situation which is detrimental to the applicant, viz., company or any member or creditor. Therefore, unless the applicant is ’aggrieved’ there is no question of making an application seeking restoration. Upon an application being made the Court is required to ascertain whether the company was carrying on business or was in operation at the time of the striking off the name from the register. In effect, it means that the reasonable belief entertained by the Registrar of Companies under section 652(1) of the 1985 Act is found to be incorrect. For the Court to record such a finding there must be some material available on record. The other alternative contention which permits the Court to exercise discretion requires that ’it is just’ that the company be restored to the register. This requirement has to be backed by facts and circumstances prevailing in a given situation so as to enable the Court to exercise discretion in favour of the applicant, namely that the action of the Registrar striking off the name of the company of the register would result in creating a situation which is unfair and unjust to the applicant. [Para 46]

In the instant case, admittedly, the plaintiff could not seek restoration on the ground that it was carrying on business or was in operation at the time when its name was struck off, as the plaintiff had applied that its name be struck off from the register as the company was not carrying on business or was not in operation. In light of the fact that an application had been moved, it was not necessary to deal with the alternative situation whether it would be permissible for the Court to exercise discretion on the basis of the consequence of striking off being unjust to the applicant. Suffice it to state that there had to be cogent and sufficient material in that regard. [Para 47]

Section 654 of the 1985 Act stipulates that property and rights of a dissolved company are deemed to be bona vacantia and, accordingly, belong to the Crown. Once this was the position, the plaintiff could not seek any relief on the basis of being owner of the property without either impleading Crown or putting it to notice. [Para 48]

In the aforesaid factual matrix even if the plaintiff had moved an application seeking restoration of the company to the register it was not necessary to await outcome of such application. Considering the fact that an order of arrest was operating against the defendant it was not possible to do so, especially in light of the fact that the plaintiff was not inclined to permit vacation of the ex parte interim order of arrest. [Para 49]

In the aforesaid fact situation it was not possible to state that these were procedural defects which did not go to the root of the matter and should not be permitted to defeat a just cause. The plaintiff had failed to make out a case. [Para 53]

In the result, the OJMCA was allowed and as a consequence the suit was dismissed. The order of the arrest of the vessel was vacated/set aside. [Para 54]

HEADNOTE: Section 457 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Powers of liquidator - Whether Company Court while exercising jurisdiction in an application under sections 433, 434 and 439 has power to appoint a provisional liquidator giving him liberty to sell properties, not merely property standing in name of company but also properties standing in names of other companies on premise that such assets have been created with funds collected by company - Held, yes

FACT: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

HELD: STATUTORY POWERS OF OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR

The powers of provisional liquidator appointed by the Company Court under section 450(3) the same powers as that the liquidator himself has. The extensive powers of the liquidator are delineated under section 457. [Para 4]

EXTENT OF DIRECTIONS THAT THE COMPANY COURT COULD PASS

Even apart from the powers of the liquidator which are co-extensive with the powers of the provisional liquidator, the Court itself has the power under section 477 at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator to summon before it any officer of the company or person knowing or suspected to have in his possession any property or books or papers of the company or known or suspected to be indebted to the company. This power which the Company Court has under section 477 is wide enough to pass even an ex parte order to secure the interest of the persons moving the application for winding up. Having regard to such wide powers of the Company Court, it is untenable to contend that the Company Court could not have directed as regards the properties which, on a prima facie finding, were also the assets of the company. The order of the Company Court was unexceptional if it was noticed that the Company Court had also given liberty to show that the assets standing in the name of other companies did not belong to the company against which liquidation proceedings had been initiated. Indeed, no prejudice could be said to be caused by such an order. Further, section 533 enables the liquidator to apply for disclaimer of onerous property. Section 535(4), while fastening the liquidator to disclaim certain properties, makes it possible for any third party for approaching the liquidator himself staking his claim to the property which is taken possession of by the liquidator or in respect of which proceedings are taken for sale. Having regard to the scheme of the Act protecting the interest of third parties and controlling the discretion of the liquidator by overall supervision of the Company Court, it would be untenable to contend that the directions given by the Company Court at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator were not in conformity with law. [Para 5]

DISPOSITION

The sole contention raised by the appellant was, therefore, without any substance and the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

FACT: The company-in-liquidation, which was a ‘Nidhi’ started by the appellant, collapsed after collecting huge amounts of deposits from the public at large under certain schemes. On winding up petitions preferred by the affected persons, the Company Judge appointed an administrator, besides the Official Liquidator, to look into the affairs of the company. Since the Company Judge also made an observation to the effect that there was prima facie fraud of massive proportions having been committed by the appellants along with other board members of company-in-liquidation, the administrator appointed by the Court filed an application under sections 542 and 543 seeking for a declaration that those persons were liable to be prosecuted for the fraudulent diversion of the funds. The appellant contested the application denying all the allegations and also raised the question of maintainability of the same, but the Company Judge, while passing penal order against the appellant, also held that the application preferred by the administrator was maintainable.

On appeal to the Division Bench :

HELD: Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13]

case, the main concern was the public interest. If it could be shown that the affairs of the company were being conducted in a manner which was prejudicial to the public interest, then the order of the CLB was justified. The powers under section 408 are to be sparingly used and it is only if the CLB is satisfied that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner which is prejudicial to public interest, that the order can be passed. [Para 12] It is also a well-settled principle of law that it is not necessary that to invoke the powers under section 408, the damage should have already taken place. The powers of the Central Government under section 408 are preventive in nature and can be exercised in order to ensure that in future the affairs of the company are not conducted in a manner which is prejudicial to the public interest. An order under section 408 may not be able to cure the illegal or prejudicial act which may already have been performed, but can be used to prevent further damage. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the admitted facts were that the company had been unable to comply with the orders of the CLB and pay off the public depositors. The explanation of the company that it could not comply with the orders of the CLB due to the fact that its produce ‘Loratadine’ could not be sold in the US market; and that the global deposit receipts could not be utilized, could not be accepted. Both those circumstances were already in existence when the earlier order was passed by the CLB. At that time, the company itself had given various options to the CLB to pay off all the depositors. The CLB passed directions. That order of the CLB had attained finality and the company should have cleared the public debt in accordance with the orders of the CLB. The company, in fact, had not fulfilled its obligations and instead had diverted the funds to various other parties. One could not lose sight of the fact that thousands of pensioners, widows and other members of the public had invested their funds in the company. The company’s accounts should be above board. No doubt, in commercial transactions, there may be instances when a company may lose money, yet the totality of circumstances has to be seen while adjudicating whether the affairs of the company are being run in a manner which may be prejudicial to the public interest. [Para 14]

There were certain facts which had not been controverted. The first was that instead of servicing the public debt and repaying the depositors, the company had invested a sum of Rs. 67.75 crores in shares of associated companies. Admittedly, the company had invested huge amounts in its sister company ‘M’ Ltd. The annual report for the year 2002-03 showed that the company off loaded its investment and ‘M’ Ltd. ceased to be a subsidiary of the company. Thereafter, that company again became a subsidiary of the company a couple of years later. There was sufficient material on record to show that more than Rs. 67 crores had been diverted to other companies out of the funds of the company. That money could have been better utilized by paying off the public debt. [Para 15]

Another factor, which showed that the affairs of the company were not being run properly, was that the company had made a provision for writing-off outstanding debts of Rs. 126.25 crores as non-recoverable on 30-9-2003. In the previous year, the outstanding debts were less than Rs. one crore. The company had failed to explain as to how an increase of Rs. 124 crores in the bad debts had taken place in a period of less than one and a half years. Despite repeated queries in the matter, no proper answer could be given by the company. [Para 16]

It would also be pertinent to mention that even as per the report of the chartered accountants of the company itself, the accounts were not being properly maintained. It was being projected that the company was doing well and was making profit. However, if the note of the chartered accountants was taken into consideration, it appeared that said projection made by the company was also incorrect. [Para 17]

Section 456 itself makes it clear that the PL shall take into his custody or under his control 'all the property' to which the company is or appears to be entitled. There can be no manner of doubt, and it is in fact not denied, that the company did place with NSEIL Rs. 1.10 crore when it became a trading member. The said sum definitely, therefore, constitutes the property of the company.

Although upon passing of the winding up order by the Court, the assets and the properties of the company came to the custody of the PL, but, in fact, the properties did not vest in the PL. Therefore, the PL acts as an agent of the company, a trustee of the properties as also the officer of the Court. He acts under the directions of the Court. This explains why under section 457(1), it is the liquidator who has been given the powers thereafter to represent the company under liquidation in all the proceedings. [Para 14]

Claims of investors had not been met out of company's fund with Defaulter Committee

In the instant case, although the company was expelled as a trading member, prior to the order of winding up, resulting in the deposit made by it with NSEIL vesting in the Defaulters' Committee, the claims of the investors had not been met out of that fund by the Defaulters Committee. It, in fact, set aside Rs. 83,91,000 pursuant to the letter written to the NSEIL by the Official Liquidator. It has met the claims of 68 investors in part out of IPFT. Therefore, the deposit made by the company with NSEIL, which constitutes its property under section 456(1), remains intact. [Para 17]

Conclusion

With the process of liquidation of the company already in progress, the scheme of section 456 will have to be followed. The inevitable result would be that wherever any property of the company-in-liquidation is available, the possession of such property would have to come to the PL appointed by the Court. Investors, who are before the Defaulters' Committee, will now have the option of pursuing their claims before the Official Liquidator in accordance with law.

Consequently, the plea of NSEIL that its Defaulters' Committee should be allowed to continue to be in possession and control of the deposits of Rs. 1.10 crore lying with it to the credit of the company cannot be countenanced. [Para 18]

Consequently, company application is to be allowed and NSEIL is to be directed to remit to the Official Liquidator the sum of Rs. 1.10 crore together with interest, if any accrued thereon. [Para 19]

Section 207 enables the Registrar or the inspector to conduct inspection and inquiry and they are vested with all powers of the Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, while trying a suit in respect of; (a) the discovery and production of books of account; (b) summoning and enforcing the attendance of persons and examining them on oath; (c) inspection of any books, registers and other documents of the company at any place. [Para 19] The Registrar or inspector is mandated to submit a report in writing to the Central Government pursuant to an inquiry either under section 206 or 207, which may include a recommendation and further investigation into the affairs of the company is necessary along with reason. [Para 20]

The power to search and seizure is provided under section 209. Section 210 of the Act, 2013 empowers the Central Government, where it forms an opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company either, (a) on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or inspector under section 208; (b) on intimation of a special resolution passed by a company that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated; or (c) in public interest. Sub-section (2) thereof mandates the Central Government to order an investigation into the affairs of that company where an order is passed by a court or the Tribunal in any proceedings before it that affairs of a company ought to be investigated. [Para 21]

The establishment of SFIO is provided in section 211 of the Act, 2013, which also provides for its constitution by experts headed by a Director appointed by a notification by the Central Government. Section 212 provides for investigation into affairs of Company by SFIO. The procedure to be adopted by SFIO is also provided in this section. [Para 22]

Section 226 indicates that where winding up proceeding in respect of a company is pending before a Tribunal, that is to say, where winding up order has not been passed by a Tribunal, an investigation in the Chapter may be initiated, and no such investigation shall be stopped or suspended by reason only of the fact that such winding up proceeding is pending. However, where a winding up order is passed by the Tribunal in a proceeding referred to in clause (c) of section 226 of the Act, 2013, the Inspector shall inform the Tribunal about the pendency of investigation proceedings before him and the Tribunal shall pass such order as it may deem fit. [Para 27]

Once the provisions of Part VII of the Act, 1956 or Chapter XX of the Act, 2013 are brought into play, then the companies become subject to provisions of winding up and orders passed by the Tribunal. [Para 28]

The Official Liquidator under the Act, 1956 and the Company Liquidator under the Act, 2013 are empowered to take into custody the company's properties and are vested with wide powers in that regard. [Para 29]

Wide ranging powers have been given to the liquidator for taking custody of the company's property under section 456 of the Act, 1956. All the properties and effects of the companies are deemed to be in custody of the Court/Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. [Para 30]

Similar powers are vested in the liquidator in section 283 of the Act, 2013, which provision also creates a legal fiction with regard to the custody of the properties and effects of the company being deemed to be with the Tribunal from the date of the order for winding up of the company. Wide ranging powers are provided by the Act, 2013 to the Tribunal which orders winding up of the company. Therefore, the purpose of the first proviso to section 226 of the Act, 2013 appears to be that since the Inspector would have taken into his custody the books and papers of the company or would have examined the various persons in exercise of his power under section 217 of the Act, 2013, or he would require papers and books for purpose of investigation initiated, he would bring to the knowledge of the Tribunal the steps taken by him or requiredto be taken, to enable the Tribunal to pass such orders as it may deem fit. This is in view of the fact that under section 283 of the Act, 2013 all the property of the company is deemed to be in the custody of the Tribunal. [Para 31]

It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that it has a panel of Chartered Accountants through whom the inspection and inquiries may be ordered. The sole purpose for which the Official Liquidator has sought for referring the matter to the SFIO was for detection of diversion of assets/funds of the company-in-liquidation. It is not denied by the Official Liquidator that the balance sheet, other books of account and documents are in possession of the Official Liquidator as well as the statement of affairs filed by the ex-director on behalf of the company-in-liquidation. FACT: CIRP was initiated against a real estate company 'C' by the NCLT, wherein, the investors/homebuyers of 'C' including the petitioner, lodged their claims against 'C' before the resolution professional of 'C'.

However, the NCLAT on an appeal filed by the directors of 'C', passed an order setting aside the entire CIRP.

The petitioner filed the instant writ petition praying for certain directions in the nature of mandamus to Registrar of Companies (RoC) to initiate and carry out appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of 'C' and its sister group of companies, for the acts of manipulating of records and siphoning off funds of the said company to its sister concern and freeze its assets.

Chapter II enables the Government to attach properties on default of return of deposits. For the said purpose, complaints have to be received by the Government from a number of depositors that the financial establishment has defaulted to return the deposits or the Government must have reason to believe that the financial institution is acting in a calculated manner with an intention to default depositors. If any of these conditions is satisfied, the Government is entitled to attach the properties and it may notify the competent authority to take control of the assets.
