This Article attempts to analyse the judgement passed in the matter of "Union of India v. Videocon Industries Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 52/[2022] 169 SCL 402 (NCLT - Mum.) wherein serious allegations of mismanagement has been taken against promoter/management of the company. The allegations were based on the forensic audit report which was conducted on directions of Resolution Professional during the insolvency process.

Brief History :

Videocon was large corporate performing in electronic hardware industry and as well as in telecom industry.

In 2018, State Bank of India, lead bank, which was Financial Creditor of the company, made an application under section 7 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC')to initiated Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against company since there was default in repayment of debts.

During Corporate Insolvency Process , Resolution Professional filed application to tribunal based on avoidance transactions identified by forensic auditor. Various application were made under section 43 and 66 of IBC wherein serious allegations were made against Promoters for conducting fraudulent transaction.

In Forensic Audit, the independent Auditor made remarks based on the information available and provided that various fraudulent transactions occurred between group companies.

Based on report of forensic auditor and other financial transaction proof with them, Regional Director, Western Region on behalf of Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed Petition for Interim Reliefs against officials of company and board of directors of group companies.

Present Case :

Various Interim reliefs were sought i.e. to direct respondents to disclose their Properties, to direct NSDL/CDSL to freeze their securities account, to direct CBDT to freeze assets of the respondents of the petition etc. and further to initiate oppression and mismanagement case against the promoter and BOD of the corporate debtor to secure or restore the assets back to catch out the real fraud and the wrong doers of the fraud along with assets to the right victim of the fraud

The respondent companies argued that matter was stayed by Appellate Tribunal and which was confirmed by Supreme court. Hence, Company is still under CIR and therefore as per Section 14 of IBC, Moratorium is in effect and therefore no judicial action can be initiated during CIRP against the company.

Brief of Section 14 related to case :

Section 14 (1) says that "Subject to provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3), on the insolvency commencement date, the Adjudicating Authority shall by order declare moratorium for prohibiting all of the following, namely :—

(a)

the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel or other authority;"

(b)

transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of by the corporate debtor any of its assets or any legal right or beneficial interest therein;

(c)

any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property including any action under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002;

(d)

the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor.

Moratorium Prohibits Petitioner to initiate Suit against company which is under CIRP. The very purpose of Moratorium is to stop multiplicity of cases, safeguarding assets pool and help resolution professional in focusing CIRP.

The argument of respondents was that the prohibitions are on both parties i.e. for and against the corporate debtor and hence these proceedings are bad in law and therefore should be set aside.

However, NCLT rejected this argument that proceedings are not proceedings against the corporate debtor but for corporate debtor. They agreed on contention that no suit or proceeding can be initiated against corporate debtor.

But in the instance case the efforts made by the Union of India were analysed and the spirit of them was seen to secure or restore the assets back to the ultimate victims of fraud and it is not any adversarial proceeding that is the proceeding in rem which has initiated by the Union of India to catch hold all the wrong doers and the fraudulent persons.

A brief about this case

1. This particular case relates to M/s. Pallava Resorts Private Limited of Chennai and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs undertook an inspection/enquiry upon this company. Let us go through this case threadbare in order to understand the compliance requirements involved in this matter and the specific non-compliance that occurred, leading to a violation of the true and fair view of the financial statements and the consequences of non-compliance resulting in penal action.

The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case. In light of above case, it is clear that the Section 32A is applicable even to those corporate debtors whose resolution has been approved. This provision has been incorporated to give boost to the prospective bidders of the corporate debtor in the CIRP or liquidation process as the case may be. Serious economic and legal issues arises in respect of Section 32A, which otherwise can lead to the misuse of the provision and defeat the purpose with which it has been incorporated.

The researcher has observed following issues w.r.t. Section 32A of the Code which needs to be addressed:-

1.

The extent to which benefit can be granted by the Appellate tribunal or Adjudicating Authority under section 32A of the Code need to be clarified. In theJSW Steel Ltd's case (supra), the Appellate tribunal went ahead to set aside all the attachments made by the Enforcement Department under PMLA. It is crucial to note that the tribunal itself has been incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013. The jurisdiction and power of the tribunal cannot be equated with that of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution. Thus, the powers of the tribunal are very limited in nature and setting aside of the attachments made amounts to overreaching the powers that are conferred on the tribunal under Companies Act, 2013 and the Code. Therefore, the legality of the order made by the tribunal is itself under suspicion. Moreover, the exercise of the power in such a manner has be frowned by the Hon'ble SC in the Case of Embassy Property Developments (P.) Ltd. v. State of Karnataka.9

2.

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has rendered the PMLA ineffective and toothless. It raises serious concerns as it can be misused as way to squander away from their criminal liability under various Acts. It makes such acts redundant and defeats the object with which these statues have been framed.

3.

Section 32A of the Code appears to resolve only the concerns of the corporate debtors and renders the victims of the crime committed by theses corporate entities from acts like money laundering.

4.

Section 32A of the Code doesn't provide for any exception over the encumbrance made in order to defeat the of the PMLA and hence it runs contrary to Section 9 of the PMLA which empowers the authority to remove any encumbrance on the property or lease if it found that it is created to defeat the provisions of PMLA.

5.

Victims of the money laundering have not been conferred any protection under section 32A of the Code. It makes them remedy-less and also encourage more and more shell companies to use corporate entity for the money laundering.

6.

It encourages more and more fraudulent practices under corporate entities until and unless proper safeguards are incorporated. For instance, where a company collects money from the public and passes it on other company for purchasing the properties, while in reality to misuse this provision and get hold over that money illegally. While the victim claim over the money is only limited to the company which received it by way of public offer and no claim can be made by the victims directly over the second company.

Conclusion

The legislative intent behind incorporating Section 32A of the Code is very clear to incentivize the bidders, give boost to the economy and incentivize the establishment of more foreign companies. Section 32A has been promulgated in order to enable the resolution applicant to take over the company which is free from all sorts of liability. However, the lot of questions flowing as a consequence of the incorporation of this provision remains to be unanswered. In order to weed out the abuse of Section 32A of the Code, the ambiguity and issues arising from the unwanted interpretation needs to be resolved at the earliest. There is need of proper checks and balance in order to minimize the abuse of the provision. Most importantly, it must be ensured that incorporation of Section 32A into the code doesn't render the provisions other statues redundant or contradicts.

Secondly, clause 245(1)(a) provides remedy to members or depositors by way of class action to seek order from Tribunal to "restrain the company from committing an act which is ultra vires the articles or memorandum of the company". This remedy can be sought when application is made by specified number of members as under: The requisite number of depositors shall not be less than 100 depositors or not less than such percentage of the total number of depositors as may be prescribed, whichever is less, or any depositor or depositors to whom the company owes such percentage of total deposits of the company as may be prescribed.

Thus, an individual member cannot approach the Tribunal unless he satisfies the criteria as per the above Table. A question arises then whether he can sue the company to restrain ultra vires acts as at present? Clause 430 of the Bill provides as under:

No civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

No injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force by the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal.

In view of clause 430 read with clause 245, it appears that once the Companies Act, 2012 comes into force individual member cannot sue to prevent ultra vires acts. He can only apply to Tribunal only if he satisfies criteria as per the above Table.

Thus, remedy against ultra vires acts made more difficult albeit unintentionally. Gist of the case

1. The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) has passed an order on 8th January 2024 vide its order no 003/2024 whereby a statutory auditor – one of the partners of M/s SVP & Associates was penalized for professional misconduct under the provisions of section 132 of the Companies Act 2013. The order passed by the NFRA pertains to the statutory audit carried out by the auditor for the financial year 2017-18 in respect of M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited, a company incorporated effective from 26th June 1990 under the provisions of the Companies Act 1956 and having the registered office at SRS Multiple, Top Floor City Centre, Sector 12, Faridabad in the state of Haryana. The company was engaged in real estate, manufacturing and trading of construction materials. NFRA initiated its investigation against the statutory auditor of M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited (earlier known as Manu Leasing Limited) for the professional conduct of the statutory auditor who carried out the statutory audit for the company.

Under the powers of section 212(1) (a) of the Companies Act 2013, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs assigned the investigation into the affairs of M/s. M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited and its group of companies to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) on 1st August 2018. M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited was listed with the Bombay Stock Exchange and therefore falls under the domain of NFRA. The company was required to prepare its financial statements for the year 2017-18 in accordance with the Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) as notified by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. The investigation conducted by the SFIO revealed that the company and its group of companies presented falsified financial statements containing the falsified statements of debtors, adopted the malpractice of round-tripping and layering the transactions that resulted in inflated purchases and sales. The investigation also revealed inter-alia siphoning of funds of Rs. 671.48 crores and diversion of funds of Rs. 645.86 crores in the company and its group companies SFIO accused the auditors of the company and its group companies under the provisions of sections 143, 147 and 448 of the Companies Act 2013.

MCA vide its letter dated 10th June 2021, directed SIFO to share the investigation report with NFRA and according the SFIO shared the report vide its letter dated 31st August 2021 with NFRA for taking necessary action against the statutory auditor of the company and also with the group companies. Pursuant to the sharing of the information the NFRA considered the case under the provisions of section 132 (4) of the Companies Act 2013, to assess as to whether any professional misconduct was committed by the auditor of M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited in his role as an engagement partner in the statutory audit of the company conducted by the auditors for the financial year 2017-18.

Let us go through the case in detail in order to understand the major lapses discovered on the part of the auditor in connection with the conduct of the statutory audit along with reference to his professional conduct which was called for under the regulations and as well as by the code of conduct prescribed by the professional body i.e., the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. The NFRA passed an order in this case levying a penalty of Rs. 3 lakh upon the auditors and also debarred him from his practice for a period of 3 years.

Background history on fraud

There have been multiple cases of scams in companies, capital markets etc. during the last decade and we could cite the following one which was known as Enron of India scam.

In the year 2009, the Satyam scam in India which was termed Enron of India happened from one of the respected business family managed company. Satyam was the fourth largest Indian information technology (IT) company listed in India and also in United States having over US$ 2 billion annual revenue size. The company was established in 1980s and grown to the size of having 53,000 employees and 600 plus customers including 185 fortune 500 companies. Not only that, the company had operations in 66 countries across the world and the financial advisors were Merrill Lynch (now Bank of America) and their auditors were one of the Big4 – i.e. Price Water House Coopers (PWc) and their bankers were Citi bank, BNP Paribas, HSBC and HDFC.

After the Satyam scam which came as a shock, the investors were panicked as stock plummeted and this particular incident resulted in immeasurable and unjustifiable damage to Brand India and Brand IT in particular. Many of the Satyam employees -stranded in many ways-morally, financially, legally and socially and people lost a staggering Rs.100 billion in Satyam in market capitalisation as investors reacted sharply and dumped shares, pushing down the scrip by 95 per cent. Regulatory action followed resulting into the arrest of Chairperson, Managing Director / Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer and key associates of the company including the partners of Audit Firm PWc.

In the capital market also the biggest scam was reported in the year 1992 known as Harshad Mehta Scam. It was reported that the Harshad Mehta scam featured an embezzlement of of Rs 1439 crores that led to a severe crunch and drastic loss of wealth in the life savings of many investors that amounted to Rs 3542 crores.

In the year 2001, Ketan Parekh scam was the second most important scam that rocked the Bombay Stock Exchange after the Harshad Mehta scam in the year 1992. . To make matters worse, Ketan Parekh was himself a protégé of Harshad Mehta and had learned stock trading from the pied piper of Bombay Stock Exchange himself. As a result, he was able to achieve a similar feat as compared to what Mehta himself had accomplished. As reported in the media, Ketan Parekh was found involved in cheating with banks by misrepresenting facts, falsifying accounts, ripping off the stock market prices and exploiting investor's decisions, mishandling the public money, bribing company directors enabling them to insider trading.

In the year 2019, the capital market witnessed Karvy scam in which Karvy frauded lakhs of investors by using their shares and securities and monetizing it by pledging the investor's shares and using the notes.

Followed the above, there has been various regulatory changes have taken place especially reporting the fraud happening within an organization, setting up the procedure for reporting of the fraud. Regulators have brought into effect vigil mechanism and whistle-blower policy to be in place in organizations. Let us look into the related provision on vigil mechanism, whistle blowing and fraud reporting.

Regulatory framework

Section 177 of the Companies Act 2013 spells out the requirement on whistle-blowing mechanism which is applicable to specified companies. In addition to this, for listed companies the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations are also applicable.

Provisions under Companies Act 2013

Under sub-section (9) of section 177 of Companies Act 2013 read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, it is mandatory for all listed companies and companies which have borrowed money from Banks and Public Financial Institutions in excess of Rs.50 crores. Sub-section(9) of section 177 of the Companies Act 2013, states that every listed company and other class or classes of companies, as prescribed, shall establish a vigil mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns in such manner as may be prescribed.

HEADNOTE: Section 12(1B) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992, read with article 142 of the Constitution of India - Collective investment scheme -Certificate of registration - SEBI filed petition in public interest stating that certain companies by issuing instrument like agro-bonds, plantation bonds, etc., were offering very high rates of return and collecting amounts from small investors and turning same amount to their sister-concern and other business instead of returning promised amount to investors and as such appropriate directions should be given by the Court to protect the interests of small investors - Whether even in absence of statutory provision since large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the aforesaid corporate veil, which might amount to a criminal offence, appropriate directions could be issued by Court to search and seize property of aforesaid companies - Held, yes

FACT: A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, wherein it was stated that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that there were entities which were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bonds, etc., offering very high rates of returns which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes.

In petition SEBI pointed out that respondent No. 1 had floated 18 Schemes and had collected approximately Rs. 16 crores from the small investors. Thereafter it was noticed that promoters of the schemes of respondent No. 1 were not traceable, respondent No. 1 had downed its shutters, the owners were not available, various offices of respondent No. 1 were closed and the said company was going through financial crises. Many investors were holding demonstrations outside the SEBI's office demanding action against the company and its directors.

Therefore, in petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. It was further contended that the bank accounts and other assets, movable as well as immovable, of respondent No. 1 wheresoever situated required to be frozen and attached to protect the investor's money from being frittered away.

HELD: Unfortunately it appeared that there is no legislation which can effectively control the mushrooming of companies which tempt small investors to deposit or invest their life-savings in such companies, promising to pay fanciful returns on their investment but actually defrauding the investors after siphoning off large amounts from such investments. It is also unfortunate that Nationalised Banks are also advancing loans to such institutions without adequate security from such companies as well as their directors. The situation on the whole, prima facie, is not very happy and knowing fully well the parameters of the powers of the Court as well as the self-imposed restrictions under article 226 of the Constitution, the Courts, cannot be silent spectators to such piquant situations.

It, was appeared that respondent No. 1 and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without their being any basis. Further, in agricultural production, this type of high returns are impossibility in this country. It appears that, because of these empty, false promises, investors are duped and the company's monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

The Apex Court in case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, held that the concept of corporate entity is evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people.

The Court has also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court was exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties.

Applying the aforesaid ratio and taking into consideration the fact that large number of investors were being defrauded by employing the corporate veil, which may amount to a criminal offence, and also the fact that under Criminal Law property acquired by fraud, cheating, etc., can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions could be issued by the Court to search and seize such property. Further, under article 226 of the Constitution, the Court can issue appropriate directions for not only enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III of constitution but 'for any other purpose', and 'any other purpose 'would include such public interest purpose.

In this view of the matter the Court passed the order directing an enquiry freezing of accounts of respondent-company and attachment of its properties.

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India - Writ petition - Whether where it prima facie appeared that investors were defrauded by respondent- company employing corporate veil and there was allegation of criminal offence of acquiring properties by fraud and cheating, appropriate directions for following properties and seizing these wherever these where lying, were required to be passed in exercise of Court's powers under article 226 of the Constitution -Held, yes

FACT: The respondent company (respondent No. 3), a residuary non-banking company, recorded a spurt in deposits from 1992-93. In 1995, on receiving complaints, the RBI conducted inspection of the respondent-company in which the RBI found an extremely unsatisfactory financial position, violation of the RBI directions and poor management. Therefore, the RBI issued prohibitory order restraining the company from accepting deposits from the public and also published notice in newspapers for the know- ledge of the general public. Receiving complaints about non-compliance of the prohibitory order, the RBI carried out a fresh inspection in 1997 in which it was found that the directors had no knowledge of and control over the affairs of the company. The registered office was not in operation and books of account had been shifted from there. Books of account had only been maintained upto 31-3-1995 and finalised upto 1993-94. Hence, the liabilities of the company to the depositors could not be determined. Substantial portion of liabilities, assets, properties and invest-ments of the company were transferred either to new companies or to its functionaries. These new companies where incorporated by officials agents and even field staff of the company. They were using premises of the assessee-company and were continuing deposit mobilisation activities violating prohibitory order of the RBI. In a branch the company itself collected deposit violating the order. The RBI also found that the company had substantial real estate, most of which had no complete documents and these were either repeatedly mortgaged or were in possession of the new companies. The RBI was also informed by the directors that investments of Rs. 152 lakhs were either realised or were encumbered.

The present writ petition under article 226 was filed by the agents and policy-holders of the respondent company. The petitioners sought appro-priate directions for protection of public interest.

HELD: There was great substance in the submission of the petitioners that the aforementioned state of affairs required immediate remedial attention. Prima facie, it was apparent that the third respondent had mobilised large deposits from the public and that innocent persons who had invested their money, had not been repaid The officials and other persons associated with the third respondent including the field-staff had formed new companies with the object of siphoning funds and assets of the third respondent to the detriment of the interest of the depositors.

Prima facie, it appeared that the respondents and such other companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their lifelong savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction Company (P.) Ltd. AIR 1996 SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose.

The Courts have also held that the absence of a statutory provision will not inhibit the Court (as the Court is exercising power under article 142 of the Constitution) while acting under the said article from making appropriate orders for doing complete justice between the parties. The Courts have also observed that in India, the Courts are not only Courts of law, but also the Courts of equity.

Considering the fact that a large number of investors prima facie appeared to have been defrauded, that the allegations of fraud and cheating if established would amount to a criminal offence and in view, of the fact that under the criminal law property acquired by fraud or cheating can be followed and seized from wherever it is lying, appropriate directions were required to be issued by the Court to search and seize the property of the company. Under article 226 the Court can issue appropriate directions not only for enforcing any of the rights conferred by Part III but 'for any other purpose' and 'any other purpose' would include a purpose for the protection of public interest. Therefore, order was passed directing the Commissioner, Police to appoint DC, Police to follow all assets and properties of respondent No. 3 company and to take necessary action for their seizure.

HEADNOTE: Section 457 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Powers of liquidator - Whether Company Court while exercising jurisdiction in an application under sections 433, 434 and 439 has power to appoint a provisional liquidator giving him liberty to sell properties, not merely property standing in name of company but also properties standing in names of other companies on premise that such assets have been created with funds collected by company - Held, yes

FACT: On complaints of large scale commission of frauds by the directors of the company involving siphoning off the company funds for private ends and for purchasing all properties in the names of other front companies and, thus, stashing away large assets from the reach of the creditors, the respondent filed winding up application against the appellant-company. The Company Court, on the basis of prima facie material that the funds of the company were transferred to other companies formed by one of the directors concluded that the affairs of the company, including assets in the names of other companies which had been created with the funds collected by the company, were required to be investigated and that such systematic investigation would bring out the extent of assets owned by the company, legal and valid so as to make available the properties for discharge of debts of the investors. The Company Court, accordingly, passed an order appointing a provisional liquidator under whose control the property, effects and actionable claims to which the company claimed to be entitled to would vest. In the instant appeal, the appellant contended that the properties that were to be brought for sale did not belong to the company and that the company could not have offered to the liquidator to take possession of all the assets, including the assets that did not stand in the name of the company.

HELD: STATUTORY POWERS OF OFFICIAL LIQUIDATOR

The powers of provisional liquidator appointed by the Company Court under section 450(3) the same powers as that the liquidator himself has. The extensive powers of the liquidator are delineated under section 457. [Para 4]

EXTENT OF DIRECTIONS THAT THE COMPANY COURT COULD PASS

Even apart from the powers of the liquidator which are co-extensive with the powers of the provisional liquidator, the Court itself has the power under section 477 at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator to summon before it any officer of the company or person knowing or suspected to have in his possession any property or books or papers of the company or known or suspected to be indebted to the company. This power which the Company Court has under section 477 is wide enough to pass even an ex parte order to secure the interest of the persons moving the application for winding up. Having regard to such wide powers of the Company Court, it is untenable to contend that the Company Court could not have directed as regards the properties which, on a prima facie finding, were also the assets of the company. The order of the Company Court was unexceptional if it was noticed that the Company Court had also given liberty to show that the assets standing in the name of other companies did not belong to the company against which liquidation proceedings had been initiated. Indeed, no prejudice could be said to be caused by such an order. Further, section 533 enables the liquidator to apply for disclaimer of onerous property. Section 535(4), while fastening the liquidator to disclaim certain properties, makes it possible for any third party for approaching the liquidator himself staking his claim to the property which is taken possession of by the liquidator or in respect of which proceedings are taken for sale. Having regard to the scheme of the Act protecting the interest of third parties and controlling the discretion of the liquidator by overall supervision of the Company Court, it would be untenable to contend that the directions given by the Company Court at the time of appointment of the provisional liquidator were not in conformity with law. [Para 5]

DISPOSITION

The sole contention raised by the appellant was, therefore, without any substance and the appeal was to be dismissed. [Para 6]

Ltd (supra ), the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose. The Court has also considered the concept of corporate entity and held that where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. After discussing other authorities, the Court has observed that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegal- ities or to defraud people and held as follows:

"Where, therefore, the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the corporate character and will look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to enable it to pass appropriate orders to do justice between the parties concerned. The fact that Tejwant Singh and members of his family have created several corporate bodies does not prevent this Court from treating all of them as one entity belonging to and controlled by Tejwant Singh and family if it is found that these corporate bodies are merely cloaks behind which lurks Tejwant Singh and/or members of his family and that the device of incorporation was really a ploy adopted for committing illegalities and/or to defraud people."

"(8) Where a property stands confiscated to the Central Government under sub-section (5), the Special Court, in such manner as may be prescribed, may also direct the Central Government to restore such confiscated property or part thereof of a claimant with a legitimate interest in the property, who may have suffered a quantifiable loss as a result of the offence of money laundering: Provided that the Special Court shall not consider such claim unless it is satisfied that the claimant has acted in good faith and has suffered the loss despite having taken all reasonable precautions and is not involved in the offence of money-laundering.

Provided that the Special Court shall not consider such claim unless it is satisfied that the claimant has acted in good faith and has suffered the loss despite having taken all reasonable precautions and is not involved in the offence of money-laundering:

"3A. Manner of restoration of property during trial.

HEADNOTE: Section 542, read with section 543, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Liability for fraudulent conduct of business - Whether Company Judge/ Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of company-in-liquidation and any such application filed by administrator of that company is not maintainable - Held, yes - Whether Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, but for penal order under section 542(3) it can only give permission to Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both can be passed by Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3) - Held, yes

FACT: The company-in-liquidation, which was a ‘Nidhi’ started by the appellant, collapsed after collecting huge amounts of deposits from the public at large under certain schemes. On winding up petitions preferred by the affected persons, the Company Judge appointed an administrator, besides the Official Liquidator, to look into the affairs of the company. Since the Company Judge also made an observation to the effect that there was prima facie fraud of massive proportions having been committed by the appellants along with other board members of company-in-liquidation, the administrator appointed by the Court filed an application under sections 542 and 543 seeking for a declaration that those persons were liable to be prosecuted for the fraudulent diversion of the funds. The appellant contested the application denying all the allegations and also raised the question of maintainability of the same, but the Company Judge, while passing penal order against the appellant, also held that the application preferred by the administrator was maintainable.

On appeal to the Division Bench :

HELD: Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13]

28.2-3 Inspection of report of Company Liquidator

Report of Company Liquidator can be inspected by creditor or contributory or his agent and can obtain its copies - section 281(5) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3 Directions by NCLT after receiving report of Company Liquidator Section 282 of Companies Act, 2013 enumerates steps to be taken by NCLT after receiving report of company liquidator. The steps include (a) fix time limit for completing winding up proceedings (b) Order sale of company or its assets as a going concern (c) Order action if fraud is suspected (d) Other order to protect, preserve and enhance value of assets of company (e) Other directions as NCLT may deem fit.

Thus, NCLT has very wide powers in winding up of company.

NCLT can review and modify its orders during winding up proceedings, on receiving quarterly report from Company Liquidator - section 288(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

NCLT has to grant hearing to Company Liquidator, Creditors, Contributories or other persons before passing order.

28.3-1 Fixing time schedule for dissolution of company

NCLT shall fix time limit to complete dissolution of company. The time limit can be revised on application of Company Liquidator, Creditor, Contributory or any other person - section 282(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.3-2 Sale of company or assets as going concern

NCLT can order sale of company or its assets as a going concern. NCLT may appoint sales committee for this purpose - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

If a unit is actually functional, sale as a 'going concern' may attract better price than sale of individual assets. This will also really speed up process of winding up.

Once NCLT sanctions sale as a going concern, the actual sale can be made by Company Liquidator as per powers under section 290(1)(d) of Companies Act, 2013.

Unit closed for long time may not be sold as going concern - If the unit is closed for long time, sale of machinery, plant and land separately will fetch a better price. The reason is that in case of sale as a going concern, employment of all employees will continue, which may cast a big liability.

In Allahabad Bank v. Arc Holding Ltd. 2000 AIR SCW 3498 = 28 SCL 394 (SC), it was held that if a unit is closed for a long time, sale as a going concern should not be normally ordered by High Court (now NCLT).

28.3-3 Action if Company Liquidator reports fraud

If Company Liquidator makes such report, NCLT shall order investigation under section 210 of Companies Act, 2013. On receipt of report of investigation, NCLT may give directions under sections 339 to 342 of Companies Act, 2013. NCLT may direct Company Liquidator to file criminal complaint against persons who were involved in the fraud - section 282(2) of Companies Act, 2013

If Company Liquidator reports that fraud has been committed in promotion, formation, business or conduct of affairs of company, NCLT can order examination of such promoters, directors or officers of the company - section 300(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

28.4 Custody of company's properties after order of winding up

Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take custody of all properties, effects and actionable claims of the company. Even if actual possession is not taken, these will be deemed to be in custody of NCLT. NCLT can order any contributory, trustee, receiver, banker, officer or employee to pay or deliver or transfer any money, property or books and papers in his custody.

28.4-1 Taking over of company's property by Company Liquidator

After order of winding up is made or after a provisional liquidator has been appointed, the Company Liquidator or Provisional Liquidator shall take into his custody or under his control, all property, effects and actionable claims of the company - section 283(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

In Pradeshia Industrial & Investment Corpn of UP v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2003) 47 SCL 126 (All HC), Court had issued order of winding up. Even then, Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) ordered Official Liquidator (later Company Liquidator) to handover property to the company. It was held that order suffers from gross error of jurisdiction and beyond powers conferred on CJM under section 451 of CrPC.

In K & Co v. Aruna Sugars AIR 1999 Mad 45, it was held that disposition of property by company after commencement of winding up can be sanctioned if necessary for general interest of company, without causing harm to creditors.

Investor Help-lines

1.50 Ordinarily, in the absence of fraud or misfeasance in relation to the company or any breach of duty to the company alleged, there is no remedy in law against loss of investment in a company as a result of the company ceasing to be a going concern, it taken as an inherent risk in carrying on a business. In order to protect themselves from loss otherwise, the investors are expected generally to be aware of their rights with due recognition of their responsibilities to keep themselves informed about the developments in the affairs of the company where they have invested and to act, like participation in its meetings in person or by proxy individually or better still as a member in a kindred group of investors.

Investors’ rights

1.50-1 The investors’ rights in respect of shares include: (a) timely receipt of share certificates, whether on allotment or transfer/transmission, the abridged annual report each year and the notices for the general meetings and prompt refund of excess money paid with the share-application, dividend warrants, offers of rights shares on approval of the issue by the general body; (b) inspection of the statutory books and registers kept by the company as per the Act or to have copies in full or as extracts from the company; (c) to exercise the right of piloting members’ requisitioned resolutions/general meetings to force a change in the company’s course of affairs; (d) to commence civil and criminal proceedings against the company or the directors for defaults or infringements of their rights like oppression or mis-management; (e) to be the residual claimants or be liable as contributories on the company’s winding up; and (f) to prosecute the company and the directors for defaults under and offences against the Act or for the company to be wound-up by the Tribunal, if appropriate. Debenture or bond-holders’ rights are limited to receive the periodic returns and the return of the investment at maturity, to receive the debenture-trust-deed copy on request, and to seek the company’s winding up, if appropriate, before the Tribunal.

Trading and transfer of securities

1.50-2 As regards trading in and transfer of securities, the channels available to investors include :

(A) Trades - purchase and sale by private arrangement or via the trading floors established by the stock exchange where the securities are listed, the stock exchange route being free of the loss due to the risk of non-performance of delivery of securities and prompt payment of the consideration in the deals apart from getting the advantage of the market price at a little extra cost to the investors. While the securities are held, as owners they can raise finances against deposit of the securities.

(B) Grievances (to the low of which property rights of citizens in company or other securities have been summarily diluted as an administrative expedient to form part of Company Law)—the redressal channels available at present include the company and its Registrars first and foremost, besides the DCA and additionally in respect of listed companies, the SEBI/Stock Exchanges where the securities are listed, and the debenture-trustee in the case of debentures. Grievances in respect of Fixed Deposit Receipts in banks or financial institutions other than the Non-banking financial companies may be addressed to the RBI, but for company public deposits it is only the DCA to be approached.

Help-lines, minimal

1.50-3 Obviously, these help-lines are minimal at any rate for the vast domestic investors in a large country like India comprising of several States and divided controls to nurture investor confidence and encourage wider participation of common people in company securities, in the absence of well-known institutional remedies against wrongs available close at hand and at small cost, including provision of some measure of compensation against the perceived loss in investing in company shares compulsorily highlighted as a disclaimer in the offer documents, without it being an end in itself on its occurrence.

Section 542 deals with the liability for fraudulent conduct of business, if found in the course of winding up of a company. If it comes to the notice of the Company Judge/Tribunal that any business of the company had been carried on with intent to defraud the creditors of the company or any other person or for any fraudulent purpose, appropriate declaration can be made and the liability of such person can be determined or appropriate order may be passed under sub-section (2) of section 542. However, such order can be passed only on the application of the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company, as is evident from section 542. [Para 8]

Section 543 enables the Company Judge/Tribunal to assess damages against the delinquent directors, manager, liquidator or officer of the company in case such person has misapplied or retained or become liable or accountable or has been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. It is only if an application to that effect is preferred by the Official Liquidator or Liquidator or any creditor or contributory within the time prescribed,that the Company Judge/Tribunal may compel the person concerned to repay or restore the money or property. While section 542 makes a person criminally liable for punishment, section 543 is civil in nature as it only enables the guilty person to repay or restore the money or property with the company. [Para 9]

So far as the criminal action as envisaged under section 542 is concerned, for the purpose of enforcement of the order of the Company Judge/Tribunal, the Official Liquidator or Liquidator can ask for permission to prosecute the guilty person by filing an application under section 457(1)(a). The Company Judge/Tribunal, in such cases, after giving a declaration under section 542, may permit the Official Liquidator or Liquidator to move the Court of criminal jurisdiction for appropriate order to ensure punishment as may be imposed under section 542(3). [Para 10]

Thus, the Company Judge/Tribunal can give a declaration and pass an order either under section 542 or under section 543 or both only if an application is preferred by the Official Liquidator or liquidator or any creditor or contributory of the company. Though the Company Judge/Tribunal may give an appropriate declaration and pass order under sections 542 and 543, yet for penal order under section 542(3) it could only give permission to the Official Liquidator or liquidator to prefer an application before the Court of competent criminal jurisdiction and no order of punishment with imprisonment or fine or both could be passed by the Company Judge/Tribunal under section 542(3). [Para 11]

It is the settled law that if a person or body is created under the statute and such express powers have been given to such person or body under the provisions of law, it would not be legitimate to have resorted to general or implied powers under the law. [Para 13]

From a plain reading of sections 542 and 543 as a whole, as it is evident that the statute itself is very clear and there is no ambiguity with regard to entitlement to filing an application under sections 542 and 543, the principle of law of casus omissus cannot be supplied by the Court in the absence of any necessity. [Para 17]

From the said finding, it would be evident that the application under sections 542 and 543 preferred by the administrator of the company-in-liquidation was not maintainable, nor the Company Judge was empowered to impose a fine in lieu of imprisonment under section 542(3). In such a background, there was no other option, but to set aside the impugned order passed by the Company Judge. [Para 18]

The impugned order of the Company Judge was to be set aside, accordingly, and the appeals were to be allowed. [Para 19]

When an order is illegal, it cannot be severed by keeping the finding alone intact and setting aside that portion of the conclusion and remiting back the matter to the company court to cure the defects. Likewise, it is also impossible for an appellate court to do the exercise of the company court, when the court has come to the conclusion that the order impugned is held to be an order passed against the statutory provisions. 14. The decisions relied on by counsel for the respondent in Koksingh v. Smt. Deokabai AIR 1976 SC 634 and P. Purushottam Reddy v. Pratap Steels Ltd. AIR 2002 SC 771, are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand inasmuch as those two decisions were rendered explaining the scope of Order 41, rule 33 prior to the amendment and Order 41, rules 23, 23A and 25 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, respectively. In Koksingh’s case, the precise dispute was whether the appellate court could grant a decree, which was not granted by the trial court in the absence of an appeal. In that case the trial court did not grant decree for charge over the property for which the respondent filed the suit, but granted personal money decree. On appeal by the appellant against that money decree, the High Court granted a decree for charge over the property. When this was disputed, the Apex Court ruled as follows :—

"6. In Giani Ram v. Ramji Lal [1969] 3 SCR 944; AIR 1969 SC 1144, the Court said that in Order 41, rule 33, the expression ‘which ought to have been passed’ means ‘what ought in law to have been passed’ and if an appellate Court is of the view that any decree which ought in law to have been passed was in fact not passed by the court below, it may pass or make such further or other decree or order as the justice of the case may require.

7. Therefore, we hold that even if the respondent did not file any appeal from the decree of the trial court, that was no bar to the High Court passing a decree in favour of the respondent for the enforcement of the charge." (p. 636)

15. Likewise, in P. Purushottam Reddy’s case (supra) the decree was granted by the trial court in a specific performance suit. On appeal, the High Court, having found that no plea was taken that the suit for specific performance was not maintainable for non-compliance with Form Nos. 47 and 48 of the Appendix A to the Civil Procedure Code, and having found that there was no specific issue framed by the trial court that whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, set aside the decree granted by the trial court and the matter is remitted for re-consideration. After referring to the Order 41 prior to and subsequent to 1976 amendment, it was observed by the Supreme Court that in view of the express provision of Order 41, rule 23A, the High Court cannot have recourse to its inherent power to make a remand as the inherent power can be availed of ex debito justitiae only in the absence of express provision in the Code. It is only in exceptional cases, where the court may now exercise the power of remand de hors the rules 23 and 23A. To wit, the superior court, if finds the judgment under appeal has not disposed of the case satisfactorily in the manner required by Order 20, rule 3 or Order 41, rule 31 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 and hence it is no judgment in the eye of law and it may set aside the same and send the matter back for re-writing the judgment so as to protect the valuable right of the parties. An appellate court should be circumspect in ordering a remand when the case is not covered either by rule 23 or rule 23A or rule 25 of the Civil Procedure Code. An unwarranted order of remand gives the litigation an undeserved lease of life and therefore must be avoided.

16. As already stated, the company law is a special law and it provides certain inbuilt mandatory safeguards to be followed by the company court while passing orders and winding up as envisaged in the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959. As already stated, the impugned order is an order against the statute and no judgment in the eye of law, the judgments referred to above cannot be made applicable to the facts of the present case. Hence, the respondent cannot improve the case under the cover of these judgments.

17. For the foregoing reasons, the order impugned in this appeal is set aside the matter is remitted to the company court to pass orders on the petition in accordance with the statutory provisions.

DDA's responsibility to reimburse the purchasers :

S/Sri Bobde and Dave, learned counsel for the purchasers, contended that inasmuch as several top officials of the DDA had colluded with Skipper and connived at their wrongdoing, the DDA must be held equally liable to reimburse the purchasers. Indeed, their submission is that the DDA stood by and took no action whatsoever while Skipper was issuing repeated advertisements (even after January 29, 1991, in open and brazen defiance of this court's orders) and, therefore, it must be made equally liable to reimburse the said purchasers in full. We find it difficult to agree. Firstly, the said contention is not factually correct. As has been pointed out hereinabove, soon after the publication of an advertisement by Skipper in the newspapers inviting the citizens at large to come and purchase the space in the proposed building on February 4,1991, the DDA came forward with a warning notice published in all leading national dailies advising citizens not to purchase space in the building in view of the orders of this court. It is true that even thereafter Skipper has been issuing similar advertisements but it cannot be said with any reasonableness that the DDA should have responded to each such advertisement by publishing a warning. It could have done that but it cannot be, faulted for not doing it. It is, therefore, factually incorrect to say that the DDA stood by and allowed Skipper to defraud the people by issuing advertisements. Secondly, even if there is any collusion between the officials of the DDA and Skipper as alleged by learned counsel, the question still arises whether the DDA can be held bound by such actions of its officials acting beyond their authority, indeed, acting adverse to the interests of the DDA intentionally. We are not suggesting nor are we laying down the proposition that the DDA is not bound by the acts and deeds of its officials but are only saying that where the acts and deeds of the officials are not only beyond their authority but are done with a mala fide intent, it may not be just and fair to bind the DDA with such mala fide acts and deeds. Be that as it may, it is not necessary for the purpose of this case to pursue this line of enquiry further or to express any definite opinion thereon.

HELD: Under sub-article (2) of article 226, the power conferred on the High Court to issue directions, orders or writs can be exercised by the Court in relation to territories within which the cause of action wholly or in part arises for the exercise of such powers. If cause of action or part of cause of action has not arisen or the person fails to demonstrate such cause of action, as having arisen within the territorial jurisdiction of the Court, issue of any writ or direction would be without jurisdiction. If the deposit was not repaid, the aggrieved party could file application before the CLB which might direct the NBFC to make payment of such deposit. There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator. The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

Any claim by or against the company is transferred to Company Court (now NCLT) under section 446(2)(b) of the 1956 Act [section 280 of Companies Act, 2013]. It was held that there is no time limit prescribed under section 477 of the 1956 Act [section 299 of Companies Act, 2013] for taking proceedings thereunder. By virtue of section 654 of the 1985 Act even if the property of the company is not sold (as per the plaintiff), the property has vested in the crown. Then there is no question of any person, including a shareholder, staking a claim to the property; and, thus, filing a plaint by self or through a power of attorney holder. [Para 39]

On a conjoint reading of provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 653 of the 1985 Act it is apparent that a company or any member or creditor can apply to a Court if the company or member or creditor feels aggrieved by the name of the company having been struck off from the register. The Court is required to be satisfied that at the point of time when the name of the company was struck off from the register, the company was carrying on business or was in operation, or otherwise, that it is just that the company be restored to the register. Therefore, the person applying for restoration has to be a person who is aggrieved. The concept of ’aggrieved’ here means that the order of striking off has resulted in a situation which is detrimental to the applicant, viz., company or any member or creditor. Therefore, unless the applicant is ’aggrieved’ there is no question of making an application seeking restoration. Upon an application being made the Court is required to ascertain whether the company was carrying on business or was in operation at the time of the striking off the name from the register. In effect, it means that the reasonable belief entertained by the Registrar of Companies under section 652(1) of the 1985 Act is found to be incorrect. For the Court to record such a finding there must be some material available on record. The other alternative contention which permits the Court to exercise discretion requires that ’it is just’ that the company be restored to the register. This requirement has to be backed by facts and circumstances prevailing in a given situation so as to enable the Court to exercise discretion in favour of the applicant, namely that the action of the Registrar striking off the name of the company of the register would result in creating a situation which is unfair and unjust to the applicant. [Para 46]

In the instant case, admittedly, the plaintiff could not seek restoration on the ground that it was carrying on business or was in operation at the time when its name was struck off, as the plaintiff had applied that its name be struck off from the register as the company was not carrying on business or was not in operation. In light of the fact that an application had been moved, it was not necessary to deal with the alternative situation whether it would be permissible for the Court to exercise discretion on the basis of the consequence of striking off being unjust to the applicant. Suffice it to state that there had to be cogent and sufficient material in that regard. [Para 47]

Section 654 of the 1985 Act stipulates that property and rights of a dissolved company are deemed to be bona vacantia and, accordingly, belong to the Crown. Once this was the position, the plaintiff could not seek any relief on the basis of being owner of the property without either impleading Crown or putting it to notice. [Para 48]

In the aforesaid factual matrix even if the plaintiff had moved an application seeking restoration of the company to the register it was not necessary to await outcome of such application. Considering the fact that an order of arrest was operating against the defendant it was not possible to do so, especially in light of the fact that the plaintiff was not inclined to permit vacation of the ex parte interim order of arrest. [Para 49]

In the aforesaid fact situation it was not possible to state that these were procedural defects which did not go to the root of the matter and should not be permitted to defeat a just cause. The plaintiff had failed to make out a case. [Para 53]

In the result, the OJMCA was allowed and as a consequence the suit was dismissed. The order of the arrest of the vessel was vacated/set aside. [Para 54]

VII Section 11 Special Courts (Trial of offences relating to transactions in securities) Act, 1992 - Discharge of liabilities Third person coming into possession of properties of notified parties under illegal agreements, cannot be allowed to retain them A.K. Menon v. Fairgrowth Financial Services Ltd. [1994] 81 Comp. Cas. 508 (Bom.) (Special Court) In case of statutory attachments which requires distribution of property it is the Special Court which has to recover the properties for the purposes of effective distribution under section 11(2) of the Act. One of the main objects of the Act being to recover large amounts of public money which have gone into private pockets and there being statutory attachment of properties of notified parties, such statutory attachments would operate even if the properties are in the hands of a third party pursuant to an illegal contract. After attachment, such properties can only be dealt with under the directions of the instant court. All such property must, therefore, be available for distribution under section 11(2). It, thus, cannot be argued that even after a statutory attachment, the third party must be allowed to deal with the properties as the notified party will not be assisted by the Court. The Court will not be assisting notified parties.The Court is safeguarding properties purchased from public monies from further alienation and ensuring that they are available for distribution under section 11. The question of applying the principle of pari delicto to such cases does not arise at all. To accept such an argument would amount to meaning that if an agreement is legal, then the Special Court can recover attached properties, but if an agreement is illegal, the Special Court must allow a transfer to take place. It can hardly be said that the third person who has come into possession of properties of notified parties, under illegal agreements, must be allowed to retain them. Such an argument cannot be accepted.

CHAPTER 284

PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER *PROSECUTION AND CONVICTION OF FRAUDULENT PERSONS UNDER SECTION 203 AND DISQUALIFICATION ORDER*

284.1 Background note284.1 Background note

The Court/Tribunal has been vested with the power to restrain fraudulent persons from managing companies under section 203 of the Act, in a case before it by way of a disqualification order passed, where —

(a) a person is convicted of any offence in connection with the promotion, formation or management of a company, or

(b) in the course of its winding up, a person is found guilty of an offence punishable under section 542 of the Act, irrespective of his conviction, or

(c) a person is otherwise guilty while being an officer of the company of any fraud, or misfeasance in relation to the company or of any breach of duty to the company.

284.2 Disqualification order284.2 Disqualification order

The Court/Tribunal may make an order that a person convicted as above shall not, without the leave of the Court/Tribunal, be a Director or, in any other way - whether directly or indirectly be concerned or take part in the promotion, formation or management of a company, for such period not exceeding five years as may be specified in the order.

284.3 Who can apply ?284.3 Who can apply ?

Any person who is or has been a member or creditor of the company or the liquidator or Official Liquidator may apply to the Court/Tribunal for making the disqualification order by following the procedure under section 203.

284.4 Violation of disqualification order284.4 Violation of disqualification order

Acting in contravention of disqualification order entails punishment by a prison term upto two years or fine extending to fifty thousand rupees or both, for each such offence.

Illustration

In a case, winding up petitions were filed, but the winding order was not passed. At that stage a petition under section 203 seeking a disqualification order was filed. The alleged breach of duty against the company consisted of further issue of capital in violation of the provision in the Articles made by the Directors allotting the shares in the names of the Directors themselves and their relatives without first offering them proportionately to the members of the company. Section 456 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Custody of company’s property - Respondent-company had collected huge sums of money by way of deposits from general public and by utilizing money so collected, various assets had been acquired by it which included land whereon superstructure had been constructed for housing registered office of company - Applicants’ case was that respondent-company had become nearly insolvent and with a view to tide over its financial distress, it, through one of its directors, viz., ‘D’, sold said land together with building standing thereon to applicants - Certain payment was made by applicants as advance and balance was to be paid at time of registration - Applicants contended that receipt of said balance amount and consequential execution of sale deed were delayed on one pretext or other and, therefore, they filed suit seeking specific performance of agreement of sale - Immediately, a compromise memo was filed before Court and, consequently, matter was referred to Lok Adalat which passed a decree duly recording compromise between parties - In terms of compromise decree, balance amount was paid and sale deed was executed - Subsequently, applicants entered into an agreement of sale of said property with ‘V’ - In meantime, respondent-company was ordered to be wound up on applications by some depositors of company to whom company had not repaid their deposits and possession of said property was taken over by Official Liquidator - Hence, applicants moved instant application seeking property to be released from custody of Official Liquidator on ground that title over property had been transferred by company in favour of applicants by way of sale deed executed between parties - It was found that market value of property was much higher than value for which property was offered for sale to applicants - There was no resolution passed by board of directors of company, in accordance with provisions contained in section 291, for undertaking sale of any of asset of company - No publicity was ever issued by company or by its directors for intended sale of said asset - It was not explained as to how applicants came to know of impending sale of said asset and how they got property valued before entering into transaction - There was no authorization issued by company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or enter into a transaction of sale at first instance with applicants - Sale consideration was paid in cash instead of secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts and no entries were found in books of company about receipt of said amount - Applicants failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to respondent in cash - Thousands of complaints had been lodged with police at various places in State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by respondent-company - Whether, on facts, it could be said that entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by applicants on District Court as well as on Lok Adalat and ‘D’ on behalf of respondent-company had joined hands with them - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no rights of any kind would ever pass to hands of applicants vis-a-vis property in question owned and belonging to company and, as such, application filed by them was to be dismissed - Held, yes

Before adverting to the reasoning, the submissions of the parties may be taken note of. [Para 6]

At the very outset it may be considered that while there is no cavil with the settled position that statutory powers cannot be curtailed by orders of Court, the special scheme of the Supreme Court demands a modified application of the powers conferred upon the ED under the PMLA. [Para 14]

■

It is noteworthy to consider that the scheme of the PMLA, as evinced from Sections 5, 8, 9, ends the civil law aspect of PMLA proceedings by vesting the attached and subsequently confiscated properties absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. The insistence of ED to seek for a deemed restitution under Section 8(8) also seems to be misplaced. For clarity, the said provision reads as under: [Para 15]

■

The restitution route provided for under Section 8(8) is an exception and not the rule. A property, under Section 5 of the PMLA, is provisionally attached with the intent of confiscating and vesting it with the Central Govt. It is only when the conditions stipulated under Section 8(8) and Rule 3A of the Confiscation Rules are met that the Special Court can direct the release of properties. This release, during trial, as per sub-rule (1) of Rule 3A, takes place after the framing of the charge under Section 4 of the Act, and post a publication-notice is caused to be made, by the Special Court, in two daily newspapers. Then, the Special Court upon being satisfied of the legitimate interests of a claimant, can order for the release of such a property. [Para 17]

■

It be noted that the Special Court is distinct from the agency which is the ED. It is the Special Court's satisfaction that could warrant a release under Section 8(8) and Rule 3A of the Confiscation Rules. The fact that those recoveries were directed to and retained by the Lodha Committee, for disbursement to investors, is an unambiguous acknowledgment by the ED that the Supreme Court scheme governs these assets and not the PMLA. [Para 18]

Applicant and its two unsecured creditors filed company applications claiming relief with regard to setting aside of aforesaid auction sale - By an order dated 12-2-2004, a committee of unsecured creditors was appointed by Court under Chairmanship of then Company Registrar of Court and other five members, which was to take steps to dispose of specified property of applicant so as to repay dues of unsecured creditors - However, then board of directors of applicant resolved to assign job of intended sale of suit property to ‘N’ and ‘D’, directors of applicant, and ‘P’, who was ex-director of ‘G’ company - Thereafter, suit property was conveyed in favour of ‘G’ company -
