Committee submitted its report on basis of which Court issued notices to respective companies and directed parties, in particular ‘K’ company to maintain status quo of suit property as on that date till disposal of proceedings - Whether since applicant-company was party to proceedings before High Court as well as before executing Court which issued order of attachment and order of sale of suit property, transfer of suit property by applicant in favour of ‘G’ company without seeking permission of Court was illegal and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, ‘G’ company had no valid title in suit property and it could not have validly transferred suit property to ‘K’ company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, sale of suit property was illegal and non-existent and could not be recognised in law - Held, yes - Whether once Court found that suit property was transferred by applicant in violation of order of Court to which it was a party and same was in force, it would necessarily follow that transfer so effected by applicant was illegal and non-existent in law - Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid, instant case was an act of commission and omission in connivance and as a part of conspiracy to act in breach of order of Court to encash property of applicant and also to defeat claims and rights of creditors of applicant - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, criminal action was to be initiated against all erring persons who were directly or indirectly concerned with transaction-in-question, which was intended to overreach orders of Court of law and to defeat claim of creditors - Held, yes - Whether both applicant company and ‘G’ company were to be directed to bring back amount of sale proceeds with interest for payment of same to ‘K’ company and property-in-question was to be reauctioned for payment of dues of creditors - Held, yes

Findings of the inspector's report

The sum and substances of the report submitted by the inspectors as per Section 207 are as follows:

1.

No registered office of the Company was located by the officer during physical inspection.

2.

No books of accounts were produced before the officer despite multiple notices and summons issued to the Company, its directors and statutory auditors.

3.

Shares of the Company were not listed on the stock exchange post its IPO in the year 1996.

4.

Company failed to file the Statutory Returns i.e. Annual financial statements and Annual Returns after the financial year 2015 – 16.

5.

The existing directors of the Company were dummy/shadow directors of the Chairman and were not traceable.

6.

Statement of one of the Directors of the Company proved that he was working as clerk and was induced by the auditor to join the Company as a Director.

7.

Statutory Auditor was not eligible to be appointed as an auditor under Section 141(3)(d) of the Act as his family members are shareholders of the Company.

8.

9.

Analysis & Conclusion

Undoubtedly, the role of the auditor is very vital from the investors' as well as stakeholders' interest point of view as they implicitly trust the financials authenticated by him. The auditor must express his opinion on whether the financial statements give true and fair view of the state of the company's affairs. In reaching his opinion, the auditor must examine the company's books of accounts and related documents, conduct enquiries, collect evidences, detect frauds and so forth. Therefore, it is the duty of the auditor to perform all his statutory obligations with integrity and objectivity. The Tribunal also stated that the auditor owes a fiduciary duty towards the entire Nation.

In the present case, the statutory auditor lacked independence as his family members held shares in the Company which makes him ineligible to become auditor of the Company u/s 141(3)(d). Also, he was negligent in conducting audit and issued his report without proper inspection and examination to which he himself admitted.

Based on the inspection report, the Hon'ble Tribunal opined that the statutory auditor failed to exercise his duties and has certified the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the company without even examining any of the records/ Books of the Account of the Company. Tribunal to prevent any further abuse of power, passed an interim order dated 03.01.2019 removing the auditor from function as statutory auditor of the Company and permitting the Company to replace him with an independent auditor. The Tribunal further held that:

"Statutory Auditor colluded with the Chairman/Director of company and has given a false Audit certificate relating to the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet of the R-2 company, without even examining and verifying the books of accounts, and the Statutory Auditor has not given any plausible explanation for such irresponsible fraudulent activities"

The Tribunal, in exercise of its powers under sections 140(5) and 147(3)(i) of the Act, passed the following order as final stating that the statutory auditor:

1.

shall not be eligible to be appointed as an Auditor of any company for a period of 5 years from the date of passing this order;

2.

shall also be liable for action under Section 447 of the Companies Act, 2013; or

3.

to refund the remuneration received by him, during the period he acted as Auditor, back to the Company.

Evidently, the Hon'ble Tribunal stressed on how the role of statutory auditor is becoming important in detecting and preventing frauds. The Auditors are appointed by the shareholders with a view to report the true picture of the company which enables them to make a well-informed decision. However, if the same auditor gets involved in fraudulent instances it will erase their confidence. Therefore, how the Ministry and the Tribunal are exercising their powers to curb such activities is an appreciable move which is trying to reinstate the faith and confidence in the audit profession.

Code of Criminal Procedure

Sections 155 to 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would oblige the State to act on information received in non-cognizable cases and cognizable cases. Section 157 would lay down the procedure for investigation. Section 158 would suggest a procedure for submission of report. Section 159 onwards would lay down the procedure till the issue is brought to logical conclusion. [Para 53] On a combined reading of the law on the subject and applying it to the present context it is found, the depositors being citizens of the country were entitled to lodge complaint with regard to the non-refund of the deposits that they made with Saradha Group and police would be obliged to act upon such complaint and bring it to logical conclusion in accordance with the procedure laid down under the Code of Criminal Procedure. Similarly, the other Central Agency being SEBI was also empowered to look into the complaint as to whether there was any illegality committed by the company in contravention of the SEBI Act and the Regulations framed thereunder and suggest remedial and penal measures to be adopted by various agencies including State Police if the company failed to act upon their direction as contained in the order passed under Regulation 73. In the instant case, SEBI would contend, time was still there. Hence, it would be premature for them to take further steps in this regard. The company did not have any registration either under the Chit Funds Act or under the SEBI Act and, thus, would attract appropriate penal measures under the relevant provisions of law and Reserve Bank of India would be obliged to advise the State in case their assistance would be needed. Sanchaita Episode

In later part of 1970s Sanchaita Investment, a partnership firm mostly operated in the urban part of the State based in Calcutta. They collected lump sum amounts as and by way of deposit refundable with high returns payable on monthly basis. The firm initially established credence by paying interest to the depositors on the firm date and obviously failed to sustain in absence of appropriate returns of investment that they made either in realty sector or film sector or otherwise. The matter reached up to the Apex Court level. The Apex Court passed an extraordinary order appointing a committee that would have an immense power including that of a Civil Court as well having summary jurisdiction. The committee would be headed by a retired District Judge to be nominated by the Chief Justice having other members on the Board. The committee would be entitled to attach any property either belonging to the firm or its agents or benamidars or anyone having nexus with Sanchaita, after forming an opinion, the property was acquired with Sanchaita money. The Commissioner would invite objection, in case any objection was put against the attachment, such objection would be considered and disposed of by a Division Bench of the High Court to be nominated by the Chief Justice and on a failure to sustain the objection by the objector the property would be sold and the proceeds would be distributed amongst the small objectors. The Civil Court was divested of the power to deal with the issue. The Apex Court passed such order presumably under Article 142. Such power, the High Court does not have. The other similar companies were wound up. In cases where companies were established under the Companies Act, 1956, the Official Liquidator disposed of the assets to pay off the dues of the creditors. [Para 64]

FACT: The case of the revision petitioners was that the first revision petitioner, being a foreign company, had applied to the Reserve Bank of India and as a matter of fact had applied to a foreign bank to invest in the share capital of the first respondent-company. Thereafter, the said foreign company had sent money by way of an inward remittance on two occasions totalling a sum of Rs. 5,87,00,000. After receipt of money, the first respondent/plaintiff-company had filed a return in Form II and had obtained certificates from the statutory auditor and the company secretary disclosing that the first respondent-company had allotted 5,87,000 shares to the first revision petitioner. The revision petitioners further submitted that within a month from the date of receipt of inward remittance by the first respondent-company, it had to allot shares to the first revision petitioner and, therefore, in accordance with the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 the first respondent-company had filed its return in the FGR Form. Out of the funds remitted by the first revision petitioner, the first respondent-company had purchased a land for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000 but the revision petitioners were not posted with information. The revision petitioners contended that to deprive the revision petitioners' investment in share capital of company, the second respondent and his family members had fabricated records as if no allotment was made to the first revision petitioner. The first respondent had also filed a suit filed before the civil court and obtained an interim injunction regarding fact that no shares had been allotted to the first revision petitioner.

On revision petition, the revision petitioners contended that the fraud had been played on the Court by the respondents as they had not disclosed either in the plaint or in the affidavit that the identical issue was pending before the CLB; that the order of the trial Court granting interim injunction was a non-speaking one and, therefore, the High Court could exercise its revisional powers under article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the same to promote substantial cause of justice. The respondent, however, submitted that the petitioners had got a remedy of appeal, in law, before the appropriate forum if they were aggrieved against the order of the trial court and, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the revision petition.

HELD: The term 'fraud' is not employed in a technical sense under the Company Law. It specifies such conduct of affairs as constitutes a discrimination of the shareholders much less of the minority shareholders to be a discriminatory conduct or a fraudulent conduct. As a matter of fact, when no specific remedy is provided under the Companies Act, 1956, the proper remedy is a suit which is to be filed in an appropriate Court, which may be a Court subordinate to the High Court. Indeed, unless a particular matter is specified in the Act to be dealt with by the Company Court it cannot exercise its jurisdiction merely because it is also a matter which relates to the company. [Para 28]

It is an axiomatic fact that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil court is not to be readily inferred and such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied, as per principles of statutory interpretation. [Para 29]

Where the investors in a private limited company are fictitious entities or untraceable, can the Department invoke confiscation proceedings under benami Act (PBPT Act, 1988) instead of the 1st proviso (2nd proviso w.e.f. AY 2023-24) to section 68?

In Macro Entertainment (P) Ltd. v. Union of India [2017] 87 taxmann.com 360 (Calcutta), the Initiating Officer (IO) issued a show cause notice u/s 24(1) of the PBPT Act which inter alia read as under:

"Material on record, marked as Annexure V, reveal that the entities which provided the consideration are either fictitious or non-traceable. It is evident from the above facts and circumstances that the consideration related to the transactions of the property in concern is provided by another person and it is held for the future benefit of another person whose identity is not known.

The above conditions satisfy the definition of the Benami transaction u/s 2(9) of the PBPT Act, 1988. Thus I have reason to believe and I am satisfied that the property in the form of Flat having details discussed above, is a Benami property as per section 2(8) of the PBPT Act, 1988."

The notice under Section 24(1) was answered by the Writ Petitioner/Company. The Company denied that the provisions of the 1988 Act are at all applicable to the facts of the present case. The Company took the stand that, if at all, the IO has jurisdiction only to inquire under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act (for short the IT Act). The reply to the Section 24(1) notice (supra) was finally considered by the IO vide his order under Section 24(4) of the 1988 Act. The IO, inter alia, concluded that both the paper and the fund trails connecting to the purchase of the scheduled property in issue, inter alia, point to fictitious/non-transparent/non-visible entities. The IO found, on the basis of the available materials, that the funds utilised in the name of the Company to purchase the property in issue belonged to person/persons whose identities have not been disclosed. The usufructs of the purchase, although ostensibly in the name of the Company, may be ultimately beneficial to the non-transparent/Fictitious/non-visible entities behind the suspected benami purchase. Therefore, the IO ordered that the provisional attachment under section 24(3) shall continue till the Adjudicating Authority (for short AA) further adjudicates under section 24(3) of the 1988 Act.

The company filed a writ petition challenging the initiation of proceedings by IO under section 24(1) and attachment of property under section 24(4) and reference to Adjudicating Authority. The company contended that, in view of the decision reported in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 at Paragraph 7 thereof, the question of fictitious entities behind the fund alleged to have been utilised by the Company for the purchase of the property in issue would not be attracted in law since, such fictitious entities are not referable to the shareholders of the Company, who carry no fiduciary interest connected to the property of the Company. The law as elucidated in AIR 1955 SC Page 74 (supra), inter alia, permits the shareholders to only participate in the profits of the Company in the form of dividends without being required to exercise any participatory involvement in its immovable assets. Therefore, the fundamentals of the proceeding initiated by the IO under section 24(1) and 24(4) are misconceived. The Respondents/Revenue contended that the profile of the investments made by the Company as evident from the facts collected by the IO connected to the purchase of the scheduled property traces its source to funds from fictitious entities which are required to be identified. On the basis of the materials available to the IO, the Company is believed to be acting as the benamidar, or, apropo the current lingo in vogue of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), Government of India, a shell or "dabba" company of investors at large.

Section 543 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Winding up - Power of court to assess damages against delinquent directors, etc. - Court is competent to proceed against non-resident foreigner directors and pass a decree   In an application under section 235 of the 1913 Act the Court can be asked to examine into the conduct of non-resident foreigner directors and compel them to pay the amount in respect of which they have committed breach of trust. The proceeding is in the nature of a suit for recovery of monies wrongfully converted by a person who happens to be a non-resident foreigner. If this proceeding is instituted by way of a suit, the provisions of sections 19 and 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable and since the cause of action arises within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, though the defendants - the persons who are liable to account - reside in a foreign territory, a suit can very well be laid and summons served in the manner provided by the rules and a decree can be passed. This does not necessarily involve any process to compel his attendance in order to submit himself for examination. If on the receipt of notice served in the manner provided under the rules, the concerned director does not choose to appear, the Court can come to a conclusion on the material placed before it on behalf of the applicant as to the conduct of the director in the matter and decide about his liability to the applicant or to the company and an order can be made directing the particular director to bring in any amount which he has misapplied, retained or in respect of which he has committed breach of trust or misfeasance which order will be in the nature of a decree. How and in what manner the decree will be treated by the foreign Court is immaterial, for, the decree is nevertheless valid though it may be treated as a nullity by the foreign Court. It is also equally unnecessary to consider whether such a decree can be enforced against such director. The Court is competent to pass such a decree by virtue of the local or municipal law governing the exercise of such jurisdiction. If the concerned director has any properties within the jurisdiction of the State, such an order can very well be executed against those properties and if there are no such properties, the order will have the same force and effect as a decree passed in a suit against a non-resident foreigner.

In instant writ, filed as public interest litigation, petitioner sought that State Government be directed to promulgate an Investor Protection Act. It was contended that about 3600 plantation companies promising uncon-scionably high returns had collected approximately Rs. 25,000 crores from poor investors. Money was not returned and post-dated cheques issued by these companies returned. It was further contended that these companies diverted deposits to non-agricultural use. However, there was no platform for redressing grievance of depositors. Therefore, promulga-tion of Act become necessary.

By an intermediate order the High Court had earlier empowered SEBI to issue advertisement against investment in such companies and the plantation companies were prohibited from publishing advertisement unless it carried a credit rating from an Accredited Rating Agency. It was also directed to State Government to issue circular to all revenue offices to prevent purchase of lands by such companies. However, in a number of other petitions various interim orders were also passed to enquire about functioning of such companies, its assets and directing attachment of bank accounts, etc. The State Government was directed to issue circulars to all revenue officers to take appropriate actions before mutation entries are made in case of such companies. The Governmental representative made statement during hearing that very recently the Government would pass an appropriate legislation to protect the interest of depositors, and the directors and promoters of these companies would be personally liable for the investment made. Section 542 imposes liability of fraudulent conduct of business by the ex-directors, found in the course of winding up ofthe company (in liquidation). The Official Liquidator or the creditor or contributory may file an application on which the court may declare that the persons, who were knowingly parties to the conduct of the business in the manner to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, shall be personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for all or any of the debts or other liabilities of the company. Section 543 gives the power to the court to assess damages against the delinquent directors. These powers can be exercised when it is found in the course of winding up petition that any past or present directors, managers, liquidators or officers had misapplied or retained or have become liable or accountable for any money or property of the company; or have been guilty of any misfeasance or breach of trust in relation to the company. [Para 7]

The Central Government, in its statutory exercise of powers under section 209A, carried out the inspections in the year 1994. Those powers had been conceded by the statutes to the Central Government for inspection of accounts of the company. The company was running into losses. There were many allegations of misfeasance and misappropriation of the company funds against the ex-directors. The report of the Deputy Director (Inspections) or the Regional Director (NR) of the Department of Company Affairs provided the details of the inspections. [Para 8]

Reporting contraventions of sections 295 and 292, it was observed in the inspections that the promoter directors and their relatives were maintaining their personal accounts in the books of the company which revealed several transactions in the nature of loans. They were withdrawing and depositing huge amount from/with the company and the company was making payments on their behalf to third parties by way of debiting to their personal accounts. Similarly, the relatives of those directors also withdrew funds of the company. The company paid interest on the loans taken from the directors, but charged no interest on the amounts advanced/lent to the directors. The inspecting officer suggested that inspections be also made under section 209A, in connection with the other group concerns detailed in the report. [Para 11]

The report detailed the contravention of section 372. The company had made various investments. [Para 12]

The company failed to make the statutory entry of the investments with Registrar within seven days. The contravention with regard to section 299/301 was recorded. It was also found that they had contravened section 43A inasmuch as during the years ending 30-6-1983, 30-6-1984 and 30-6-1985, the turnover was Rs. 6,64,483, Rs. 1,23,27,937 and Rs. 2,16,36,263, respectively, which turnover attracted the provisions of section 43A and that the company became a public limited company with effect from 1-10-1995, but the management and auditors of the company treated the company as a private company till the year 1998-99 and up to 27-11-1999, the date on which ROC changed the certificate of incorporation. [Para 13]

All those and other statutory violations and withholding of large amount of money without interest amounted to misfeasance within the meaning of sections 542 and 543. The business of the company with turnover in crores of rupees was run and managed as a private company; the amounts were advanced to the directors without interest and/or retained by them for long periods; the investments were made and shares were sold without seeking approval of the board of directors. The company ultimately went into severe losses and was wound up by the Court. [Para 14]

The findings in the inspections supported by the accounts of the company annexed to the application prima facie amounted to violation of section 542/543. Therefore, the preliminary objection did not have any force and the same was to be rejected. [Para 15]

The respondents were, thus, to be charged accordingly. [Para 16]

6. The Indian Financial Code, drafted by the Financial Sector Legislative Commission, would address these issues in the following ways:

The whole system of investigation is formalised under an investigator appointed by the regulator. The terms of reference for the investigator, the system of investigation and the time for investigation have to be written down at the onset. Since all incomplete investigations will require extensions, there will be system of raising alarms for an unusually long investigation – (see draft clause 394 of the IFC). The Code would allow the investigator to apply for a warrant for the search and seizure of documents. The investigator does not have to go to the area where the scheme is operating. He can apply for a warrant to the Magistrate where the head office of the regulator is situated. This allows the government to create a special Magistrate's office. This Magistrate can be trained in issues of finance and fraud and serve as a proper judicial check for warrants (see draft clause 396 of the IFC).

The Code also allows the financial agency to make an order preventing transfer of any money or assets pending an investigation, if there is a reasonable fear that the assets of clients are at risk. Any violation of such orders is also punishable by imprisonment up to five years (see draft clause 398 of the IFC).

The Code empowers the Central Government to set-up special Courts to try cases involving the violation of investment laws. This allows for far quicker and more efficient disposal of cases. These Courts will be district Courts and would follow all due process of law required under the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code. However, unlike general Criminal Courts, Judges in these Courts can be experts in securities and investment laws (see draft clause 417 of the IFC).

Finally, the Code envisages that the financial sector regulator appoints its own lawyers to prosecute cases of criminal offences. These lawyers will have the same powers as a prosecuting lawyers under the criminal procedure law. Since most financial regulators have legal officers on staff today, this allows specialised expertise to head the prosecution of these crimes, rather than a generalist public prosecutor.

The strategy used in the IFC is similar to that used in securities laws in the U.S., where dedicated federal Court benches are used to prosecute securities frauds. Even in India, special Courts and prosecutors have been created for the CBI and for prosecution of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The longer a Ponzi scheme lingers on the more victims it would accumulate. The Indian Financial Code provides a system to effectively shut down schemes like these ones and a specialised criminal law system to prosecute violators.

The loss of critical savings by many people have raised demand for retribution. A hurried response to such demands can be bringing in laws which dilute the principle of 'innocent until proved guilty' or reduce the procedural and evidentiary standards. The Code scrupulously avoids this by placing the power of issuing warrants and convicting offences on the same standards as are envisaged in the laws of evidence and criminal procedure. However, it addresses the problems of a slow judicial system and dedicated expertise in resolving financial crimes.

Defining financial products and services

7. In the IFC, the definitions of financial products and services are broad ones and principles-based, with no statutory exemptions. All kinds of deposit-taking and investment schemes (including chit funds) are covered by these definitions. A deposit is defined as a contribution of money, made other than for the purpose of acquiring a security, which may be re-payable on the demand of the contributor. In section 2(90), an investment scheme means following:

"any arrangement with respect to property of any description, including money, the purpose or effect of which is to enable persons taking part in the arrangement, whether by becoming owners of the property or any part of it or otherwise, to participate in or receive profits or income arising from the acquisition, holding, management or disposal of the property or sums paid out of such profits or income, where:

persons participating in such schemes do not have day-to-day control over the management of the property, whether or not they have the right to be consulted or to give directions; and

the arrangement has either or both of the following characteristics:

the contributions of the participants and the profits or income out of which payments are to be made to them are pooled; or

the property is managed as a whole by or on behalf of the operator of the scheme."

Anyone in the business of accepting deposits or managing investment schemes would need to get authorisation from the UFA. Accordingly, both Saradha and MMM would be covered under the IFC, the former as a deposit-taking firm, and the latter one as an investment scheme. In case of the MMM scheme, a unit of MAVRO is the underlying property in which the members invest in. The other tests of the definition are also met as the member of the scheme do not have the ability to control the unit, which is managed by the operators of the scheme.

The IFC also empowers the Central Government to expand the definitions of financial products and services. When a new financial product or service is taken note of, instead of waiting for an amendment to the law, the Central Government can include the new product or service in the definition.

Section 5(1)(d) of the WBPIDFE Act provides that where the State Government is satisfied that any financial establishment committing a default in repayment of deposit fraudulently, has transferred any of the property otherwise then in good faith and for consideration, it may in order to protect the interest of the depositors of such financial establishment by an order to be published in official gazette and recording reasons in writing attach the money or other property acquired either in the name of such financial establishment or in the name of any other person on behalf of such financial establishment. [Para 27]

Sub-section (5) of section 5 of the WBPIDFE Act provides that the Competent Authority may make an application to Special Court or Designated Court for adjudicating any issue or subject matter pertaining to money or property or assets belonging to or ostensibly belonging to a financial establishment or any person mentioned in the order under sub-section (1) situated within the territorial jurisdiction of the Designated Court may be, for passing appropriate orders to give effect to the provisions. [Para 28]

Section 14 of the WBPIDFE Act provides the powers of Designated Court regarding attachment. Section 14(1) provides that upon receipt of an application under sub-section (4) of section 5, the Designated Court shall issue to the Financial establishment or to the person, whose property has been attached and vested in the competent authority under section 5, a notice accompanied by a copy of the application and affidavit together with an extract of evidence calling upon such financial establishment and person to show cause as to why the order of attachment should not be made absolute and property so attached sold in public auction. Section 14(3) provides that any person claiming an interest in the property attached or any portion thereof, may notwithstanding that no notice has been served upon him under this sub-section, raise an objection as aforesaid before the designated court at any time before an order is passed under sub-section (5) or sub-section (6). [Para 29]

With the aforesaid provisions, it is clear that under the WBPIDFE Act, the property acquired either in the name of a financial establishment or in the name of any other person on behalf of such financial establishment can also be attached. In the present case, the property of the corporate debtor is attached on the allegation that corporate debtor is one of the Companies of Group and the Group had fraudulently accepted the deposits and all the money went to corporate debtor and the corporate debtor had purchased the attached properties with the money of the depositors. In this regard, the appellant placed reliance on the findings of the designated court. [Para 30]

Prima facie, it appears that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and such other Companies, which are mushrooming in the country under the corporate veil, are committing fraud by tempting middle-class persons to invest their life-long savings in the high hope of having fanciful returns, without there being any basis. It appears that, because of these empty false promises, investors are duped and the Companies' monies are siphoned off either to sister Companies or firms of the directors or their relatives.

9. In the case of Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction (P.) Ltd. 1996 AIR SCW 2401, the Apex Court has referred to the discussion on the topic of corporate veil in Palmer's Company Law and has quoted with approval the observations that Courts have shown themselves willing to lifting the veil where the device of incorporation is used for some illegal or improper purpose. The Court has also considered the concept of corporate entity and held that where the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the entity with regard to corporate Company and its association of men and women and will do justice between the real persons. After discussing other authorities, the Court has observed that the concept of corporate entity was evolved to encourage and promote trade and commerce but not to commit illegalities or to defraud people and held as follows :—

"Where, therefore, the corporate character is employed for the purpose of committing illegality or for defrauding others, the Court would ignore the corporate character and will look at the reality behind the corporate veil so as to enable it to pass appropriate orders to do justice between the parties concerned. The fact that Tejwant Singh and members of his family have created several corporate bodies does not prevent this Court from treating all of them as one entity belonging to and controlled by Tejwant Singh and family if it is found that these corporate bodies are merely cloaks behind which lurks Tejwant Singh and/or members of his family and that the device of incorporation was really a ploy adopted for committing illegalities and/or to defraud people."

Power of Company Law Board to review: On behalf of ORE and Athappan, it was mainly contended that the CLB has no power to review its own order, especially, in the guise of a clarification. [Para 137] It is fairly well-settled that the CLB does not have the power of review. It is, however, open to the CLB to exercise its inherent powers and to make such orders as may seem necessary to meet the ends of justice. The CLB has power to review and recall its orders which have been wangled through fraud or misrepresentation. [Para 141]

In its earlier order dated 13-8-2008, the CLB has recorded categorical findings:- (i) conduct of KCP having regarded CEPL's funds as though his own funds is burdensome, harsh and wrongful; (ii) movement of funds from CEPL as traced by the auditors is not supported by any approvals from the Board of CEPL. (iii) KCP had taken enormous steps in safeguarding and enhancing the value of CPL properties as well as bringing VML out of sickness thereby saving its vast extent of properties and settling all dues of workmen which is in contravention of the JVA/Articles of CEPL. (iv) KCP is accountable for not having diligently discharged its statutory duties cast on him. On those factual findings, in its order dated 13-8-2008, CLB observed that the very purpose of CEPL could not have been achieved in terms of JVA and in the light of those factual findings directed CEPL to return a sum of Rs. 75 crores and Rs.4 crores invested by ORE and Athappans respectively along with interest at 8 per cent. In the said order, the CLB also permitted KCP to utilise the money to return the said amount to ORE and Athappans and in the meanwhile directing that VML shall not alienate or sell any of its immovable properties till payment is made to ORE. The CLB also made provision that in the event of failure to make the repayment within the specified time, CEPL, CGH, KCP and VML were to duly convey the immovable properties of VML, i.e., 17.15 acres of land in favour of ORE and 7.80 acres of land in favour of Athappans. When the CLB has recorded categorical findings that CEPL neither carried out nor could accomplish its business plan in accordance with terms of JVA and directed return of sum of Rs.75 crores and Rs.4 crores, it was not justified in modifying its earlier order permitting KCP to deal with 50 per cent of the money lying with State Bank of India. [Para 142]

Given the sequence of events, if KCP is placed in position to manage CEPL, he would again try to divert the amount to innumerable subsidiary companies floated by him, the CLB was not justified in directing ORE and NA to deposit the share certificates with the Bench Officer. Having found that KCP had not discharged his statutory duties and that he was not prudent in managing CEPL, the CLB was not justified in directing payment of 50 per cent of the deposit lying with the State Bank of India. [Para 143]

HELD: Section 210 empowers the Central Government to investigate into the affairs of a company/(companies), if it is of the opinion that such investigation is necessary for the reasons mentioned therein, including public interest. For the purpose of the said provision, the Central Government may appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate into the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The SFIO has been established under section 211 of the Companies Act, 2013, which has jurisdiction to investigate into the company/(companies), where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary to investigate into the affairs of a company by the SFIO for different reasons, including the public interest. Where any case has been assigned by the Central Government to the SFIO for investigation under the Act, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or any State Government can proceed with investigation in such case in respect of any offence under the Companies Act and other cases before such agency are required to transfer the relevant documents and records in respect of such offences under the Companies Act to the SFIO. Sub-section (8) of section 211 empowers certain Officers of the SFIO to arrest any person, if on the basis of material in his possession there is reason to believe, which is to be recorded in writing, that any person has been guilty of any offence punishable under sub-section (6) of section 212. [Para 30]

Investigation into company's affairs in other cases can also be done under section 213 on an application made by the eligible members as mentioned in clause (a) of section 213 or on an application made by any other person or otherwise, if it is satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company etc. has been conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213. [Para 31]

From section 213, it is clear that the Tribunal on an application made to it or 'otherwise', if satisfied that there are circumstances suggesting that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members etc. as mentioned in clause (b) of section 213, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, direct the Central Government to investigate. [Para 32]

From section 221, it is clear that the Tribunal has power to direct that the transfer, removal or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company shall not take place during such period not exceeding three years'. In case of any removal, transfer or disposal of funds, assets, or properties of the company in contravention of the order of the Tribunal under sub-section (1) of section 221, the company is punishable with fine and imprisonment as prescribed under sub-section (2) of section 221. Introduction

The Supreme Court's recent judgment in National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) v. Union of India & Ors (Writ Petition (Civil) No. 995 of 2019) is a landmark in the domain of financial fraud litigation and asset recovery. The decision, delivered on 15 May 2025, addresses the complex interplay between the Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (MPID) Act, the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), and central statutes such as the SARFAESI Act, Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

At its core, this decision represents a careful recalibration of the legal hierarchy between secured creditors, government agencies, and public interest protections in cases involving tainted assets.

Background: The NSEL Scam and Legal Tangle

NSEL, a commodity trading platform promoted by 63 Moons Technologies Ltd. The collapse of the National Spot Exchange in 2013 triggered a Rs. 5,600 crore default, affecting about 13,000 traders and investors. The fallout led to multiple FIRs, civil suits, and the attachment of assets by both the Enforcement Directorate (under PMLA) and the State of Maharashtra (under the MPID Act). The NSEL itself secured decrees and arbitral awards worth around Rs. 3,365 crore against defaulting members, but faced significant hurdles in executing them due to overlapping attachments and competing claims from secured creditors (primarily banks) under SARFAESI/RDB Act. IBC proceedings also initiated against several entities.

Genesis of the Supreme Court Committee

To streamline the complex situation, involving execution of multiple decrees and avoid conflicting proceedings, the Supreme Court, invoking Article 142, constituted a high-powered committee chaired by Justice (Retd.). This committee was vested with the powers of a civil court to execute all decrees, orders, and arbitral awards obtained by NSEL, including the authority to sell properties attached under PMLA and MPID Act and oversee distribution to verified claimants. In short, Article 142 was used as a constitutional "safety valve" to harmonize conflicting statutory regimes, centralize execution, and prioritize investor restitution in a manner that ordinary statutory processes could not have achieved efficiently.

Power under Article 142 is extraordinary, discretionary, and unique to the Supreme Court. It allows the Court to:

Fill legal gaps where no statute provides an adequate remedy. It Complements statutory law, but does not override it—cannot be used to violate or contradict existing statutes

Issue binding directions, even if not strictly aligned with procedural law. Curative in nature—used to resolve issues when ordinary law falls short or causes injustice

Craft equitable solutions, especially in complex, multi-party, or sensitive matters.

However, Article 142 cannot be used to create a new law or override substantive rights conferred by legislation. It must be used judiciously and only when regular statutory or procedural remedies are inadequate or unjust. Article 142 cannot be used to achieve something indirectly what cannot be achieved directly.

While initially hailed as a pragmatic consolidation, the order's breadth brought it into direct strain with key statutory provisions of PMLA, SARFAESI, RDB Act, and IBC—particularly regarding the priority of secured creditors and the moratorium under insolvency law.

Key Legal Questions before the Supreme Court

Two main issues crystallized before the Court in the later stages of the litigation:

1.

Do secured creditors have priority over assets attached under the PMLA and MPID Act by virtue of SARFAESI and RDB Act?

2.

Are properties attached under the MPID Act immune from the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC?

These questions weren't just technical—they strike at the heart of India's recovery framework, challenging the hierarchy of creditor rights in fraud scenarios.

Supreme Court's Ruling on Secured Creditors' Priority

The Court held that the MPID Act and PMLA take precedence over the SARFAESI Act and RDB Act when it comes to assets attached as "proceeds of crime" or for the protection of depositors. The rationale is rooted in constitutional law: the MPID Act is a state law enacted to maintain public order and protect depositors, while SARFAESI and RDB Act are central laws focusing on banking and secured creditors' rights. Since these statutes operate in distinct legislative fields, the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254 does not apply.

When the company failed to return nearly Rs. 18 crores collected from thousands of depositors, one of the creditors filed petition for winding-up of the company. In the meantime, the company filed an application under section 391 for obtaining sanction to a scheme of compromise, which was refused by the court. The court, however, formulated a scheme for running the business without allowing to receive fresh deposits and appointed provisional liquidator. The company had diverted a huge amount to its sister company by unlawful means in violation of the provisions of law and the directions issued by the Reserve Bank of India. Despite repeated directions of the court, the company and its managing director did not furnish the books of account, registers and the securities including the gold to the Official Liquidator, and even those registers which were produced before the Official Liquidator, were found to be forged and fabricated with false entries. The court, thereupon, passed an order directing the crime branch police to register a case and to recover the books of account, register, etc. It also issued certain directions to the effect that all the genuine registers, account books, etc., should be seized/recovered and that the investigating officer should further enquire whether any properties had been acquired by the directors in the name of others as benami with the company's funds. Further, it would be open to him to arrest the respondent-managing director as well as directors of the company. The police, accordingly, registered a criminal case against the directors of the company as well as accused 5 and 6 who had joined them in diverting considerable sum to a sister concern. Subsequently, the court directed that all matters including bail matters, should be placed before the company court. At that stage the company court found it necessary to give notice to all the accused, why the bail granted to all of them should not be cancelled. The case of the accused was that the company court had no jurisdiction to cancel the bail which was granted by another bench of the court and the petition for cancellation of bail should also go before the same bench which granted the bail.

A complaint was received from an investor alleging that the complainant had been induced for making investments. The promoters and senior management of National Spot Exchange Limited (NSEL) made false representations and assurances with a deliberate intention to dishonestly misappropriate his funds and the complainant had been cheated by NSEL.

An ECIR was registered by the Enforcement Directorate and investigation was undertaken under the Act. Consequent to the investigation, provisional attachment order was passed by the Enforcement Directorate. In the said order the plant of Naraingarh Sugar Mills, comprising of land and machinery were attached.

The appellant, a government company, submitted that the related co-generation project had been set-up with the loan of the appellant. The sugar project which was sought to be attached was a part of the security against the financial assistance granted by the appellant, and was made, constructed and built, out of the loan amount of the appellant and different lenders, which were nationalized banks, and none of the alleged funds raised out of alleged money laundering were available with the accused at that point of time. As such all those assets were built out of the due and valid legal modes. Those assets were under the charge of the appellant as security for the term loan of Rs. 10,339 lakhs for setting up of co-generation project.

The appellant was not made a party either in original complaint or by the Adjudicating Authority. However, when the appellant came to know about the pendency of the adjudication of the original complaint before the Adjudicating Authority, on the information of the Enforcement Directorate, the appellant appeared and contested the proceedings.

However, the Adjudicating Authority confirmed the provisional attachment order holding that the property which had been attached were involved in money laundering and that the defendants were in possession of proceeds of crime and that the defendants had committed the scheduled offences, generated proceeds of crime and laundered them.

| 'Property'/Section 452 of the 2013 Act |  | Beguram v. Jaipur Udhyog Ltd. [1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 744 (Raj.) The word 'property' used in section 630(1)(a) of the 1956 Act [corresponding to section 452(1)(a) of the 2013 Act] includes within its purview both movable as well as immovable property and there are no words, express or implied, in this section which can restrict the application of the word 'property' to only movable property. The words 'deliver up' very well apply to the delivering up of the possession of immovable property. These words are on the other hand, indicative of the fact that immovable properties are also covered in the scope of section 630 of the 1956 Act. Harkishin Lakhimal Gidwani v. Achyut Kashinath Wagh [1982] 52 Comp. Cas. 1 (Bom.) The user of both the terms 'any such property' and 'wrongfully obtained' would strongly indicate that both are independent of each other and not mutually inclusive or overlapping. The term 'any such property' in section 630(2) of the 1956 Act [corresponding to section 452(2) of the 2013 Act] governs all the three categories and is not restricted to only one, viz., 'wrongfully obtained'. Baldev Krishna Sahi v. Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd. [1988] 63 Comp. Cas. 1 (SC) There is no warrant for the constraction placed by the High Court of Calcutta in Amritlal Churr's case [1987] 61 Comp. Cas. 211 on the words 'any such property' in clause (b) to section 630(1) of the 1956 Act [corresponding to section 452 of the 2013 Act] as applicable to 'such property' of a company, possession of which is wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the company, i.e., refers to the whole of clause (b). According to the plain construction, the words 'any such property' in clause (b) relate to any property of a company as mentioned in clause (a). |

25.7-16-1 RECOVERY OF DAMAGES OR PROPERTY [SECTION 244] - If warranted in public interest in the opinion of the Central Government on perusal of the Inspector’s report, that any proceedings should be initiated for the recovery of damages or property due to any fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct in connection with the promotion or management of the affairs of the company or body corporate investigated, the Central Government may itself bring the proceedings for the purpose. 25.7-16-2 EXPENSES OF INVESTIGATION [SECTION 245] - The costs of investigation are met in the first instance by the Central Government and reclaimed from the persons who are prosecuted and convicted as ordered by the Court convicting him, or in whole or in part of the expenses as may be decided by the Central Government from the company or body corporate to the extent of its property recovered and restored; and if no prosecution is instituted, the expenses are recoverable from the company/managing director/manager indicated in the Inspector’s report, as well as the applicants if the investigation arose out of section 235(2). The amount levied against the company or body corporate against property restored forms a first charge on such property, and in other cases the claim ranks as arrears of land revenue by operation of law, any shortfall in such recovery going to be met from the moneys provided by the Parliament.

Further, the expenses in respect of investigation of ownership shall be met from the funds of the Central Government unless it decides to recover the same from the applicants who sought the investigation of ownership, for which there is no express provision in the section enabling anyone to apply to the Central Government but implied as permissible, section 247(5) and (6).

Presumptive Restrictions/Prohibition on Transfers [Section 250/187D]

25.7-18 In connection with any investigation of ownership of shares/debentures under section 247 and on its conclusion the following presumptive restrictions may be imposed displacing the burden of proof from prosecution on to the Companies for any relief against it following the most extreme threat against companies wrong doers, provided under the Act :

(i) the Central Government or any person may make a reference to the Tribunal, or any person may make a complaint to the Tribunal, in that behalf, in either case showing that there is good reason to find out the relevant facts about any shares/debentures, whether issued or to be issued by the company. Section 187D confers power on the Central Government co-extensive with section 250 to investigate the beneficial ownership of shares of any company. In either case if the Tribunal comes to the same opinion, it may by order direct that the related shares/debentures shall be subject to the following presumptive restrictions for a period not exceeding three years as it may determine and serve the order on the company within 14 days of its passing :

u Any transfer of the shares/debentures shall be void;

u Where those shares/debentures are to be issued, they shall not be issued; and any issue thereof or any transfer of the right to be issued therewith, shall be void;

u No voting right shall be exercisable in respect of those shares;

u No further shares shall be issued in right of those shares or in pursuance of any offer made to the holder thereof; and any issue of such shares or any transfer of the right to be issued therewith, shall be void; and

u Except in a liquidation, no payment shall be made of any sums due from the company on those shares, whether in respect of dividend, capital or otherwise.

(ii) Where as a result of a transfer of shares/debentures that took place a change in the composition of the Board of directors of the company is likely to take place, and the Tribunal is of the opinion that any such change would be prejudicial to the public interest, it may by its order impose the following restrictions valid up to three years as it may determine, and serve the order on the company within 14 days of its passing :

u The voting rights in respect of those shares shall not be exercisable for such period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the order;

u No resolution passed or action taken to effect a change in the composition of the Board of directors before the date of the order shall have effect unless confirmed by the Tribunal.

(iii) If the Tribunal has reasonable ground to believe that there is an impending transfer of shares/debentures in a company to bring about a change in the composition of the company’s Board of directors and is of the opinion that any such change would be prejudicial to public interest, it may direct that any such transfer shall be void in the period next up to three years as it may determine and serve the order on the company within 14 days of its passing.

The first petitioner, a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) registered under the Companies Act, 1956 having its registered office in Madhya Pradesh, was promoted by the second respondent with the objectives of carrying on the business of financing, money-lending, bills discounting, hire-purchasing, leasing, etc. The company evolved a scheme known as SFDR whereunder deposits collected from the investors were to be utilized for allotment of shares to them and also to be invested in other companies. The petitioners alleged that they collected non-interest yielding/profit-sharing investments in the form of equity and invested in equity shares. According to them, there were baseless rumours of cheating against first petitioner and, therefore, some of the members of public filed complaints against them in various police stations. It was alleged that there were serious threats to their lives and in spite of repeated requests to the SHOs to extend proper protection, the police officer was instead of protecting the petitioners, were compelling them to repay deposits collected by the company, and that some investors had attacked the office of the second petitioner and threatened him with physical abuses. Therefore the petitioners sought protection from third respondent - police officer. The third respondent, on the other hand, denied all the allegations.

On writ, the petitioners sought for relief (i) to declare the action of the respondents in not taking necessary prohibitive steps for the safety of the petitioners as illegal and unconstitutional, (ii) to declare the action of respondents in calling upon the petitioners to make payments on the basis of civil transactions between petitioners and their investors/shareholders as arbitrary, illegal and unjust and violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 14, 19, 20 and 21 of the Constitution of India and constitutional guarantees under articles 50 and 300A of the Constitution of India; (iii) to issue a direction to first respondent, namely, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), New Delhi, to centralize all the alleged complaints against petitioners, if any, and carry out investigation in accordance with law, (iv) to issue a consequential direction to police to take such steps as were necessary for protection of petitioners and not to harass petitioners on the back of civil complaints; and (v) to direct respondents to carry out their investigations, if any, on the complaints against petitioners strictly in accordance with the procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

The Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner to take charge of the movable and immovable properties, who after visiting various places, reported that there were no substantial money deposits in the name of the company but there were deposits in the name of the second petitioner’s wife and personal accounts. According to the report, properties were sold under Revenue Recovery Act by the bank, cold storage units were still under construction and the Indore office was seized by the police in some criminal case. A letter from a depositor informed that all the depositors belonged to New Delhi and Indore, and that they were cheated by the petitioners against whom FIR was lodged at New Delhi. The Inspector of Crime Branch, New Delhi, enclosed a list of 94 investors who were cheated and all of them did not belong to Andhra Pradesh.

On the basis of the earlier order of the Court the properties of the directors of Respondent No. 1 were attached. Further, the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Economic Offences Wing, Crime Branch, Mumbai, had carried out investigation which revealed that, out of Rs. 1,893.54 lakhs collected only Rs. 482.23 lakhs were expended fruitfully for business operations of the company. The investigation also revealed in detail the mismanagement by the directors of the respondent No. 1 company. As the investigation was still in progress, no further directions were required to be issued for the present.

However, considering the facts narrated above and various other similar petitions filed before the Court complaining against the mismanagement by such companies and their directors, the Central Government or the State Government would have to take appropriate action in framing appropriate Regulations/enactment as early as possible as suggested by the petitioner and respondent No. 6.

It would be open to the official liquidator to take physical possession of the premises located at Goregaon and Malad which were under his lock and key.

At this stage, it would be relevant to refer the order of the Apex Court. The order produced before this Tribunal is dated 28-3-2023 where a detailed order was passed for settling the dues of the investors and therein it was made clear that the property attached by the ED can be released for realization of the dues if the prospective purchasers are willing to deposit the amount of Rs.641 crores and in that case, the attachment of the ED would be lifted but leaving the parties to take remedies for their respective rights. The detailed order is, however, passed by this Tribunal to clarify the claim of the appellants. With the aforesaid observation, there is no case to cause interference in the orders. The appeals accordingly fail and are dismissed. [Para 29]

The petitioner, who was a homebuyer, claimed to have purchased a plot from ‘TCSPL’, in a real estate project named ‘Greenopolis’, which was envisioned to be developed in Gurugram, Haryana. Petitioner filed writ petition against TCSPL and its Ex-promoters / directors / management, accusing them of allegedly siphoning off approximately Rs. 1,664 crores collected from innocent homebuyers into its various shell/sister concerns. This misappropriation led to TCSPL being subjected to proceedings under the IBC before the NCLT with nearly 536 investors/claimants/homebuyers lodging their claims before the IRP.

■

While the matter was pending before the NCLT, three reports were submitted by the IRP and the Status Report, which, inter alia demonstrated as to how and in what manner the Ex promoters/directors/management of TCSPL had been siphoning off the funds.

■

The petitioner vide said petition was seeking invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of Writ Court under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, 1950, seeking certain directions against Registrar of Companies (RoC) and Union of India (UoI) through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for taking cognizance, initiation and conduction of appropriate inquiries and investigation against the management of TCSPL, as well as its shell/sister group of companies, for alleged action of manipulation of records and siphoning of funds to shell/sister companies based in Kolkata and elsewhere. Additionally, the petitioner sought reliefs in the nature of freezing the assets of such unscrupulous companies and their promoters/directors to safeguard the legal rights of the investors/claimants/homebuyers like the petitioner.

■

This, to safeguard the interest of the petitioner, as well as other similarly placed investors/claimants /homebuyers, RoC and UoI, were conjointly directed to initiate action and ensure step-wise compliance in terms of Section 206 to 210 of the Companies Act, 2013 and other analogous provisions in Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013, and thereby inspect the affairs of TCSPL and the related.

■

During the course of proceedings before Writ Court, an application was moved on behalf of the ACE Group, a renowned Real Estate Developer in Delhi and NCR for impleadment, which was allowed. Subsequently, ACE Group moved an application for the recall of the order. Prior to this, TCSPL had also moved an application to recall / modification of order.

■

The ACE Group submitted that although the order was directed at RoC and UoI to inspect the affairs of the TCSPL, they were directly affected, as the IRP had endeavoured to reclaim or repossess certain properties belonging to them, which have no nexus or connection with the TCSPL.

■

According to ACE Group, impugned order had wrongly portrayed it as a proxy of TCSPL. It was further stated that penal provisions under the Companies Act, 2013, appear to have been set in motion against the ACE Group of Companies without impleading them or issuing notice.

they raised loans initially to pool up the sale consideration. When they realised that the debt burden was mounting day-by-day, they sold off this very property to ‘V’. However, now the additional material papers certificates from the mandal revenue officer were produced to show that they were oozing with excessive cash yielded by their Horticultural activities. Was it not said that ‘dolosus versatur in generalibus’ - a person intending to deceive deals in general terms. [Para 10] Tricksters are on the prowl in the society. They will not hesitate to do all that is necessary for securing a ring of authenticity and acceptability for every deceitful action of theirs. If a sale deed for a very expensive immovable property is got executed pursuant to a decree passed by a civil court, it is assumed that such transactions will automatically acquire the ring of credibility around them. Little do such people realize that in a suit wherein upon contest and after full fledged trial on every issue at stake, the same is decided in favour of the plaintiffs and a specific performance is ordered by a Court, as a follow up measure, then it will undoubtedly carry a ring of authenticity around it. Not every attempt made to beat the clock and see to it that a valuable property is knocked down, irrespective of the fact whether the consideration paid for it is adequate or not and that the means employed are fair and not foul, would matter a great deal. In the instant case, the applicants had failed to demonstrate their financial capacity to have pooled up such a huge sum at one go, to pay to the respondent in cash in the year 2002. It passed one’s comprehension that they had failed to pool up from all their resources a meagre sum of Rs. 25,000 for the transaction to be over on the same day. The affairs of the company had been adversely reported in the press ever since 2004 and it was a matter of common knowledge in the city. Hundreds and thousands of complaints had been lodged with the police at various places in the State by depositors alleging fraud and misrepresentation indulged in by company. These depositors had been duped of their monies. Hence, this mode was devised by the applicants to knock off a valuable asset of the company. [Para 11]

The High Court had already intervened in the matter in the year 2004 itself by directing the CID of the police to act promptly on the complaints lodged against the company and its directors. Therefore, to beat all these circumstances, the above transaction had been engineered and a sale deed had been got executed on 14-7-2005. There was no whisper of any authorization issued by the company in favour of ‘D’ to enter into a compromise or to enter into a transaction of sale at the first instance with the applicants. No such agreement could be enforced, even if it was entered into with the sanction of the Judge at the trial of the proceedings to which it related. [Para 12]

Properties of the companies are not liable to be sold like items of general merchandise across the shelves. The poor attempt of camouflage made by all the parties was visible with the fact that no entries were found anywhere in the books of account of the company about receipt of Rs. 49,75,000. This apart, it passes one’s comprehension as to how such huge sums of money were preferred to be parted in cash instead of through commonly known secured instruments like cheques or demand drafts. [Para 13]

Fraud vitiates every transaction. No rights can ever flow to a party from a fraudulent transaction. [Para 14]

When an opportunity had been provided to the applicants to demonstrate their financial wherewithal to pool up such a huge sum of Rs. 49,75,000 in the additional material papers filed, material had been placed in the form of ‘pattedar’ passbooks and certificates issued by the revenue authorities that commercial crops were raised in the lands owned by the applicants and that they were deriving huge sums of money therefrom. These certificates issued by the Tahsildar were only needed to be looked at to be disbelieved. They were so contradictory in terms and content. When these contradictions were brought to the notice of the applicants, realizing the difficult situation brought about, they urged the High Court to fix up a reasonable market value for the property and then direct the applicants to pay up the balance amount in favour of the company so as to regularize the sale transaction. It was submitted that since the applicants had already entered into a transaction of sale relating to this very property with ‘V’, for a total sale consideration of Rs. 90 lakhs and they had already received Rs. 50 lakhs as advance, the balance money would be paid to the company, in case the High Court comes to the conclusion that the consideration paid by the applicants was hopelessly undervalued. [Para 15]

The aforesaid requests made by the applicants could not be acceded to. A wrong doer ought not to be permitted to make a profit out of his own wrong. The entire transaction was vitiated by fraud played by them on the District Court as well as on the Lok Adalat. ‘D’ on behalf of the respondent-company had joined hands with them. What was the authority in the hands of the said individual vis-a-vis the company under liquidation was anybody’s guess. [Para 16]

Respondent also argued that as per section 241(1) Central Government may itself apply tribunal only in case ,if it is of opinion that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest. Here "acts" in this case are past acts and not present acts.

Bench said that "The use of words "are being conducted", does not mean it does not cover the past acts. APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER BY COURT *APPOINTMENT OF INSPECTOR FOR INVESTIGATION INTO AFFAIRS OF A COMPANY ON ORDER BY COURT*

387.1 Background note387.1 Background note

It is mandatory that the Central Government appoint one or more inspectors to investigate the affairs of a company, if an order is issued by the Court to that effect.

387.2 Issue of order by Court387.2 Issue of order by Court

If, on an application made by any interested person, the Court feels that an investigation into the affairs of the company is required, it may issue an order to the Central Government to this effect and direct the appointment of one or more competent persons as inspector[s].

387.3 Appointment of inspectors387.3 Appointment of inspectors

On receipt of the order from the Court, the Central Government shall appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon.

387.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)387.4 Investigation by Inspector(s)

The inspector(s) shall investigate the affairs of the company and submit a report thereon to the Central Government. A copy of the report should be sent by the Central Government to the Court. Refer paras 384.8 to 384.14 for provisions relating to appointment of inspectors, powers of inspectors, inspector’s report, action by Central Government and expenses on investigation which are also applicable in case of appointment of inspector at the instance of Court.

Background history on fraud

There have been multiple cases of scams in companies, capital markets etc. during the last decade and we could cite the following one which was known as Enron of India scam.

In the year 2009, the Satyam scam in India which was termed Enron of India happened from one of the respected business family managed company. Satyam was the fourth largest Indian information technology (IT) company listed in India and also in United States having over US$ 2 billion annual revenue size. The company was established in 1980s and grown to the size of having 53,000 employees and 600 plus customers including 185 fortune 500 companies. Not only that, the company had operations in 66 countries across the world and the financial advisors were Merrill Lynch (now Bank of America) and their auditors were one of the Big4 – i.e. Price Water House Coopers (PWc) and their bankers were Citi bank, BNP Paribas, HSBC and HDFC.

After the Satyam scam which came as a shock, the investors were panicked as stock plummeted and this particular incident resulted in immeasurable and unjustifiable damage to Brand India and Brand IT in particular. Many of the Satyam employees -stranded in many ways-morally, financially, legally and socially and people lost a staggering Rs.100 billion in Satyam in market capitalisation as investors reacted sharply and dumped shares, pushing down the scrip by 95 per cent. Regulatory action followed resulting into the arrest of Chairperson, Managing Director / Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer and key associates of the company including the partners of Audit Firm PWc.

In the capital market also the biggest scam was reported in the year 1992 known as Harshad Mehta Scam. It was reported that the Harshad Mehta scam featured an embezzlement of of Rs 1439 crores that led to a severe crunch and drastic loss of wealth in the life savings of many investors that amounted to Rs 3542 crores.

In the year 2001, Ketan Parekh scam was the second most important scam that rocked the Bombay Stock Exchange after the Harshad Mehta scam in the year 1992. . To make matters worse, Ketan Parekh was himself a protégé of Harshad Mehta and had learned stock trading from the pied piper of Bombay Stock Exchange himself. As a result, he was able to achieve a similar feat as compared to what Mehta himself had accomplished. As reported in the media, Ketan Parekh was found involved in cheating with banks by misrepresenting facts, falsifying accounts, ripping off the stock market prices and exploiting investor's decisions, mishandling the public money, bribing company directors enabling them to insider trading.

In the year 2019, the capital market witnessed Karvy scam in which Karvy frauded lakhs of investors by using their shares and securities and monetizing it by pledging the investor's shares and using the notes.

Followed the above, there has been various regulatory changes have taken place especially reporting the fraud happening within an organization, setting up the procedure for reporting of the fraud. Regulators have brought into effect vigil mechanism and whistle-blower policy to be in place in organizations. Let us look into the related provision on vigil mechanism, whistle blowing and fraud reporting.

Regulatory framework

Section 177 of the Companies Act 2013 spells out the requirement on whistle-blowing mechanism which is applicable to specified companies. In addition to this, for listed companies the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations are also applicable.

Provisions under Companies Act 2013

Under sub-section (9) of section 177 of Companies Act 2013 read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, it is mandatory for all listed companies and companies which have borrowed money from Banks and Public Financial Institutions in excess of Rs.50 crores. Sub-section(9) of section 177 of the Companies Act 2013, states that every listed company and other class or classes of companies, as prescribed, shall establish a vigil mechanism for directors and employees to report genuine concerns in such manner as may be prescribed.

They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

The second issue is regarding non-compliance of section 8(1). It submited that the notice under section 8 was to be given to a person who claims the possession and the control of the property. He was required to be afforded an opportunity of hearing. It was stated that the properties attached was under the control of Official Liquidator. The Adjudicating Authority passed the impugned order without an opportunity of hearing, to the Official Liquidator. Thus, also, the impugned order deserves to be set aside.

It was also submitted that section 8(2) and (3) of Act of 2002 have not been complied rather Adjudicating Authority recorded finding going beyond its power under those provisions. The Adjudicating Authority had no power to hold that a predicate offence had been committed by the defendants. In fact, the jurisdiction for it lies with the Special Court, yet a finding for commission of offence had been recorded. Thus, for the aforesaid reasons also, the order deserves to be set aside.

HELD: The provision for hearing is given under section 8(1). Section 5(1) provides for attachment against 'any person' in possession of proceeds. At the relevant time defendant was in possession of the proceeds. The Competent Authority passed the order of attachment was not having information that an Official Liquidator has been appointed. The information was given only to the Adjudicating Authority.[Para 17]

Section 66 shall test question of facts whether director or personnel of the Corporate Debtor or any outsider has acted diligently with honest intention to avoid any connivance in the fraudulent transactions. The element of dishonesty may not be there but sufficient evidence shall entail the conduct of business and dereliction of duties which may lead to negligence on the part of that person to enable fraud to be committed and losses incurred by the Corporate Debtor.
