the learned Tribunal has not received any objection from any regulatory body raising any concern for reopening/recasting books of accounts;

(g)

the impugned cannot be said to be in violation of the principles of natural justice as alleged; and

(h)

the report of the RBI dated 22-3-2019 demonstrates and establishes beyond any doubt about the complete correctness, validity and legality of the order under Section 130 of the Act.

Making the above submissions, it was prayed to dismiss the present appeal, more particularly, considering the larger public interest as, in the present case, thousands of crores of the public money is involved.

Observations by the Hon'ble Supreme Court

While considering the issue, the Hon'ble Supreme Court noted amongst others that -

(a)

in the preliminary SFIO report, there are specific findings with respect to mismanagement of the affairs and also with respect to preparing fraudulent accounts;

(b)

in the preliminary report, the ICAI has mentioned that "accounts for the post five years have been prepared in a fraudulent and negligent manner by the erstwhile auditors"; and

(c)

the Registrar of Companies prima facie concluded that mismanagement and compromise in corporate governance norms and risk management has been perpetuated indiscriminately raising long term and short-term loans/borrowings through public sector banks and financial institutions.

It was observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that -

(a)

on a fair reading of Section 130 of the Companies Act, if the Tribunal is satisfied that either of the conditions precedent is satisfied, the Tribunal would be justified in passing the order under Section 130 of the Companies Act;

(b)

it cannot be said that the conditions precedent while invoking the powers under Section 130 of the Act are not satisfied;

(c)

it was more than satisfied that in the facts and circumstances of the case, and also in the larger public interest and when thousands of crores of public money is involved, the Tribunal is justified in allowing the application under Section 130 of the Companies Act; and

(d)

it cannot be said that the order passed by the learned Tribunal is per se in violation of the principle of natural justice as alleged.

Further it was observed that the order passed by the Tribunal under Section 130 of the Companies Act does not suffer from any illegality and the same is passed in the larger public interest.

Final Order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court

The Hon'ble Supreme Court relied heavily on the merits of 'larger public interest', for passing the Order.

It was ordered that the Hon'ble Supreme Court had no reason to interfere with the impugned order dated 1-1-2019 passed by the learned Tribunal under Section 130 of the Companies Act for reopening of the books of accounts and recasting the financial statements for the last five years, viz. from Financial Year 2012-13 to the Financial Year 2017-18.

Accordingly, the present appeal was dismissed and order of the learned Tribunal was upheld.

Consequences of re-opening and re-casting of books of accounts

The books of accounts once reopened and recasted are deemed to be final under the provisions of Section 130(2) of the Companies Act, 2013. It means recasted books of accounts are to be considered as final for the relevant period for all purposes.

Recovery of remuneration

Section 199 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits the Company to recover remuneration from any managing director/whole-time director/manager/Chief Executive Officer (by whatever name called) who has received the remuneration (including stock option) in excess of what would have been payable to him as per the restated financial statements. This would be applicable for all the period(s) for which financial statements were restated.

Conclusion - some unanswered questions

There are many frontiers opens when an order is passed to re-open/re-cast the books of accounts and the law does not answer to all such questions in the statues. For example, recovery of dividend which was distributed based on previous accounts and claim of damages by the investors who have suffered losses.

It was seen that the company Judge had directed almost a detailed questionnaire and sought the information which was extremely relevant and which would give the complete picture regarding the financial status, etc., of the company. The information sought also appeared to be extremely relevant in coming to the conclusion as to whether the transactions were of bona fide nature or not. There was also a second affidavit filed on record before the order of the Court dated 17-8-2000 seeking further information and even in this affidavit, the financial scenario of the company and its dealings generally were highlighted. In fact, from a reading of those affidavits, it was clear that the company had access to all that was filed before the Court including the petitions. The Single Judge had painstakingly and studiously gone into the whole financial aspects giving a thorough picture of the financial status of the appellant-company itself as also vis-a-vis the other companies floated by it. The Judge had also taken stock of the various transactions with reference to the figures involved in those transactions. It was true that the Judge had made a reference to that report. However, he was completely convinced that there was no necessity of supplying the copy of every document on which the RBI had relied in support of its petitions. The company had a complete idea as to what was the stand of the RBI and what were the precise grounds on which the RBI was moving against it. The company not only got the notice of the petitions but a complete opportunity to show the reasons against it in writing besides the hearing in the open Court. Therefore, this was not a case of breach of natural justice on account of the denial of the opportunity.

There was no doubt that the considerations enumerated by the company Judge for the appointment of provisional liquidator were abundantly available in the present case. Therefore, the Single Judge was justified in admitting the petitions and in appointing the provisional liquidator.

The Judge had given the directions that the report forwarded by the RBI to the Additional Director General of Police, in-charge of the Economic Offence Wing, to whom the RBI had forwarded the report of the Special Auditor should be treated as the first information report with regard to the apparent fraud committed by the company and those in-charge of the company. This action, according to the Single Judge, would be in addition to any of the cases that might have been registered against the company. The Judge then directed that steps should be taken against those involved in the apparent conspiracy to siphon off or divert the funds of the company. The observations made by the Single Judge directing an investigation to be made had got nothing to do with sections 541 and 542. Section 543 also speaks about the assessment of damages for any mis-application, retainer, misfeasance or breach of trust by the directors. Even that section had got nothing to do with the directions given by the Single Judge. That is a general power of the court and there can be no doubt that every court has that power and the Single Judge also had the same power.

Section 443 provides for the powers of the court. Clause (c) of section 443(1) thereof speaks of the Court's powers to make any interim order which the Court thinks fit to order an investigation. This has got no connection with sections 541 to 543 and, therefore, the argument that that part of the order was without jurisdiction was to be rejected.

The Court has ample powers including the power under section 443 to recommend an investigation. After all, an investigation into the affairs of the company does not mean a final conviction of the Directors. This argument, therefore, was to be rejected. The criminal liability would be decided by the competent Criminal Court on the evidence tendered before it by the prosecution. The question of the bail and release would also be decided by the Criminal Court which was dealing with the matters. The release of a person on bail in this case was the exclusive right of the Criminal Court dealing with the accused persons, viz., the directors of the company. The payment of Rs. 50 crores might have been considered as one of the considerations for grant of bail but, that did not divest the Criminal Court of its powers to deal with the bail matter and to deal further with the criminal matter pending before it in its own rights.

Accordingly, the application was disposed of.

COMPANY LAW/SEBI : Where CBI issued freeze orders against appellant company during an investigation into an alleged crime committed by 'D' however, appellant company was in no way connected to concerned investigation, freeze orders made against appellant company's properties were redundant qua investigation and condition imposed to furnish bank guarantee in furtherance of said orders was to be set aside

A complaint was registered against 'Birla Power' and its Directors for offence under sections 406, 420, 120B of IPC. After registration of FIR, an ECIR was recorded.

It was alleged that accused company 'Birla Power' and their group entities issued an advertisement to invite fixed deposits on an attractive interest. The accused in coalition with each other had accepted the amount of more than 260 crores from around 20,000 victims/investors in 'Birla Power', 'Birla Shlok', 'Zenith' and 'Birla Cotsyn' After maturity of the amount, the companies failed rather refused to return the amount deposited with it and accordingly an amount of 57.04 crores and Rs. 214 crores remains unpaid towards Fixed Deposit and ICD depositors.

During the course of Investigation, the statement of the complainant/investors were recorded.

The complainant apart from many invested their hard earned money but the amount deposited by them remained unpaid. Thus, they filed a complaint. The statement of other investors were also recorded. They made reference of 163 investors filed the complaint against 'Birla Power' and its Director. In the investigation, it was found that the money collected from the investors was siphoned off and laundered by transfer to other companies and mainly the entities of 'Birla Power'.

The statement of the accused were also recorded who submitted that the investment were invited to expand the business and to cover the shortage of capital. The deposits so received from the investors was transferred to the group of companies which includes 'Birla Surya' which alleged to have siphoned of the money thus, an offence of money laundering was found.

The respondent finding a case of money laundering sought to attach the properties to safeguard the interest of the investors during the pendency of the criminal case. They accordingly attached several properties of 'Birla Surya' to whom the money was transferred by 'Birla Power' and its Directors. It was to secure the proceeds of crime so transferred to 'Birla Surya'.

The attachment order was confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority finding a case of money laundering. It had been questioned by the appellant principally on three grounds.

According to the appellant the proceeding before the Adjudicating Authority was suffering from mis-joinder of parties. The appellant was not in possession of proceeds of crime and those who were in possession of the proceeds were not impleaded. Thus, the attachment of property becomes illegal. The investment received from different persons said to have been transferred to 'Birla Surya' was also not in possession of the proceeds of crime because 'Birla Surya' went in liquidation at the time of attachment. The said company was not in a possession and control over the proceeds of crime rather it was lying with the Official Liquidator who was appointed by the High Court in the petition for winding up of the company. The Official Liquidator was having the possession and control over the proceeds attached by the respondent. The official liquidator was not impleaded as defendant while impleading appellants having no control and possession of the proceeds. Thus, the appeal was suffering from mis-joinders of the parties. Yet, the provisional attachment order was confirmed without a notice to the Official Liquidator.

When compounding is granted, it operates as a bar against prosecution, section 621A(2)(c). In compounding of an offence when prosecution is pending before the court, the Registrar shall bring it in writing before the court whereupon the court shall discharge the company and/or the accused. The compounding may be conditional with a direction to file the return or document with the Registrar within specified time together with the fee and additional fee payable, the non-compliance of which is again punishable. Section 456 itself makes it clear that the PL shall take into his custody or under his control 'all the property' to which the company is or appears to be entitled. There can be no manner of doubt, and it is in fact not denied, that the company did place with NSEIL Rs. 1.10 crore when it became a trading member. The said sum definitely, therefore, constitutes the property of the company.

Although upon passing of the winding up order by the Court, the assets and the properties of the company came to the custody of the PL, but, in fact, the properties did not vest in the PL. Therefore, the PL acts as an agent of the company, a trustee of the properties as also the officer of the Court. He acts under the directions of the Court. Conclusion

With the process of liquidation of the company already in progress, the scheme of section 456 will have to be followed. Dilatory part of court procedure is a dampener 1.40-13 In addition to the question on the proper Court of competent jurisdiction discussed above, companies and company affairs that happen to be brought before the courts for adjudication in whatever context are equally subject to the common curse of endemic court delays and related costs largely due to the archaic, outmoded and staid procedural laws made by the imperialist British regime around the 1850’s remaining firm at the core through six decades of India’s Independence to the present electronic era, as a consequence of the law-makers’ choice of creating multiple fast track courts or forums parallelly, to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of ordinary civil courts which are nearer to people and familiar to them in the view that those courts are super-saturated with other cases and allowing their jurisdiction over company cases to continue would only add to further delays, instead of overhauling the procedural laws to rid them off the dilatory parts for faster disposal of cases by the common law courts and creating more. Unfortunately, seeing the victims sapped by prolonged litigation for years lasting for a generation or over in many cases, there is a misgiving present generally as an aside in the minds of people on ‘who is watching what they do’ about the Judiciary in our system. These factors have contributed to encourage people at large to keep away from approaching the Courts on their disputes with others and swallow the losses unless compelled not for some little money alone as in the case of the common investors, or it forms the lesser evil faced by them, or it found advantageous to show as inescapable and vindicate their own position at any cost to the company or others. Overall, so far as companies are concerned, the combined incidence of these factors has gone in favour of the managements to do what they prefer rather than what they should under the laws in matters of the corporate investors or others.

In Motilal case, Motilal and brothers were silver merchants, in operative proceedings of Customs and Central excise Department, sizeable quantity of silver was seized, this seizure was officially notified to the merchants. Further on, the fresh case was filed by Income tax department and new proceedings were started against them specifically towards attaining the silver bullions so seized by excise department. These proceedings were like in the present case within the ambit of Section 132 (1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It was held by Allahabad High Court that the proceedings of search and seizure under the said Section can be essentially towards assets that are not disclosed/secreted and/or hidden and not towards specifically disclosed assets which the court considered in this case to be the silver bullions since the information for the same was officially recorded by the excise department thereby the use of aforesaid mentioned Section being rendered invalid. This case was in principle upheld to the extent of disclosure invalidating the usage of said Section.

In H.L. Sibal case, it was held that searches made under Section 132 are particularly towards those in possession of undisclosed incomes or assets and that this power has to be exercised in an honest manner and search warrants cannot be indiscriminately issued purely as a matter of policy.

The contentions here in lines of Vivo case are that the bank accounts are not hidden from any authority and thereby not something that are in a secret vacuum of undisclosed data, an unknown factor whether the accounts so freezed were directly owned by Vivo or by the alleged shell companies, in the former case the accounts cannot be deemed undisclosed or something that government was completely unaware of, since the reporting of this information is prima facie done by banks under the ambit of applicable regulatory frameworks, however in the latter case scrupulous veil over the shell companies' bank accounts even though the same may have been reported but conclusively in respect to this case being incomprehensive information in furtherance of alleged motive of money laundering could have been brought within the ambit of Section 17 (1A) of PMLA and/or Section 132 (1) of the Income Tax Act.

Also, Vivo claims that companies' existence itself cannot be criminal but this fundamentally is against the Supreme Court's judgement in Standard Chartered Bank v. Directorate of Enforcement [2006] 67 SCL 2 which states the principle that company can have criminal liability in form of fines and penalties in cases where it is criminally liable and cannot escape the same even on the ground that a company has no Mens Rea.

Specifically, the cases of shell companies can be even on existential ground be criminal since prima facie intention of these companies is to commit fraud on Indian laws, in accordance with Section 5 of PMLA, ED has authority to seize 'proceeds of crime' which is defined under Section 2(u) that covers the ambit of scheduled offences as well as transferring such illegal proceeds out of India, both of which are alleged by ED in the present case.

Conclusion

Through this article, the authors intend to provide legal aspect from both the sides of the case whereby this case can be considered essential in developmental jurisprudence of understanding the grey areas of distinction in operation of law by enforcement agencies in terms of search and seizure operations where prima facie the liquidity is in legal form in the economy but the tools are so deployed so as to evade taxes or commit fraud on Indian laws. It has been a generalised presumption that multiple shell companies do not show clean hands of the parent holding especially when in such a case whereby the directors have fled the country, also Indian enforcement agencies need to have a broader perspective of the powers conferred upon them for instance, the preliminary ground of search and seizure operations under Section 17 (1A) of PMLA and Section 132 (1) of Income Tax Act could have been avoided had the operation been under the ambit of Section 222 and 226(5) of Income Tax Act which provides for similar power but in a slightly restrictive manner. The ingredients of this case would have a deep imprint in Indian jurisprudence since a sizeable quantum of India's foreign based companies back-track money to their parent country or their registered tax-haven countries. Also, specifically India's continued sweet and sour Chinese relations would have an impact since the trail just jumps from one company to other like from Xiaomi to Vivo and with Oppo next on the radar, development in this case would lay a significant political risk assessment parameter for Chinese companies' investment in Indian markets.

Obligations of financial institution and intermediaries

7.1 Maintaining record of certain transactions - Clause 11 of the Bill is considered to be the main cause of worry for financial institutions and other intermediaries. It proposes to make it obligatory for every financial institution and intermediary to maintain a record of all transactions or series of inter-connected transactions exceeding the value of rupees twenty-five lakhs held within a month.

7.2 Furnishing information about certain transactions to income-tax department - It is also proposed that they would be required to furnish information of these transactions to the Commissioner of Income-tax having jurisdiction over such financial institutions or the intermediaries. The financial institutions and intermediaries would also be required to verify and maintain the records of the identity of all of their clients in the prescribed manner for a period of five years from the date of cessation of transactions between the clients and financial institutions.

The provisions of the clause are likely to impose a severe burden on banks, financial institutions and other intermediaries. In view of the fact that the process of computerisation of banks may still take some time to complete, the compliance with these provisions may be very difficult, if not impossible. Even the Reserve Bank has criticised the provisions due to the fact that financial markets have significantly matured in recent years and the number of daily transactions exceeding Rs. 25 lakh runs into lakhs. Therefore, unless the limit is raised to Rs. 1 crore, it would be a nightmarish and back-breaking exercise for banks, financial institutions etc., to report every Rs. 25 lakh plus deal to the authorities.

Also, it is learnt that financial institutions etc. will be required to maintain the record of such transactions for a period of 5 years. This will further add to their headache as they would be required to preserve the records in their original forms. Thus, they would be under tremendous strain for not only maintaining the specified records but also for forwarding the same to the Commissioner of Income-tax. This information on financial trans-actions would be utilised by the enforcement agencies, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, to investigate offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Legislation (after the Bill is enacted into an Act).

Clause 12 proposes to empower the Director to impose a fine on a financial institution if the institution has failed to maintain or retain records in accordance with the provisions of clause 11. The company furnished a detailed statement of its reasons for its failure to repay all the matured deposits and also a scheme for repayment of both outstanding matured deposits and also the deposits that would be maturing in future. The company submitted a scheme for repayment of deposits during the period of five years, the gist of which had been quoted in the order of the CLB itself. Another scheme was given on behalf of the depositors asking for repayment scheme of 48 months. The company submitted a revised repayment schedule for 48 months and had published the scheme in two newspapers. [Para 27]

Thereafter, various dates were fixed by the CLB in which the company absented though representatives of the depositors and a large number of depositors attended the proceedings. The CLB, therefore, after observing that due opportunity had been given to the company to make its submission on the suggestions given by the depositor but no one was present on behalf of the company and directors had also chosen to remain absent whereas large number of depositors were involved who had put in their hard earned money with the company, found that the matter could not be allowed to be dragged. The CLB on going through the revised scheme submitted by the company and suggestions made by the advocate on behalf of the depositors, and with a view to balance the interest of the company and the depositors and also the public interest at large issued a detailed order as to payment of deposited amount. [Para 28]

Despite that order, the record revealed that not a single penny was paid nor any effective step was taken by the company or its directors for making any payment to the depositors. Since the company failed to make the repayment even as per the directions and the scheme and the company did not take any interest in the proceedings nor the directors attended the proceedings despite themselves having come to the Board for getting the scheme approved for payment, the investors were well within their right to approach the Court for winding-up of the company on the ground that the company had failed to make the payment and it was unable to pay its debts. [Para 30]

For allowing the winding-up petition, it is essential that there are dues of the creditors against the company, namely, debt, and that the company has failed to make the payment at the given intervals or at such intervals in time when the depositors have asked for payment and that the company is unable to pay its debts. In case all the three ingredients aforesaid are established, besides other contents, if, at all, required to be proved, the creditors would be justified in asking the winding-up of the company. [Para 31]

This Article attempts to analyse the judgement passed in the matter of "Union of India v. Videocon Industries Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 52/[2022] 169 SCL 402 (NCLT - Mum.) wherein serious allegations of mismanagement has been taken against promoter/management of the company. The allegations were based on the forensic audit report which was conducted on directions of Resolution Professional during the insolvency process.

Brief History :

Videocon was large corporate performing in electronic hardware industry and as well as in telecom industry.

In 2018, State Bank of India, lead bank, which was Financial Creditor of the company, made an application under section 7 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ('IBC')to initiated Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against company since there was default in repayment of debts.

During Corporate Insolvency Process , Resolution Professional filed application to tribunal based on avoidance transactions identified by forensic auditor. Various application were made under section 43 and 66 of IBC wherein serious allegations were made against Promoters for conducting fraudulent transaction.

In Forensic Audit, the independent Auditor made remarks based on the information available and provided that various fraudulent transactions occurred between group companies.

Based on report of forensic auditor and other financial transaction proof with them, Regional Director, Western Region on behalf of Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed Petition for Interim Reliefs against officials of company and board of directors of group companies.

Present Case :

Various Interim reliefs were sought i.e. to direct respondents to disclose their Properties, to direct NSDL/CDSL to freeze their securities account, to direct CBDT to freeze assets of the respondents of the petition etc. and further to initiate oppression and mismanagement case against the promoter and BOD of the corporate debtor to secure or restore the assets back to catch out the real fraud and the wrong doers of the fraud along with assets to the right victim of the fraud

The respondent companies argued that matter was stayed by Appellate Tribunal and which was confirmed by Supreme court. Hence, Company is still under CIR and therefore as per Section 14 of IBC, Moratorium is in effect and therefore no judicial action can be initiated during CIRP against the company.

Brief of Section 14 related to case :

Section 14 (1) says that "Subject to provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3), on the insolvency commencement date, the Adjudicating Authority shall by order declare moratorium for prohibiting all of the following, namely :—

(a)

the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel or other authority;"

(b)

transferring, encumbering, alienating or disposing of by the corporate debtor any of its assets or any legal right or beneficial interest therein;

(c)

any action to foreclose, recover or enforce any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property including any action under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002;

(d)

the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor.

Moratorium Prohibits Petitioner to initiate Suit against company which is under CIRP. The very purpose of Moratorium is to stop multiplicity of cases, safeguarding assets pool and help resolution professional in focusing CIRP.

The argument of respondents was that the prohibitions are on both parties i.e. for and against the corporate debtor and hence these proceedings are bad in law and therefore should be set aside.

However, NCLT rejected this argument that proceedings are not proceedings against the corporate debtor but for corporate debtor. They agreed on contention that no suit or proceeding can be initiated against corporate debtor.

But in the instance case the efforts made by the Union of India were analysed and the spirit of them was seen to secure or restore the assets back to the ultimate victims of fraud and it is not any adversarial proceeding that is the proceeding in rem which has initiated by the Union of India to catch hold all the wrong doers and the fraudulent persons.

To which the first respondent's counsel opposed the same arguing that this Bench did not pass these orders by keeping this applicant in the dark, the company served notice upon the applicant as and when it moved extension application before this Bench, but this applicant never and ever raised objection for the extension. The applicant did not even move section 10F appeal against the order dated 13-11-2009. Now, this applicant cannot seek recall of the order passed by this Bench as because there is no provision under the Company Law Board Regulations, 1991, entitling this Bench to recall its own order passed in accordance with law and because there is an express provision for setting aside of the order passed by this Bench and a provision of appeal. The applicant having failed to have recourse under any of these provisions, is not permitted for the relief of recall of the order invoking regulations 43, 44 and 48 of the Company Law Board Regulations, 1991. The first respondent's counsel with these submissions, sought for dismissal of this application as not maintainable.

13. Having heard the arguments of either side, the points for consideration are :

Is this application maintainable ?

If maintainable, is the applicant entitled to the reliefs sought by it ?

14. As to the first point, it is evident that there is no provision for review of the order passed by this Bench, in fact the provision of review in force until 1992 was deleted. No doubt, there is a provision of inherent power analogous to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which could be invoked as and when felt necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of this Bench. There is also a provision giving power to this Bench to dispense with the requirement of regulations as mentioned in regulation 48 of the Company Law Board Regulations, 1991. As to this aspect, the hon'ble Apex Court held that this inherent jurisdiction cannot be exercised so as to nullify the other provisions of any Act when the code deals with a particular matter, the provision should normally be regarded as exhausted. Since there being a provision of appeal and there is a set aside provision, this applicant is not expected to file this application for recall of the very order passed by this Bench when review authority was expressly omitted in the year 1992. Inherent power could be invoked only when a matter is dealt with leading to perpetuation of fraud, or abuse of process of law. Here, in this case, the opportunity was given to the applicant as and when the first respondent moved for extension, but never availed the same. Now, if the applicant comes and says this order as abuse of the process of law cannot be considered because no fraud is played against this Bench, moreover this Bench is competent to pass extensions, of course veracity of the order is always open to the scrutiny of the appellate authority.

15. The Apex Court in Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) (P.) Ltd. [1998] 92 Comp. Cas. 149, speaks as follows :

"The judiciary in India also possesses inherent power, specially under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, to recall its judgment or order if it is obtained by fraud on the court. In the case of fraud on a party to the suit or proceedings, the court may direct the affected party to file a separate suit for setting aside the decree obtained by fraud. Inherent powers are powers which are resident in all courts, especially of superior jurisdiction . . ." (p. 163)

16. The same is reiterated in between K. Rama Rao v. M. A. Bari & B. Shyamasundara Rao, Advocates-Receivers-cum-Commissioners [2007] 6 ALT 177, wherein his Lordship T. Ch. Surya Rao held the classification of fraud as a fraud played on a party to the suit and a fraud played upon the court. In the former case, the affected party shall be directed to file a separate suit for setting aside the decree obtained by fraud and in the latter case; the court by exercising its inherent jurisdiction can recall its order.

17. The applicant counsel relied upon Rai Ram Nath Bhargava Bahadur v. Sri Swami Goverdhan Rangacharia AIR 1936 All. 97 and Sita Ram Sahu v. Kedarnaih Sahu AIR 1957 All. 825, to state that inherent powers could be invoked to the ends of justice, but having the Supreme Court held in Jaipur Mineral Development Syndicate v. CIT [1977] 106 ITR 653, filed by the applicant's counsel himself that the inherent power could be invoked only in the absence of express or implied prohibition, those two citations supra relied upon are not applicable in the given situation.

Whether petition is maintainable for recovery of amounts by invoking sections 397-398, read with sections 406, 542 and 543? Whether such kind of relief (recovery of amounts) can be sought? Admittedly the instant petition was filed for recovery of amounts from the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 in the petition. The grievance of the Union of India that the applicant and the 3rd respondent were the directors of the company and acting in a fraudulent manner had retained the funds and had become liable and accountable for their illegal acts. The case of the Union of India was that they had ordered investigation on 23-3-2004 by appointing inspector. The inspector had investigated into the matter and submitted the detailed report pointing out various illegal and fraudulent acts of the respondents, thereby it was of the view that it was a fit case to file the instant petition before the CLB. The main allegations were that from October, 1998 to January, 1999 the management of the company created an equity capital of Rs. 7093 crores through dubious method of rotation of cheques and by swapping of shares among group associates. The management was found to have indulged in falsification of accounts of the company. Further the allegation of the petitioner that the company adjusted the application money in the form of deposit for software, rigging of share price through manipulation of working results in financial statements, shares reprinted and sold in the market and whole original jumbo share certificates were under seizure of Income-tax Department for contravention of section 41, read with sections 372/372A, 78, 293, 295,370 etc. of the Income-tax Act, 1961. From the pleadings, it was apparent that the petition was filed basing on the report of the Investigating Officer. In that regard the provision under which the Union of India approached the CLB was necessary to emphasize. Section 397 empowers the CLB to make such order as it thinks fit, may with a view to bringing to an end the matters complained off by any member of a company who complains that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interests or in a manner oppressive to any member or members. Section 398 empowers the CLB in case of mismanagement in the affairs of a company and may apply any member of a company who complained that the affairs of the company are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or that a material change not being a change brought about by or in the interests of any creditor including debenture holders or any class of shareholders of the company. The CLB may with a view to bringing to an end or preventing the matters complained of are apprehended make such order as it thinks fit. Section 399 provides for the right to apply under sections 397-398 by the category of persons as mentioned in that section. Admittedly, there were no complaints before the Bench by any member/members or creditors of the company alleging/complaining the acts of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs of the company and the nature of allegations of the Union of India required a detailed trial by examining the witnesses and the veracity of documents. The proceedings under sections 397-398 are summary in nature. Therefore, the nature of allegations could not be decided by the CLB. The contention of the respondents was that no notice was given for the inspection which was ordered under section 209 or even under section 234. The petitioner submitted that opportunity was given to the respondents. The inspection was carried out in the year 2004 and a final report was submitted to the Government. It was open to the respondents to challenge the investigation report if it would have violated the principles of natural justice in conducting the inspection. The petitioner alleged violation of various provisions of law in the instant petition. Prima facie the petitioner could initiate prosecution for the said contraventions in appropriate Court of law. Further, the CLB would not intrude the functions of the other statutory bodies such as SEBI, RBI and the civil court, company court and exercising powers under IPC. It is well settled law that to invoke the provisions of sections 397 and 398 by any member, creditor a case has to be made out that facts would justify the making of winding up order and that winding up would unfairly prejudice the members. In the instant case the petitioner had not made out any case for winding up of the company on just and equitable ground. The petitioner was not remediless. Most of the allegations were in the nature of grievances for which specific alternate course of action was available under various provisions of the Act and other laws which could be resorted to by the petitioner. The petitioner also invoked the provisions of sections 542 and 543. Section 543 is relevant provision to be applied by the petitioner. However, to apply under that provision, only a creditor or a member can make an application. In the instant case admittedly the petitioner was neither a member nor creditor of the company. Hence, the petitioner could not invoke the provision of section 543 where the CLB has the power to order for repayment or restore the money or property. The sole prayer in the petition was for recovery of money

Nevertheless, these sales were a means whereby the American company carried on its European business and it was held that the substance of the arrangement was that the American company traded in England through this agency of its subsidiary". 10.7-4a Exception is admissible either as public purpose or no real connection - A clutch of 13 foreign companies alleged to be belonging to one family trust formed into a ring to buy the shares of a company in India effectively for one man under NRI Schemes sponsored under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973, by the RBI to attract investments by NRIS, and it was urged before the Supreme Court that, in totality, the purchase of shares violated the FERA and that the corporate veils should be lifted to see the reality. It was refused on the ground that doing so would be defeating instead of promoting the aims of FERA which is a statutory enactment to attract investments into India, LIC v. Escorts Ltd. AIR 1986 SC 1370; Carrasco Investments Ltd. v. Special Director, Enforcement Directorate (1991) 2 Comp. LJ 339. A decree passed against a company cannot be satisfied by attachment and sale of properties belonging to other companies managed by the same group of directors, Punjab National Bank v. Breja Knipping Fasteners Ltd. [2001] 30 SCL 456 (Punj. & Har.).

10.7-4b Mere make-up found as a fact warrants lifting the veil - In Juggilal Kamalapat v. CIT, AIR 1969 SC 932, it was held that collusive foreclosing of managing agency agreement and assigning the managing agency by the partnership firm to a limited company in which the erstwhile partners of the firm became directors and continued as the managing agents, did not render the amount paid as compensation for loss of office as revenue expenditure in the hands of the paying managed company and a capital receipt in the hands of the dissolved partnership firm, avoiding tax at both ends, and the new company was no different from the dissolved firm, and that the Income Tax authorities were entitled to pierce the veil of the corporate entity and levy the tax.

10.7-4c Where the statute contemplates, veil can be lifted - The corporate veil may be lifted where the statute itself contemplates it or fraud or improper conduct is intended to be prevented, or a taxing statute or a beneficent statute is sought to be evaded or where associated companies are inextricably connected as to be, in reality, one concern, Life Insurance Corpn. of India v. Escorts Ltd. [1986] 59 Comp. Cas. 548 (SC). The Court observed in Union of India v. Playworld Electronics (P.) Ltd. AIR 1990 SC 202, that: "The Court is entitled to lift the mask of corporate entity, if the concept is used for tax evasion, or to circumvent tax obligation, or to perpetuate fraud. However, tax-planning may be legitimate provided it is within the framework of the law. Colourable devices cannot be part of tax-planning". Various provisions of the Companies Act maintain a clear distinction between a company’s legal entity and its actions, assets, rights and liabilities and those of its shareholders’ from which it legally follows that lifting of the corporate veil is not permissible in law unless the statute clearly provides for it OR very compelling reasons exist such as prevention of fraud etc., Cotton Corpn. of India Ltd. v. G.C. Odusumathd [1999] 34 CLA 458/22 SCL 228 (Kar.).

10.7-4d Where experience claimed is experience on paper in the company’s name with the people of that experience not with it who left and made a new company, the claim is empty - With respect to experience to be reckoned for a tender and company mergers in the line, the Supreme Court observed that experience is not experience simply on paper in the name of a given company for the required duration when it has no experienced persons with it in order to ignore the new company having on its rolls the persons experienced in the field, in New Horizons Ltd. v. Union of India [1997] 89 Comp. Cas. 849/[1998] 15 SCL 148 (SC).

10.7-4e Illegal activities warrant lifting the veil - Where it is found that the corporate character has been used for committing illegalities and for defrauding people, corporate veil can be lifted with a view to rendering full justice to the affected parties, Delhi Development Authority v. Skipper Construction (P.) Ltd. [1996] 4 Comp. LJ 233 (SC).

10.7-4f On a speculative plea, veil cannot be lifted - The doctrine of lifting of corporate veil cannot be applied to a plaintiff who is not a shareholder of a company but claims that the real holder will emerge on its lifting.

A petition was filed by the Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI) as a public interest litigation, stating that it had come to the notice of the Government of India that certain plantation companies were issuing instruments such as agro bonds, plantation bond, etc., offering very high rates of return which were not consistent with the normal returns in such schemes. In petition SEBI prayed that in public interest, till regulations were framed under section 12(1B), appropriate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle-class people, and immediate action be taken against the directors who had siphoned off large amounts belonging to investors under the guise of corporate veil. The Court ordered search and seizure and for an investigation by the Police into the affairs of the company with the assistance of the auditors and staff to be provided by the RBI. Consequently, investigations were made and prop- erties of directors of the company were attached. At this stage SEBI sought direction that till such regulations were framed and finalised, the Court may direct the RBI to issue orders to all commercial banks and/or cooperative banks, where Respondent No. 1 Plantation company had accounts, restraining Respondents No. 1 to 5 and 7 from withdrawing any money from the said accounts, and for certain other reliefs. The company opposed the prayer contending that it is the function of SEBI or the Central Government to frame the regulations at the earliest, if they think it necessary in the interests of investors/depositors in such plantation companies. It was contended that instead of moving the Central Govern- ment to frame and finalise the Regulations, they have approached the Court and it amounted to abuse of the process of law, because the court had issued various directions, including the direction to freeze the bank accounts of the directors.

The respondent-company had floated various schemes by which it was offering fanciful returns which were highly disproportionate and com-mercially not viable. On the basis of these complaints, the SEBI filed petition in the interest of the members of public, stating that the Central Government was concerned with the high elements of risks associated with such schemes and hence, in order to ensure that investors make investment in such schemes only after they are fully acquainted with or made aware of the high risk factors involved in such schemes, it was felt necessary to decide an appropriate regulatory framework for regulating entities which issue such schemes.

It was prayed that in public interest, till regulations are framed, appropri- ate directions be given to protect large amounts invested by middle class people. The petitioner filed the petition under sections 397/398 and 402 read with section 406, alleging that the promoters of the company, by giving a rosy picture of the prospectus of the company, had cheated the public to the tune of more than Rs. 460 lakhs. In terms of the prospectus, the commercial production was to commence by June, 1993 but had not been yet started. To get away from their responsibilities, the respondent Nos. 2 to 8 being the signatories to the prospectus, had transferred their shares in 1996 to the 9th respondent, that too in violation of the terms of the prospectus according to which the promoters were not to transfer their shares for a period of 5 years. In the instant case, the admitted facts were that the company had been unable to comply with the orders of the CLB and pay off the public depositors. The explanation of the company that it could not comply with the orders of the CLB due to the fact that its produce ‘Loratadine’ could not be sold in the US market; and that the global deposit receipts could not be utilized, could not be accepted. Both those circumstances were already in existence when the earlier order was passed by the CLB. At that time, the company itself had given various options to the CLB to pay off all the depositors. The CLB passed directions. That order of the CLB had attained finality and the company should have cleared the public debt in accordance with the orders of the CLB. The company, in fact, had not fulfilled its obligations and instead had diverted the funds to various other parties. One could not lose sight of the fact that thousands of pensioners, widows and other members of the public had invested their funds in the company. The company’s accounts should be above board. No doubt, in commercial transactions, there may be instances when a company may lose money, yet the totality of circumstances has to be seen while adjudicating whether the affairs of the company are being run in a manner which may be prejudicial to the public interest. [Para 14]

There were certain facts which had not been controverted. The first was that instead of servicing the public debt and repaying the depositors, the company had invested a sum of Rs. 67.75 crores in shares of associated companies. Admittedly, the company had invested huge amounts in its sister company ‘M’ Ltd. The annual report for the year 2002-03 showed that the company off loaded its investment and ‘M’ Ltd. ceased to be a subsidiary of the company. Thereafter, that company again became a subsidiary of the company a couple of years later. There was sufficient material on record to show that more than Rs. 67 crores had been diverted to other companies out of the funds of the company. That money could have been better utilized by paying off the public debt. [Para 15]

Another factor, which showed that the affairs of the company were not being run properly, was that the company had made a provision for writing-off outstanding debts of Rs. 126.25 crores as non-recoverable on 30-9-2003. In the previous year, the outstanding debts were less than Rs. one crore. This is in line with the earlier draft Bill that had been formulated by the Inter-Ministerial Group. The Committee noted that repaying depositors' money is the most critical part of the process of restitution of depositors. Where financial creditors, especially regulated businesses such as banks and financial institutions fail to exercise due diligence and give credit/lending to operators of unregulated securities schemes or schemes where fraudulent default is taken place, the law does not protect and give them priority and precedence. It does not incentivize lending to operators of unregulated schemes and those engaging in fraudulent default in regulated schemes. In this respect it may be noted that the US Bankruptcy Code is more explicit in excluding from the bankruptcy estate, "property in which the debtor holds, as of the commencement of the case, only legal title and not an equitable interest … becomes property of the estate … only to the extent of the debtor's legal title to such property, but not to the extent of any equitable interest in such property that the debtor does not hold."5 The property is part of the estate of the bankrupt only to the extent of his legal right, if he has any, and subject to the equitable interest of another. Thus, where the debtor holds bare legal title without any equitable interest, the estate acquires bare legal title without any equitable interest. Especially given the fact that in cases where the defaulter did not have the legal authorization to collect monies through the issuance of securities, the defaulter may not even have the prima facie legal right to create a security interest in the trust asset.

Collective Investment Schemes and the role of trust in insolvency

Generally, in a Collective Investment Scheme a trustee holds the pooled money on behalf of the beneficiary and in case the trust goes into insolvency the application of insolvency law poses certain important questions as to what happens to the pooled assets which the trustee has raised from the investors. In the famous international bankruptcy cases relating to Lehman Bros. Lehman Brothers International (Europe), In re6 the judge in that case explained the law on the above point maintaining that although the trust relationship may give rise to unsecured claims against the trustee for breach of trust or even negligence and may sometimes exist in a wider contractual framework, it remains at its core a different legal relationship. Subject to the terms of the trust instrument, the trustee holds the trust property for the benefit of those beneficially entitled to it and has a primary obligation to maintain those particular assets (or any which replace them) to the exclusion of all other claims. The trust property does not form part of the trustee's estate in the event of insolvency so as to be available to meet the claims of general creditors and the beneficiary is entitled to the property in specie free of any such claims.

Thus, where a trustee becomes insolvent, all the assets belonging to the trustee are divided up amongst his or her creditors. But if a beneficiary has an equitable property right to assets held by the trustee, it cannot be said that those assets belong to the trustee beneficially. Those assets are, therefore, removed from the pool of the trustee's assets, as they belong in equity to the beneficiary. Only the remaining assets that belong to the trustee beneficially are then distributed amongst the remaining creditors (generally paripassu, or proportionally). Clearly, this puts a beneficiary in a much stronger position than other creditors. The beneficiary is not a 'creditor' for the purposes of insolvency law; his position is higher than that of a creditor.

US Approach and the Berkeley Applegate Principle

Since the previous management of the company admitted to insolvency loses the power to deal with the company assets, it cannot discharge the burden of identifying the trust assets vis-à-vis the company assets. Under the IBC, the power to deal with the company assets, the right to manage the company and deal with its books of accounts primarily vest with the Insolvency professional. The Berkeley Applegate principle7 is useful for making the insolvency discharge the duty of differentiating the trust assets from other assets of the company and to be paid out of such funds. As a corollary of the rule that only the company's assets are available to the creditors, the liquidator has no power as the liquidator, to sell assets not beneficially owned by the company. But to apply this principle there needs to be some procedure to file this claim whereby the Insolvency Professional would then differentiate the assets. In civil matters, where property of a third party has been sequestered or a receiver has been appointed, a petition for examination pro interessesuo is permitted to prove the title and release of their assets.8 A petition for examination pro interessesuo would have to be filed under Section 60 of the IBC, for lack of a well-defined procedure under the IBC9. A well-defined procedure under the IBC at the outset would help in protecting the trust assets from being dissipated towards any creditor-oriented resolution or liquidation.

Reliance Industries Ltd. [2000] 26 SCL 355 (Cal.). The civil court’s jurisdiction with regard to a dispute of a civil nature is extensive in terms of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure unless barred by the statute either expressly or by implication. Even when the jurisdiction is specifically barred, if the provision so barring is not notified to have come into effect or after that the Tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure, the Civil Court’s jurisdiction to entertain the dispute of such nature is not barred. In other words, where there is no adequate and efficacious remedy available under the Act with regard to the dispute raised in the plaint, the Civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the dispute: Vijay Kumar Gupta v. The IL&FS was originally promoted by the Central Bank of India, HDFC Ltd., the Union Trust of India and it have SBI, LIC, ORIX Corporation of Japan and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA) as largest shareholders.

Before going into nitty gritty of section 130 of the Companies Act, 2013 lets us first read section 130:-

Section 130 - Re-opening of Accounts on Court's or Tribunal's Orders Trigerring Event (Section 241 – 242)

Everything started after ICRA downgraded IL&FS' long-term loans and debentures for the first time from AAA to AA+, citing mounting debt, slow asset-monetisation and deteriorating credit profiles of hundreds of its subsidiaries, after which IL&FS started slipping into hot water.

Generally, the Central Government do not usually take the cognizance of the matter, whereas in IL&FS case, the financial impact was of Rs. 90,000 Crore on economy. Therefore, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed a petition before the learned Appellate Tribunal under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act alleging mismanagement by the Board of IL&FS and that the affairs of IL&FS were being conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest.

Invoking of Investigation (Section 212)

In order to unearth the series of irregularities committed by IL&FS and its companies, the provisions of Section 212(1)(c) of the Companies Act were invoked for investigation into the affairs of the company by Central Government. The investigation was carried out by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office under Section 212 of the Companies Act wherein an interim report dated 30.11.2018 to the Central Government placing on record that the affairs in respect of IL&FS group Companies were mismanaged, and that the manner in which the affairs of the company were being conducted were against the public interest.

REPORT OF ROC and ICAI:-

The Registrar of Companies, Mumbai had also conducted an enquiry under Section 206 of the Companies Act and prima facie concluded following:-

a.

"mismanagement and compromise in corporate governance norms and risk management has been perpetuated on IL&FS and its group companies by indiscriminately raising long term and short term loans/borrowings through public sector banks and financial institutions"

b.

It was also observed that IL&FS company has been presenting a rosy picture by camouflaging its financial statements, and concealing and suppressing severe mismatch between its cash flows and payment obligations, total lack of liquidity and adverse financial ratios.

c.

It was also found that IL&FS company has first defaulted on commercial paper and then on short term borrowings i.e. inter corporate deposits, negative cash flows in operating activities etc.

d.

It was further observed that the consolidated balance sheet of IL&FS company indicated the extremely precarious financial position, and was virtually in deep red.

Further, ICAI had also conducted an enquiry and mentioned that "accounts for the past five years have been prepared in a fraudulent and negligent manner by the erstwhile auditors".

Reopening of accounts Application u/s. 130

The Central Government after considering the fact that thousands of crores of public money is involved and in the public interest, moved the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Mumbai seeking for reopening the books of accounts and re-casting of the financial statements of IL&FS and two other companies for the past five years viz. FY 2012-2013 to 2017-2018 under Section 130 of the Companies Act, to ascertain financial mismanagement, after issuing notice to all concerned including the Central Government, Income Tax Authorities, SEBI, other Statutory Regulatory Body and even to the erstwhile Directors of IL&FS and other two companies.

The Hon'ble NCLT had allowed the application filed by the Central Government and had directed/permitted reopening of the books of accounts and recasting the financial statements of IL&FS and other two companies for the last 5 years, viz., F.Y 2012-2013 to 2017-2018.

The order passed by the learned Tribunal was affirmed by the learned Appellate Tribunal and finally ended up at Apex Court for consideration.

Whether can it be said that the order passed by the learned Tribunal is illegal and/or contrary to Section 130 of the Companies Act based the facts and circumstances of the case?

The Apex court noted that the Tribunal after considering the larger public interest and on the basis of the reports/preliminary reports of SFIO, ICAI and ROC held that books of accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner and the affairs of the company were mismanaged. Though the accounts of companies cannot clearly be said to have been prepared in a fraudulent manner though there are some observations with respect to role of the auditors, it is observed that the affairs of the company and its subsidiary were mismanaged during the relevant period and as per Section 130 of the Act, the Tribunal may pass an order of reopening of accounts if the Tribunal is of the opinion that

(i)

the relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner; OR

(ii)

the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period casting a doubt on the reliability of the financial statements.

1.40 Administration of Law and Justice

Company Court

1.40-1 Primarily, Company Court is the High Court of the State in which the registered office of a given company is situated (it being reckoned by the longest time duration in the immediately preceding six months for winding up) section 10(1)(a) read with sub-section (3), or the jurisdictional District Court in the State to the extent the jurisdiction has been conferred by the Central Government in section 10(1)(b) read with sub-section (2) vide Notification GSR 663 of 29-5-1959 and GSR 1626 of 13.10.1966 conferring jurisdiction in respect of sections 89, 113, 118, 141, 144, 163, 196, 219, 234, 304, 307 and 614—generally—with some conditions. Consequent to the coming into force of Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which is yet to be notified, the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) would be established (sections 10FB and 10FQ), in replacement of the Company Law Board which was in operation since 1-1-1964 introduced by the 1963 Amendment Act (section 10FA), and ousted the jurisdiction of High Court altogether so far as companies are concerned. With this, all Civil Court jurisdiction is barred with the exception of Constitutional powers of the High Court. Appeal against the orders of the Appellate Tribunal lies to the Supreme Court on questions of law. As against this, Taxation laws provide for reference of questions of law to the High Court [since shifted to the National Tax Tribunal formed recently, but halted by the ad interim order of the Bombay High Court in P.C. Joshi v. Union of India [2006] 282 ITR 39/152 Taxman 285] while jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is barred otherwise.

Puzzling mis-joinder of executive, civil and criminal adjudication

1.40-2 Under the Taxation and the economic laws enormous discretionary powers are vested in the Executive, subject to review of special Tribunals. In the same token, though companies are no Government, these are more or less equated to it in the philosophy of self-regulation subject to the purview of State-controlled Regulators of which SEBI partakes of the character both of a Corporate Regulator as well as a quasi-judicial Tribunal with powers of a Civil Court conferred on it in respect of calling for information from, undertaking inspection, conducting enquiries and audits of stock exchanges, mutual funds, other persons associated with the securities market, intermediaries and self-regulatory organizations in the securities market [section 10(i) and (3) of SEBI Act] and imposing penalties and/or fastening cease and desist orders.

Civil Court’s jurisdiction

1.40-3 Civil Court jurisdiction lies still in matters falling outside the purview of the NCLT in respect of protection of the property or prevention of invasion of related rights of the investors in shares or compensation for loss or damage like the remedies provided under section 62 (read with section 10), civil liability for mis-statements in prospectus under the Act and other civil matters connected to meetings, appointments of directors, debts and commercial disputes and torts subject to the jurisdiction being vested in the Court by Government Notification under section 10 and the Civil Procedure Code, and otherwise companies have been distanced from the Civil Court in the largest ever measure so far as shareholders are concerned.

Further, he became director of the company, with understanding that the second petitioner would not participate in the day-to-day affairs of the company on account of his critical physical condition. Accordingly, the second petitioner had kept with the second respondent signed blank cheques in advance for facilitating issuance of cheques in favour of the creditors or suppliers of the company. Similarly, the second petitioner had executed bank loan as well as security documents giving his personal guarantee and collateral security of his immovable property in favour of the respondent Nos. 6 and 7 for the credit facilities extended by them in favour of the company. However, later it transpired that the second respondent failed to conduct the affairs of the company on sound business principles and corporate practices, without settling the dues of creditors but embezzled substantial amounts of the company and deliberately committed acts of fraud and misfeasance with mala fide intentions, resulting in removal of the statutory records, furnitures, computer systems and other movable assets of the company and closure of the factory as well as the corporate office premises without any intimation to the staff members, workers and other members, including the petitioners, and absconded himself. The second petitioner had to face several of civil and criminal proceedings at the hands of the financial institutions, suppliers and other creditors on account of the fraudulent conduct of the second respondent in collusion with the officials of the respondent Nos. 6, 7 and 9. Therefore, the petitioner filed the instant petition under sections 235, 237, 397 and 398 read with sections 402 and 403 for appointment of one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company.

The petitioner-company for expanding its manufacturing activities approached R for investment. R invested certain amount and was correspondingly allotted shares of petitioner-company.

During search undertaken at premises of petitioner-company, certain incriminating material was seized and an appraisal report was shared according to which petitioner-company and its group concerns generated unaccounted money by inflating the purchase cost of plant and machinery as well as showing bogus expenditures and said money was used to acquire properties in name of benamidars and to introduce the same as share capital in the books of petitioner-company and its group concerns in the name of the benamidars. The Initiating Officer thus, issued show cause notice to R and petitioner company under section 24(1) on ground that investment made by R on 14-12-2011 in the property of petitioner was a benami transaction as constituted under section 2(9). Consequently, the Initiating Officer passed an order of provisional attachment under section 24(3).

In instant writ, petitioner challenged the impugned order on ground that the transactions took place in the year 2011, thus, the Amendment Act, 2016 which came into effect from 1-11-2006 could not be applied retrospectively:

The One-Man Committee was constituted by the Court for the purpose of identification, recovery and distribution of proceeds from sale of assets of various chit fund companies to verified claimants.

■

The Enforcement Directorate was directed to extend all necessary assistance to the Committee, as and when sought, for the purpose of implementation of the various orders of this Court, particularly with respect to identification, recovery and allied matters concerning the assets of the respective companies or any issue incidental thereto.

In short, a balance-sheet is an historical document. A balance-sheet must not be a mere inventory. Cas. 180 (Mad.) but shares are not equivalent to 'goods' before the allotment. As a matter of fact, an applicant for allotment of shares is a prospective investor, though he is not an immediate 'buyer of goods'. No wonder, the shares are simply bundle of intangible rights against the company which has issued them. After all, share certificates are just evidences of true property, which are the proportionate interests of the shareholders in the ownership of the company. As such, each share certificate with the depositary evidences the same bundle of rights, and each bundle of rights can satisfy the client's proprietary interest as any other interest. To put it differently, a 'share' is a right to a particular amount of the share capital of a company, carrying with it certain rights and liabilities, while the company is a going concern and when it is wound up. INVESTIGATION OF OWNERSHIP OF A COMPANY

Central Government can order investigation into ownership to decide who are really financially interested and who are in real control of the company.

Section 216(1) of Companies Act, 2013 provides that where it appears to the Central Government that there is a reason so to do, it may appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on matters relating to the company, and its membership for the purpose of determining the true persons—

(a)

who are or have been financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

(b)

who are or have been able to control or to materially influence the policy of the company.

(c)

who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company [clause (c) inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018].

Section 90 of Companies Act, 2013 substituted w.e.f. 13-6-2018 provides for declaration and register of beneficial interest. To support this provision, section 216 is amended w.e.f. 13-6-2018 to provide for investigation into beneficial ownership.

Central Government can appoint inspectors to investigate and report matters relating to company and its membership for purposes of determining the true persons who have or had beneficial interest in shares of a company or who are or have been beneficial owners or significant beneficial owner of a company - section 216(1)(c) of Companies Act, 2013 inserted w.e.f. 13-6-2018

Investigation if NCLT directs - Without prejudice to its powers section 216(1), the Central Government shall appoint one or more inspectors under that sub-section, if NCLT, in the course of any proceeding before it, directs by an order that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated as regards the membership of the company and other matters relating to the company, for the purposes specified in section 216(1) - Section 216(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Investigation under section 216 can be initiated or continued even if special resolution for voluntary winding up is passed or application in respect of oppression and mismanagement has been made or any winding up petition is filed or pending - section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250A of the 1956 Act].

Section 226 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016. Of course, this section is not relevant now as provisions relating to voluntary winding up have been omitted vide Insolvency Code, 2016.

Imposition on restrictions during investigation on securities issued or to be issued by company - During investigation under section 216, NCLT can impose certain restrictions upon securities. Such restriction can be upto three years - section 222(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 250(1) of the 1956 Act].

If despite such order, there is issue or transfer of securities, company as well as every officer who is in default is liable for punishment of fine and imprisonment - section 222(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

Applicability of provisions to foreign company - The provisions of investigation of ownership apply to foreign company also [section 228 of Companies Act, 2013]

Conclusion - some unanswered questions

There are many frontiers opens when an order is passed to re-open/re-cast the books of accounts and the law does not answer to all such questions in the statues. For example, recovery of dividend which was distributed based on previous accounts and claim of damages by the investors who have suffered losses. The Board of Directors, Auditors and professionals must take due care while finalising/approving books of accounts and must take into account 'larger public interest' than concerning only for limited group of people directly connected with the Company.

A greater responsibility is bestowed to the management in preparation of annual accounts and to the statutory auditor to give its true and fair view. Both the management and statutory audit is equally responsible for an account which is found to be not providing true and fair view. The power to re-open accounts should be carefully applied keeping in mind the broader interest of stakeholders and perhaps clarifying unanswered questions not dealt under the statute.

11.9-8 A similar range of law reform has not yet been attempted in our Act and other laws, and accordingly, the ultra vires doctrine, approved by the Supreme Court in Dr A. Lakshmanaswamy Mudaliar v. LIC AIR 1963 S C 1185, holds good. Now with the change in section 17(2) of the Act by the 1996 Amendment Act with effect from 1-3-1997, restricting the confirmation procedure for the alteration of the memorandum so far it relates only to a change in the situation of the registered office from one State to another, and doing away with it for alteration of Objects, discussed earlier in this Chapter, it’s relevance may seem to be largely diluted unless a petition is filed by the shareholders alleging oppression or mismanagement under sections 397 and 398 of the Act bound up with the alteration of Objects effected by the majority in passing the required special resolution. But, it is not so because the statute change regarding confirmation of alteration of the objects has no effect on the inherent nature of the objects and their effect in whatever shape they exist at a given point of time, in law, which determines the scope of the company’s capacity to act. Accordingly, the doctrine of ultra vires holds good, and in all probability it will be held unlawful for any company, not necessarily section 25 company, to abuse its power to alter the objects by merely passing a special resolution with any retrospective force or to ratify a past act ultra vires the company merely for the reason that the objects may be altered simply on its own behind the Court.

11.9-9 Present position and required Act change as to ultra vires

11.9-9a Powers of company implied - "A company can only lawfully deal with its assets in furtherance with its objects. The corporators may take assets out of the company by way of dividend, or, with the leave of the Court, by way of reduction of capital, or in a winding up. They may of course acquire them for full consideration. They cannot take assets out of the company by way of voluntary disposition, however described, and if they attempt to do so, the disposition is ultra vires the company"-said Pennyquick, J. in Ridge Securities Ltd. v. IRC (1964) 1 All ER 275. This case was referred to in Aviling Barford Ltd. v. Perion Ltd. 1989 BCLC 626 Ch. D. where it was held that it would be a breach of the fiduciary duty of directors to undersell a property rendering them accountable as constructive trustees. While the objects are to be specified in the memorandum, the powers exercisable may be implied on the consideration that a company has power to do all that is reasonably necessary for attaining its objects, like the power to purchase land implying the power to sell it or lease it or the power to compromise, but, the power to borrow needs to be expressly specified, whether the company is a trading or a non-trading company and it cannot be implied, Baroness Wenlock v. River Dee (1885) 10 App. Cases 354 (HL).

11.9-9b Powers not implied - The power to acquire business of another, to carry on business in partnership, acquiring shares in another company whose business does or does not fall within the company’s objects, promoting other companies or extending financial support to them, selling the whole undertaking of the company, political contributions, giving away as gifts, donations and charities for purposes unrelated to the company’s objects, entering into suretyship or guarantee contracts etc. are not implied unless any statute confers the power on the company or are specifically included in the memorandum.

11.9-9c Shareholders’ right to restrain the company - An ultra vires contract is not illegal but is null and void and the shareholders have the right to seek to restrain the company from going ahead with it by an action laid in the name of the company for the company’s benefit, as an exception to the rule in Foss v. Harbottle Smith v. Croft [No. 2 (1987) 3 All ER 909] by way of an injunction, enforcing the personal liability of the directors, or as breach of warranty of authority of an agent.

11.9-9d Property acquired by company under an ultra vires contract - Property acquired by the company under an ultra vires transaction is the company’s property vested in it and a suit is maintainable for securing it, Ad Sait v. Bank of Mysore 59 MLJR 28 (1930).
