Secondly, clause 245(1)(a) provides remedy to members or depositors by way of class action to seek order from Tribunal to "restrain the company from committing an act which is ultra vires the articles or memorandum of the company". This remedy can be sought when application is made by specified number of members as under: The requisite number of depositors shall not be less than 100 depositors or not less than such percentage of the total number of depositors as may be prescribed, whichever is less, or any depositor or depositors to whom the company owes such percentage of total deposits of the company as may be prescribed.

Thus, an individual member cannot approach the Tribunal unless he satisfies the criteria as per the above Table. A question arises then whether he can sue the company to restrain ultra vires acts as at present? Clause 430 of the Bill provides as under:

No civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

No injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force by the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal.

In view of clause 430 read with clause 245, it appears that once the Companies Act, 2012 comes into force individual member cannot sue to prevent ultra vires acts. He can only apply to Tribunal only if he satisfies criteria as per the above Table.

Conclusion

3. So far as ultra vires is concerned, the Companies Bill (i) mentions the words ultra vires-this word found no mention in 1956 Act (ii) defined ultra vires to cover breach of articles also (iii) the "Tribunalisation" of company law matters and the good intent to provide class action remedy has led to existing remedy of any member irrespective of his shareholding to sue to restrain ultra vires acts taken away and replaced with requirements more stringent to apply to Tribunal to seek the remedy. Thus, remedy against ultra vires acts made more difficult albeit unintentionally. It would be better that when the Bill is considered in Rajya Sabha, this numerical requirements to be satisfied by members to apply to Tribunal to restrain ultra vires acts be done away with.

Can a Consumer Forum stay a public issue ?

3. In a landmark judgment in case of Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund v. Kartick Das, [1994] 1 SCI 19 (SC) the Supreme Court on May 20,1994 barred the Consumer Courts from entertaining complaints of 'prospective inves-tors'. The Supreme Court has also laid down guidelines for the civil courts for granting interim relief on petitions challenging public issues. A three-Judge Bench comprising Chief Justice M.N. Venkatachalliah, Justice S. Mohan and Justice A.S. Anand passed the order while allowing an appeal of Morgan Stanley Mutual Fund challenging an order of the Calcutta District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum, which by an ex parte order dated January 1, 1994 had stayed the issue of Rs. 300 crore Morgan Stanley Growth Fund units which opened on January 6, 1994.

Justice S. Mohan, while delivering the 31 pages judgment, held that: ( i) the prospective investor could not be a consumer within the meaning of the CP Act; (ii) the appellant-company did not trade in shares; and (iii) the Consumer Protection Forum have no jurisdiction to entertain complaints from the prospective investors.

Is a prospective investor consumer ?

4. The Supreme Court held that in order to satisfy the requirements of a consumer, as defined under section 2(c) of the CP Act, there must be a transaction of buying goods for consideration under the relevant section of the Act. The definition contemplated the pre-existence of a completed transaction of a sale and purchase.

When can an investor challenge the public issue of company ?

5. The Apex Court has made it clear that an investor has a right to challenge the public issue of a company only after allotment of shares and not before allotment, because before allotment he is only a prospective investor of future goods. A 'prospective investor' is not a consumer under the terms of CP Act and it is only after becoming a shareholder that he gains the locus standi of a litigant.

What is the correct interpretation of section 14 of the CP Act ?

6. The Consumer Forum has no power under section 14 of the CP Act to grant any interim relief or even ad interim relief. The jurisdiction of the forum to grant interim relief is confined to remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory from the goods in question, to replace the goods with new goods, to return to the complainant the price or to pay such amount as may be awarded by it as compensation to the consumer for any loss or injury suffered by him due to the negligence of the opposite party. Only final relief could be granted within the provisions of section 14.

When civil court can pass ex parte injunction ?

7. While laying guidelines for the civil courts to pass ex parte injunctions, the Court stated that as a principle, ex parte injunction could be granted only under exceptional circumstances. The factors which should weigh with the Court in grant of ex parte injunctions are as under:

- Where irreparable or serious mischief will ensure to the plaintiff;

- Whether the refusal of ex parte injunction would involve greater injustice than the grant of it would involve;

- The Court to consider the time at which the plaintiff first had notice of the act complained so that the making of an improper order against a party in his absence is prevented;

- The Court to consider whether the plaintiff had acquiesced for some time and in such circumstances it will not grant ex parte injunction;

- The Court would expect a party applying for ex parte injunction to show utmost good faith in making the application. Even if granted, the ex parte injunction would be for a limited period of time; and

- General principles like prima facie case, balance of convenience and irreparable loss would also be considered by the Court.

Where should a complaint be filed ?

8. The Supreme Court has held that normally cases should be filed only where the registered office of the company is situated. In cases where the registered offices of companies are far away from civil courts and an aggrieved person approaches the Court, the Court must ensure that the plaintiff comes to it well in time so that notice may be served on the defendant and he may have his say before any interim order is passed.

The Court observed that invariably, suits are filed seeking to injunct either the allotment of shares or the meeting of the Board of Directors or against the general body meeting. The Court is approached at the last minute. If injunction is granted even without notice to the respondent, it will cause immense hardships and administrative inconvenience to the defendants.

How long the injunction should be valid ?

9. The injunction, even if granted by a Civil Court, should be valid for a limited period till the need is there.

Exchange deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company in compliance with the order passed by the Custodian. Section 3(5) lays down that the Custodian can take assistance of any other person while exercising his powers or for discharging his duties under this section and under section 4. When a fax message was sent to the Calcutta Stock Exchange for information and necessary action, the Calcutta Stock Exchange had no option but to deactivate the terminal of the petitioner-company. [Para 11] The plea taken by the petitioner-company was that K was one of the shareholders of the petitioner-company (though he resigned later on) and his holding which was raised to 97.94 per cent was subsequently brought down to 68 per cent. But the fact remained that K was practically the owner of that company; though in order to escape the clutches of law, he had resigned as one of the directors. But the fact remained that the petitioner-company was started by K in 1994 and it was a debatable question as to whether the company was established by K from the tainted money earned by him during 1-4-1991 to 6-6-1992. That matter was yet to be decided by the competent forum. But the petitioner-company rushed to file the instant writ petition and challenged the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange as well as the National and Mumbai Stock Exchanges. It was not the action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was sought to be challenged but in fact what was sought to be challenged was the order passed by the Custodian. Therefore, the view taken by the Single Judge to the extent that that could not be interfered with in extraordinary writ jurisdiction was well-founded. It was a question which was yet to be decided by the Special Court as to whether all the money for establishing the petitioner-company was tainted money or the petitioner-company which had been established by K was from any other source which did not have the tinge of that tainted money. That question could not have been decided in the instant pro- ceeding. More so, by virtue of the notification dated 20-11-2001 and the public notice issued on 24-11-2001 all the properties of all the persons who were notified and that of K stood attached. The 20-11-2001 not- ification clearly said that all the properties movable or immovable or both belonging to persons/entities would stand attached by virtue of section 3(3) of the Act of 1992 and similarly in the public notification dated 24-11-2001, the same was reiterated for notice of all concerned that from the date of the aforesaid notification any property movable or imm- ovable or both belonging to the notified persons/entities would stand attached and it would only be dealt with by the Custodian in such manner as the Special Court may direct. It was also made clear in the public notice dated 24-11-2001 that the provisions of the Act of 1992 have overriding effect on all other laws and all the companies and firms were directed to take notice that the property belonging to the notified persons/entities stood attached and it was not permissible to have any transaction of any kind relating to the attached properties of the notified persons/entities except with the direction of the Special Court. It was also mentioned in the public notice that all those who had dealings with such attached properties of the notified persons/entities should intimate to the Custodian the details of such properties. Therefore, in view of those facts, the assets and properties of K were attached and if the petitioner-company sought any remedy, the remedy lay in the Special Court which alone has jurisdiction to provide remedy and that Court is held by no less than a sitting Judge of the High Court. Therefore, the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the matter which was within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Special Court. There was no occasion for the Single Judge to have unnecessarily entered into the question whether the Calcutta Stock Exchange was a ‘State’ within the meaning of article 12 or not. In fact, that question did not directly fall for determination. In substance what the petitioner-company wanted to challenge was the basic order of the Custodian, as the Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted in terms of the direction issued by the Custodian. Therefore, it was only an incidental action, and the basic challenge was to the notification notifying K as a notified person under section 3(2) of the Act of 1992. No executing agency who has implemented the order can be held responsible. The Calcutta Stock Exchange was only an executing agency and since the said K was notified person and he floated the company in 1994, all his assets stood attached, and, therefore, it deactivated the terminal of the petitioner-company preventing it from doing any trading activity in Calcutta Stock Exchange. Therefore, it was not an action of the Calcutta Stock Exchange which was under challenge. The Calcutta Stock Exchange had only acted as per the direction given by the Custodian as executing agency and if the petitioner-company had any grievance against the order passed by the Custodian, then it had remedy under the Act of 1992

M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited and its group of companies to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) on 1st August 2018. M/s SRS Real Infrastructure Limited was listed with the Bombay Stock Exchange and therefore falls under the domain of NFRA. The investigation conducted by the SFIO revealed that the company and its group of companies presented falsified financial statements containing the falsified statements of debtors, adopted the malpractice of round-tripping and layering the transactions that resulted in inflated purchases and sales. A joint reading of the above decisions reveals that while an interim order generally merges into the final order under the Doctrine of Merger, the application of the Doctrine, in itself, is not universal or absolute. The application of the said Doctrine is subject to significant exceptions such as Principles of Equity; When the final order is non-speaking or dismissed in limine; The nature of jurisdiction exercised by the superior forum and the content or subject matter of the challenge/dispute. It is therefore the settled legal position that the Court is duty-bound to harmonise the principles of judicial comity with equitable doctrines so as to prevent abuse of process and ensure that no party unjustly benefits from procedural lapses or silence in final adjudication. The Delhi HC ruled that the petitioner is entitled to the benefit under section 32A of the Code as the instant case falls within the clear language used in Section 32A and hence corporate debtor cannot be made responsible for the offence committed prior to commencement of CIRP even when the resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority, when it is expressly prohibited by the provision. Therefore, the contention of the petitioner was upheld and liable to be discharged in the merits of the case. In light of above case, it is clear that the Section 32A is applicable even to those corporate debtors whose resolution has been approved. This provision has been incorporated to give boost to the prospective bidders of the corporate debtor in the CIRP or liquidation process as the case may be. Serious economic and legal issues arises in respect of Section 32A, which otherwise can lead to the misuse of the provision and defeat the purpose with which it has been incorporated.

The researcher has observed following issues w.r.t. Section 32A of the Code which needs to be addressed:-

1.

The extent to which benefit can be granted by the Appellate tribunal or Adjudicating Authority under section 32A of the Code need to be clarified. In theJSW Steel Ltd's case (supra), the Appellate tribunal went ahead to set aside all the attachments made by the Enforcement Department under PMLA. It is crucial to note that the tribunal itself has been incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013. The jurisdiction and power of the tribunal cannot be equated with that of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution. Thus, the powers of the tribunal are very limited in nature and setting aside of the attachments made amounts to overreaching the powers that are conferred on the tribunal under Companies Act, 2013 and the Code. Therefore, the legality of the order made by the tribunal is itself under suspicion. Moreover, the exercise of the power in such a manner has be frowned by the Hon'ble SC in the Case of Embassy Property Developments (P.) Ltd. v. State of Karnataka.9

2.

Promulgation of Section 32A in the Code has rendered the PMLA ineffective and toothless. It raises serious concerns as it can be misused as way to squander away from their criminal liability under various Acts. It makes such acts redundant and defeats the object with which these statues have been framed.

3.

Section 32A of the Code appears to resolve only the concerns of the corporate debtors and renders the victims of the crime committed by theses corporate entities from acts like money laundering.

4.

Section 32A of the Code doesn't provide for any exception over the encumbrance made in order to defeat the of the PMLA and hence it runs contrary to Section 9 of the PMLA which empowers the authority to remove any encumbrance on the property or lease if it found that it is created to defeat the provisions of PMLA.

5.

Victims of the money laundering have not been conferred any protection under section 32A of the Code. It makes them remedy-less and also encourage more and more shell companies to use corporate entity for the money laundering.

6.

It encourages more and more fraudulent practices under corporate entities until and unless proper safeguards are incorporated. For instance, where a company collects money from the public and passes it on other company for purchasing the properties, while in reality to misuse this provision and get hold over that money illegally. While the victim claim over the money is only limited to the company which received it by way of public offer and no claim can be made by the victims directly over the second company.

Conclusion

The legislative intent behind incorporating Section 32A of the Code is very clear to incentivize the bidders, give boost to the economy and incentivize the establishment of more foreign companies. Section 32A has been promulgated in order to enable the resolution applicant to take over the company which is free from all sorts of liability. However, the lot of questions flowing as a consequence of the incorporation of this provision remains to be unanswered. In order to weed out the abuse of Section 32A of the Code, the ambiguity and issues arising from the unwanted interpretation needs to be resolved at the earliest. There is need of proper checks and balance in order to minimize the abuse of the provision. Most importantly, it must be ensured that incorporation of Section 32A into the code doesn't render the provisions other statues redundant or contradicts.

In addition, information could also be called by the investigator from any other company with the previous approval of the Central Government. Only such a kind of investigation would establish the link, if any, between the ultimate beneficiary and those incharge of the management of the funds of the company. Ultimately, the investigation might not be able to establish any link. However, prima facie opinion could be formed on the basis of facts available to warrant the investigation. It might be only through a detailed probe that the intention, if any, behind the above acts resulting in substantial loss to various interests in society through the company could be established. If the above acts were done intentionally (mens rea), adverse consequences may follow including penalising the guilty. Establishing mens rea is the purpose behind any legal framework of this kind. It is essential to invoke such provisions where the funds of public and creditors are vested in the hands of a few individuals for the benefit of the former. Thus, the affairs of the company had to be investigated in respect of the years 1990-91, 1991-92 and 1992-93 including the role of any of financial institutions in this regard.

385.1 Background note385.1 Background note

The Central Government is empowered to appoint inspectors to investigate and report on the ownership of the company under certain circumstances.

385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company385.2 Investigation into ownership of the company

An investigation into the ownership of the company may be ordered under the following circumstances :

385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own385.2-1 Investigation by Central Government on its own

The Central Government may, when it appears that there is good reason to do so, appoint one or more inspectors to investigate and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board385.2-2 Investigation at the instance of Company Law Board

Where in the course of any proceedings before it, the Company Law Board declares that the affairs of the company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall appoint one or more investigators and report on the membership of any company and other matters relating to the company for the purpose of determining the true persons who are or have been—

u financially interested in the success or failure, whether real or apparent, of the company; or

u able to control or materially influence the policy of the company.

385.3 Scope of investigation385.3 Scope of investigation

While appointing inspectors, the Central Government may define the scope of investigation with regard to matters, period to which such inspection extends and limit the investigation to matters connected with particular shares or debentures.

385.4 Powers of Inspectors385.4 Powers of Inspectors

The inspectors shall have powers to examine persons on oath, inspect the books and papers. Refer para 384.9 for other provisions.

385.5 Inspector’s Report385.5 Inspector’s Report

The inspector shall forward his report to the Central Government. However, the Central Government shall not be bound to furnish the company or any other person with a copy of such report or any portion thereof, if there is a good reason for not divulging the contents thereof. In such a case, the Central Government shall require the Registrar to keep a copy of such report or parts of such report which could be divulged.

385.6 Expenses of Investigation385.6 Expenses of Investigation

The expenses of investigation shall be defrayed by the Central Government out of the moneys provided by the Parliament, unless it directs that the expenses or part thereof should be met by the applicants on whose application the investigation was ordered.

385.7 Imposition of restrictions385.7 Imposition of restrictions

Where it appears to the Company Law Board that for the purpose of investigation into ownership of the company, it is necessary to impose restrictions, it may by order direct that the shares shall be subject to the following restrictions for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the order viz.

u transfer of those shares shall be void;

u where shares are to be issued, they should not be issued and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void;

u no voting right shall be exercisable;

u no further shares shall be issued in right of those shares or in pursuance of any offer made to the holder thereof and any issue thereof or transfer of any right to be issued therewith shall be void ;

u except on liquidation no payment should be made for any sums due from the company on those shares, whether in respect of dividend or capital or otherwise.

385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures385.8 Restriction on transfer of shares or debentures

Where a transfer of shares or debentures in a company has taken place and as a result thereof a change in the composition of the Board of Directors is likely to take place which would be prejudicial to the public interest, the Company Law Board may, by order, direct that—

u the voting rights in respect of those shares or debentures shall not be exercisable for a period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order.

u no resolution passed or action taken to effect a change in the composition of the Board of Directors before the date of the order unless it is confirmed by the Company Law Board.

u the transfer of shares in the company during such period not exceeding three years as may be specified in the Order, shall be void.

Investor education and protection fund shall also be out of the purview of CARO order

12. It is very surprising to note that at a time when CSR activities are being promoted by government, due importance is not given to the transfer of amount to IEPF. Reporting relating to timely transfer of amount to IEPF has been done away with. Over the years, this clause has acted as a check point to ensure the timely transfer of unclaimed and unpaid amounts to IEPF. Reporting on accumulated losses would no longer be required

13. With a view to provide further ease of doing business, government has lifted another important reporting feature, under which auditor was to report on whether a newly incorporated company (Company registered for a period not less than 5 years) has accumulated losses at the end of financial year minimum 50% of its net worth. The clause was also required to report on cash losses in the financial year under review and in the immediately preceding financial year. Now the auditors are not at all required to report on these issues. However, this exemption is only allowed in case of newly incorporated companies. Probably the move is to see growth in the start-up companies.

Reporting on repayment of dues

14. Keeping in view rising debts and NPAs of the banks/financial institutions, the reporting format of auditors on the repayment of dues has been changed drastically. In addition to the earlier provisions of CARO applicable to the repayment of dues, now auditors are also required to report on lender-wise details. This move will surely act as an important check on further increase of NPAs and bad loans. Now the default in repayment of dues shall have its own language, as the name of the lenders and their respective amount shall be reported. It will be possible for all users of balance sheet to know/ascertain the dues to be paid to banks/financial institutions.

Default to government should also be specifically disclosed

15. Besides banks and financial institutions, now auditor shall also be required to report any default to the government. Thus, now onwards the government would also be construed as a party. In case of default to government, same type of lender-wise details have to be provided.

Corporate guarantee is no longer an item of CARO

16. CARO 2016 made another surprise move by deleting the clause for reporting of corporate guarantees given by the Company for loans taken by others from Bank or financial institutions. Subsequently, auditors are also not required to mention the interest of Company prejudicially affected by corporate guarantee.

Extensive and vast reporting on use of moneys raised through public issues as well as term loans

17. The recent scams of corporate sector seem to have widely effected the perception of the Ministry. The earlier CARO order was limited to the reporting on use of term loan for the purpose for which the loans were obtained. But keeping in view the public scams and frauds, the order is set to cover the whole gamut of fund raising in its coverage area.

Now onwards auditors have to be very cautious as they have to retain their identity of public trustees. Now they have to provide complete record for use of money raised through pubic issues and all other ways of raising finance, including debt instruments and term loans. Further reporting has to be on all kind of delays/defaults and subsequent rectifications, if any, and if applicable.

Two ways of fraud reporting

18. Earlier order was centered around reporting of fraud on or by the company. However, fraud on the company does not specifically mention the name of its officers/employees. Instead of that the new order specifically mentions the fraud on the company by its "officers/employees" as well as fraud by the Company. Thus, any kind of fraud, whether committed internally by the officers/employees or externally affecting public, shall have to be reflected in Auditor's report along with the nature of fraud and amount involved in the fraud.

Remuneration of managerial personnel would not be only a hidden item

19. Till now managerial remuneration has been reflected as a balance sheet item. But now onwards specific reporting by auditor has to be made on managerial remuneration. The auditor has to ensure that the remuneration paid to managerial personnel has been in accordance with section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act. Beyond that if amount paid or even amount provided has been in excess of section 197 and Schedule V of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor has to mention the amount in excess of section 197, read with Schedule V and the steps taken by the company for recovery of the same. Thus, the Board or management shall have no right to waive off the amount to be recovered from managerial personnel.

Extensive exposure to related party transactions

20. The earlier order did not have any requirement of reporting on related party transactions. But the new one shall have extensive reporting feature, which shall cast direct responsibility on auditor and audit committee.

Auditor has to mention that all the related party transactions are in compliance with section 188 as well as in compliance with section 177. Section 177 which requires omnibus approval of audit committee, shall have to be counter reported in auditor's report. Thus, it should not be the prerogative of only audit committee to sanction the related party transactions as it will be counter checked by statutory auditor.

In terms of section 397 read with section 408, in regard to a Board-managed company—profit earning and dividend—paying the Government sought for the appointment of 12 Government directors on the Board to effectively safeguard the interest of the company, its shareholders and the public at large having regard to the allegations of mismanagement of the company’s affairs, particularly diversion of company’s money to subsidiaries which were unlisted companies, purchase of shares with a view to finally help the directors at the company’s cost. Cas. 846/19 SCL 235 (CLB - New Delhi), wherein it was held that "under section 408 of the Companies Act 1956, the purpose of appointment of Government directors is to prevent the affairs of the company being conducted either in a manner which is prejudicial to the interest of the company or to the public interest. In the present case, since the company, on its own, by inducting reputed professionals in various fields, had taken remedial steps to tone up the working of the company, which was also reflected in the latest inspection report of the Reserve Bank of India and its affidavit before the High Court, there was no reason to order appointment of Government directors at this juncture especially when the Reserve Bank of India was monitoring the affairs of the company on a continuous basis". While independent steps were taken by FMO in arranging its investment structure carefully, the present case is important for corporate lawyers to ensure that any of their proposed structure is not only 'form compliant' but also has substantial 'substance' in it to pass the judiciary test.

However, there are no end-use restrictions under the FDI Policy like the ECB guidelines- which mandate that the money received should be used only in a particular manner. A perusal of the notes to the statements of accounts at random bears testimony to this. Law is never of fundamental importance in company contracts, and if the law really or supposedly matters, contracting around is the answer, to give a semblance of compliance.

Need for performance and propriety audit of company contracts 1.27-5 It is a paradox that the law never dictates how companies are run although companies are the creatures of the law. Law is just a factor but not the key factor, and there is a serious limitation to law reform in company affairs, which in the main are nothing but company contracts and their working. Private individuals entering into commercial contracts as they like are, inter alia, subject to the rule of caveat emptor, or beware buyer, and it ought to stand to reason to ask why the same cannot and should not apply to company contracts brought about by the Managing Director or Chief Executive or his cronies personally, who at best is an agent for a term with nothing for him to lose under the contracts that he makes day-in-and-day-out for and on behalf of the company, and everything to gain personally for himself if he chooses with no questions to be asked by any. The legality of the arbitrary character of the shrouded company contracts under cover of the so called business secrets, and the large number of compromises and waivers of obligations under them commonly found in any company of considerable size, are prima facie questionable on grounds of propriety but in the face of the general apathy of the Boards of directors are going unchallenged, though these form the bulk of company management in its essence, and it is an impropriety of the highest degree to leave it totally free and invitingly open to misuse.

1.27-5a Question of good and proper dealing - Such questions of propriety do not fall to the lot of the statutory auditor, either. The C&AG of India has evolved a sound tradition, observed over the last five decades, of formal delegation of powers for contracting as well as the performance and propriety audit in Government companies in exercise of his power under section 619 of the Act; but, this has not caught on in general corporate audit in the country. The Company Law is sheltering the companies and company managers by not providing any deterrence in that behalf except in the case of a prospectus for public offer of securities, and expressly not conceding the locus standi to the shareholders or depositors or debt instrument holders, who stand on a different footing from sundry trade creditors, in the name of avoidance of multiplicity of litigation against the companies, on the British model, where there are other modes of deterrence like the public run scare apart from legal redress familiar to many in matters of this kind since ages unlike in India.

Shareholders’ control on company contracts negligible

1.27-6 The important question that arises here is whether this arrangement provides even a semblance of balance between private interest and public interest in the so called public company in India, where the scare of public run is operative against the banks, and it is absent in every other walk of life. In companies, the residuary control of the general body at a duly convened meeting is limited to the slated subjects and those present and voting, in line with the legislative procedure except the matters reserved to the postal ballot in which company contracts do not figure, and the shareholders’ interest is nil as to the company’s affairs as those are disallowable for want of prior notice to the company, reducing the general meetings of companies to a near farce; while the legal remedies available against erring companies as to their contracts are scanty and little known unless those accumulate and amount to ‘mismanagement’, and therefore ineffectual. External voucher audit coupled with internal audit of the so called ‘commensurate level’ and the Audit Committee of Directors introduced by section 292A of the Act, without specifying the items to be seen and leaving the whole to the august Board of Directors to decide, is no answer to it, because the businessmen would not brook it and the law-makers would not get to it, for obvious reasons. Perhaps, conditioned in our mind-set as we are by the UK model, though it is patently unsuited in the Indian milieu without re-formulation, our Company Law will never find an answer to this core question of exercise of unqualified power with non chalance; or, it should be accepted in law whether fair or unfair that there is nothing ‘public’ in a public company except it being synonymous with their right to tap the capital markets at large by public offers to fund private contracts.

Judicial review of contracting power of company management affecting public interest is another remedy

1.27-7 The trend now is towards judicial review of contractual power affecting public interest, generally : Jones v. Swansea City Council (1989) 3 All ER 162 (CA).

On a complaint made by the appellant (through its Managing Director), under section 156(3) CrPC, an FIR was registered under section 420, 120B of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). In this FIR, it was alleged that the appellant received a phone call by a person impersonating himself as their client 'B', to purchase 1 lakh shares of a company named 'APM Ltd.' After the purchase was executed, the said 'B' was called to confirm the purchase but he denied making any such call to the appellant for the above said purchase. A, an agent of the appellant company was said to have connived with the seller of the shares in question to defraud the appellant. ■

Further, the charge sheet mentions that to ascertain the role of respondent no. 2, it would be necessary to arrest and interrogate main accused. Thus investigation was still underway. A meanwhile was absconding.

■

Subsequently, respondent no. 2 filed an application before Magistrate Court for the release of the money withheld by the BSE. This application was dismissed by an order dated 16-9-2016, holding that the role of respondent no. 2 was under investigation, and until investigation was finalized the release of the funds should not be allowed. Respondent no. 2 then filed a revision petition against the order dated 16-9-2016, which was also dismissed by an order dated 8-12-2016 passed by the Revisional Court.
